en: Sarasvatīvilāsa:
Section on Judicial Procedure (Vyavahārakāṇḍa).
We pay homage to the Most Exalted One, who bears matted locks hanging down to his feet.
That which is the science of grammar takes the form of the tinkling sound of bracelets. || 1 ||
May the son of Śaṅkara, whose throat is fragrant with the flow of unimpeded nectar, extend welfare to you as long as the moon and sun endure; for around his neck,
swarms of young bees joyfully sport and repeatedly form into lines.
They spread the splendor of a wave of arrows for the slayer of Śumbha and Jambha. || 2 ||
The knowers of Brahman say:
O Vani, if this [universe] were itself dependent upon you, then...
What praise could there be? This salutation with joined palms is for you. || 3 ||
We pay homage here to Hanumān, who is tranquil, who personally instructs the foremost teacher of the Raghus, and who,
possessing incomparable fame that has spread like gold, belongs to this assembly of self-controlled ascetics.
The son of the lion, the conqueror of the Lord of Laṅkā, whose emblem is valor.
[2] I remember intensely that sapphire-peak mountain, whose body is a mass of split blue gems;
within its luminous form, there exists a whiteness other than [the blue].
It is surely because of Kañjekṣaṇa’s very nature as the sky. || 5 ||
The infant who is the deceptive Yādava, the illusory protector of those who take refuge in him;
who subdued the bull-demon Vṛṣabha; the radiant mirror of the Vedas;
whose mind is united with Ramā; and who shattered the haughty pride of Bhīma with his speed.
I remember that lotus-eyed one for a moment during the preparation of the meal.

I bow at the feet of the Lord of Beings (Paśupati), who is the husband of Śacī; whose garment is the quarters of the sky, whose bow is the abode of the gods (the rainbow), and who is the seat of the mind’s dwelling place;
who is free from manifold afflictions and consists of the cloud-like intellect of the stainless mind.
I go once more to the enemy of Śaka, who has overcome his two-fold enemies. || 7 ||
May the pair of lotus-feet of the Lord of the Blue Mountain bestow prosperity upon King Śrī Vīrarudra—
those feet which are meditated upon by yogis within the center of the lotuses of their hearts.
As if from its suppression, it has emerged with a state of redness.
May the pair of Durgā’s feet, reddened by streams of blood arising from the chest of the demon Mahiṣa, protect King Pratāpaśrīrudra;
may the parting line on the brow of the maiden of the Vedas bestow auspiciousness upon him.
It was rendered intensely red by the vermilion of the city gates through long-standing contact.
[3] Now,
the lineage of the author of this work is set forth.

Indeed, it is not my opinion that the description of the descent of the lineage of His Honor [the author] is inappropriate here; for, truly, even a most beautiful pearl necklace, though fashioned from strings of pearls of excellent quality, only comes to full bloom through its being strung upon a central gem (*nāyakamaṇi*). Or rather, just as a heroine, though she is the source of extraordinary wonder, achieves her true purpose only through her connection with a suitable hero; or as the host of stars, though they bring joy to the eyes, possess their excellence of beauty only through their association with the moon; or as rivers, though their waters are capable of eroding the banks, attain their preeminence in splendor only by the spreading of their waters along the edges of the shore; or as rays of light, though skilled in dispelling darkness, become the cause of delight for the entire world only through their conjunction with the Sun; or as the multitude of virtues of the Lord Vāsudeva, though they already exist, bring forth great dignity and enchant the mind only through their connection with the descent of his assumed form in his divine play (*līlā*); in the very same way, literary works achieve their proper arrangement for the wise only through the description of the descent of the lineage of the Great Hero [the author]. What more need be said? The description of the descent of the lineage of both the work and its author is like the manifestation of fragrance in a golden flower, or the emergence of blossoms on a sandalwood tree, or the production of fruit on an *aśoka* tree.
Moreover:
For those who are endowed with auspicious conduct, no downfall exists.

Thus, even according to the Smṛtis, the performance of auspicious rites (*maṅgalācaraṇa*), which has the fruit of averting misfortune, must necessarily be observed. That alone is the performance of auspicious rites which consists in the description of the prowess of holy men (*puṇyapuruṣa*). Indeed, there is no holy man other than the Supreme Person (*paramapuruṣa*); therefore, He alone—whose form is assumed out of the delight of His divine play (*līlā*)—is to be described, along with His infinite incarnations (*avatāra*). These are infinite, being past, present, and yet to come; their infinity lies in this. My mind is unable to enter into the pastness of the past incarnations, and likewise regarding those yet to come. As for the present ones, my mind does not find it easy to pass over that particular king, Vīrarudra—the lord of elephants of majesty, a fierce Rudra to his enemies, and an ocean of profundity—in whom all the fruits of merit have been continuously gathered by the beloveds of the earth. Therefore, I seek him alone to fulfill the purpose of my speech. Consequently, since Vīrarudra is the very incarnation of the Ancient Person (*purāṇapuruṣa*) himself by virtue of being the husband of the goddesses Lakṣmī and Earth, his description is precisely what we ought to describe. And the crest-jewel of his lineage, the sun in the sky, is shining most brilliantly with countless rays.
This eighth form of Īśvara, bestowing well-being and possessing radiant light, now stands upon the summit of the lord of the western mountain;
his single hoof-tip has barely cleared the peak of the mountain of sunrise.
Among the majestic, he is like a gateway; he is majesty itself and the very ground of honor. Pratāparudra’s Pratāpabhānu is the foremost of his lineage, as the first among the planets.

In the lineage of Aṃśumat there arose kings whose play was equal to that of the guardians of the quarters; they were lords of the earth with the strength of their arms capable of crushing the dwellers in mountain caves, and by their might they brought the entire circle of the earth under their dominion. (3)
In his lineage, the Lord of the Raghus appeared, having attained power through the grace of Rāmakavi;
his son was the crest-jewel among the kings of the Bāhuja clan, whose majesty was celebrated throughout the three worlds. (4)
Therefore, Indumatī gave birth to a son who was like a digit of the moon, who partook of the boons fashioned from the blossoms of the Kalpa tree,
and who was a treasury of fame resulting from the sacrifice of battle against Indra.
O Paṅktiratha, you are indeed worthy of that esteemed title.

Beyond Paṅktiratha there was the Supreme Person named Rāma, whose flood of fame reached the very limits of existence; he possessed a splendor equal to the moon, was wise, and was ranked foremost among the most steadfast of the wise. (6)

The Lord of Śrī, having desired the purpose of his own incarnation—namely, the destruction of the powerful Lord of Laṅkā—certainly performed this task as a secondary consequence of his practice of following the Guru’s instructions; such is the nature of the deeds of the virtuous.
Thereafter, the lord of Kuśāvatī, whose crest-jewel was an elephant-goad and whose seat was a lotus, became emaciated;
then there arose one named Atithi, whose prowess was kindled, who surpassed all other guests through his hospitality.
In the lineage of the Raghus was born a king, a lord of the earth whose splendor was kindled like the sun;
he bore the form of Rāma, was named the illustrious Kapilendra, and possessed a majesty equal to that of the Supreme Lord who transcends all bounds.
He whose sun never sets; he whose nature is free from falsehood and voidness; the son of Dharma;
the sorrowless leader of the Raghus; the moon devoid of its spot;
and the son of the Ocean who never dries up, yet is a constant source of charity.
How can Gajapati Pratāpakapileśvara be described? || 10 ||
She is a mine of kindness, a forest that destroys the wretchedness of beggars,
a river of good fortune, and a wind that sweeps away her fame; she is the means for accomplishing righteousness,
a cascade of beauty, a cave for crawling serpents, and the cleverness of her enemies.
The earth of the Great Lord, whose sole great festival is majesty, remains awake as Jāgeśvarī.

[6] He who is as white as camphor powder— smooth, pervasive, and clearly manifest— produced by the friction of the two frontal globes of the elephant Airāvata (the foe of Jambha) against the lovely breasts of Śacī;
he whose fame is the delight of the mature Karṇāṭa woman, who takes pleasure in mocking the autumnal moon.
It is the play of the splendor of the laughter of the art of love, shimmering from the moon-like faces of beloved women. 12.
When King Kapilendra was enraged in battle, the fame of Karṇāṭa spread throughout Cola, Draviḍa, Nepāla, Pāṇḍya, Mālava, Kerala, and Keralā. (13)
She, named Pārvatī— her name being true to its meaning— having taken the hand of Kapileśvara, who was accompanied by his wife Āmilā, she made the earth free from co-wives.

That Pārvatī gave birth to him from that king— who possessed a preponderance of all countable virtues and whose footstool was adorned by the jewels in the crowns of monarchs— to one named Puruṣottama, who eclipsed the fortune of the lords of the earth among his enemies.
The heroic Śrī Puruṣottama Gajapati is the serpent Śeṣa within the assembly of the learned; he is the Lord who is ever-present in the legends of the valiant;
he is the friend of the bracelet on the arm of his enemies when they count them; he himself is the very limit of beauty.
He must be contemplated daily by those whose bold words declare, "This is his son."

[7] Rūpāmbikā, whose character was as delightful as form itself, was the wife of the king Māle, that best of men; she, with eyes as broad as lotuses, was equal to Umā in beauty and to Ramā in speech. 17.

By means of recitations and austerities earned by himself, he begot from this Sāmajayā of beautiful form— she who was preeminent among the foremost ladies of the lineage of Savitṛ— the illustrious Varavīrabhūpati, who excelled in statesmanship.
Vīraśrī Rudradeva became the lord of elephants; the mountain of his majesty grew ever higher through the fanning of the wind from the ears of his rutting elephants.
He reduced the golden vessel of the universe to ruin, seizing the golden earrings of his enemies' wives.
Thinking thus, the Creator indeed brought about a rainy season consisting of water there. || 19 ||
The illustrious Vīrarudra, rejoicing in the glory of his sovereignty over the elephant-kingdom, surely enjoys all fourteen worlds;
for otherwise, how could the movement of the sun and the moon proceed incessantly through the regions of the sky by night and by day? (20)
When the lord of stars rises, I clearly perceive that the ocean has reached its full extent due to the rutting elephant of the majesty of my enemies toward those with curved brows;
for were it not so, there would surely be no confluence of the rivers formed by the flowing streams of tears from their eyes.
How can there be fullness for this salt-water ocean, whose waters are covered by clouds? 21.
If this Karna had existed for only half a day, it would have been the sport of abandoning the sun; if he had existed for an entire day, it would have been the true nature of his majesty;
and if he had existed for only a single night, it would have been the playful glory of his fame.
What can we do with human lifespans? King Śrīvarirudra is praised by the wise. || 23 ||
Victorious is the fire of the majesty of King Śrī Vīrarudra, which, under the guise of the submarine fire (*vaḍabāgni*), having encircled the oceans,
has consumed the oceans of his enemies who had gone as far as the horizon.
A fellow-student of the playful fire blazing at the end of the eon, equal to the limit of the duration of the lamentations of the wives of the lords of enemies,
[he was surrounded] by the staff-like arms of the lord of Varāha, throbbing as they swallowed the necks of those who were haughty and small.

The mention of "lord of horses" (*aśvapati*) [applied] to lordly elephants, which are turbid with rut-fluid (*rathyā*), ichor (*ḍillī*), and ichor-drops (*kalamba*), is a single instance [of poetic deviation]. (25)

Pratāparudra, whose renowned solar heat of valor is peerless even throughout the three worlds, ascends the scales of the fierce-rayed sun by means of his passage through the constellations Citrā, Ardhā, Svātī, and Viśākhā;
he is the God of Love for beautiful women, the mountain of the earth's lineage, and the wish-fulfilling cow for poets. (26)

This very Śrī Vīrarudra, the lord of elephants, whose form surpasses that of the Lord of Beings (Śiva), is a Pārijāta tree for those who bow before him, a lotus-eyed one for the subjects at his lotus-feet, a treasure-trove for the wretched and the blind, and a dispeller of the mass of darkness provoked by the rays of the sun.

Moreover—Śrī Vīrarudra is like Airāvaṇa among elephants, mounted upon a bull; like Puṇḍarīka, intent on beholding Kapilā; like Vāmana, vibrating with the desire to follow Piṅgalā; like Kumuda, resting in incomparable sovereignty; like Añjana, skilled in the playful excursions of the abundant Tāmraparṇī; and like Puṣpadanta, devoted to the touch of the hands of beautiful-toothed women.

Moreover—he was like a sovereign of the whole earth, yet a sovereign of the whole earth; like Supratīka, yet Supratīka; like Kumāra, yet Kumāra; like Māra, yet Māra; like the four-faced one, yet four-faced; like Viṣvaksena, yet Viṣvaksena; like Rudra, yet Rudra; like a lotus-pond, yet a lotus-pond; like Nṛsiṃha, yet Nṛsiṃha; like Rāma, yet Rāma.

Moreover—he who, like Nṛsiṃha, bears the marks of wounds inflicted by claws; who, like the son of Daśaratha, has sprout-like hands skilled in slaying the forest of the world; who, like Paraśurāma, possesses the form of a peerless hero; who, like the Himālaya, is a mountain of his lineage; who, like the ocean, is filled with living beings; who, like the moon, causes the lilies of joy to bloom; who, like the sun, radiates the brilliance of his body; who moistens the rays of the moon on Śiva’s head with the moonlight of his fame sung throughout all the quarters; whose own majesty serves as the light for the enjoyment of the Lokāloka mountain; and who, resembling the elephant of the quarter, has surpassed the power of Bṛhaspati.

Moreover—like Indra (*puruhūta*), he possesses great renown (*vṛddhaśravas*) and a fame as thunderous as the clouds; yet, though honored by the thousand-eyed one, he is not Viṣṇu, for he is not Duścyavana (Indra), but rather exceedingly well-established. Like Agni (*vītihotra*), he is radiant with the fire of his knowledge (*jātavedas*); yet, though a friend to the breath of the world (*jagatprāṇa*), he is not Vāyu, for he is pure and not a consumer of fuel (*āśrayāśa*), but rather a protector of those who seek refuge. Like Yama (*dharmarāja*), he is impartial (*samavartin*) and a wielder of the rod of punishment (*daṇḍadhara*); yet, though a descendant of Vivasvat (*vaivasvata*), he is not the Lord of the Ancestors (*pitṛpati*), but rather devoted to the service of his elders and sovereign over the entire circle of the earth. Like Varuṇa (*varuṇa*), he is wise (*pracetās*) and a lord of the world (*bhuvanādhīśvara*); yet, though possessing no new noose (*navyapāśa*), he is not bound to the waters, but rather attached to stainless people. Like Vāyu (*śvasana*), he has the form of the wind (*anilākṛti*) and the power of the ancient leader (*purāṇanetṛvibhava*); yet, though his movement is constant (*sadāgati*), he is not accompanied by serpents (*bhujaṅga*), but rather a subduer of wicked men. Like the Lord of the Kinnaras (*kinnareśvara*), he is a supreme king (*rājādhirāja*) and a giver of wealth (*dhanada*); yet, though he is kind to the excellent ones who tread at his feet, he is not Kubera, but rather possesses the powerful physique of a lion (*siṃhasaṃhanana*). Like Śambhu, he is the lord of great elephants (*mahāgajādhīśvara*) and omniscient (*sarvajña*); yet, he is not the wielder of the broken axe (*khaṇḍaparaśu*), but rather possesses an unimpeded array of weapons.

Indeed, the enemy kings—who, like elephants dwelling in the heart of the Vindhya forest, do not fear even the sight of lions, arrows, tigers, and gaṇḍakas, but rather, through the memory of śarabhas, tigers, gaṇḍas, and bheruṇḍas manifested by the banners of his army, mistake him for them and hide within the depths of caves, trembling with fear—he is truly the wondrous Vīrarudra. Though his body is embraced by Padmā, he is a *hari-candana* (a sandalwood tree for those who seek refuge); though he has made Śrī-Candana a servant, he is himself like a *vidyādhara*; though he is himself the Supreme Person (*Puruṣottama*), he is the son of the Supreme Person; though he is himself the son of the Supreme Person, he is the father of the Supreme Person; and though he is himself the father of the Supreme Person, he is the beloved servant of the Supreme Person.

Moreover—though resembling the son of the Three-Eyed One (Śiva), he was like the son of Atri (Soma); though comparable to Nala, he was like Anala (Fire); though exceedingly beautiful through ornaments, he was exceedingly beautiful even without ornaments; though his affection was attached to the Earth, he was not attached to the lower lip; though his mind was dependent on strength, his wealth was not dependent on women; and though he protected those who sought alms, he did not protect those who were not seekers of alms.

Moreover: he was the speaker among speakers, the listener among listeners, the author among authors; the leader of the path of the righteous, the discipliner of those who wander from it; the composer of narratives (*ākhyāyikā*), the performer of dramas (*nāṭikā*); the remover of misdeeds, the resolver of doubts regarding dharma; the husband of Padmāvatī, Padmālayā, Elā, and Mahilā; and the protector of the entire circle of the earth.

Moreover, he is a reflection of Vivasvat; he is the repetition of Manu and Vainya; he is the ellipsis for Ikṣvāku; he is the synthesis of Dilīpa; he is the dialogue of Raghu; he is the wager of the prince Raghu; he is the representative of Daśaratha; he is another incarnation of Rāmabhadra. He is the Janārdana who brings joy to all people; he is the crusher of the pride of the Lord of Gauḍa; he is the field of heroism, more fragrant than the spring breeze and exceedingly noble; he surpasses the elephants of the quarters with his rutting elephant that wanders like a moving principal mountain; he is the adamantine cage for the Shāhi Suratrāṇa Huśana who sought his protection; he is the King of Kings, the Supreme Lord, the Lord of Elephants named Pratāparudra.

In this context, although the description of the caste (*varṇa*) and the description of the father’s caste (*pitṛvarṇya*) are invariably identical, their distinction is stated due to a difference in state; this is not contradictory, just as a single poet may possess both the status of a poet and a connoisseur (*sahṛdaya*). And this very Vīrarudra Gajapati [ruled over] Ayodhyā-like-Ayodhyā, Madhurā-like-Madhurā, Dvārāvatī-like-Dvārāvatī, Avanti-like-Avanti, Māyā-like-Māyā, and Vāraṇāsikā-like-Vāraṇāsikā; furthermore, like Kāśī, presided over by Viśveśvara; like Ayodhyā, possessing the noble path of the Ikṣvākus; like Kāñcī, endowed with millions of merits and millions of desires; like Madhurā, protected by Ugrasena; like Dvāravatī, filled with the sound of Ānakadundubhi; situated in the midst of the waters of the great river; a city that was the armor for the waist of the Earth-bride, like a reflection of the celestial river (Gaṅgā). Honoring Padmā, Padmālayā, and Mahilā equally, and practicing the performance of dharma in the form of daily, fixed royal administration, he—fearing lest there arise excessive hardship resulting from the necessity of investigating the consistency (*ekavākyatā*) among many treatises such as those of Vijñānayogin, Bhāruci, Aparārka, Medhātithi, Asahāya, Candrikā, and others—composed and introduced this work, which is a compendium of all the Smṛtis, exceedingly profound, yet not overly diffuse.
Herein, the method of interpretation is as follows:
"Amā" refers indeed to the lords of sages, Manu and Vasiṣṭha-Yogīśvara;
and even those who composed the legal treatises, Bhāruci and Kulārka-Yogīśvara.
May she who has gone beyond all envy be pleased; may the Lord of Bhavānī be even more gratified by this verbal expression of mine, bound to memory.
Oho! There is no pride at all toward the inferior, and certainly no pride toward the superior;
but toward an equal, one might fear pride—may there be no such equal for us.
Thus [the title of] the Vīraśrī-Gajapati-Gauḍeśvara, Navakoṭi-Karṇāṭaka-Lubbarigeśvara, Lord of Yamunāpura, Refuge of the Emperor Huśana Sāhi Suratrāṇa,
Purifier of the Conduct of the Son of Śrī-Durgā, King of Kings, Supreme Sovereign—
In the *Sarasvatīvilāsa*, a compendium of law (*smṛtisaṅgraha*) composed by the illustrious Great King Pratāparudradeva, [this is] the section titled "The Genealogy of the Authors."
The First Vilāsa [13].
Now begins the Second Vilāsa.

The experts in logic (nyāyavid) have accepted that the *Manusmṛti*, as well as other *smṛtis* not in conflict with it, various *upasmṛtis*, and the *purāṇas*, *itihāsas*, and so forth, possess authority because they are rooted in the Veda. Regarding this, some maintain that although those *smṛtis* are in certain instances based on reasoning (*nyāya*), since that reasoning itself is rooted in the Veda, those *smṛtis* are equal in status to the Veda.

Others, however, say: "Because the *nyāyas* (legal maxims) reveal the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) for the purpose of the Veda, those various *smṛtis* have their root in the Veda. Still others, however, say: "In the injunction 'The king shall look into legal disputes' (*vyavahārān nṛpaḥ paśyet*), the act of looking (*darśana*)—as that which fulfills the requirements of the injunction—is included within the category of valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*); therefore, it possesses authority. Consequently, there is no dispute that the dharma taught therein is to be practiced by all social classes (*varṇas*), and the adharma to be propounded therein is not to be practiced. And since this cannot be established if the true nature of Manu and the others is unknown, that is now investigated: [The text continues with the investigation of Manu's identity.]
The authors of the Dharmaśāstras.

The *Smṛtis* were composed by Manu, Aṅgiras, Vyāsa, Gautama, Ātreya, Yama, Vasiṣṭha, Dakṣa, Saṃvarta, Śātātapa, Parāśara, Viṣṇu, Āpastamba, Hārīta, Śaṅkha, Kātyāyana, Guru, Pracetas, Nārada, Yogīśvara, Bodhāyana, Pitāmaha, Sumantu, Kaśyapa, Babhru, Paiṭhīnasi, Vyāghrapāda, Satyavrata, Bharadvāja, Gārgya, Kārṣṇājini, Jābāli, Jamadagni, Laugākṣi, Vatsa, Marīci, Devala, Pāraskara, and Likhita. The *Upasmṛtis* were composed by Jābāli, Āciketaska, Skanda, Laugākṣi, Kaśyapa, Vyāsa, Sanatkumāra, Śaṃtanu, Janaka, Vyāghra, Kātyāyana, Jātūkarṇika, Piñjala, Bodhāyana, Kaṇāda, and Viśvāmitra (as well as Paiṭhīnasi and Gobhila). Jābāli, Laugākṣi, Vyāsa, and others mentioned here are not included among those previously named [as authors of the primary *Smṛtis*].

[14] As for the ancient Purāṇas: the Brāhma, Pādma, Vaiṣṇava, Śaiva, Bhāgavata, Nāradīya, Mārkaṇḍeya, Āgneya, Bhaviṣyat, Brahmavaivarta, Laiṅga, Vārāha, Skānda, Vāmana, Kaurma, Mātsya, Gāruḍa, and Brahmāṇḍa— these are the eighteen Purāṇas.
The names of the Itihāsas.

The *itihāsas*—such as the narrative of Satyatapas, the origin of Soma, and so forth—are included. For this very reason, Viṣṇu has stated: "The Dharma of Manu, the Veda with its auxiliary limbs (*aṅgas*), the Purāṇa, and medical science (*cikitsita*)—these four are established by authoritative command (*ājñāsiddha*). By the phrase "the Dharma of Manu," all *smṛtis* that are not in conflict with the *Manusmṛti* are subsumed. Furthermore, the word "Purāṇa" serves as an indicator (*upalakṣaka*) for the *itihāsas* and other such works. Thus, the authority of the texts composed by the authors of the *Gṛhyasūtras* is also not contradicted; for these too serve as the basis for the ritual procedures (*saṃskāra-kalāpa*) composed by Manu and others, by means of the application of mantras (*mantra-viniyoga*).

"Since the authors of the Gṛhyasūtras are independent [authorities] who employ those [rites] prescribed therein," according to the Devalasmṛti—this being the case—the commentators Vijñānayogin and others, as well as the authors of digests (nibandhakāras) such as Kulārka and Lakṣmīdhara, have, out of a desire to favor the world, commented upon all the Smṛtis under the guise of explaining them, even though there already exist digests composed by earlier authors who were supported by the learned and who caused everyone to perform [the rites]. Since the purpose is achieved by one alone, the effort of others would lead to uselessness. My endeavor is that [my work] may be made a subject of study alongside these earlier treatises.

The meaning of the verse is as follows: while my own work exists, the maxim of "uselessness" (*anarthakyanaya*)—which holds that when there is identity of subject matter (*viṣayaikya*), one work is redundant in light of the other—finds its resting place in the earlier treatises (*pūrvanibandha*). Alternatively, even though those earlier treatises exist in every house, being composed by authors such as Vijñānayogin, Bhāruci, Medhātithi, Asahāya, Aparārka, the author of the *Candrikā*, Kulārka, and Lakṣmīpati, each of which enforces the performance of Smārta rituals, and despite their presence, one must say that the maxim of "uselessness" does not apply here because the purpose is already served by a single one. In the same way, the maxim of the uselessness of the others does not apply to my work; this is my endeavor. This is the sense of the verse.

Regarding the fact that legal procedure (*vyavahāra*) is dependent upon custom (*ācāra*): here, the dependence of legal procedure on custom exists because custom is the basis for the administration of justice. For it is through the administration of justice that the suppression of the wicked occurs; when the wicked are suppressed, the stability of the duties of the castes and stages of life (*varṇāśramadharma*) is maintained; and only when those are stable does the performance of the duties prescribed therein take place—thus, custom is dependent upon legal procedure.
First, as for the precedence of the section on legal procedure (*vyavahārakāṇḍa*).

Consequently, the section on legal procedure (*vyavahārakāṇḍa*) is commenced first, even though in the *smṛtis* of Manu and others, the section on customary conduct (*ācārakāṇḍa*) is presented first, followed by the section on legal procedure, and thereafter the section on penance (*prāyaścittakāṇḍa*). In this work, which is a compendium of *smṛtis*, it would have been appropriate to present the section on legal procedure immediately after the section on customary conduct, following the sequence established in those respective *smṛtis*. Nevertheless, in accordance with the desire of the great king Vīrarudra Gajapati, the section on legal procedure is undertaken first. Regarding that, the right to preside over legal proceedings belongs exclusively to the king; for the protection of subjects—which entails the maintenance of the duties of the castes and stages of life (*varṇāśramadharma*) and the suppression of the wicked—is a duty restricted solely to the king. And so says Yājñavalkya:
The king who punishes those deserving of punishment and causes those to be punished to be executed properly,
has effectively performed sacrifices completed with the most excellent sacrificial fees.

[16] Punishment consists of a fine, corporal punishment, and clearly, execution. By that, it means that the king should have performed sacrifices with abundant sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*); the sense is that the king obtains the fruit of sacrifices characterized by many fees. Furthermore, since it has been determined that the word *yat* (which) does not subvert the injunction, the word *yat* is not to be interpreted as "when" (as in the case of the *yad-āgneya* mantra), as was explained previously during the investigation into ownership. Nor should it be thought that the infliction of punishment is optional (*kāmya*) because of the mention of a reward; for there is a scriptural declaration of sin (*pratyavāya*) incurred by its non-performance. And so says Manu:
A king who punishes those who do not deserve punishment, and fails to punish those who do deserve it,
incurs great infamy and goes to hell.

Regarding the expiation for kings and others in the administration of punishment, Vasiṣṭha states: "Upon the release of one deserving of punishment, the king shall fast for one night; the domestic priest (purohita) for three nights; and in the case of punishing one who does not deserve punishment, [the king shall perform] the Kṛcchra penance, while the priest shall fast for three nights. From this, it is stated that punishment must be properly applied against the wicked.
Since the identification of the wicked cannot be accomplished without the examination of legal proceedings (vyavahāra), the king must examine such proceedings day by day in order to identify them.

For this very reason, Viṣṇu states: "The protection of the subjects alone is the inherent duty (*svadharma*) of kings; otherwise, they would fall away from their own duty. The intention is that the administration of justice (*vyavahāradarśana*), because it serves the purpose of protecting the subjects, is equal to the performance of twilight prayers (*saṃdhyāvandana*) and other such rites. For this same reason, Yājñavalkya says:
"Having thus reflected, the king [should perform] these [duties], which individually yield fruits equal to those of sacrifices..."
"Every day, surrounded by his courtiers (*sabhyas*), he should personally oversee legal proceedings.

The meaning of this is: "In the manner stated," namely by the verse beginning with "it would be as if performed by sacrifices," the word "separately" (*pṛthak*) means according to the order of the social classes (*varṇa*) and so forth. Regarding the order of the social classes and so forth, that same author says:
For those who have strayed from their own duty, the king, having disciplined them according to their offense, shall establish families, castes, guilds, corporations,
and districts once more on the path.

Families are those of the Brāhmaṇas and so forth; castes are the Mūrdhāvasikta and others; guilds are those of the betel-sellers and so forth; corporations are those of the heretics; and local communities are the barbers, artisans, and so forth—having disciplined these, that is, having punished them. For this very reason, Bṛhaspati says:
"In accordance with the treatises on Dharma, the king, together with his ministers and his domestic priest, should examine legal cases for the sake of protecting his subjects."
"Free from anger and greed, truthful, and having conquered his senses.

By the phrase "in accordance with the *dharmaśāstra*," the abandonment of anger and greed is already established; thus, it is demonstrated that the abandonment of anger and greed is an inherent quality of the king. For this very reason, Yājñavalkya says:
"One who possesses great energy, is liberal, grateful, and serves the elders..."
Disciplined, endowed with goodness, of noble birth, truthful in speech, and pure.
One who is not procrastinating, possesses mindfulness, is neither mean nor harsh, is righteous,
free from calamity, wise, brave, and a knower of secrets.
"The protector of his own weak points [should be proficient] in the science of inquiry (ānvīkṣikī) and likewise in the science of government (daṇḍanīti);
furthermore, O lord of men, he should be well-versed in the science of economics (vārtā) and in the triple Vedas (trayī)."

*Utsāhaḥ* means manliness; he who possesses great *utsāha* is "one of great energy" (*mahotsāhaḥ*). *Sthūlalakṣaḥ* means one who gives much—specifically, one who gives many goods—is called *sthūlalakṣaḥ*, that is, a liberal giver. *Kṛtajñaḥ* means one who knows and remembers what has been done, whether it be a favor or an injury. A *vṛddhasevakaḥ* is a servant of the elders. *Vinītaḥ* means free from pride. *Satvasampannaḥ* means one who cannot be overcome by enemies. *Kulīnaḥ* means born into a noble family. *Satyavāk* means one who speaks the truth even at the cost of his life. *Śuciḥ* means possessing external and internal purity. *Adīrghasūtraḥ* means one who acts quickly. *Smṛtimān* means one whose nature is to retain the Veda he has studied. *Akṣudraḥ* means one whose disposition is profound. *Aparuṣaḥ* means one whose habit is not to reveal the faults of others. *Dhārmikaḥ* means devoted to the performance of obligatory and occasional rites. According to Vijñāneśvara, [he is] endowed with the duties of caste and stage of life (*varṇāśramadharma*). *Avyasanaḥ* means free from the eighteen types of vices. And so says Manu: [Manu 7.49–50] "Drinking liquor, gambling, hunting, sleeping during the day, idle wandering, whistling, playing musical instruments, singing, dancing, and telling stories; "Using perfumes, garlands, unguents, excessive indulgence in fine clothes, and sexual intercourse with women—these are the ten vices for a king arising from pleasure. "Malicious speech, violence, theft, calumny, backbiting, false testimony, seizing property, and hostility toward those worthy of honor—these are the eight vices for a king arising from wrath. "A king who is addicted to these eighteen vices becomes deprived of both his wealth and his kingdom."* *Note: The verse regarding the eighteen vices is cited from Manu 7.49–50.*
Hunting, gambling, sleeping during the day, slander, women, intoxication,
the triple symphony [of song, dance, and instrumental music], and wasteful expenditure— this is the tenfold group born of desire.

The meaning of the statement is that because hunting and the like are rooted in desire (*kāma*), the group of ten arises from desire. He himself states that the group of eight arises from anger (*krodha*):
"Slander, violence, malice, envy, calumny of others' wealth, and harshness of speech and punishment—this is the group of eight arising from anger."
It is reckoned as being eight in number. Regarding these two groups, he himself stated that among the ten [vices] rooted in desire, drinking, gambling, and hunting are the most grievous:
"Drinking, dice, women, and hunting—in this sequence, one should know that this tetrad is the most grievous within the group born of desire."

Regarding the phrase "in this order" (*atra yathākramam*): the intended sequence is based solely on the basis of desire (*kāma*) and anger (*krodha*), and not by intending to express a mutual disparity among drinking, gambling, women, and hunting. This is because those forms—drinking, gambling, women, and hunting—are equal in their extreme severity, as indicated by the term "fourfold" (*catuṣka*). He himself states that within the group born of anger, these three are more severe: "The infliction of punishment, verbal abuse, and the embezzlement of wealth"—he himself states that within the group born of anger, these three are the most severe.
"One should know that even in a group born of anger, these three always bring suffering. Thus it is said.

Vijñāneśvara explains that he is "wise" (*prājñaḥ*), meaning one who perceives the subtle meaning of the scriptures and is capable of discerning profound matters; "heroic" (*śūraḥ*), meaning fearless; and a "knower of secrets" (*rahasyavit*), meaning one whose nature is to understand matters that must be kept confidential—Bhāruci, however, interprets this as one whose nature is to know the secrets of others. He is a "guardian of his own vulnerabilities" (*svarandhragoptā*), meaning one who protects the points of entry for others. He is "learned" (*viditaḥ*) and renowned in *ānvīkṣikī* (the science of the self), in *daṇḍanīti* (the science of government, which serves the acquisition and preservation of wealth), in *vārtā* (agriculture, commerce, and cattle-rearing, which are the means for the accumulation of wealth), and in the *trayī* (the three Vedas known as Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma). Vijñāneśvara provides an alternative reading, *vinītaḥ* ("disciplined"), and explains it thus: "one who has been led to special proficiency," with the understood sense being "by those experts in each respective field. As Manu says: [text follows].

"One should learn the threefold Veda from those learned in the three Vedas; the science of government (daṇḍanīti) from those not [learned] in that; logic (ānvīkṣikī) from those who know the Self; and the undertakings of commerce and agriculture from the world.
When it is asked for what purpose this thorough knowledge is intended, Hārīta says:

"In *ānvīkṣikī* (philosophical inquiry), however, one finds discernment; dharma and adharma reside in the *trayī* (the three Vedas); profit and loss in *vārtā* (economics); and right policy and wrong policy in *daṇḍanīti* (statecraft). This means that discernment and the other qualities should be understood as residing in *ānvīkṣikī* and the other sciences. The phrase "he should be consecrated" (*abhiṣiktaḥ syāt*) is to be connected with every item. Here, while discussing the internal duties of a king who has undergone consecration, the external characteristics are incidentally described therein. Regarding this, Kātyāyana says:

"A king should appoint as his domestic priest (purohita) a learned Brāhmaṇa who is beneficial, accomplished in Vedic study, free from greed, and truthful. In this [verse], the singular number is intended, because [the office] is something to be produced, just as in the expression "he cuts the sacrificial post" (*yūpaṃ chinatti*). And so says Yājñavalkya:
And he should appoint as his domestic priest one who is renowned for his learning, skilled in astrology,
and likewise proficient in the science of government as well as the Atharvāṅgiras [Veda].

Regarding the term *uditoditam*: Vijñāneśvara explains that it means "prosperous" (*samṛddha*), having arisen through [the king's] learning, noble birth, religious observances, and so forth. Bhāruci, however, maintains that it refers to what is to be accomplished at the time of the king’s coronation (*paṭṭabandha*). To this effect, Hārīta says:
"At the occasion of the coronation, there should be only one domestic priest (*purohita*);
by him alone should all the king's funeral rites (*aurdhvadaihika*) be performed."
"Because of the short lifespan in the Kali age, one should always perform it twice. Thus [it is said].

In this context, the mention of *aurdhvadaihika* (rites for the deceased) is intended as an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*) for all ritual acts. As for the rites pertaining to this world (*aihika*), they should be performed by the domestic priest (*purohita*) alone on behalf of the king when the latter is unable to do so. At that time, during the very moment of the binding of the turban (*paṭṭabandha*), he should appoint two: one as the primary and the other as the subordinate. In the event of the failure of the primary, the subordinate assumes primacy. At the time of the subordinate priest’s assumption of primacy, another subordinate priest must be appointed, because the maxim “due to the short lifespan in the Kali age” applies here as well. [21] Although the specific number is not intended to be restrictive here, nevertheless, since the subordinate is included within that very category, there is only one priest; thus, this does not contradict the number two. The phrase “in the Atharvāṅgirasa” means one who is skilled in rites such as propitiatory ceremonies (*śānti*). The rest has a meaning that is not obscure. The rule that “there is only one priest” is intended to exclude any further priests, but it is not intended to exclude the astrologer (*jyotirvid*), because the astrologer must be appointed separately from the priest. For this very reason, Viṣṇu states: “The astrologer and the priest should be appointed.”
And so it is stated in the *Rājalāsaka*: "An astrologer, a domestic priest, and ministers should be appointed.
Regarding the term "ministers" (*mantriṇaḥ*), *mantraṇa* refers to the deliberation on matters of state. Although Yājñavalkya has said:
"One should appoint a domestic priest who is an eminent astrologer..."
Thus, some explain that this is intended to mean that if the domestic priest himself is an astrologer, no other astrologer should be employed.

Regarding the injunctions, “one should appoint a domestic priest (purohita)” and “one should appoint an astrologer (daivajña),” when there arises the expectation as to *when* this should be done, the text says: “at the *uditodita* [moment]. The term *udita* means rising (*udaya*); the suffix *-ta* is used here in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāve*). Thus, *uditodita* is a compound with the ablative case (*pañcamī-samāsa*), meaning “that which has arisen from the time of rising. This implies that the selection of the astrologer (*jyotirvid-varaṇa*) occurs prior to the rising [of the king], while the appointment of the domestic priest (*purohita-varaṇa*) occurs immediately after the binding of the turban (*paṭṭabandhana*). For this very reason, it is stated in the *Rājalāsaka*: “One should perform the consecration (*abhiṣeka*) at the auspicious moment (*muhūrta*) indicated by the appointed astrologer. Here, *vṛtopadiṣṭa* means “indicated by one who has been appointed” (*vṛtena jyotirvidā upadiṣṭa*).

[22] As for what was stated by Viṣṇu: “Having appointed a domestic priest (*purohita*) who is learned in the *Atharvaveda*, the Purāṇas, and the treatises on Dharma, he should thereafter appoint an astrologer (*jyotirvit*)”—that statement is intended merely to establish the necessity of appointing an astrologer. Regarding the appointment, the use of the suffix *ktvā* (in the word *vṛtvā*) serves only to indicate that the two actions have the same agent, not to necessitate a sequence of time; for it is observed that the suffix *ktvā* is restricted to expressing identity of agent even when no temporal sequence exists, as in the expression “he sleeps with his mouth open” (*mukhaṃ vyādāya svapiti*). This has been elaborated by Hari (Patañjali) in the rule *samānakartṛkayoḥ pūrvakāle*. Therefore, we consider it correct to view the passage as being primarily intended to establish the duty of employing an astrologer. Consequently, the statement by Rājalāsaka—“At the auspicious moment (*muhūrta*) prescribed after the appointment, one should perform the consecration (*abhiṣeka*)”—becomes consistent. For this very reason, in the deliberation of royal affairs...
"He should deliberate on the kingdom together with them, and then with a Brahmin himself"—
in this statement from Yājñavalkya, the word "Brahmin" (vipra) refers specifically to the astrologer. [This concludes] the section on the selection of ministers, priests, and others.

Following the deliberation by ministers skilled in state affairs, it is appropriate that there be a deliberation by astrologers (*daivajña*), and not a deliberation by the domestic priest (*purohita*). However, Vijñānayogin has stated that the word *vipra* refers to the domestic priest. If the domestic priest himself is an astrologer, then it should be understood as referring to him. Likewise, Viṣṇu states that ministers must also be appointed: "For the protection of his own kingdom, he should appoint hereditary ministers who are knowers of statecraft. The meaning of "hereditary" (*maulyān*) is those descended through one's own lineage; "knowers of statecraft" (*arthavidaḥ*) means those who know the means of acquiring wealth. The sense is that in their absence, the protection of the kingdom does not exist; therefore, they must necessarily be secured. [23] The plural number in "hereditary" (*maulyān*) indicates that seven or eight ministers should be appointed. And so says Manu:
"One should appoint seven or eight ministers who are hereditary, learned in the scriptures, brave, protected [by their status], of noble birth, and well-tested.
Regarding this, Yājñavalkya states a specific qualification:
"He should appoint ministers who are hereditary, wise, pure, and steadfast;
with them he should deliberate on the kingdom, and thereafter with a Brahmin, and finally by himself. Thus it is said.

That king, endowed with qualities such as great energy (*mahotsāha*), is wise and skilled in discerning what is beneficial and what is harmful. Regarding the term *maula*, Vijñāneśvara explains that they are "stable," meaning they remain free from agitation even in situations of great joy or sorrow. Bhāruci, however, holds that "stability" means remaining in one's natural state even when friends are divided, which signifies a desire for the welfare of the master. They are "pure," meaning free from blemish. Thus, the king, together with his ministers, should deliberate on the affairs of the kingdom, such as peace and war. Then, having deliberated on the matter with a Brāhmaṇa astrologer who is proficient in the meaning of all the scriptures, he should thereafter reflect upon it himself by his own intellect. Regarding this, Viṣṇu states a specific rule: "He should appoint four officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) and a fifth as the presiding member (*sadasya*) for the successful accomplishment of rites prescribed by the Śruti and Smṛti. Some say the four officiating priests are the Brahman, Hotṛ, Adhvaryu, and [Udgātṛ]. Others say the four great officiating priests are the Brahman, Adhvaryu, Hotṛ, and Udgātṛ. The meaning is that he should appoint four officiating priests with the presiding member as the fifth for the purpose of accomplishing the performance of Śrauta and Smārta rites.
Gautama, however, states a specific qualification: "The supervisor (*upadraṣṭṛ*) must also be appointed. For this very reason, Yājñavalkya has stated without such qualification:
"For the sake of performing rites prescribed by revelation (*śruti*) and tradition (*smṛti*), one should indeed appoint officiating priests (*ṛtvij*);
and one should perform sacrifices according to the rules, accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*)."

He performed sacrifices such as the Agniṣṭoma, and by the word "and" (cakāra), those such as the Rājasūya. Immediately after that, Vasiṣṭha stated the definition of *yogakṣema*: "Effort must be made for the sake of acquisition (*yoga*) and security (*kṣema*)."

The meaning of this is as follows: *yoga* is the acquisition of what has not been obtained; *kṣema* is the preservation of what has been obtained. Both of these must be carried out strictly in accordance with the Dharma. Therefore, Yājñavalkya said: "One should seek what is unobtained through righteousness; one should preserve with effort what has been obtained; one should increase what has been preserved through prudent policy; and one should bestow what has increased upon worthy recipients."

One should exert effort, in accordance with the Dharma, to acquire what has not yet been acquired; but that which has been acquired should be protected by oneself through careful consideration. *Nīti* refers to trade routes and the like. One should deposit the surplus (*vṛddham*) into the three worthy recipients (*pātreṣu*), namely, for the sake of Dharma, Artha, and Kāma. Here, although the plural *pātreṣu* is used, it is restricted to exactly three, according to the principle of the *Kapiñjala-adhikaraṇa*; this is the view of Bhāruci. This explanation by Bhāruci is intended to establish the threefold nature of the worthy recipients, and not to restrict the number of recipients. For this very reason, Hārīta stated: "Having understood income and expenditure... This should be understood as having the same meaning as the statement of Yājñavalkya: "One should increase what has been protected through *nīti*. This is because, after the full knowledge of income and expenditure, it is improper to give if there is equality or a deficit between them; furthermore, as will be stated later, if the treasury is empty, it is difficult for a king to maintain his own kingdom or conquer another's kingdom. As for that which was stated by Viṣṇu: "[25] One should give wealth acquired through security (*yoga*) and prosperity (*kṣema*) to Brāhmaṇas, guests, and those engaged in sacrificial sessions (*satrin*); for the sake of sacrifices and charitable works (*iṣṭāpūrta*), to actors and dancers; and to a powerful king, the tax (*kara*), the gift for a bride (*saudāyika*), and a reward (*pāritoṣika*)."... [text continues] ...he should give to the powerful king. [End of citation].

*Yogakṣema* has been explained. [Wealth] should be given to Brahmins who are worthy recipients (*pātrabhūta*) in the form of gifts such as the *tulāpuruṣa* and others. To guests (*atithi*) who have arrived spontaneously at the conclusion of the five great sacrifices; to those engaged in sacrificial sessions (*satrin*), who have come for the sake of sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*). This term *satrin* is indicative of those who beg for wealth for the purpose of accomplishing religious acts that generate merit (*dharma*). Consequently, something should be given to the builders of tanks and other such works. For the sake of *iṣṭāpūrta*: *iṣṭa* is sacrifice (*yāga*), and *pūrta* is tanks and so forth. By the word *yāga*, the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) is implied; by the word *pūrta*, the wages of the builders of such works are indicated. Both of these should be understood as being for what one has personally performed. Otherwise, there would be a redundancy with the term *satrin*. And this is the method of expenditure rooted in the purpose of *dharma*. Taxes paid to the powerful king constitute expenditure rooted in the purpose of *artha*. The remainder, however, is expenditure rooted in the purpose of *kāma*. The wages of farmers are expenditure common to all three goals (*trivarga*). *Saudāyika* is women’s property (*strīdhana*); *pāritoṣika* is what is given to women out of a desire to please them. And that term *pāritoṣika* generally applies to any gift based on satisfaction, setting aside its specific application in certain cases, such as: "The king gives a reward (*pāritoṣika*) to his soldiers. That too is intended to mean that it should be given according to one's capacity after a review of income and expenditure. When it is asked what should be done according to one's capacity after reviewing income and expenditure, Yājñavalkya [provides the answer].
[26] And he should bestow enjoyments and various kinds of wealth upon the Brahmins;
for that which is bestowed upon Brahmins is an inexhaustible treasure for kings.

One should give enjoyments and pleasures to Brahmins who are worthy recipients by means of their instrumental causes; that is to say, one should give the means for attaining happiness. One should give various kinds of wealth, such as gold, silver, and so forth. The rest is clear in meaning.
Since the injunction to give is already established as a common duty, Yājñavalkya’s repeated statement that "the king's wealth is essential" serves to introduce that very point:
[wealth] which is unspilled, imperishable, and untainted by the need for expiations.
It is said here that what is offered into the fire by a brahmin is superior to [what is offered] from the presence of Agni himself.

The meaning of this is as follows: it is said that an offering made to the fire of a Brahmin is superior even to offerings made to the sacrificial fire—such as the Rājasūya or Aśvamedha—which require abundant sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*). This is because what is given to Brahmins is *askanna* (unspilled), *akṣaya* (undecaying), *avyatha* (free from distress), and free from the injury of animals and the like, as well as the need for expiatory rites (*prāyaścitta*). Thus says Manu: "For this is an imperishable treasure of kings; it is deposited in the Brahman-treasury.
Neither thieves nor enemies carry it off, nor does it perish."
Therefore, a king should deposit an inexhaustible treasure with the Brahmins;
it does not spill over, it does not suffer distress, and it never perishes.
An offering made into the mouth of a Brahmin is superior to offerings made in the sacred fires. Thus it is said.

Regarding this, Yājñavalkya states the specific rule: "Having given land or having established a fixed endowment (nibandha), the king should cause a document to be prepared for the information of future virtuous monarchs."

[27] *Nibandha* is the wealth that may be obtained under the authority of a master according to an agreement (*prabhusamaya*), whereby the officials in charge of trade must give some small amount of money from their own trade-proceeds every year or every month to this Brāhmaṇa or to this deity. Although in this case the status of being the giver of wealth belongs only to the trade-officials, nevertheless the merit (*puṇya*) belongs to the one who establishes the *nibandha* alone, because the other party acts solely with that person’s intent. In the phrase "having given land" (*bhūmiṃ datvā*), the word "land" is indicative of gardens and so forth. For this very reason, Bṛhaspati says: [Section on Royal Edicts].
Having bestowed land and other gifts, the king should cause a righteous edict to be made upon a copper plate or a cloth, recording the location, lineage, and other relevant details.
On this point, Yājñavalkya says:
"The lord of the earth, having inscribed his own lineage, himself,
the dimensions of the gift, and a description of the boundaries of the donation,"
He should cause a firm edict to be issued, completed with his own hand and the date,
either on a cloth scroll or a copper plate, marked with his own seal above.
And this will be explained in the section on written documents (*lekhyaprakaraṇa*). Now, he describes the fort as the king's place of residence.
One should construct a wilderness fort (*jāṅgala-durga*) for the protection of the treasury;
"wilderness" refers to a fort situated in a wilderness region, but the wilderness itself is not the fort.
As Yājñavalkya says:

He should enter a region that is pleasant, suitable for cattle, providing a livelihood, and of the *jāṅgala* type; there he should construct fortresses for the protection of the people, the treasury, and his own person.

[28] It is delightful due to its groves and other features; it is "pastoral" (*paśavya*), meaning beneficial for livestock; and it is "sustaining" (*ājīvya*) by means of bulbs, roots, fruits, flowers, and so forth. Although a region with little water, trees, or foliage is *jāṅgala*, Vijñāneśvara maintains that here a *jāṅgala* refers to a region with abundant water, trees, and mountains. A fortress (*durga*) is of six kinds:
a desert-fortress (*dhanvadurga*), an earth-fortress (*mahīdurga*), a water-fortress (*abdurga*), and likewise a tree-fortress (*vārkṣadurga*).
One should dwell in a city, taking refuge in either a human fortress or a mountain fortress.

Thus it is from the *Manusmṛti*. Regarding this, there is a specific rule in another *Smṛti*: "One should employ those who know the Dharma in matters of Dharma, the learned in matters of wealth, eunuchs among women, and low-born men in low tasks."
With this very intention, Yājñavalkya stated:
"In various matters concerning income, production, and expenditure, he should appoint supervisors who are experts, skilled, pure, and diligent."
In this context, the phrase "in the positions of the Dharma-minister and so forth" is to be understood as the ellipsis. The meaning of this has been clarified by the elders [as follows]:
"Wisdom, integrity in private matters, vigilance, dedication to one's duties, freedom from addiction to worldly affairs, and devotion to the master—these constitute fitness."

Yājñavalkya states that the fruit of giving is even greater when it concerns wealth acquired through the prowess of kings: "There is no higher duty for kings than this: that wealth acquired in battle is bestowed upon Brahmins and constant fearlessness is granted to their subjects."
He (the same author) says that even in the absence of wealth acquired in battle, since that wealth cannot be obtained, death in that very situation is better:
“Those who fight in battles for the sake of land, never turning their backs and using weapons free from deceit, go to heaven just like yogins. [29]
The king takes the merit of those who do not retreat when their ranks are broken, as well as the steps of those who are slain while fleeing.
One should strike down him who speaks of "I," the impotent, the weaponless, the one who has allied with another,
the one who has retreated, and the one who merely looks on like an elder.

"He who says 'I am yours' means he should say 'I am your subordinate. The rest is easy to understand. By the inclusion of the word 'etcetera,' those deprived of their chariot or charioteer and so forth are included. As Gautama says: 'There is no fault in killing in battle, except in the case of those without horses or a charioteer, those with joined palms, those with disheveled hair, those with their backs turned, those seated, those standing on the ground, those mounted on trees, messengers, those with arms raised, and Brahmins. Śaṅkha also states a specific rule: 'One should not kill one drinking water, nor one eating, nor one taking off his sandals, nor one without armor, nor one covered in dust, nor a woman, nor a horse, nor a king. Viṣṇu, however, says: 'One should not kill one who is consecrated for a sacrifice, one surrounded by women, one dressed as a woman, one with joined palms, one who has fled, or one who has discarded his weapons.'"
Manu, however, states a specific rule:
"While fighting his enemies in battle, one should not strike them with deceptive weapons,
nor with barbed ones, nor with poisoned ones, nor with those whose tips are set ablaze with fire."
One should not strike those who have climbed onto dry land, nor eunuchs, nor those with palms joined in supplication;
nor one with disheveled hair, nor one who is seated, nor one who says, "I am yours."
[30] One should not strike one who is asleep, nor one who is unarmored, nor one who is naked, nor one who is unarmed,
nor one who is not fighting, nor one who is looking on, nor one who has encountered another opponent.

Recalling the dharma of the virtuous, he did not strike one who was suffering from a weapon-wound, nor one who was distressed, nor one who was severely mangled, nor one who was terrified, nor one who had turned away in flight.

Regarding the observation of legal proceedings (*vyavahāradarśana*), Viṣṇu states a specific rule: "The daily examination of income and expenditure must be performed just like the observation of legal proceedings. With this intention, Yājñavalkya says:
"Having ensured protection, he should rise and personally inspect his income and expenditure."
"Therefore, having observed legal proceedings, one should bathe and eat according to one's desire."

Having performed the protective rites for the city and for himself, he should rise every morning and personally inspect income and expenditure. Then, having attended to legal affairs, he may eat at midday according to his desire and pleasure; thus Vijñāneśvara states the intended sequence. Bhāruci, however, maintains that the sequence is not intended here; therefore, after bathing and eating in the morning itself, the inspection of legal affairs should be carried out. Regarding the duties following the meal, Vasiṣṭha says: "Inspection of the treasury, dispatching spies and envoys, acceptance of tributes and the like, and deliberation on counsel with ministers. *Upāyana* refers to the tribute sent by neighboring kings. *Cāras* are secret agents disguised as ascetics, while *dūtas* (envoys) are public officials, as the Lord of Yogins (*Yogīśvara*) has stated.
[31] “Gold brought from various sources should be deposited in the treasury;

thereafter, he should observe his spies and, in consultation with his ministers, dispatch messengers. Regarding this, Vijñāneśvara says: “Spies are of three kinds: those with discretionary power (*nisṛṣṭārtha*), those with a specific mission (*saṃdiṣṭārtha*), and those carrying royal edicts (*śāsanahasta*). Among these, those with discretionary power are capable of speaking for themselves on royal affairs as appropriate to the place and time. Those with a specific mission merely report to others exactly what they have been told. Those carrying royal edicts, however, are the bearers of the king’s written documents. [1]
Viṣṇu states what must be done immediately thereafter: "In the afternoon, he may enjoy himself in the inner apartments as he desires. For this very reason, Manu says:
"Having eaten, he should always enjoy himself with the women in the inner apartments;
and having enjoyed himself as he pleases, he should again attend to his duties."
Regarding the inquiry as to "with whom [should he be]," Yājñavalkya says:
"Then he may move about at his own will, or remain composed with his ministers;
having inspected the forces, he should deliberate together with the commander-in-chief."
"Then" means in the afternoon. Regarding what he should do after that, Hārīta has stated:
"Having performed the twilight worship (saṃdhyā), the king, bearing his weapon, should listen within the inner apartments to the activities of those stationed in secret and of his spies."

And likewise Viṣṇu states: "In the evening, with weapon in hand, he should summon those spies stationed somewhere and hear their secret reports. With this very intention, the Lord of Yogins (Yājñavalkya) said:
"Having performed the twilight worship (saṃdhyā), he should listen to the secret speech of the spies;
then he should enjoy himself with dance and song, and recite his own sacred study (svādhyāya)."

"Vijñāneśvara states: 'The repetition of the twilight worship (*saṃdhyopāsana*), although already generally established, is for the purpose of ensuring its performance and preventing forgetfulness. Bhāruci, however, says: 'It is intended to make known that even when occupied with other duties, if one has the capacity, the twilight worship must not be performed by a domestic priest. When the question arises as to what should be done immediately thereafter, Yogīśvara [Yājñavalkya] says:
"One should go to sleep to the sound of musical instruments, and likewise awaken in the same manner.
One should reflect upon the scriptures with the intellect, as well as upon all that is to be done."

For this very reason, Vasiṣṭha says: "Having risen during the *brāhma-muhūrta*, one should contemplate the scriptures together with three or four learned men. However, one should personally reflect upon all that ought to be done; this refers to matters that are clear. As Hārīta has said: "A lord of the earth, being in good health, should carry out this conduct; but when unwell, he should entrust all of this to his chief minister."

Śaṅkha and Likhita state the duty immediately following that: "He should bring in trustworthy spies and send them elsewhere. Viṣṇu states the duty immediately following that: "Having performed the twilight worship (saṃdhyopāsana), having accepted the benedictions of the officiating priests (ṛtvij) and the domestic priest (purohita), and having first consulted with an astrologer, conversed with him, and disclosed his secret intentions, he should report the condition of his own body and issue instructions for its treatment; then he should give gifts of gold, sesame seeds, and other items to those learned in the Vedas (śrotriya). [33] The reporting of one's own body refers to physicians. For this very reason, Yājñavalkya says:
Then, having been greeted with blessings by the officiating priests, the family priest, and the teachers, he should respectfully dispatch spies among his own people and those of others.
Having seen [these omens], one should give cows, gold, and land to astrologers and physicians,
as well as dwellings and houses to those learned in the Vedas (śrotriyas).

"A king should be patient toward Brahmins, straightforward toward his affectionate [ministers], and wrathful toward his enemies; he should be like a father toward his circle of servants and his subjects.
The phrase "toward Brahmins" implies "even when they are insulting him."
Viṣṇu states the specific fruit resulting from a king’s protection of his subjects: "The status of receiving a sixth part [of the merit];
for by pleasing his subjects, the king receives a sixth part of their asceticism."

The meaning of this is as follows: one is designated by the word "king" (*rājan*) solely because of pleasing the subjects, and not on account of merit. Regarding the phrase "he takes a sixth part," Vasiṣṭha says for this very reason: "A king who acts according to justice is the taker of a sixth part. "Just" (*nyāyya*) means not deviating from justice; the remainder of the sense is that he takes a sixth part of their ascetic merit (*tapas*).
Yājñavalkya likewise states that the fruit of protecting the subjects belongs to the king for this very reason.
"Protecting [his subjects] according to the law, he takes a sixth part of their merit;

for the protection of subjects is superior to all gifts. The meaning is that, because it is superior to all gifts, it must necessarily be performed. Vijñāneśvara, however, says: "Because the fruit is greater, therefore he should be toward his subjects just like a father—this is the connection with what has preceded."

[34] Regarding this, Hārīta states a specific rule: “Having learned the conduct of those appointed over the kingdom through spies, one should protect the subjects. “Protecting the subjects” means the protection of the people. Having learned the conduct of those appointed by the king—the officials—through spies, he should punish the wicked and honor the virtuous. As Vasiṣṭha says: “One should especially guard against scribes who live by bribery. This has been explained by the author of the *Saṃgraha*: “In the construction ‘from scribes who live by bribery,’ if the scribes are those who live by bribery, then protection must certainly be provided against them. In that context, “scribes” (*kāyastha*) refers to accountants; they are specifically those who live by bribery. And this protection even from those who live by bribery is indeed distinct [from other forms of protection].
Therefore Yājñavalkya says:
"Having learned through spies the conduct of those who hold office in the kingdom,
the king should honor the virtuous but put to death those who are the opposite."
Having deprived those who live by bribery of their wealth, he should banish them;
meanwhile, he should settle there learned Vedic scholars (śrotriyas) who are provided with gifts, honor, and respect.
"He shall protect the subjects being oppressed by rogues, thieves, evildoers, violent criminals, and the like, and especially by scribes (kāyastha).
The meaning is that because scribes are favorites of the king and are exceedingly deceitful, they are difficult to restrain. "Cāṭas" refers to deceivers.
In filling the treasury through unjust means, there is ruin for the king;
that monarch who increases his own treasury from the kingdom by unjust means will, before long, lose his royal fortune and go to destruction along with his kinsmen.
The fire born from the suffering caused by the oppression of subjects does not turn back until it has consumed the lineage, the fortune, and the very lives of kings.
Whatever merit belongs to a king from the protection of his own kingdom,
that same merit in its entirety he obtains by bringing another's kingdom under his control.

“Whatever custom, family tradition, or legal practice has existed in a particular region exactly as it was before, that very same thing must be maintained, provided it is not contrary to the sacred scriptures,” says Vijñāneśvara (on Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 1.343). By the phrase “when he has come under one’s control,” it is shown that there is no fixed rule prior to bringing him under control. And so Pitāmaha says: “One should remain besieging the enemy and harass his kingdom; one should constantly spoil his fodder, food, and water supply.”

Regarding this, Śaṅkha and Likhita state a specific rule: "The secrecy of counsel [must be maintained] until the emergence of the fruit. "Until the emergence of the fruit" means up to the attainment of the result. "Counsel" refers to the deliberation on matters of state. As Yājñavalkya says:
"Since the kingdom has its root in counsel, one should keep that counsel well-guarded, so that others do not know of his actions until the emergence of their fruits."
Of this king’s actions, such as peace and war;
furthermore—artificial, natural, and ordinary enemies and friends:
"The enemy, the friend, and the neutral one; the immediate neighbor, the one beyond him, and the one further still."
The maṇḍala should be visualized in sequence by means of the expedients such as conciliation and the rest.

[36] An enemy (*ari*) is one who hates; a friend (*mitra*) is a companion. One distinct from these is the neutral (*udāsīna*), meaning one devoid of both friendship and enmity. These are of three kinds: innate (*sahaja*), natural (*prākṛta*), and acquired (*kṛtrima*). Innate enemies include stepbrothers, nephews on the father’s side, and so forth. Acquired enemies are those by whom one has been wronged or by whom one has wronged. A natural enemy is the ruler of the territory immediately adjacent to one's own. An innate friend includes sisters' sons, paternal cousins, maternal cousins, and so forth. An acquired friend is one by whom one has been helped or to whom one has rendered help. A natural friend is the ruler of the territory separated by one intervening state. Those lacking the characteristics of both innate and acquired friends are innate and acquired neutrals. A natural neutral is the ruler of a territory separated by two intervening states.

Furthermore, the enemy is of four kinds: one to be marched against (*yātavya*), one to be cut off (*chettavya*), one to be oppressed (*pīḍanīya*), and one to be weakened (*karśanīya*). Among these, the immediate neighbor king is the one to be marched against. One who is in calamity, deficient in strength, whose subjects are disaffected, who lacks a fortress, who is without allies, or who is weak, is to be cut off. One who is deficient in the power of counsel (*mantra*) is to be oppressed. But one who possesses powerful counsel is to be weakened.
As it has been said: "Cutting off is uprooting and destruction; oppression is the suppression of power."
"Furthermore, they say that 'emaciation' (karśana) results from the depletion of treasury and army.
Thus, allies are of two kinds, distinguished as those to be strengthened (bṛṃhaṇīya) and those to be emaciated (karśanīya).

An ally (*mitra*) is of two kinds: one to be strengthened (*bṛṃhaṇīya*) and one to be weakened (*karśanīya*). An ally who lacks strength and treasury is to be strengthened. Vijñāneśvara states: "One with a depleted treasury is to be strengthened; one with an excess of treasury and power is to be weakened. This circle of kings (*rājamaṇḍala*) is to be considered in sequence, starting from the east and so forth. With three kings each in front, behind, and on the flanks, and the king himself as the center, there are thirteen kings in the circle of kings. As for the rear-enemy (*pārṣṇigrāha*) and others, they are not mentioned separately in the *Dharmaśāstra* because they are already included within the categories of enemy, ally, and neutral.

[37] In the system of Uśanas and others, however, a plurality of circles (*maṇḍala*) is taught based on the distinction between the number—such as unity—and the entities to be numbered. For this very reason, Uśanas says: "Because the enemy and the seeker of victory are mutually engaged, the state of being an enemy and the state of being a seeker of victory constitute a single constituent element (*prakṛti*)."

The meaning is that even an enemy who has been attacked by one desiring victory (*vijigīṣu*) is a constituent element (*prakṛti*) in the form of a counter-attacker. According to the opinion of Parāśara, however, Uśanas says there are two constituent elements:
"Parāśara stated that only two constituent elements are logical.

This is the meaning: the one desiring victory is primary because he is the attacker; the enemy is also primary because he is the object of attack. Since the others are included within their respective circles (*maṇḍala*), they are subsumed under those two; thus, there are only two constituent elements.

“Even a triad is proper,” says Viṣṇu. [This refers to] one who is attacked by a middle king, a neutral king, and an enemy—the word “enemy” being understood as the remainder [of the phrase]. The “success” here is the accomplishment of the task; the point is that even the *vijigīṣu* (the seeker of victory) is included within the category of the enemy at the time of counter-attack, because he too acts as an enemy.
For this very reason, Uśanas said: “They say the circle consists of three: the *vijigīṣu*, the enemy, and the middle king.”
Others say that the mandala consists of four [deities]. As it is stated in the *Rājalāsaka*:
"These four are proclaimed as the root natures;
one skilled in tantra has said that the mandala is a group of four."
[38] "Four" refers to the enemy, the conqueror, the inferior, and the neutral. Some say there are five, for it is said:

"The circle of states (*maṇḍala*) is rightly considered by the wise to consist of five, or else three. The meaning is that for a conqueror (*vijigīṣu*) attacking an enemy, the successful accomplishment of his task requires the following five: ensuring the safety of his rear (*pārṣṇigrāha-nivṛtti*), securing his base (*mūlaka-śuddhi*), purifying his flanks (*pṛṣṭha-śuddhi*), producing provocation against his ally (*mitrotpādita-kopa*), and provoking internal dissent among his enemies (*paścāt-kopa*). Thus, the group of five is logical.
Some say there is a hexagon of states (*maṇḍala-ṣaṭka*):
"The seeker of victory, the enemy, the friend, the rear-attacker, the middle state, and the neutral state—these two, Puloman and Indra, spoke of the hexagon of states. Thus it is said.
The intended meaning is that the middling king and the neutral king, having been assisted, both attack their respective enemies;
thus, Uśanas describes the circle of kings (*rājamaṇḍala*) as consisting of ten:
the enemy, the friend, the enemy’s friend, and beyond that, the friend of the friend.
Now, the enemy's friend and the conqueror's own friend are the two who march ahead of the one seeking victory.
"Then behind him is the rear-attacker (pārṣṇigrāha), and immediately after that the ally of the rear-attacker (ākranda);
these two are the supports (āsāra) of the one seeking victory (vijigīṣu)—such is the circle [of states]."

The meaning of this is as follows: In that context, for one who desires victory (*vijigīṣu*), the enemy is the territory immediately adjacent on all sides, while the friend is separated by one intervening territory. Likewise, the friend of the enemy is immediately adjacent to that, and the friend of the friend is beyond that. For the one desiring victory who has set out to attack the enemy, these are designated by such names in front of him. One who seizes the rear (*pārṣṇi*) for the benefit of the enemy is called the "rear-seizer" (*pārṣṇigrāha*). One who is called upon or summoned by the one desiring victory is the "ally" (*ākranda*), namely the friend of the one desiring victory. Regarding the two types of "supporters" (*āsāra*): one who supports the rear-seizer by granting permission is the "supporter of the enemy" (*amitra-āsāra*). Similarly, the supporter of the ally is the "friend of the friend of the one desiring victory" (*vijigīṣu-mitramitra*). This constitutes the circle (*maṇḍala*) of the one desiring victory. [39] Because it is to be conquered, the entire earth is described from the perspective of a universal monarch (*cakravartin*); however, from the perspective of a mere king, it is as follows:

"Outside the circle [of states], there is one who is neutral and possesses superior power; he is the master in favoring those who are allied and in slaying those who are divided. It should be understood that when the neutral party is included, the circle consists of eleven types. The twelfth and thirteenth circles have already been explained previously. Others say there is a fourteenth circle; and so says Bṛhaspati:

"That which consists of seven constituents for both the seeker of victory (*vijigīṣu*) and the enemy (*ari*), this very fourteenfold circle (*maṇḍala*) is what they describe. Thus, the teachers say that because there are seven constituents each for the seeker of victory and the enemy, there are fourteen; however, some say there are eighteen.

"But one who is allied with both the enemy and the friend, as well as the enemy of both, and the enemy himself—these twelve are the hereditary kings; thus, the teacher [Vṛhaspati] says there is a circle of eighteen.

This is the meaning: together with the two—the enemy and the conqueror—who stand outside the relationship of harm-doer and benefactor, and along with the six consisting of one's own friends and enemies, there are twelve hereditary kings. Thus, it is a circle of eighteen. Others, however, speak of a circle of twenty-one, as Uśanas said:
"All those—the conqueror, the enemy, and the intermediate state—are of seven constituent types," so say some opponents. Others, however, say there are twenty-one;
still others say there are thirty.
The two eastern ones are for the desire to conquer, and the two western ones as well; thus there is a group of five.
Including the ministers and others separately for each of these, thirty are proclaimed.
[40] There are twenty-five beginning with the ministers and five royal constituents; thus, there is a group of thirty.
Those who know the mandala say that the mandala consists of thirty-six;
they declare it to be a group of thirty-six. Thus it is said.
Others say there are forty-eight maṇḍalas. As it is stated in the Bṛhaspatya:
"The four rulers of the earth, each with their separate allies, making eight;
and these, together with the ministers and others, are composed of the syllables of the Jagatī metre."
Regarding the syllables of the *jagatī* meter—the syllables of the *jagatī* *chandas* are forty-eight. Viśālākṣa states that there are fifty-four; this is said in the *Rājalāsaka*:
"Of these eighteen, Mitra and Śatru are each separate;
Viśālākṣa declares them to be fifty-four. Thus it is said.

Others say that a *maṇḍala* consists of sixty [rulers]. Those who know the *maṇḍala* declare that a *maṇḍala* numbering sixty is formed by the ministers and other officials of ten sovereigns, each acting separately.

In this context, "ten kings" means fifty, including enemies, friends, and so forth. According to the system of Manu, the circle of states (*maṇḍala*) consists of seventy-two.
