There are twelve sovereign lords, each with five distinct constituent elements (*prakṛti*) beginning with the minister; thus, the number of human beings here is infinite.
These twelve, beginning with the ministers, are the hereditary [officials]; likewise, there are seventy-two others—this indeed constitutes the entire circle of constituent elements.

This is the meaning: there are sixty constituent elements (*prakṛti*) of substance and twelve constituent elements of sovereignty; thus, the entire circle of constituent elements (*maṇḍala*) consists of seventy-two. Uśanas speaks of a circle of one hundred and eight:
"Of these eighteen [elements], the ministers and so forth are each distinct;
the wise know this circle to consist of one hundred and eight. Thus it is said.

[41] There are eighteen basic types of kings and ninety basic types of substances; such is the meaning. According to the view of some, the maṇḍala consists of three hundred and twenty-four [deities]. As it is stated in the *Rājalāsaka*: "The ministers and other attendants of fifty-four kings, each distinct [from the king], together with these twenty-four, are considered this maṇḍala of three hundred."

In this context, there are two hundred and seventy *dravyaprakṛtis* (material constituents), meaning fifty-four *svāmiprakṛtis* (personal constituents). Thus, although the circle of kings (*rājamaṇḍala*) consists of many varieties, it is subsumed within the group of twelve. This very point has been stated by the authors of the *Dharmaśāstras*, such as Yājñavalkya, even though circles of one up to eleven kings are not actually included within the twelve. Nevertheless, because the circle of twelve kings is well-known in the world and because circles of one king and so forth are difficult to ascertain, the group of twelve alone was accepted by Yājñavalkya and others. Even in the systems of Auśanasa and others, where various alternatives for the circle exist, the group of twelve is intended. As Uśanas said:
"In these various ways, they describe the maṇḍala in many forms;
yet that which is clearly recognized by all the world is the twelvefold royal [maṇḍala]. Thus, there are four kinds of means (upāya).

Regarding this, Viṣṇu states the means: "The means are fourfold: conciliation (*sāman*), gift-giving (*dāna*), sowing dissension (*bheda*), and force (*daṇḍa*). Conciliation is pleasant speech. Gift-giving is the bestowal of gold and other valuables. Sowing dissension is the act of creating mutual enmity among neighboring kings and others. Force is injury ranging from secret or open seizure of wealth to the taking of life. These, beginning with conciliation, are the means for accomplishing one's objectives against adversaries and the like. Although their number as four is established by the mere mention of them, the explicit inclusion of the word "four" is for the purpose of demonstrating that force may be employed either as a last resort (*agatika*) or when no other alternative exists (*sagatika*). Therefore, it is correct to say that there are only three means; for this very reason, the Lord of Yogins (Yājñavalkya) has said: [The verse follows: *sāma dānaṃ ca bhedaś ca daṇḍaś ceti catuṣṭayam | upāyāḥ kathitā hy ete...* etc. (Note: The provided text fragment ends mid-verse; the full verse typically concludes with *tatra trayo 'py upāyāḥ syur daṇḍas tv antye prayujyate*.)
"The means are conciliation, bribery, sowing dissension, and likewise force;
when properly applied, they may achieve success, but force is the resort of the desperate."

Regarding the phrase "four," they say that by means of the number four, there is an exclusion of non-connection (*ayoga-vyavaccheda*) alone, and not an exclusion of connection with something else (*anyayoga-vyavaccheda*). In this way, the three means consisting of *māyā*, *akṣa*, and *indrajāla* are included. Together with these, the means (*upāyas*) are exactly seven. *Māyā* is the means of concealment; that is to say, the production of false knowledge. *Akṣas* are well known, as in the case of the bird [Śakuni] seizing King Yudhiṣṭhira’s kingdom through dice. In the treatises on statecraft (*nītiśāstra*) such as those of Auśanas and others, the seven [means] consist of *sāma* and the rest, together with *māyā*, *akṣa*, and *indrajāla*. In the slaying of Kīcaka, *māyā* refers to Vṛkodara (Bhīma) assuming the form of a woman. In that same context of Kīcaka’s killing, it is said that Virāṭa maintained indifference, thinking, "Let this Kīcaka die. *Indrajāla*, however, is the fabrication of objects possessing the nature of illusion. For example, the capture of the King of Vatsa through the creation of an illusory elephant by a magician. Thus, there is a distinction between *māyā* and *indrajāla* based on their relationship as cause and effect. Even though *māyā* exists within the *akṣas*, the distinction lies in the fact that *māyā* is denoted by the word "deception" (*pratāraṇa*). For this very reason, the triad beginning with *māyā* is considered difficult because it is rooted in deception. Therefore, it is stated in the *Gautama-sūtra* that there are four means. The authors of the legal digests (*smṛtis*), such as Yājñavalkya, have also established only four means. Accordingly, the *Gautama-sūtra* states: "Resorting to the four means, one should employ the strategic qualities (*guṇas*) known as peace (*saṃdhi*), war (*vigraha*), marching (*yāna*), halting (*āsana*), duplicity (*dvaidhībhāva*), and seeking refuge (*samāśraya*)."
The qualities of peace, war, and so forth:

*saṃdhi* (peace) is the making of an agreement; *vigraha* (war) is injury; *yāna* (marching) is an expedition against an enemy; *āsana* (sitting encamped) is indifference; *dvaidhībhāva* (double-dealing) is the division of one's forces; *āśraya* (seeking protection) is taking refuge with a powerful one.
[This concludes the section on] the time for marching.
Regarding vehicles, Yājñavalkya said:
"When the enemy kingdom is endowed with the excellence of crops, then one should march;
provided that the enemy is weak and one's own self has joyful mounts and men."

Since the science of polity (*arthaśāstra*) depends upon human effort (*puruṣakāra*), Vasiṣṭha states the predominance of human effort: "Between fate (*daiva*) and human effort, human effort is stronger; some say that both are one. This means that Yājñavalkya and others hold this view. In his own opinion, however, human effort alone is predominant, because it is so observed in the world; otherwise, treatises on medicine and the like would be useless. Furthermore, skills such as those involving the wheel (mechanical arts) which have visible purposes would be in vain. For example, when a skillful man determines in a battle, "He shall be struck in this limb by this [weapon], and by this blow he shall die," and a steel band or similar object is placed in concealment on that limb, the blow from that steel band occurs; yet he does not die [because of the protection]. Thus, the sense is that human effort is stronger than fate, and the purpose of the treatise is thereby established. As for the opinion of Yājñavalkya and others:
The accomplishment of action is established upon both destiny and human effort;
therein, destiny is that which is manifest, while human effort is what was performed in a previous life.
"Acquired in a previous life" means earned in a former body. The view that "human effort alone is called destiny" is the opinion of some partial schools (*ekadeśimata*).

Other views, however, are as follows: some hold that human effort arises from the strength of the body and from time; some maintain that the attainment of desired or undesired results comes from destiny alone; some say it is from inherent nature (*svabhāva*) and does not depend on any cause; some say it is from time; and some say it is human effort alone. Having stated these, the Lord of Yogins (*yogīśvara*) declares his own view:
"Those of wise intellect maintain that the result arises from the conjunction [of all factors]."
The meaning is that the fruit does not arise from either one alone. Regarding this, he provides an illustration:
"For just as there would be no movement of a chariot with only a single wheel, so too destiny is not accomplished without human effort."
Hārīta stated that there are five constituent parts:
assistants, the means of accomplishment, the division of place and time, [the determination of the result, and the removal of obstacles].
And the remedy for misfortune; success is held to have five factors.

The attainment of success (*kāryasiddhi*) consists of three kinds of acquisitions: the acquisition of gold, the acquisition of land, and the acquisition of friends. Among these, the acquisition of friends is the most excellent; therefore, the means to achieve that is the most excellent. Consequently, one should apply effort toward the means for attaining it. And that very means is truthful speech; thus Vasiṣṭha says: "The acquisition of friends through truthful speech is superior to [the acquisition of] gold and land. Likewise, Yājñavalkya states: "Since the acquisition of friends is better than the acquisition of gold and land..."
"Therefore, one should strive for its attainment and, being composed, protect the truth"—
thus [it is said regarding] the vital points.

One must not be negligent regarding even the five *marmas* (critical moments). Thus, the *Gautama-sūtra* states: “The times for eating, sexual intercourse, shaving, oil-massage, and sleep—these are the five *marmas*; one must not be negligent during them. The time for eating (*bhojana-kāla*) indicates the period of consuming food in general. The time for chewing betel leaves and the like is also a *marma*-time. The time for sexual intercourse (*nidhuvana-kāla*) indicates contact with another person; likewise, the time of sharing a bed or seat with a friend is also a *marma*-time. The time for shaving (*kṣaura-kāla*) indicates the time of contact with weapons. The time for oil-massage (*abhyañjana-kāla*) indicates periods of physical exertion and the like. The time for sleep (*svāpa-kāla*), however, indicates a state of being alone—so it has been explained by the commentators. Therefore, it was said by Manu:
Having thus deliberated on all this with his ministers, the king,
after exercising himself and bathing at midday, should go to the inner apartments to eat.
There, one should eat food that has been thoroughly examined by attendants who are like his own self, who know the proper time, who are incorruptible, and who have neutralized poison with mantras.
One should purify all objects with water containing anti-venomous herbs;
and, being self-restrained, one should always wear gems that destroy poison.
And women, thoroughly tested and adorned with their dress and ornaments, being composed, should touch him with fans, water, and incense.
In this manner, one should exert effort regarding vehicles, beds, seats, and food,
as well as in bathing, purification, and all forms of personal adornment.

"Having eaten, he should indeed enjoy himself with women in the inner apartments; and having enjoyed himself at the proper time, he should again deliberate upon his duties. Thus [are stated] the seven constituent parts.

The seven constituents (*saptāṅga*) are the sovereign and so forth. Thus states the *Gautama-sūtra*: "The sovereign, ministers, allies, fortresses, treasury, army, and subjects. The sovereign is well known. Ministers are counselors. Allies are those who are natural, acquired, and ordinary. Fortresses are the seven types, such as mountain fortresses. The treasury is a heap of wealth consisting of gold and other valuables. The army is the fourfold military force. The subjects are the social classes beginning with the Brahmins. And likewise, Yājñavalkya says:
"The sovereign, ministers, subjects, the fortress, the treasury, and likewise the army."
"These subjects are friends; the kingdom is said to have seven constituent parts. Thus it is said.

The *prakṛtis* are the primary constituents [of sovereignty]. Therefore, Sumantu states that the seven limbs must be protected in every way: “One should protect the sovereign by oneself; ministers by honoring them; the social classes (*varṇas*) by pleasing them; the people by pleasing them through the duties of their respective classes; the fortress by abundance of wealth, grain, and so forth; the treasury by appropriate expenditure; the army by its own duty; and a friend by truthful speech. Here, the term *daṇḍa* does not refer to the fourfold army. Rather, corporal punishment or monetary fines should be prescribed according to the nature of the offense. This is the underlying intention: in Sumantu’s view, the fourfold army is included within the treasury itself. Gautama says, “But the treasury must be protected in every way,” because “the constituents are rooted in it. This means the six constituents [excluding the sovereign]. It must be protected in every way—that is, in all manners—by avoiding improper expenditure and by guarding it against thieves, scribes, and others.

For this very reason, the *Gautama-sūtra* states: "The powers of sovereignty, counsel, and energy have that as their root. "Having that as their root" means having the treasury (*kośa*) as their root; such is the implied meaning. And so says Yājñavalkya:
"Having obtained that [kingdom], the king should inflict punishment upon the wicked;
for punishment was fashioned of old by Brahmā in the form of Dharma."
[47] "That" refers to sovereignty.
When practiced by one who is true to his word, pure, possessed of good allies,
and wise, according to the scriptures, it [subdues] the world including the gods, asuras, and humans.
One should gladden the entire world; otherwise, one would provoke its wrath—even if it be a brother, a son, a venerable guest, a father-in-law, or even a maternal uncle.
There is no one who, having deviated from his own dharma, is not subject to punishment by the king.
And this refers to cases other than those involving one's mother, father, and so forth:
"The mother and father are not to be punished, nor is the bath-graduate (snātaka), nor the domestic priest,
nor wandering mendicants (parivrājaka) or forest-dwellers (vānaprastha)."
Thus, according to the recollection of Viṣṇu.

It has now been stated that the king must generally conduct the examination of legal proceedings (*vyavahāra*). What is that legal proceeding like? Of how many kinds is it? And how is it conducted? This is now demonstrated.

What is called *vyavahāra* (legal procedure) is the statement of one's own position in relation to oneself, without contradicting another. This is because it consists of truthful speech and is dedicated to non-violence. When a matter known as *dharma*—which is to be accomplished through effort—is interrupted by greed, hatred, and the like, then in cases such as the non-payment of debts (*ṛṇādāna*) for the sake of recovering one’s own property, or in matters of customary law (*samayadharma*) for the sake of avoiding the duties of others, a judicial inquiry (*nyāya*) is conducted. In that context, the dispute among men which is rooted in what is to be accomplished is called *vyavahāra*. Nor should it be suspected that a dispute concerning theft or assault is not *vyavahāra*; for the definition of *vyavahāra* is accepted as being a dispute concerning any one of the eighteen types of subject matters. For instance: [The eighteen titles of law follow: Non-payment of debt, deposits, sale without ownership, joint concerns, rescission of sale and purchase, non-delivery of gifts, non-payment of wages, breach of contract, cancellation of purchase and sale, disputes between owners and herdsmen, boundary disputes, verbal assault, physical assault, theft, robbery and violence, adultery, defamation, gambling and betting, and miscellaneous matters. Thus it is said: "The eighteenfold subjects of dispute are the eighteen titles of law. Therefore, all these are indeed *vyavahāra*. Furthermore, since the term *vyavahāra* is derived from the root *hṛ* (to carry/take), it signifies the carrying forward of a dispute; and because it is preceded by the prefix *vi*, it denotes the separation or distinction of the parties involved. Thus, it is established that *vyavahāra* is a dispute concerning the eighteen titles of law. It is not merely a dispute, nor is it simply a lawsuit; rather, it is a specific kind of dispute characterized by the aforementioned definition. Consequently, the term *vyavahāra* is used in its primary sense (*mukhya-vṛtti*) with respect to the eighteen titles of law, while it is used in a secondary or figurative sense (*gauṇa-vṛtti*) in other contexts. Therefore, there is no contradiction. Thus ends the discussion on the nature of *vyavahāra*. Now, the purpose of this treatise is stated: [The purpose is] the protection of the world and the maintenance of the eternal *dharma*. "Protection of the world" means the preservation of the four castes and stages of life (*varṇāśrama*). "Maintenance of eternal *dharma*" means the establishment of the duties of the four castes and stages of life, which are based upon the Vedas. By the word "and" (*ca*), it is indicated that the purpose is both the protection of the world and the maintenance of eternal *dharma*. This is because the protection of the world is impossible without the maintenance of eternal *dharma*. Therefore, the author of the treatise undertakes the composition of this work for the sake of both purposes. As it has been said: "The king who protects the world according to *dharma* attains imperishable worlds hereafter, and in this world he gains fame and long life. Thus, the connection between the subject matter and the purpose is established. For the subject matter is the eighteen titles of law, and the purpose is the protection of the world and the maintenance of eternal *dharma*. And since the subject matter is contained within the treatise, the relationship between the treatise and the purpose is that of the means and the end (*sādhyasādhanabhāva*). Thus, the introduction is concluded. Now, the first title of law is described: "Non-payment of debt is the first title of law. Here, "debt" refers to gold, grain, cattle, and so forth, which have been lent out. Its "non-payment" is the failure to return it at the proper time. That is the first title of law. It is called the first because it is the foremost among the eighteen titles of law. It is called a "title of law" because it is a subject of dispute. The word "first" indicates its priority over the others. Thus, the meaning is that the non-payment of debt is the very first title of law. Now, the definition of a "debt": a "debt" is that which is borrowed from another for the purpose of consumption or trade, and which is to be returned with interest at a later time. It is of four kinds: based on a document (*kāyika*), based on witnesses (*sākṣika*), based on a deposit (*bhogya*), and based on a bond (*lekhya*). Among these, a "document-based" debt is one where a written agreement is made before a judge or an arbitrator, specifying the amount, the interest, and the time of repayment. A "witness-based" debt is one where the transaction is recorded in the presence of witnesses. A "deposit-based" debt is one involving the lending of goods such as grain, oil, or sesame. A "bond-based" debt is one where a formal bond is executed. The non-payment of such a debt is the first title of law. Now, the procedure for the plaintiff: the plaintiff, having approached the king, should state his case clearly and concisely, beginning with the date and place, and including the names of the witnesses and the nature of the claim. He must speak the truth and avoid falsehood. If he speaks falsely, he shall be punished. Now, the procedure for the defendant: the defendant, having heard the plaintiff's claim, should answer it truthfully. If he denies the claim, he should be summoned by the king through messengers. If he does not appear, he may be imprisoned or fined. If he appears, the judge should examine the evidence. There are five means of proof: documents, witnesses, possession, ordeals, and divine proof. Among these, a document is the best proof. Witnesses are those who have seen or heard the transaction. Possession is the enjoyment of property. Ordeals are the balance, fire, water, poison, and sacred libation. Divine proof is the oath. These are the means of proof. Now, the rules for witnesses: witnesses should be honest, virtuous, and knowledgeable in the scriptures. They should be of the same caste as the parties, and they should be examined in the presence of the king. If they speak falsely, they shall be punished. Now, the rules for the judge: the judge should be learned in the *Dharmaśāstra* and capable of discerning truth from falsehood. He should decide the case according to the evidence. If he decides wrongly, he shall incur sin and punishment. Thus, the first title of law, non-payment of debt, is explained. Now, the second title of law is described: "Deposits are the second title of law. Here, a "deposit" is an object placed in the custody of another for safekeeping. Its "recovery" is the second title of law. It is called the second because it follows the first. It is called a "title of law" because it is a subject of dispute. Thus, the meaning is that the recovery of deposits is the second title of law. Now, the rules for deposits: a deposit should be returned exactly as it was received. If it is damaged or lost, the custodian is liable unless the loss was due to force majeure or negligence on the part of the depositor. If the deposit is stolen, the custodian is not liable if he proves his innocence. Thus, the second title of law is explained. Now, the third title of law is described: "Sale without ownership is the third title of law. Here, "sale without ownership" is the sale of an object by one who is not the owner. Its "recovery" is the third title of law. It is called the third because it follows the second. It is called a "title of law" because it is a subject of dispute. Thus, the meaning is that the sale without ownership is the third title of law. Now, the rules for sale without ownership: if a person sells an object belonging to another without permission, the true owner may reclaim it. The seller is liable for the price and damages. If the sale was made in good faith, the buyer may keep the object, but the seller must pay the price. Thus, the third title of law is explained. Now, the fourth title of law is described: "Joint concerns are the fourth title of law. Here, a "joint concern" is a partnership in business. Its "settlement" is the fourth title of law. It is called the fourth because it follows the third. It is called a "title of law" because it is a subject of dispute. Thus, the meaning is that joint concerns are the fourth title of law. Now, the rules for joint concerns: partners should share profits and losses equally. If one partner withdraws from the partnership, he is entitled to his share of the profits but liable for his share of the losses. If a partner dies, his heirs shall inherit his share. Thus, the fourth title of law is explained. Now, the fifth title of law is described: "Rescission of sale and purchase is the fifth title of law. Here, "rescission" is the withdrawal of a transaction after it has been completed. It is the fifth title of law. It is called the fifth because it follows
The eighteen bases of legal dispute.

The eighteen titles of legal dispute (*vivādapada*) are: non-payment of debt, deposits, partnerships, non-delivery of what has been given, breach of contract for service, non-payment of wages, sale without ownership, non-delivery of gifts, rescission of purchase, disputes concerning boundaries, disputes concerning fields, disputes between husband and wife, partition of inheritance, violence, verbal abuse, physical assault, gambling, and miscellaneous matters. It should not be argued that the definition [of legal dispute] is under-extended (*avyāpti*) because other titles such as "deposit" (*nikṣepa*) are recorded in the law-books (*smṛti*). This is because deposits and the like are included within "deposits" (*upanidhi*) and the other categories mentioned. The systematic grouping of these eighteen titles of legal dispute is now stated: in all *smṛtis*, the determination of the eighteen titles of legal dispute follows immediately after the determination of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Since it is logical to determine the objects of knowledge (*prameya*) after determining the means of knowledge, the object of knowledge known as the eighteen titles of legal dispute is determined immediately thereafter.

In this context, since legal procedure (*vyavahāra*) is defined as being established by all means of proof—both human and divine—it is first examined as the title of dispute (*vivādapada*) called "Recovery of Debt" (*ṛṇādāna*), following the order of enumeration starting from the first. For this very reason, Manu stated: "Of these, the first is the recovery of debt."

Regarding the non-payment of debt (*ṛṇādāna*): a debt is that which is given into the hand of another with a view toward profit (*upacaya*). A deposit (*upanidhi*), however, is property given into the hand of another solely for the purpose of safekeeping, without such a view toward profit. Thus, the occasion for the section on deposits follows immediately after that on the non-payment of debt. Furthermore, while the profit arising from the interest applied in the non-payment of debt rests upon a single person, in joint enterprise (*sambhūyasamutthāna*) it rests upon many; therefore, it would be logical for joint enterprise to follow immediately after the non-payment of debt. Nevertheless, since there is no room for the term "deposit" immediately after that [section on joint enterprise], the entry of the section on deposits occurs right after the non-payment of debt according to the aforementioned reasoning; thus, the connection of this section's occasion is established later.

The connection (*saṅgati*) of *Dattāpradānika* (Non-delivery of what has been given) is as follows: because it establishes that certain types of property—such as those obtained through deposits, trusts, theft, or similar means—are not to be given away, it is a supplement (*śeṣa*) to *Ṛṇādāna* (Recovery of Debts), *Upanidhi* (Deposits), and *Sambhūyasamutthāna* (Partnership). It is also a supplement to *Dāyavibhāga* (Partition of Inheritance); nevertheless, one should understand that by the principle of the majority, it is considered a supplement to these three. In *Dattāpradānika*, it is stated that what was promised must be returned if it was given under a condition (*sopādhika*). [49] In the title of dispute called *Abhyupetyāśuśrūṣā* (Failure to Perform Agreed Service), even when there is no such condition, it must be returned; thus, there is a thematic connection (*saṅgati*). However, these two do not belong to the same section (*prakaraṇa*), because in the preceding section, the non-taking of what was given concerned material objects (*dravya*), whereas here, the failure to perform what was agreed upon concerns a dependent (*upajīvaka*). Since their subject matter (*viṣaya*) is different, they are to be explained in separate sections; therefore, they do not constitute a single section. In the title of dispute called *Abhyupetyāśuśrūṣā*, it is stated that for those who have entered into service for wages or for the sake of fulfilling a promise, a substitute may be employed. Here, however, in the title of dispute called *Vetanānapākarma* (Non-payment of Wages), the connection is with wages for the purpose of fulfilling a promise. Yet, this [latter] is not included within *Dattāpradānika*. In that [former], it was stated that what was given is treated as if it were not given, but not that there is a seizure of what was given. Therefore, there is a distinction between these two. With this in mind, Manu says:
"Hereafter, I shall explain the remedial treatment for Vetasī. Thus [it is said].

The meaning is that this follows after the section known as *abhyupetyāśuśrūṣā* (non-performance of promised service), which is why it is called "the subsequent" (*anantaram*). In the preceding section titled *vetanānapākarma* (non-payment of wages), it was stated that wages are not to be withheld; here, in the section titled *asvāmivikraya* (sale by one who is not the owner), it is stated that what has been purchased is to be returned—this is the connection. In the section on *dattāpradānika* (non-delivery of gifts), it was stated that what has been given is practically equivalent to what has not been given; here, however, there is simply the returning of what has been purchased, and not the fact that what has been purchased is practically equivalent to what has not been purchased—therefore, there is a distinction between them. In the section on *asvāmivikraya*, it was stated that when an object is purchased from one who is not the owner, ownership does not arise, and thus it must be returned. Here, in the section on *vikrīyāsaṃpradāna* (failure to deliver after sale), although ownership arises through purchase, it is subject to a restriction and must therefore be returned—this is the connection. Nor should this be included within *ṛṇādāna* (recovery of debts) despite the ownership being conditional, like a pledge for custody (*gopyādhi*); in the case of a pledge for custody, the conditionality of ownership is rooted in a specific agreement (*paribhāṣā*), whereas here it is rooted in the right of rescission (*anuśaya*)—thus is the difference between these two. Nor can this be subsumed under *dattāpradānika*, because of the difference between giving and buying. Furthermore, in the former case, what is given is treated as if not given; here, however, there is the reversal of what has been sold—the logic previously stated is indeed correct, and for this very reason, it is not included in *vetanānapākarma* and the others. In the section on *vikrīyāsaṃpradāna*, there is the reversal of the sold item; here, in the section on *krītvānuśaya* (rescission after buying), there is the reversal of the purchased item—this is the connection. Nor can this be included in the preceding sections, because the reversal here is distinct from the transactions involving what has been bought or sold. Now, if it is argued that since buying and selling are mutually dependent, like a pair of scales (*vīvadhakalaśa*), they ought to be treated as a single topic, that is true. However, in the statement "the period for rescission regarding a purchase is ten days," the word "purchase" (*kraya*) is indicative of both exchange (*parivṛtti*) and barter (*vinimaya*). This is because of the traditional teaching of Viṣṇu: "Barter is the exchange of two objects of the same kind, while exchange (*parivṛtti*) is that of two objects of different kinds. Nor should it be said that exchange is merely included within purchase; for in a purchase, the price is equal to the value of the goods for three years' yield, whereas in exchange, the value is exactly equal. Although it may appear that according to Gautama’s Sūtra on inheritance, purchase, and so forth, exchange and barter are not enumerated as causes of ownership, nevertheless, because the purchase of sesame seeds is prohibited and receiving them as a gift is highly censurable, it is a worldly fact that in cases where one gives sesame and receives sesame, rice, and so forth, it is precisely exchange and barter that produce ownership. As for the statement, "A pledge is lost when it becomes double [the debt]," etc., in such cases, the doubling of wealth through the exchange of sesame seeds does not produce ownership; rather, it is said that ownership is produced because it culminates in a purchase. That statement is not intended to deny that exchange produces ownership, but rather that in that specific instance, ownership is produced only because it culminates in a purchase. Elsewhere, however, in cases such as the exchange of sesame seeds, it is impossible to deny that exchange and barter produce ownership just as much as purchase and the rest—it is a worldly fact. Thus says Bhāruci.

In reality, however, it has been stated in that very same place that, by means of the technical terminology of *vinimaya* (exchange) and *parivṛtti* (barter), those two are indeed established as causes for ownership in the form of a formal gift (*vācanika-dāna*). Consequently, while in the preceding section there was the non-delivery after sale (*vikrīyāsaṃpradānatā*), here there is the rescission of a barter (*parivṛttyanuśaya*). Bhāruci, moreover, says that the designation (*samākhyā*) applies to both exchange and the rescission of a barter.

In the preceding section, the transgression regarding purchased goods and the transgression regarding exchange were discussed under the headings of *krītvānuśaya* (repentance after buying) and *parivṛttyanuśaya* (repentance after exchanging). Here, however, the transgression regarding an agreement (*samaya*) is stated under the title of the legal dispute (*vivādapada*) known as *samayānapākarma* (non-fulfillment of agreements); this is the connection. Furthermore, in the preceding section on the legal dispute titled *samayānapākarma*, the transgression of a contract (*saṃvidvyatikrama*) was treated in relation to merchants and others; this is the connection. Although it would have been more logical for these two to constitute a single topic (*aikādhikaraṇya*), they are nevertheless treated as separate topics because the former is relevant to the legal dispute concerning men and women, while the latter is relevant to the determination of houses, fields, and so forth—this should be understood. In the preceding section, disputes concerning fields were adjudicated. Fields are of two kinds: the connection here is that following the dispute concerning immovable fields, there is the adjudication of disputes concerning movable fields in the form of women. In the preceding section, the law (*dharma*) concerning men and women was expounded; here, however, in the legal dispute titled *dāyavibhāga* (partition of inheritance), the dispute proceeds specifically concerning men and women. Thus, the connection between them is one of dependence and dependency (*upajīvyopajīvakatā*). Now, the connection for the section titled *sāhasa* (violence): in the previous thirteen legal disputes, the consideration of what is to be given and what is not to be given was conducted, as Viṣṇu says: "Legal procedure (*vyavahāra*) has two origins. Two causes of legal procedure were thus stated. Likewise, Gautama’s Sūtra says: "From its two origins, it has two courses"; the word "legal procedure" is supplied from the context. Regarding this, the author of the commentary (*Nibandhanakāra*) stated: "From the beginning of *ṛṇādāna* (non-payment of debt) up to *dāyavibhāga* (partition of inheritance), the basis is 'what is to be given'; from *sāhasa* (violence) onwards, the basis is 'punishment' (*daṇḍa*). This is the meaning of "having two origins. Even though [the matter] was [treated] by Manu and others... [text ends].
Of these, the first is non-payment of debt, followed by deposit, sale without ownership, partnership,
and the non-delivery of what has been given.
Non-payment of wages, breach of contract,
rescission of purchase and sale, and disputes between owners and herdsmen;
The law concerning the division of boundaries, verbal and physical assault,
theft, violence, and the abduction of women.
Matters concerning women, partition of property, gambling, and betting—
these eighteen points the wise know to be the subjects of legal procedure.

In this manner, the sequential titles of legal procedure (*vyavahārapada*) have been stated. Among them, the division of inheritance (*dāyavibhāga*) follows immediately after verbal abuse, physical assault, and adultery. However, the author of the *Nibandhana* has stated that inheritance is the thirteenth title of dispute. There is a great contradiction between these two views, which shall now be resolved. Thus it was said by Nārada, in presenting the statements enumerating the eighteen titles of legal procedure: "Recovery of debts, deposits, and partnership... and so forth.
Taking back what has been given, refusing to show obedience, and failing to fulfill a promise;
Non-payment of wages, as well as sale without ownership,
non-delivery after having sold, and likewise rescission after having purchased;
Non-performance of agreements, disputes, and the son born of the field; the relationship between man and woman, partition of inheritance, and then violence.
"Abuse in speech, as well as assault, gambling, and betting—these are the eighteen titles of law. Thus it is said.

[53] The statement of the commentator follows the words of Nārada; therefore, it should be understood that even the statement of Gautama’s Sūtra follows the words of Nārada. It is precisely according to this that we have also explained the mutual connection between the titles of law (*vivādapada*). Consequently, the section from the non-payment of debts (*ṛṇādāna*) up to the partition of inheritance (*dāyavibhāga*) is established as being based on what is to be given (*deya*); whereas the group of five beginning with violence (*sāhasa*) is based on punishment (*daṇḍa*). To indicate this distinction in subject matter, the word "atha" (now/then) is employed in the phrase "partition of inheritance, then violence. Thus, the connection (*saṃgati*) is that the exposition of punishment follows immediately after the exposition of what is to be given. Although there is no essential difference between verbal abuse, physical assault, and violence, they are treated separately for the sake of distinguishing between light and heavy punishments, as will be explained later. In the preceding section, theft was defined. Since gambling and betting share the same nature and consequences as theft, their connection follows immediately after theft. Alternatively, another connection exists between the seventeen titles of law and the miscellaneous title (*prakīrṇaka*): previously, the imposition of punishment was stated only for the defeated party, whereas here, the imposition of punishment is stated for the victor as well; this constitutes the connection between these two.
But having seen legal proceedings wrongly decided by the king,
the members of the court, along with the assessors and the scribe, shall be fined twice the amount of the dispute.

Thus, according to Yājñavalkya, the prescription of punishment for the victor is recorded as being included within the category of legal disputes known as *prakīrṇaka* (miscellaneous matters). However, there is much that remains to be said on this point; that will be explained in its proper place. Alternatively, there is another connection: "The two-fold nature [of the lawsuit] has been illustrated in accordance with the actual facts and the pretext."

Thus, two courses for legal proceedings have been stated: following the quibble (*chala*) and following the truth (*tattva*). Among these, by following the truth, the seventeen titles of dispute (*vivādapada*) have been enumerated; by following the quibble, the title of dispute known as "miscellaneous" (*prakīrṇaka*) has been enumerated. And so, Bṛhaspati says in this context:

"In the case of the disqualification of witnesses, assessors, or litigants, there is a retrial. However, for those who have been defeated by their own words, no rule for a second trial has been declared."

In this context, the injunction "the king shall examine the legal disputes" relies solely on the pretext (*chala*) of following his own word, because the dispute is concluded by his own decree; it does not involve the search for other means of proof (*pramāṇa*), as that would cause delay, which contradicts the purpose of the injunction. Furthermore, consistency can also be asserted with the sequence in Manu’s work, beginning with "Of these, the first is the non-payment of debt," though it is not stated here for fear of excessive prolixity. This exposition of all the consistencies has indeed been thoroughly established even during the detailed explanation of each specific subject of dispute (*vivādapada*); however, since the author—desiring to make the meaning of the scripture as clear as a myrobalan fruit in the palm of one's hand and being unwilling to tolerate further bulk—has presented it here in brief, there is no tautology. A debtor must repay the loan after the minority of the son, grandson, or other heirs has passed, according to the methods such as the doubling of the time period.

A debt incurred by a father or others for the purpose of giving what should not be given, gambling, and other such despicable acts, or for maintaining a family, or for purposes other than those that are necessary, is "indebtedness not to be paid" (*adeyam*). That subject of dispute in which the rules regarding the lending of money through the taking of pledges and so forth, as well as the rules regarding the gradual receipt of large sums of wealth from merchants and others, are explained, is subsequently termed "Recovery of Debts" (*ṛṇādāna*). [An object] placed in a casket, uncounted, unnamed, and not shown.

The second head of dispute (*vivādapada*) is "Deposits in the Hand of Another" (*parahaste dattam upanidhikam*). If this very same thing is specified by its number, it is called a "Deposit" (*nikṣepa*), and thus it is not a separate head of dispute. When property is placed in another's house out of fear of heirs or fear of kings and thieves, it is called a "Consignment" (*nyāsa*); thus, it is not a distinct head of dispute. When merchants engage in trade, priests in sacrifice, farmers in agriculture, goldsmiths and others in their crafts, dancers and others in dance and the like, and thieves in theft—where they act together—the activity performed collectively is called "Joint Venture" (*saṃbhūyasamutthāna*). This is a head of dispute derived from the etymology: "that by which trade and other activities arise. Where property given to goldsmiths and others out of affection or similar motives is later to be reclaimed due to negligence or other defects, it is called "Non-delivery of What Was Given" (*dattāpradānika*), because in this case there exists the non-giving of what was given. "Non-removal of What Was Given" (*dattānapākarma*)—meaning the non-taking back of what was given due to the lack of negligence on the part of the laborer and others—is also a head of dispute; therefore, it is not mentioned separately. Consequently, the fourfold classification according to the nature of the object—as "what is to be given," "what is not to be given," "given," and "not given"—is not contradictory. "What is to be given" (*deyam*) is that which effects an unrestricted act of giving. "Given" (*dattam*) means that once the gift has occurred, it cannot be taken back from the recipient. "Given but to be taken back" refers to when a student or similar person, having agreed to service and the like, fails to perform the duties of obedience toward the teacher and others; this is the head of dispute known as "Breach of Agreement" (*abhyupetyāśuśrūṣā*). Since the word "student" (*śiṣya*) implies apprentices, hired laborers, workmen, and slaves, it is not divided separately from them; thus, it is a single head of dispute. It has been stated that for such a person something is to be given, for such a person it is not to be given, for such a person what was given may be recovered, and in some cases double the amount is to be received, and so forth. In a dispute where there is the non-removal—that is, the non-payment—of wages or hire, that is the head of dispute known as "Non-payment of Wages" (*vetanānapākarma*). When another's property, such as borrowed goods, items held for delivery, or deposits, is sold in the absence of the owner, that is "Sale Without Ownership" (*asvāmivikraya*). Because that must be adjudicated in this legal proceeding, it is called the head of dispute "Sale Without Ownership. When the merchandise being sold is not delivered to the buyer even after payment, that is "Non-delivery After Sale" (*vikrīyāsaṃpradāna*).
Merchandise is of six kinds.

Merchandise (*paṇya*) is of six kinds, categorized by calculation, weight, measurement, labor, luster, and form. *Gaṇita* (calculated) refers to coconuts and the like. *Tulita* (weighed) refers to asafoetida and the like. *Meya* (measured) refers to rice and the like. *Kriyā* (labor) refers to the work of driving, milking, and so forth, performed by cattle, buffaloes, and the like. *Kāntyā* (by luster) refers to gems and the like. *Rūpataḥ* (by form) refers to courtesans and the like. Therefore, since betel nuts and similar items are specific types of weighed merchandise, this legal subject matter (*vivādapada*) does not constitute a separate category from that [of *tulita-paṇya*]. When a buyer, having purchased merchandise for its price, later regrets the purchase without prior reflection, that is the legal subject known as "repentance after purchase" (*krītvānuśaya*). The non-abandonment—that is, the non-violation—of a compact (*samaya*) established for the purpose of forming a guild, a corporation, or an association, is "non-abandonment of compact" (*samayānapākarma*). By means of indirect indication (*lakṣaṇā*), this constitutes the legal subject called "non-abandonment of compact," just as the term "new moon" (*darśa*) indicates the sacrifice. It is another name for "violation of agreement" (*saṃvidvyatikrama*). "Pāṣaṇḍas" refers to corporations (*pūga*) and guilds (*naigama*). A "corporation" (*samūha*) is a union of Brahmins. A "vrāta" is a company of those who bear weapons. A "vratati" is a group of those bound by religious vows.

That legal matter concerning fields which involves the determination of boundaries for ploughed and unploughed plots, such as those involving irrigation channels and embankments, is termed *kṣetravivāda* (dispute over fields). It is of six kinds, distinguished by [the issues of] excess or deficiency. 1. A dispute based on excess arises when, regarding a certain plot of land, there is a contention as to whether there is more land beyond it or not. 2. One caused by deficiency occurs when, upon being told "this much land is yours," one replies, "I have this much. 3. One caused by the existence of a share arises when, upon being told "I have a share in this land," the other says "no. 4. One caused by the non-existence of a share occurs when, upon being told "you have no share here," the other says "it exists. 5. One whose seed is non-enjoyment versus enjoyment arises when, upon being told "my land is being enjoyed by you now, though it was not enjoyed before," the other replies "there was enjoyment even previously. 6. One arising from boundaries occurs when, upon being told "this is the boundary of my land," the other says "no. Therefore, since deficiency and the other categories are not distinct from that [general category], they do not constitute separate divisions based on their own specific roots.

[57] There are five types of boundary disputes (*sīmāvivāda*), because they are brought about by flags, fish, water-channels, mutual consent, or royal edicts. Therefore, the subject of dispute is divided separately according to these distinctions, beginning with "flags. "Flags" refers to a boundary marked by trees and the like. "Fish" refers to one marked by water. "Water-channels" refers to one marked by the washing away of husks and such. "Mutual consent" refers to one agreed upon by both disputing parties. "Royal edict" refers to one established by the king's will. That case where the sexual union of a man and a woman is made the subject of dispute is called the legal topic of "relations between men and women" (*strīpuṃsasaṃbandha*); it has another name, "seduction" (*strīsaṃgrahaṇa*). That case where the division of ancestral property and so forth is determined among sons and others is the legal topic named "partition of inheritance" (*dāyabhāga*). Whatever act—such as killing, theft, or violating another's wife—is committed suddenly by force by those arrogant in their strength, and is then adjudicated, that is "violence" (*sāhasa*); this is the legal topic known as violence. That speech which, by being offensive to a region, caste, family, or the like, causes extreme suffering, is the legal topic of "verbal abuse" (*vākpāruṣya*). That case where the determination of an assault on another's body—committed with hands, feet, weapons, and so forth—or an injury caused by ashes and the like is made, is the legal topic known as "physical assault" (*daṇḍapāruṣya*).

[Objection: Since the two types of harsh speech (*pāruṣya*) and sexual intercourse with a woman (*strī-saṃgrahaṇa*) are specific forms of violence (*sāhasa*), it is not appropriate to state them as separate categories. [Reply: True; however, because violence is distinguished by its reliance on force, arrogance, or deception, they are mentioned separately for the purpose of imposing a higher penalty. The title of the legal dispute known as *dyūta* (gambling) refers to that case where playing with dice and so forth, preceded by a wager, is conducted through fraudulent means. Likewise, the title of the legal dispute known by the same name refers to that case where gambling is conducted with false witnesses, preceded by a wager. There is no difference between these two, as both are rooted in playing with a wager. Thus says the *Nighaṇṭu*:
"That which is performed with inanimate objects is called 'gambling' (dyūta) in the world;
however, that which is performed with animate beings should be known as 'betting' (samāhvaya). [58]

That which must be adjudicated by the king—having adopted the role of an opponent against one who has violated his own commands and so forth—and that which was not mentioned among the previously stated titles such as non-payment of debt (*ṛṇādāna*) and the rest, is the title known as *prakīrṇaka* (miscellaneous). Furthermore, this legal procedure (*vyavahāra*), divided into eighteen sub-categories, is again of two kinds: with a wager (*sapaṇa*) and without a wager (*apaṇa*). Nārada and others, however, say it is "with a counter-claim" (*sottara*) and "without a counter-claim" (*anuttara*). In a legal proceeding where, prior to the formal writing of the plaint (*pratijñā*), a wager exceeding the fine is accepted by both parties or by one of them, that is a proceeding "with a counter-claim"; any other is "without a counter-claim. Consequently, there is no separate distinction between the categories of "with wager/without wager" and "with counter-claim/without counter-claim" mentioned by Yājñavalkya and Nārada respectively. Nevertheless, other distinctions have also been stated by Nārada and others: "It consists of having four feet, four means, four elements, four pervasions, and four functions; and it has eight limbs, eighteen titles, a hundred branches, three origins, two types of accusations, two types of disputes, and two types of outcomes."

Dharma (righteousness), vyavahāra (legal procedure), caritra (customary practice), and royal edict—these are the four feet. Therefore, legal procedure is four-footed. In this regard, each subsequent one sublates the preceding. Thus says Hārīta:
"By means of dharma, vyavahāra, caritra, and the king’s command—this legal procedure is four-footed; each subsequent one sublates the preceding."

If it is objected that the fourfold nature [of legal procedure] consists of the plaint, the reply, the investigation of evidence, and the final decision (*nirṇaya*), and not of *dharma* and the other factors, we say: not so. The "foot" consisting of the final decision is of four kinds according to the pursuit of *dharma* and the rest. In this regard, whatever final decision is made in accordance with whichever factor, it is designated by that very term. Therefore, it is entirely appropriate to describe the fourfold nature as consisting of *dharma* and the others. The "foot" called *dharma* is that in a dispute where, through a final decision rooted solely in *dharma*, the wrongdoer incurs guilt and the owner of wealth recovers his own property; that is called *dharma*. The "foot" known as judicial procedure (*vyavahāra*) is the final decision reached in accordance with the plaint and the reply as defined in the *Dharmaśāstras*. The "foot" called custom (*caritra*) is when a matter is decided by relying on local usage due to a lack of distinction between *dharma* and *adharma*; the final decision following that is likewise so called. A final decision based on other means of knowledge (*māna*) but conceived solely by the king’s will is a royal edict (*rājaśāsana*). In this context, each of these—*dharma* and the rest—is twofold. The final decision termed *dharma* is of one kind when it follows the actual truth (*tattva*); it is the second kind when it is made without following the truth, either by means of a "truth-based" reply (*tattvottara*) or by means of divine proof (*divya-pramāṇa*). Judicial procedure (*vyavahāra*) is of one kind when determined by human means of knowledge; it is the second kind when it follows immediately upon a verbal quibble (*vākchala*). Custom (*caritra*) is of one type when decided by signs such as a torch in hand; it is the second type when it follows the established stability of the region.

If that is so, then the statement "the latter sublates the former" is incorrect; for, due to its superior conformity with the true nature of reality, it is actually the former that sublates the latter. As Yājñavalkya stated: "The king should conduct legal proceedings by setting aside deception and relying on what is factual."

It is said: True, this is the general rule (*utsarga*), but it is not always the case that it is so everywhere. In certain instances, however, the subsequent [authority] indeed becomes a sublater of the preceding one. To illustrate: suppose some person, such as a member of the royal family, out of delusion has somehow committed an act such as touching the queen; having done so, he denies it due to fear for his life, and there are witnesses present. If they give false testimony, saying "he did not do it," then because the fault-perpetrator does not attain the status of being the doer, the *dharma* (the moral/legal principle) is sublated by the *vyavahāra* (the judicial proceeding). And here, the sublation of *dharma* is stated in the verse beginning, "where there is the killing of those belonging to the [caste] classes...," because of the injunction for witnesses to speak falsely. On the other hand, when someone accused says, "He has committed adultery with another's wife, and there are witnesses to this," and replies, "This is true as spoken by the witnesses; nevertheless, I am not to be punished because of the strength of my character (*caritra*). I did this, and I have recorded it on a stone slab, in a book, and so forth, by the King"—then in that case, the *vyavahāra* is sublated by *caritra*. This is because the punishment obtained through the judicial proceeding is set aside by the established character. Even *caritra* is sometimes sublated by a royal decree (*rājājñā*). For example, a custom (*caritra*) may have been established that no royal official is to enter the interior of a private residence. Then, an offense is discovered and someone enters the inner apartments. Thereupon, the King commands a certain official: "Entering even the interior of the house, that wicked man is to be brought forth. In that case, even *caritra* is sublated by the royal command. Because the suppression of the wicked must necessarily be carried out, the royal command is stronger than *caritra*. The term *catuḥsthāna* means that which has four bases: namely, truth, witnesses, written records, and royal decrees. This is what is meant: truth is the basis of *dharma*; witnesses are the basis of *vyavahāra*; written records are the basis of *caritra*; and the royal decree is the basis of the written document (*lekhya*). The mention of "witnesses" is intended to indicate the inclusion of other means of proof, such as the *dharma-śāstra* and ordeals (*divya*). *Catur-sādhana*: that in which the four means—conciliation (*sāma*) and the others—are the instruments (*sādhana*). *Catur-hita*: beneficial to the four [classes], namely the castes and stages of life (*varṇāśrama*). *Catur-vyāpī*: it pervades the four—the litigants (*kartṛ*), witnesses, court members (*sabhyāḥ*), and the king. *Catuṣ-kārī*: it produces the four—virtue (*dharma*), wealth (*artha*), fame (*yaśas*), and the affection of the world (*loka-anurāga*). *Aṣṭāṅga*: that which has eight limbs (*aṅga*): namely, the King, the royal officials, the court members, the treatises (*śāstra*), the assembly of people, the scribe, gold, and water. Their application will be explained later. The eighteen titles of law (*vyavahāra-pada*) have been explained.

*Śataśākhaḥ* (having a hundred branches)—the word "hundred" is indicative of numbers such as a thousand; that is to say, it has many branches. *Triyoniḥ* (having three sources)—it is called "three-sourced" because it proceeds from the three [defects], namely desire (*kāma*), anger (*krodha*), and greed (*lobha*), as the case may be. *Dvyabhiyogaḥ* (having two types of accusations)—he who has two types of accusation is "dvyabhiyoga. These are the accusation based on suspicion (*śaṅkābhiyoga*) and the accusation based on facts (*tattvābhiyoga*). An accusation based on suspicion arises from association with wicked people, such as gamblers, thieves, and the like. An accusation based on facts consists of a formal charge, a partial reproach, or direct observation. In some cases, a suspicion regarding a deposit or similar matter may arise even from association with virtuous people; therefore, it should be understood that "association with the wicked" is mentioned merely as an illustration. *Dvidvāraḥ* (having two doors)—there are two doors: the commencement of the action and the prior claim and the subsequent defense (*pūrvapakṣa-uttarapakṣa*) in the debate; the lawsuit in which these exist is "dvidvāra. *Dvigatiḥ* (having two courses)—he who has two courses is so called; the two courses are reality (*bhūta*) and deception (*chala*). Reality is that which is connected with the true meaning; deception is that which is joined with negligence and the like.

Hārīta has also mentioned certain divisions: it has one root, two risings, two trunks, and two fruits. Kātyāyana, however, explains them as follows: that which has one goal (*sādhya*) as its root is "one-rooted" (*ekamūla*). It has "two risings" (*dvirutthāna*): that in which there are two risings, where "dviḥ" means occurring twice; this is a compound formed according to the rule *sup-supā*. This is what is meant: it is "two-rising" because it consists of the two types of risings, namely non-payment of what is due and injury (*hiṃsā*); that is to say, it has two risings. It has "two trunks" (*dviskandha*): that which has two trunks consisting of the *Dharmaśāstra* and the *Arthaśāstra*. It has "two fruits" (*dviphala*): that which has two fruits in the form of victory and defeat. Kātyāyana has also shown another division: legal procedure (*vyavahāra*) is four-footed (*catuṣpād*) due to the division into the plaint (*pūrva-pakṣa*), the reply (*uttara-pakṣa*), the investigation (*pratyākalita*), and the stage of proof (*kriyā-pāda*). "Investigation" (*pratyākalita*) refers to the deliberation by the judge and others after the statements have been accepted, regarding which of the two litigants should be required to present evidence. The "stage of proof" (*kriyā-pāda*) is the presentation of evidence such as written documents and so forth. Since the investigation and the stage of proof also constitute part of the legal procedure—which is essentially the dispute—they are included within "legal procedure. Thus, the state of being four-footed is stated in this view, with the "investigation" (*pratyākalita*) being the third foot, as the sequence is intended here. In the opinion of those for whom "investigation" (*pratyākalita*) is the deliberation following the presentation of evidence—designed to dispel doubts regarding fallacious evidence and resulting in victory or defeat—the number alone is intended, not the sequence, because in their view the investigation constitutes the fourth foot. As it has been said:
"The first quarter is *bhāṣā* (the statement), the second is likewise *marśana* (investigation),
another is the *kriyā* (action) quarter, and the fourth is recorded as *nirṇaya* (decision).
Thus [ends the work] of the heroic and illustrious Gajapati Gauḍeśvara, Navakoṭi Karṇāṭaka Kuburigeśvara.

Composed by the great king Śrī Pratāparudradeva— the sovereign of kings, whose pure life was sanctified by his being the son of the illustrious Durgāvarman, the protector of the refuge of Huśana Sāhi Suratrāṇa, the lord of Yamunāpura, who had come for protection.
In the *Smṛtisaṅgraha*, within the *Sarasvatīvilāsa*,
in the section on judicial procedure (*vyavahārakāṇḍa*), this is the second chapter, titled "The Definition of the Nature of the Source of the Treatise."
Now begins the third chapter:
An Exposition on the Seats of Dharma.

Now, immediately after the definition of the nature of legal procedure (*vyavahāra*), legal procedure—which is divided into eighteen categories—will be defined in detail. For its utility, it is proper first to define the location where justice is administered (*dharmasthāna*). Although the location of justice should have been defined first because of the injunction for the king to observe legal procedure while stationed at that place, there is no rule that the determination of all legal procedures must occur only at the seat of justice; therefore, defining it after the definition of legal procedure is not a fault.
The Establishment of the Court of Justice (*dharmādhikaraṇa-vyavasthā*).

Alternatively, legal procedure (*vyavahāra*) was previously mentioned only in brief; now, after the exposition of the court of justice (*dharmasthāna*), legal procedure is explained in detail, so there is no fault in this. That place where the determination of the facts to be reported is carried out by judges through an investigation based on the treatises of law (*dharmaśāstra*) is called the "court of justice" (*dharmasthāna*). This very place has another name: the "judicial seat" (*dharmādhikaraṇa*). It is called the judicial seat because it is presided over (*adhikriyate*) by means of the treatises of law. And that judicial seat should be established in the eastern direction, according to the traditional teaching of Śaṅkha: "One should establish the court of justice in the eastern direction, provided with fire and water. The phrase "in the eastern direction" implies "from the royal palace. Here, one should prepare a distinguished assembly hall facing east, equipped with perfumes, garlands, incense, seats, seeds, gems, images, paintings, deities, fire, and water. Having prepared the assembly hall in this manner, the king should enter it in the morning.
Having duly honored these— his gurus, astrologers, physicians, deities, brahmins, and domestic priests— with fine flowers, ornaments, and garments as was appropriate for each;
Having paid homage to his teachers and others, he, with a cheerful countenance, should enter the assembly hall.
Thus it has been stated by Bṛhaspati.

[64] Here, the plural number in the phrase "the domestic priest and others" (*purohitādīn*) denotes the category of action alone, as in the case of the word "nooses" (*pāśān*), and not plurality itself, because the domestic priest is singular. The king, too, should enter accompanied by Brāhmaṇas; for the king desiring to see legal cases, however, [should enter] together with Brāhmaṇas.
Disciplined by ministers who are experts in counsel, he should enter the assembly hall.

This is because it was stated by Manu. The word *ca* (and) is for the purpose of indicating that [the king] should act together with the judge (*prāḍvivāka*), the royal chaplain (*purohita*), the members of the court (*sabhyas*), the ministers (*mantris*), the astrologer (*gaṇaka*), the scribe (*lekhaka*), the keeper of the legal deposits (*sādhyapāla*), gold, and the treatises on Dharma (*dharmaśāstra*). This is according to the traditional teaching (*smaraṇa*) of Gautama: "The king, endowed with the means consisting of men, members of the court, the astrologer, the scribe, gold, fire, water, the judge (*prāḍvivāka*), and so forth, shall oversee legal proceedings.
Furthermore: "He asks questions in a dispute and likewise asks counter-questions;
he speaks first with kindness—therefore he is remembered as the *prāḍvivāka* (the one who speaks before)."

He asks the plaintiff and the defendant, thus he is a *prāṭ*; he speaks specifically the decision, thus he is a *vivāka*. These are his etymological designations. The term *prāḍvivāka* is correct by virtue of belonging to the *pṛṣodarādi* group [of irregular compounds]. A Brahmin who is an expert in the eighteen titles of law, who knows their eight thousand subdivisions, who is devoted to the *Śruti* and *Smṛti*, and who is skilled in *Ānvīkṣikī* (logic) and other sciences, is the *prāḍvivāka*.
As it is said: "The king who presides with the *prāḍvivāka*, the ministers, the Brahmins, the domestic chaplain, and the members of the assembly, remains in heaven according to dharma."

The *prāḍvivāka* (judge) is one who possesses the characteristics previously described; he with whom [the king] is associated is "with the judge" (*saprāḍvivāka*). He is "with ministers" (*sāmātya*), being joined by those characterized by the marks of a minister. The characteristics of a minister are: knowledge of all scriptures, lack of greed, skill in legal discourse, wisdom, and acting according to established order.
Regarding the prohibition against a Śūdra deliberating on legal proceedings, such a person must be one of the Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, or Vaiśyas, and not a Śūdra. [65]
He who, setting aside the twice-born, should look after affairs together with the low-born (vṛṣalas),
his kingdom becomes agitated, and his army and treasury perish.

Because it has been stated thus by Vyāsa: "One should appoint members of the court for the purpose of overseeing legal proceedings. This establishes the necessity of providing a livelihood for the court members.

Just as they do not abandon their integrity in the assembly, so should he employ them through means such as the granting of wealth and honor. And these—those endowed with learning and study, knowers of dharma, speakers of truth, who are impartial toward both enemy and friend—should be appointed to the assembly. One should not appoint those ignorant of local customs, atheists, those devoid of scriptural knowledge, the insane, the cruel, or the greedy. In this regard, there should be seven, five, or even three members of the assembly. Here, the judges (*prāḍvivāka*) and others possess only dependence upon the assembly due to their seeking of wealth, like sacrificial priests; their formal authority, however, belongs to the king alone in the administration of justice, as stated at the beginning of the section. For this very reason, his primacy is indicated by the phrase "together with the judge" (*saprāḍvivākaḥ*). In this administration of justice, the authority belongs to the king—whoever he may be, whether consecrated or unconsecrated, of the Kṣatriya caste or another caste—who performs the protection of the subjects and other duties. Therefore:
"The king shall examine legal cases together with learned Brāhmaṇas," so says Yājñavalkya.
Having risen in the morning and performed purification according to the rule, the king [should proceed].
Teachers, astrologers, physicians, deities, brahmins, and family priests.
Having honored these as was fitting, adorned with fine flowers, ornaments, and garments,
and having greeted his teachers and others with a cheerful countenance, he should enter the assembly hall.

Thus says Bṛhaspati. As for the observation of legal proceedings (*vyavahāra*) by a consecrated king which was stated by Prajāpati, that is not intended as an exhaustive enumeration (*parisaṃkhyā*). Otherwise, there would be a contradiction with the statement of Yājñavalkya: "The king shall observe the legal proceedings" (YDh 1.359), and so forth. The use of the word "king" (*rājan*) applies to one who performs the duties of sovereignty in a figurative sense (*gauṇavṛtti*), as has been explained in the very section concerning the *Aveṣṭi* sacrifice. When the monarch himself does not decide a case due to being preoccupied, then he should appoint therein a Brāhmaṇa who is highly learned, capable, of noble birth, impartial, a master of the scriptures, free from agitation, steady, fearful of others, devoid of anger, and most righteous. Where no Brāhmaṇa is available, he should employ a Kṣatriya.
Or he may appoint a Vaiśya who knows the treatises on dharma, but he should take great care to avoid a Śūdra.
For that king in whose realm a Śūdra performs the discernment of dharma, his kingdom perishes like a cow in the mud while he looks on.
For the purpose of pleasing the kingdom, the king should sit in the assembly together with a few merchants;
four merchants who perceive justice should be appointed there,
as well as an accountant and a scribe.
They should be made knowledgeable in the true nature of words and their denotations, skilled in calculation, and proficient in various scripts.

Likewise, in that assembly, one should appoint an astrologer who is proficient in the three branches of knowledge consisting of *horā*, *gaṇita*, and *saṃhitā*, who produces clear evidence, and who is endowed with learning and study. The guardian of the matter (*sādhyapāla*), however, must be a *śūdra* by birth, hereditary, firm, approved by the members of the court, and the one to perform the duties such as summoning the plaintiff, the defendant, and the witnesses. When ordeals such as fire and water are to be prepared, gold, a vessel, cow-dung, and *darbha* grass should be placed there for the purpose of oaths; thus has the excellent place of adjudication been described by Manu and others.
Common grounds for legal decision.

Soldiers are the judicial authority for soldiers; forest-dwellers for forest-dwellers; caravan-traders for caravan-traders; and villages for those residing in both [towns and villages]. Because they are approved by both [parties], these are thus fixed for each respective group. There are ten types of common judicial authorities, distinguished as: the village, the city-dwellers, the guild, the corporation, the group of the four Vedas, the assembly, the family-heads, the appointed officials, and the king. A "village" (*grāma*) refers to people settled in the form of a village. "City-dwellers" (*paura*) is the collective body of those living in a city. A "guild" (*gaṇa*) is a collection of families. "Corporations" (*śreṇi*) are the eighteen low castes, beginning with the washermen. "The group of the four Vedas" (*cāturvidya*) refers to one endowed with the four branches of knowledge, such as *ānvīkṣikī* (logic/metaphysics) and so forth. By the word "and" (*ca*) in the phrase "the fourfold scholar" (*caturvidyaś ca*), the inclusion of learned men, royal officers, and others is accepted.
There is a prohibition against one person being the controller of dharma;
therefore, it should not be said that even by a single person who knows the injunctions, [dharma may be determined] according to dharma.
This is because Pitāmaha prohibited a single person from expounding dharma. "Vargins" refers to groups and the like.

"Gaṇas, groups of heretics (pāṣaṇḍapūga), corporations (vrāta), guilds (śreṇi), as well as other assemblies known by the name 'vargya'—these are called *bṛhaspati*," so says Bṛhaspati. The mention of Bṛhaspati is intended to show that this designation was already well-established for the *gaṇas* and the others. A "corporation" (*vrāta*) is an assembly of those who bear arms. "Families" (*kula*) refers to the lineages of the plaintiff and the defendant. "Family elders" (*kulika*) are certain elderly members of the lineage of the plaintiff and the defendant. "Appointed officials" (*niyukta*) are the three members of the court together with the presiding judge (*prāḍvivāka*). The "king" (*nṛpati*) is accompanied by Brahmins and others.

That court is of four kinds: unsettled (*apratiṣṭhitā*), settled (*pratiṣṭhitā*), sealed (*mudritā*), and governed by scripture (*śāstritā*). A court located in the three places beginning with the forest hermitage (*āraṇyaka*) is "unsettled," because it generally involves traveling to other regions; it is "settled" in the ten locations accepted by both disputants, as such travel is absent there. Furthermore, in a designated place, it is "sealed" when presided over by a judge (*prāḍvivāka*) who holds the seal and so forth. In the king’s location, it is "governed by scripture" because it is regulated by the treatises (*śāstra*). [68] A court in a city or village is "settled"; that which is mobile is called "unsettled."
But that which is sealed, accompanied by a supervisor, and joined with the king is indeed authorized by the treatises.

Thus says the Smṛti. The *adhyakṣa* is the judge (*prāḍvivāka*). Among these, each subsequent one possesses greater authority than the preceding. "Families, guilds, assemblies, the appointed official, and the king are the foundations of legal procedure; each succeeding one is superior to those preceding it."

Thus, from the statement of Nārada, the king’s authority is established. And therefore: "Legal proceedings that have reached the previous stage, whether based on dharma or even on adharma, resort to the king’s court and thereby uphold the original claim."

Thus the father has stated the *pūrvavāda*—meaning the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*). Here, in this assembly, the king shall sit facing the east; the members of the court (*sabhyas*), however, facing the north; the calculator (*gaṇaka*) facing the west; and the scribe (*lekhaka*) shall sit facing the south. This undertaking is for the purpose of establishing such a rule. Apart from the king, the chief justice (*prādvivāka*) and others should perform only the formal adjudication (*nirṇaya-mātra*); however, in cases of violent crime (*sāhasa-vivāda*), even the mere adjudication is not to be performed. As Bṛhaspati says: "Those families, guilds, corporations, and so forth, who have been duly appointed by the king..."
"They should carry out the legal affairs of men, avoiding acts of rashness.
Thus it is said: "The punishment of speech and the punishment of censure are both declared to depend upon the Brahmins;
the punishment of fines and the punishment of death are both declared to depend upon the king."
Thus it is stated in the Smṛti:
"The fruit of establishing the Dharma is for those possessed by the darkness of ignorance and covered by the film of doubt."
"He who rectifies the treatises with the probe of public opinion makes them free from defects;
he attains fame in this world and gains a destination in heaven. Thus [it is said].
He who, having abandoned greed, hatred, and the like, should carry out the determination of legal cases...
By means of the procedure prescribed in the scriptures, he shall obtain the fruit of that sacrifice.
But the members of the court must not overlook an action that has proceeded contrary to dharma;
by overlooking it, those kings go headlong to hell.
"O Lord of the Earth, having recognized that the king's mind has strayed from the path of justice, one must speak what is unpleasant; a member of the assembly does not thereby incur sin.
Whether out of affection, ignorance, delusion, or even greed..."
Where a member of the assembly speaks otherwise [than the truth], he is to be punished; for he is considered an unrighteous member.

"Sneha" means passion (*rāga*); "moha" means erroneous knowledge (*viparītajñāna*). Regarding this, Yogayājñavalkya states that one who speaks falsely out of passion, greed, or fear should be punished with a fine double the amount of the fine for defeat in the dispute:
"Those members of the court who act contrary to the legal tradition (*smṛti*) out of passion, greed, or even fear, shall each be punished individually with a fine double the amount of the dispute."

The meaning accepted by many commentators—that one who is defeated in a dispute shall be made to pay double the fine that was imposed—is what should be adopted; however, the interpretation of some commentators, that it should be double the value of the object under dispute, is not to be followed. Kātyāyana states that both the judge and the members of the court are to be punished even for merely conversing with the plaintiff in private before the decision of the lawsuit: "If the judge or the members of the court converse in secret with the plaintiff while the matter is not yet decided, they shall be punished, there is no doubt."
He (Yājñavalkya) himself states the punishment even after the decision has been reached, should a fault of the members of the court be subsequently discovered:
"But whatever has been lost due to a fault of the members of the court must then be paid by that member;
however, a decision already finalized for the litigants shall not be overturned. [70]
Even a decision rendered by a corrupt assembly member shall not be overturned; rather, the meaning is that one should cause the person who lost through audacity to pay the debt.
That is no assembly where there are no elders; they are no elders who do not speak according to Dharma;
that is no Dharma where there is no truth; and that is no truth which is permeated by deceit.

Free from envy and impartial toward all beings, the king, upholding the vow of Vaivasvata, shall oversee legal proceedings. Regarding the vow of Vaivasvata, Yama has said: "Just as Dharma restrains both the beloved and the hated when the time arrives, so too must the subjects be restrained by the king; for that is the vow of Yama."

Thus, according to the traditional teaching (*smaraṇa*): "The king, examining the course of legal proceedings without conflict between the *dharmaśāstra* and the *arthaśāstra*, should lead [the case]. The *dharmaśāstras* consist of the Vedas with their auxiliary limbs (*sāṅga*), the *smṛtis*, Mīmāṃsā, the Purāṇas, and the treatises on logic (*nyāyaśāstra*). The meaning is that a *smṛti* has as its subject matter matters perceived through other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Thus, following both types of scriptures is possible only when there is no mutual contradiction between them. If a contradiction should arise, then the text of Yājñavalkya applies. And so says Yājñavalkya:
"In the case of a conflict between two Smṛtis, however, the reasoning (nyāya) is stronger on account of worldly practice (vyavahāra).

This means: by virtue of a specific decision known as *vyavahāra*. The meaning is that when there is a conflict between two Smṛtis rooted in Śruti, one should understand that their respective settlement is established through the force of reasoning (*tarka*), such as the determination of the scope (*sāvakāśatva*) of each as understood from the traditional practice (*vṛddha-vyavahāra*) of the elders; this is how it must be grasped. This decision is not to be made by relying on the scripture alone, but rather by relying on the scripture as assisted by reasoning.
