"He who investigates with reasoning knows Dharma, and no other. [71]

Because of this traditional teaching (*smaraṇa*), legal proceedings must not be conducted without investigation; rather, they must be conducted only after investigation. To this effect, Pitāmaha says:
"Untruths appear like truths, and truths appear like untruths; they are seen to produce delusion. Therefore, investigation is appropriate."
For the Blessed Dharma is subtle, difficult to perceive, and difficult to discern;
therefore, one should lead the course of worldly affairs by means of direct perception.

The path of direct perception is the clear path. The means for observing legal proceedings was shown by Manu: "Just as a hunter tracks the footprints of a deer by drops of blood, so should a king track the course of *dharma* through inference."
One should discern the internal state of men by means of external signs.
Through voice, complexion, gestures, appearance, the eyes, and speech,
it is declared to have two courses, because it conforms to both reality and deception.

A legal decision may be reached by relying on conformity with reality (*bhūta*) in some cases, and by relying on conformity with artifice (*chala*) in others. However, when it is impossible to always follow reality, a decision based on evidence such as witnesses must certainly be made even by following artifice; for Gautama has stated regarding conflicting claims: "The determination [of truth] is based on witnesses. Legal procedure is thus declared to have two courses, because it follows both reality and artifice.
According to this traditional teaching (*smṛti*), even when pursuing a legal pretext, the king is not tainted by unrighteousness.
Whatever a superior person practices, whether it be righteous or unrighteous,
that is proclaimed as *caritra* (established custom), based on the local practices of the community and so forth.
[72] The settlement that has been determined by the approval of the district shall always be recorded in writing and sealed with the royal seal.
"The king, having examined it with care according to the scriptures, should reach a decision.
The sense is that a legal case (*vyavahāra*) must be decided on the basis of local custom (*caritra*).
[This applies to] those residing in districts, towns, cow-pens, cities, or villages.
"By their own rules according to the Dharmaśāstras, [one should decide] among others together with them.
And where these grounds of proof do not exist, Bṛhaspati declares that the decision shall be by the king's command:
"Where neither a document exists, nor witnesses, nor possession..."
There are no means of valid cognition; in that regard, O King, there is but one means of valid cognition.
"Those disputes which cannot be determined and whose nature is doubtful—for these, the king shall be the authority, since he is the lord of all. And:
"He should personally examine legal cases every day, surrounded by his courtiers."
The King himself—this [rule] applies to days other than the fourteenth and so forth.
For the fourteenth day, the new moon, the full moon, and likewise the eighth:
on these lunar days, the King shall not look upon matters of legal dispute.
Thus it is stated by Hārīta. On other lunar days as well, the administration of justice should take place only before the turning of the sun (āvartana).
As it is said: "That time which consists of three parts of the day following the eighth part of the first [watch] is declared in the scriptures to be the supreme period for legal proceedings."
The meaning is that one should oversee legal proceedings during this period measured by three parts.
The scribe, the accountant, the legal treatise, the bailiff, the members of the court,
gold, fire, and water— this is remembered as the eightfold constituent of the court (karaṇa).
[73] Having presided over that, he should constantly examine the cases reported by the citizens;
but the king, out of a desire for power or greed for wealth, must never himself initiate legal proceedings against men who are not disputing.
"Cases" means legal disputes.
"The king, in his own palace, shall not [decide] matters not brought forward by others out of passion, greed, anger, or even according to his own whim. Thus it is said.
Regarding this, Pitāmaha states an exception: "The king himself should take cognizance of these— words, offenses, and pretexts— even without the litigants."

The points are: reproach, destruction of crops, arson, the abduction of a maiden, the unauthorized use of a watering place, the cutting of embankments or thorns, the destruction of a grove, trespassing on fields, administering poison, committing treason against kings, breaking their seals or secret counsels, the release of prisoners, the seizure of property or fines, the giving away of gifts, arrogance, the sounding of drums and other instruments, the appropriation of ownerless property, the appropriation of property seized by the king, and the mutilation of limbs—these twenty-two points are to be known by the king; having learned of them either directly or through the words of informants, they must be investigated by the king.

The offenses, however, are: disobedience of commands, killing a woman, causing the intermixture of castes (*varṇasaṃkara*), adultery, theft, pregnancy without a husband, verbal abuse, unspeakable conduct, physical assault, and causing an abortion. These he should investigate himself, without the need for a complainant. The deceptive acts (*chala*), however, are: breaking another's [property], throwing [objects] at another, leaping over a wall, destroying watering places or dwellings, filling up moats, revealing the king's secrets, entering the inner apartments, the residence, the treasury, or the kitchen; inspecting food without authorization; the desire to discharge feces, urine, phlegm, or wind in the presence of the king; serving those hated by the king; sitting on a seat not granted; wearing gold, clothing, or ornaments; chewing betel taken by oneself; speaking without being appointed; reviling the king; wearing a single garment; being unanointed; having disheveled hair; being unwrapped [in a cloak]; having limbs decorated with various colors; wearing garlands; shaking one's lower garment; covering the head; intentness on seeking faults; associating with wicked people; looking at one's teeth, ears, or eyes; scraping the teeth; and cleaning the ears, nose, and so forth—these are the fifty deceptive acts.
Having understood the treatises, the duties of the social classes, the natures of the subjects, and the true nature of legal procedure, the king should carry out his duties.

The *prakṛtis* (dependent subjects), however, have been shown by the Grandfather [Brahmā] to include washermen, leather-workers, actors, basket-makers, fishermen, barbarians (*mlecchas*), forest-dwellers (*bhillas*), and so forth; they always stand outside the castes (*varṇas*) and stages of life (*āśramas*). Although these people are to be adjudicated solely within the legal category known as "Miscellaneous" (*prakīrṇaka*), they are mentioned here because of the context. As for legal procedure (*vyavahāra*), it consists of eighteen titles and has already been defined previously.
Placing the Dharmaśāstra before him and abiding by the opinion of the judge,
he should examine the legal cases in due order with a concentrated mind.
The meaning is "in accordance with the sequence of the plaintiff's statements.
Regarding the fourfold nature of the examination of legal proceedings:
first, the traditional source (āgama) must be established; thereafter, the subject matter of the legal proceeding (vyavahārapada).

Investigation (*vicāra*) and the final decision (*nirṇaya*): thus, the judicial process (*darśana*) is fourfold. First, the scripture (*āgama*) and the hearing of the plaintiff’s statement must be carried out. Then, that statement must be included within one of the legal titles (*pada*), such as the non-payment of debt (*ṛṇādāna*). Following that is the investigation (*vicāra*) of the plaint, the reply, and the means of proof (*pramāṇa*). Finally, there is the determination of victory based on those means of proof. Having deliberated in this manner, the king or the members of the court (*sabhyāḥ*) shall issue the final decision on the lawsuit.
Having entered the court, he should ask: "By whom? Against whom? When? For what reason? Thus he should inquire.
Thus Kātyāyana explains the *Manusmṛti*:
"At the proper time, he should question the petitioner who stands before him with a bowed head:
'What is your business? What is your grievance? Do not fear; speak, O man!'"

The question "What is the matter? is for the purpose of making known whether a gift is being withheld; and "And what is your grievance? is for the purpose of making known whether there has been violence. Thus questioned, the plaintiff should then inform him of the matter to be stated. This is the manner of questioning the complainant: "Have you been oppressed by others through a course of action contrary to the Smṛti and established custom?"
For that indeed is a matter of legal dispute which one reports to the king.

By this statement, the implied meaning is understood to be that one should personally report a wrong committed by another. The plural number in the word *paraiḥ* (by others) is merely illustrative (*upalakṣaṇa*), because we observe the singular ending in Manu’s own verse beginning with *kena* (by whom). By the word *cet* (if), it is made known that the reporting must be done by the accuser through his own volition, and not by the king's command. By the word *ādharṣitaḥ* (assaulted), those who have authority over the parties in dispute are also indicated; it does not refer to the mere agent alone. As Kātyāyana says:
"Whether commissioned by the plaintiff or even sent by the defendant,
whoever litigates on behalf of another, victory and defeat belong to those two [parties].
Thus says Pitāmaha.
If a father, brother, friend, relative, or even a kinsman should provide attendance [to a monk],
one may engage him in debate thereon.
Regarding the instruction on authorization:
"Whatever anyone may cause to be done by anyone through authorization, that is to be known as done by that very person; for it is declared to be irrevocable. Thus [it is said].
And thus it should be understood that the plaint must be filed by the claimant himself or by his agent, and not by anyone else.
As for those other than fathers, brothers, friends, or relatives who act as appointed agents, there is a penalty:
"He who is neither a brother, nor a father, nor a son, nor an appointed agent... [and so forth].
One who speaks for another's sake, speaking falsely in legal proceedings, should be punished.

Thus it is stated by Nārada. Kātyāyana, however, states a specific distinction: "Laborers, disciples, those appointed [to a task], and likewise kinsmen—these litigants shall not be punished; whoever is other than these is liable to punishment."

"The discipline for one who makes a formal accusation is as follows: otherwise, there shall be punishment. One who is armed, one without an upper garment, one with disheveled hair, one eating together [with others], or one wearing a garland while speaking with the left hand, shall incur the penalty. [77]
Therefore, the intention is that one who has become such [a judge] should not speak in this manner.
The commencement of the administration of justice:
having occupied the seat of dharma, with his limbs properly covered and his mind composed.
Having prostrated before the guardians of the world, one should begin the examination of the case.
Now follows the procedure for restraint (*āsedha*).
In this context, this refers to verbal abuse occurring immediately after the restraint. As Nārada says:
"Regarding a matter that ought to be discussed, [one who] stands still or departs from those words..."
The plaintiff shall keep the defendant under restraint until the appearance for the summons. Thus it is said.

Even when a matter is doubtful, one should restrain—meaning suppress by royal command—the litigant who disregards the petitioner’s statement that "one must proceed toward a decision while remaining impartial even regarding a doubtful point," up to the point of summoning him for the purpose of observing the legal proceedings; this is the meaning of "seeking a decision in a dispute. This restraint (*āsedha*) is fourfold, distinguished by its application to place, time, travel, and activity. Restraint of place (*sthānāsedha*) is the prohibition: "You must not move from your current location, such as your home or a temple. Restraint of time (*kālakṛta*) is of the following kind: "On the fifth day and so forth, you must present your true nature; otherwise, you shall have transgressed the royal command. Restraint of travel (*pravāsāsedha*) is the prevention of departure. Restraint of activity (*karmāsedha*) is the prevention of religious merit, such as pilgrimage and the like. However, in cases such as the inspection of evidence or the restraint of the senses, because of the difficulty involved, a transgression of the royal command does not incur fault. Furthermore, one who is under restraint shall not be guilty of an offense if he departs during river crossings, wildernesses, difficult terrains, or times of calamity. Nārada says that one who restrains someone who should not be restrained becomes liable to punishment.
"He who violates a seizure that has been effected at the time of seizure, or he who acts otherwise on that day, shall be liable to punishment as the one who carried out the seizure. Thus it is said.
Furthermore, those who are not subject to seizure have been declared by Kātyāyana:

Those mounted on elephants, horses, chariots, boats, trees, or mountains; those in difficult circumstances; those afflicted by disease, those in distress, and those engaged in sacrifices; as well as those occupied with other tasks—these should not be obstructed at that time. However, the intoxicated, the insane, and the mentally deficient are never to be obstructed. Farmers [should not be obstructed] during the sowing season, and soldiers during the time of military mobilization. One who has set a specific time [for a transaction] is not to be obstructed in the interim. Herdsmen are exempt while herding their cattle for the purpose of breeding, and artisans during their working hours. A minor (*aprāptavyavahāra*) is one who has not yet reached sixteen years of age. "One in difficult circumstances" refers to one whose entire property has been plundered by thieves or the like. Regarding "soldiers," the phrase "when near battle" is to be understood as the ellipsis.

Thus [the one] whose most holy life is that of the son of Śrī-Durgāvarpu, the King of Kings and Supreme Lord (Rājādhirāja-Rājaparameśvara), who is the hero, the illustrious Gajapati, the Lord of Gauḍa, the Lord of Navakoṭi-Karṇāṭaka-Kulbarige, the Sovereign of Yamunāpura, the protector of the refuge of Huśanasāhi-Suratrāṇa—
In the *Sarasvatīvilāsa*, a compendium of law (*smṛtisaṅgraha*) composed by the illustrious Great King Pratāparudra Mahādeva,
within the section on legal procedure (*vyavahārakāṇḍa*), this is the chapter titled "The Determination of Procedural Duties" (*itikartavyatānirūpaṇa*).
The Third Chapter;
now begins the Fourth Chapter:
The Duty of the Determiner.
When the litigant thus utters insults immediately after the issuance of the summons (*āsedhakaraṇa*), Nārada states what the judge must do next:
"Then one should inscribe all those words upon a wooden board or similar surface.
Gobhila also says the same.
Whatever one declares when provoked by passion or other such emotions,
all of that should be written as "om" by the petitioner on the wooden board or other surfaces.

The grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is: "that which one might say through any one [of the passions] such as attachment, aversion, greed, or delusion. Regarding the instrument (*karaṇe*): "in the presence of the king. Subsequently, having deliberated upon that statement together with the Brahmins who serve as court members (*sabhyas*), if it is found to be just, the *sādhyapāla*—a royal official—should summon the defendant. This is what is meant: if what is written on a wooden board or similar surface were not fit for investigation—such as "In another birth, I gave this wealth to him, but he does not return it"—then the *sādhyapāla* should be dispatched to summon the opposing party (*pratyarthī*). A *sādhyapāla* is a royal official authorized by the king and approved by the court members to summon both the plaintiff (*arthin*) and the defendant. The mention of the *sādhyapāla* is intended to indicate the royal seal, as Bṛhaspati has said: [The *sādhyapāla* is the one who carries out the king's command.]
"Against whomsoever he makes a charge, whether based on truth or even out of suspicion, the king shall cause that very person to be summoned by means of a seal or by a messenger.
Here, "summoning" (*ākāraṇa*) means calling forth; the intention is that such a person alone has the authority to provide an answer. Thus it was stated by Kātyāyana:
[80] “The right belongs to one who is engaged, not to another, because of the lack of connection.

This is its meaning: for another who is not engaged, there is no right to provide a reply in this dispute due to the absence of a relevant connection. He states that the status of being a respondent for another is threefold: those entitled to the reply...
The other is also considered one who has been made a defendant by the plaintiff;

he is another person who, having been presented by the claimant before the court of justice, is to be known as the respondent (*prativādī*), as well as this one who has submitted himself [to the case]. Thus it is said.

The meaning is as follows: even another person, though unrelated to the dispute, may be made an opponent (*pratirodhī*) by the plaintiff—that is, made a defendant (*prativādī*)—according to Manu and others; this is the ellipsis. "Another" means a second defendant. A "third," though unrelated to the dispute, may be presented by the plaintiff before the judge (*dharmādhikārin*, *prāḍvivāka*), or one who has been accepted by the claimant himself as a defendant. This status of being a defendant for those who lack legal capacity (*anadhikārin*) should be understood as applying to cases involving the incapacitated (*akalya*) and so forth, because it is extremely difficult for those with legal capacity (*adhikārin*) to act as direct parties in such circumstances. Here, "incapacitated" refers to a sick person; by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the unskilled, the dull-witted, the insane, the elderly, women, and children are intended.
The substitution of those who are indisposed and so forth is by virtue of their being appointed.

For this very reason, Hārīta stated: "It is improper to summon those who are indisposed, children, the elderly, those in a state of distress, those preoccupied with ritual acts, those burdened by family affairs, those overcome by calamities, those addicted to vices, those occupied with royal business, those distracted by festivals, the intoxicated, the insane, the heedless, the afflicted, and servants. The term *akalya* (indisposed) has been explained. *Viṣamastha* means one who has encountered a crisis. *Kriyākula* means one who is busy with obligatory and occasional rites (*nitya-naimittika-karma*). As for one who is coming...

[81] One who neglects a more important duty is "one who fails in his obligation" (*kāryātipātī*). "One in distress" (*vyasanī*) is one who possesses suffering (*duḥkha*) arising from misfortune, such as separation from what has been lost. "Intoxicated" (*matta*) is one whose intellect is impaired by intoxicating substances such as honey-wine. "Insane" (*unmatta*) is one [afflicted] by planetary influences, bile disorders, and so forth. "Negligent" (*pramatta*) is one devoid of all attentiveness. "Afflicted" (*ārta*) is one pained by sensual objects and the like. The mention of "servants" is intended to include women who lack independence. Consequently, the rule for appointing a substitute (*pratinidhi*) is established only for those who are unfit due to illness and similar conditions. In a case involving a grave accusation (*mahābhiyoga*), all persons are fit to be summoned.

But when the accomplishment of the legal business cannot be achieved through a substitute sent by one who is ill or otherwise incapacitated, then even those who are ill and so forth must be summoned; for in cases of serious charges (*mahābhiyoga*), the summoning of the accused himself is mandatory. Serious charges consist of: homicide, theft, adultery, and drinking forbidden liquors. Even in cases of indecent speech (*asabhyavāda*), those who are ill and so forth must indeed be summoned. Indecent speech includes: eating forbidden food, violating a maiden, verbal abuse, forgery, treason against the king, and the like. In these matters, no substitute is permitted. On this point, Vyāsa says:
"He who commits violence or does not give what is due to one who begs for it, because of his wickedness, shall be dragged away by order of the king. Thus,
if one summoned fails to appear, he shall receive a punishment corresponding to the charge.
Bṛhaspati states the punishment for one who does not come by the king’s command:

"If one who has been summoned does not come out of pride, even though supported by the strength of his kinsmen, the king shall determine his punishment in accordance with the nature of the legal claim. Thus it is said.
In the case of a minor offense, the fine shall be fifty; for a middling offense, it shall be at least one hundred;
and for serious matters, the punishment shall always be at least five hundred.
This is to be calculated in *kārṣāpaṇas*.
Whatever punishment has been prescribed for a particular offense according to one's capacity,
there shall be the collection of fines in paṇas, or else its equivalent value, to be paid to the king.

Thus it was said by Kātyāyana. By the statement "according to his capacity," no punishment is to be prescribed in the case of a calamity; rather, upon recovery, he should be summoned again. And if that [recovery] is genuine, well and good; but if it is not genuine, then, having punished him, the king should subsequently cause him to proceed according to justice.
One who is to be reinstated must be established with effort; otherwise, he would be subject to punishment. Having punished him, the king should thereafter cause him to proceed according to justice.

Thus, by whatever means possible, the plaintiff shall cause the defendant—who has been summoned—to stand before the court or in another location where he cannot conceal his physical characteristics. Once he is stationed there, the accused, when questioned by the king, shall report the facts of the charge against him. Since it is impossible to investigate the truth based solely on the plaintiff’s report, the procedure for examination follows after both parties have been determined to be speaking deceptively; therefore, it should be understood that the defendant also possesses the knowledge of the facts.
Regarding the taking of sureties for both the plaintiff and the defendant:
"A capable surety should be taken from both parties who is able to settle the matter of the case.

Based on this traditional teaching of Yājñavalkya, the meaning is that after the determination of whether the arguments of the two litigants involve fallacies (*chala*), the judge should take a surety from both the plaintiff and the defendant—one who is capable of easily securing the fulfillment of the matter of the case, namely the delivery of the proven debt and the payment of the fine.

In this matter of acting as a surety (*pratibhūkarma*), certain individuals are prohibited from serving in that capacity: enemies, masters, their officials, those under arrest, those punished, those in a state of uncertainty, empty-handed friends, lifelong residents (*atyantavāsī*), those engaged in royal service, renunciants (*pravrajita*), those incapable of giving wealth, and those who are unknown. Those "in a state of uncertainty" include the accused (*abhiśasta*). "Lifelong residents" refers to perpetual celibates (*naiṣṭhika-brahmacārin*). "Renunciants" refers to those who have taken up the life of renunciation (*saṃnyāsin*). Regarding one who is unable to provide a surety, Kātyāyana says: "Now, if there is no surety for either of two litigants..."

"Having protected him until the end of the day, he should give the messenger his wages. Here, "messenger" (dūta) refers to the guardian of the defendant; "wages" (vetana) refers to the salary. Two caravans mean twenty million [paṇas]. Having accepted this, the plaintiff should be made to proceed according to justice. This is the sequence for the complainants and others to present their respective cases.
Kātyāyana has stated the manner of speech for the plaintiff and the others:
"The plaintiff shall speak first, and the defendant immediately thereafter;
when both have spoken, the members of the assembly [shall deliberate], and after that, the presiding judge. Thus it is said.
"One should speak first" means that one should make the formal proposition (*pratijñā*). He states an exception to the rule that "the plaintiff is the one who speaks first":
"To whomsoever the suffering is greater, or for whom the wrongful act is more serious, to him the right to speak as the plaintiff must be granted, even if he did not present his case first."

The meaning is that prior notification is not a determining factor. The plaintiff's statement constitutes the *pūrvapakṣa* (the prima facie case). Where both parties simultaneously desire to be the plaintiff due to a difference in their respective objectives, the rule of Bṛhaspati applies: "When both the plaintiff and the defendant vie with one another to be first, the lawsuit shall be accepted according to the order of the social classes (*varṇa*), or by considering the degree of suffering."
It should be understood that the consideration of injury to the object of perception applies only when two witnesses of equal status are present.
However, when several pairs of witnesses appear simultaneously, Manu states:
"Having ascertained both the benefit and the harm, as well as the merit and demerit alone..."
He should oversee all the affairs of litigants according to their caste and stage of life.

The stabilization of the meaning of the plaint has been explained; only that which is the *sādhya* (the matter to be proved) should be written down, not something other than the *sādhya*. Yājñavalkya states the correct principle that it is not the case that everything exactly as it was announced must be written: "The plaintiff shall write before the defendant exactly as it was announced."
For this very reason, Yājñavalkya says:
"Marked by the year, month, half-month, day, name, caste, and so forth.

Having read the text as *yad āveditam* ("that which was stated"), the author of the *Candrikā* explained it as *yat sādhyam* ("that which is to be proven"). Vijñānayogin, however, reads it as *yathāveditam* ("as it was stated") and explains: "In whatever manner (*yathā*)—by whichever means—it was stated at the time of the initial deposition, in that same way and not otherwise; for if one were to state it otherwise, there would be the consequence of defeat (*bhaṅga*)."

"One who speaks otherwise, one who hates the performance [of the legal act], one who does not appear, one who is unable to provide an answer, and one who absents himself after being summoned— these five are recorded as those who have lost their case."

Since the plaintiff’s statement has already been recorded at the time of the formal plea (*āvedana*), writing it again would be redundant; therefore, he says "the year, month," and so forth. Vijñāneśvara, explaining by treating the suffix *-thāl* in *yathā* as expressing a manner, intends that while everything written at the time of the plea should indeed be written down, only the *sādhya* (the point to be proved) must be recorded. This is because of the example given regarding the speech of another party (*anyavādin*). Being a "party of another" (*anyavāditva*) means accepting a different point to be proved after abandoning one's own original *sādhya*. Thus, there is merely a difference in the method of explanation between Vijñāneśvara and Yogīndrācārya, the author of the *Candrikā*, and not a difference in the meaning itself; one may accept whichever one prefers. By the word "etc. (*ādi*), the substance, its quantity, place, time, capacity, gender, and so forth are included.
The procedure for drafting a petition:
It should be meaningful, consistent with the Dharma, complete, and unconfused;
it should contain words that state the point to be proven and be connected to the subject matter at hand.
The method of proof should be well-known, non-contradictory,
certain, concise, coherent in meaning, and consistent with place and time.
It is characterized by the year, season, month, fortnight, day, time, location, and entry;
as well as by place, dwelling, the name of the person to be accomplished, caste, physical form, and age.
It was marked with the number of the means of proof for the case to be established, as well as the names of himself, his adversaries,
his ancestors, and many other kings.
"That which one reports to the king—characterized by patience, an embrace, self-inflicted pain, or what is taken away and given back—is called *bhāṣā*. Thus it is said.

* Bhāṣā*, *pratijñā*, and *pakṣa* are synonymous. Although specifications such as the year are not required in all legal proceedings (*vyavahāra*), there is no fault here because they are useful for reaching a decision in matters of mortgages, gifts, and purchases. *Arthavat* means purposeful. *Dharmasaṃyuktam* means endowed with qualities such as being concise in syllables and well-composed. *Paripūrṇam* means not requiring ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*). *Anākulam* means having unambiguous syllables. *Sādhyavat* means not lacking the matter intended to be proved. *Vācakapadam* means free from figurative or secondary meanings (*gauṇa-lakṣaṇā*). *Prakṛtārthānubandhi* means not contradicting the matter previously stated. *Prasiddham* means concerning a subject matter well-known in the world. *Aviruddham* refers to that which is not contradicted by the city, the kingdom, the judge, the king, and so forth; likewise, it refers to that which is not internally inconsistent, not contradicted by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) such as perception (*pratyakṣa*), and not contrary to the conventional law (*vyāvahārika-dharma*). *Niścitam* means free from confusion with other matters. *Sādhanakṣamam* means fit for proof. *Saṃkṣiptam* means not overly prolix. *Nikhilārtham* means containing everything that ought to be said without omission. *Deśakālāvirodhi* means not contradicting place and time—for example, a betel-nut plantation in the Middle Country (*madhyadeśa*), or "a thousand mangoes were stolen in the autumn"—being free from such contradictions. *Śiṣṭam* (the remainder) has a clear meaning.
The specific requirements for drafting a document concerning immovable property are as follows:
caste, name, and residence; the dimensions and the name of the field;
its paternal and ancestral lineage; and the mention of previous kings.
In disputes concerning immovable property, one should present these ten [means of proof].

Thus it is from the traditional law (smṛti). Location, place, and so forth, are applicable only in the case of immovable property. "Neighbors" (adhivāsa) refers to people living in the vicinity. "Measure" (pramāṇa) refers to the dimensions such as those of a *gocarma* (cow-hide area) and so on. "Name of the field" (*kṣetranāma*) is for the sake of clarity, specifying the particular field such as one for rice and so forth. This is what is meant: the purport of Yājñavalkya’s statement is that in whatever legal proceeding the year, month, and so forth are relevant, they should be written down to that extent. Hārīta also says: "A seat, a bed, a vehicle, [an object] made of bell-metal, copper, or iron..."
Grain, stone-made objects, clothing, bipeds, and quadrupeds.
If there should be a collection of substances such as gems, pearls, and the like, diamonds, silver, and gold, then the number must be calculated in that very same manner.

"In whatever region and with whatever measure a quantity is measured, by that [measure] and in that [region], that number must be established by those engaged in worldly transactions. The meaning is that the number should be determined after having measured with that specific measure.
[87] Regarding the legal procedure for non-acceptance,
Kātyāyana, however, has stated a specific distinction.
A plaint that is devoid of place and time, lacking in substance and number,
and deficient in action and proof, is considered unacceptable.

The meaning is this: wherever something is required, that very thing should be written down there. In its absence, because one would be unable to accomplish the goal to be proven (*sādhya*), a thesis (*pakṣa*) devoid of utility is simply not to be accepted. The measure of action (*kriyāpramāṇa*) is the measure of what is to be proven; since it would be devoid of purpose, a thesis lacking even the [proper] definition is indeed to be rejected. This is because of the traditional rule: "Unestablished, unassailable, useless, purposeless, impossible to prove, and contradictory—these are fallacious theses (*pakṣābhāsa*). The author of the *Candrikā* explains this. As the author of the *Candrikā* says: "Among those, the 'unestablished' (*aprasiddha*) has been defined by Bṛhaspati."
That which has not been recorded by anyone is known as *aprasiddha* (unestablished).

An example of this is: "A palm tree made of a thousand *palas* was seized. *Nirābādha* means free from disturbance; for example: "This person is conducting his business in his own house by the light of the lamp in our house. *Nirarthaka* (meaningless) and *niṣprayojana* (purposeless), however, were shown by Bṛhaspati: "That which has a slight fault or a slight purpose is known as *nirarthaka*."
But that which is devoid of both a purpose and a sublation of its effect should be known as useless.

A "pointless" (nirarthaka) plaint is one that is not included within the eighteen titles of law, such as non-payment of debt, and is accompanied by matters like verbal abuse which are useless for establishing the proof of the claim; this is the meaning. By that same [definition], the "unprovable" (asādhya) and the "contradictory" (viruddha) are also shown:
"He must give me a bow made from the horn of a hare."
The wise say that a position which is impossible and unachievable is not to be pursued.
"When that side which has been stated is found to be contrary to the city or the kingdom before the judge or the king, it is called 'contrary' (viruddha).

However, Vijñānayogin has explained it differently; having stated the definition of a "pseudo-side" (pakṣābhāsa) as "those things which appear to be sides but are devoid of the characteristics of a side," he says:
One should avoid a fallacious thesis (pakṣābhāsa) that is unestablished, free from contradiction, devoid of meaning, purposeless, impossible to prove, or contradictory.

Having thus stated the specific characteristics (*viśeṣalakṣaṇa*), they have been explained. As for the method of explanation, as the Vijñānayogin said: "Unestablished" (*aprasiddha*) is, for example, saying, "He does not give me my hare's horn," and so forth. "Unassailable" (*nirābādha*) is, for example, saying, "By the light of the lamp in our house, he conducts his affairs in his own home," and so forth. This example is common to both. "Meaningless" (*nirarthaka*) is that which lacks a denotable object, such as *kacaṭatapam* or *gajaḍadabam*, and so forth. "Purposeless" (*niṣprayojana*) is, for example, saying, "This Devadatta recited aloud in the vicinity of our house," and so forth. Both of these are common [to the two]. "Impossible to prove" (*asādhya*) is, for example, saying, "I was laughed at by Devadatta with a frown," and so forth. "Contradictory" (*viruddha*) is, for example, saying, "I am cursed by him," and so forth; or it may be contradictory to the Purāṇas and other authorities. The author of the *Candrikā* has treated the example of the impossible as an example of the meaningless. A statement of little significance is not a fault according to the tradition of the meaningless; here, the example of the impossible has been treated as an example of the impossible.

"There must be given to me by him a bow made of hare-horn"—because of such a statement, there is no fault. Thus, the fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*) have been explained by Vijñānayogin with reference to worldly convention. However, the author of the *Candrikā* has explained them in accordance with the literal wording; this is the extent of the difference. These [cases], such as "Devadatta laughed with a frown" and so forth, are non-provable (*asādhya*) because it is impossible for them to serve as means of proof. Because the time was short, witnesses are not possible. A written document is out of the question due to its insignificance, and an ordeal (*divya*) is likewise excluded because of the triviality of the matter.

However, other defects of the plaint (*bhāṣā-doṣa*) have been shown by Nārada and others; all of these should also be understood as being included within the characteristics of a "pseudo-plaint" (*pakṣābhāsa*), though they are not elaborated upon here for fear of excessive prolixity. For this very reason, the Lord of Yogins (Yājñavalkya) did not mention pseudo-plaints separately, since their status as pseudo-plaints—appearing as a plaint while lacking the true characteristics of a plaint—is already established. Nevertheless, it should be understood that he has stated them merely by way of illustration. As for what was stated by Pitāmaha:
"A plaint consisting of multiple confused points is not successful."

Thus, if the word *pada* here were to denote a "substantive object" (*vastu*), then there would be no fault; for [otherwise] there would be no such thing as "my gold, clothing, silver coins, and so forth have been stolen by him. Furthermore, if the word *pada* here denotes a "place" (*sthāna*), and it is argued that there would be an absence of a legal "plaint" (*pakṣa*) due to the confusion of various grounds for litigation such as non-payment of debt (*ṛṇādāna*) and the like, that too is not the case. For it is precisely what is intended that "my silver coin was taken by him on interest," "gold was deposited in his hand," and "he is seizing my field," and so on, constitute a plaint. However, due to the difference in the actions involved, the legal proceedings occur sequentially and not simultaneously—this is all that is meant.
Even a case involving many assertions that has been settled in legal proceedings,
the king may, if he desires, take it up again out of a wish to discover the truth.

Thus, according to the traditional teaching of Kātyāyana, the meaning of the statement is that a plaint (*pūrvapakṣa*) consisting of multiple confused points cannot be established simultaneously. The word "ground" (*bhūmi*) is indicative of the fruit-stand and other such items.

[90] Those who know the plaint recognize it as being free from defects of the proposition (*pratijñā*), containing the matter to be proven (*sādhya*), accompanied by valid reasons (*satkāraṇa*), recorded in writing, and established in common worldly usage.

"Established in the world" (*lokasiddham*) means not contradicted by conventional dharma and well-known in the world; since such a meaning is already covered by the phrase "free from defects of the thesis" (*pratijñādoṣanirmuktam*), [it need not be stated separately]. The fourfold nature of the legal charge (*abhiyoga*) is that this side (*pakṣa*) is fourfold, consisting of: a charge based on suspicion (*śaṅkābhiyoga*), a charge based on reality (*tathyalabdhābhyarthana*), and a charge based on renewed legal procedure (*punarnyāya*).
One should examine the plaintiff's claim until the defendant's reply is seen;
whatever was not stated by the plaintiff, whether through delusion or deceit,
should be accepted from both parties if it is included within the defendant's reply.
"Included within the reply" (uttarāntargata) means that which is stated by the plaintiff while the reply is being given. Bṛhaspati, however, states a specific rule:
"When the accuser, due to lack of confidence, does not venture to speak, time should be granted to him in accordance with his capacity for the task. Thus it is said.
Then, regarding the respondent: Bṛhaspati states that when the plaintiff's case has been thus determined, the reply must be given:
"When the plaintiff's case has been fully determined and distinguished as to what is admissible and what is inadmissible..."
Once the plaint has been established and made firm, one should then cause the reply to be written.

"The characteristics of a superior rejoinder are that it is pervasive, essential, free from doubt, unconfused, and not requiring further explanation; the wise know a rejoinder to be such. Thus [it is said].

[91] Regarding the phrase "not to be understood through explanation," this refers to [an expression] that is either difficult to construe due to the use of well-known conventional usage, or because of the employment of awkward case-endings, compounds, or ellipses, or because of the use of a non-standard dialect (*adeśabhāṣā*). The remainder is easy to understand. The author of the *Saṃgraha* also states:

"That which has no other purpose, whose meaning is not divided, which is endowed with both logic (*nyāya*) and scripture (*āgama*), which is neither deficient nor redundant, which is free from corruption, and in which no other syllables could possibly occur."
"Regarding the statement 'in the language [of the plaint],' this means immediately after it has been written down on the documents;
this is the time for the defendant, having heard the matter, to provide his answer."

The meaning is that this refers to the deposition being written down in such a way that it possesses characteristics such as having no other purpose. Furthermore, this restriction of time applies only to disputes concerning cattle and the like:
"In cases involving cattle, land, gold, theft, verbal abuse, urgent matters, acts of violence, and false accusations, one should litigate immediately."

An *abhiśāpa* (imprecation) is the pronouncement of a death sentence. Although it is a form of verbal abuse (*pāruṣya*), it is mentioned again out of respect for its gravity. Yājñavalkya also says: "In cases of violence, theft, verbal abuse, imprecation, the loss of cattle, or matters concerning women, one should seek a legal decision immediately; in other cases, the time is prescribed according to one's own wish."
The meaning is: "except in cases such as the non-payment of debts.
Regarding loans, deposits, pledges, gifts, joint undertakings, agreements, and the partition of inheritance, the time [for litigation] must be observed with diligence.

*Samayaḥ*—the removal of the time-limit. This is the meaning: in cases that have arisen immediately, one should litigate immediately; in cases where time has elapsed, one should grant a period of time. For this very reason, Pitāmaha says:
“In cases that have arisen immediately, one should litigate immediately;
or in cases where time has elapsed, the lord (the judge) should grant a period of time to the defendant.”
The term "respondent" (*pratyarthī*) is also indicative of the "plaintiff" (*arthin*). As Nārada has said:
"If the mind of one who wishes to speak in a dispute does not find the courage, then time must be granted to both the plaintiff and the respondent."
He himself states the measure of time:
"In cases such as debts and the like, it shall be immediate, one day, five days, three days, a month, three fortnights, or seven days, depending on the gravity or lightness [of the matter]."

Kātyāyana, however, states a specific rule: "The king, having considered whatever local custom has been handed down through successive tradition, should cause a reply to be given according to justice."
The sub-divisions of the *uttara* (rejoinder) and their characteristics:

this *uttara* is of four kinds, namely *mithyā* (denial), *saṃpratipatti* (admission), *pratyavaskandana* (counter-attack), and *pūrvanyāya* (prior judgment). Kātyāyana states the definition of *mithyā*:
"If one who is accused should deny the accusation..."
"But one should recognize that as false on account of the subsequent legal proceeding.
That "false" (mithyā) plea, moreover, is of four kinds:
"This is false," "I do not know [it]," "At that time I was not present there," and so forth.
And "I was unborn at that time"—these four types [of views] are false.
He himself states the definition of the reply of admission (*saṃpratipatti*):

"The statement of truth regarding the matter to be proven is declared to be admission" (verse 93). An example for both is as follows: when it is said, "He owes me a hundred pieces of gold," the response "I truly owe it" is admission; "I do not owe it" is a falsehood. That which is called "counter-attack" (*pratyavaskandana*) refers to what was received back after being taken, or obtained through a formal gift. As Nārada says:

"That matter which has been written by the plaintiff, and likewise that which has been stated by the defendant—if one should state a reason after having accepted it, that is known as *pratyavaskandana* (counter-pleading).

As for the *prāṅnyāya* (prior judgment), however, it is where the very person who is being accused says: "I was accused of this matter, and in that case, I was defeated according to the course of legal procedure. As it was stated by Hārīta:
Regarding this matter, I previously had a dispute with him;
if he should then say, "I was defeated," that subsequent statement would constitute a prior judgment.
The northern appearances.

Thus, since the definition of a valid rejoinder (*uttara*) has been established, it follows by implication that those which lack the characteristics of a valid rejoinder, yet appear as such, possess the nature of a pseudo-rejoinder (*uttarābhāsa*). Consequently, this was not explicitly stated by the Lord of Yogins (*Yogīśvara*) and others because it is clearly established [by them]. Nevertheless, for the sake of providing clear examples from other traditional works (*smṛtis*), a mere indication is cited here: Pseudo-rejoinders (*uttarābhāsas*) are those that possess faults such as being unestablished (*aprasiddha*), contradictory (*viruddha*), too little (*atyalpa*), too much (*atibhūri*), doubtful (*saṃdigdha*), improbable (*asaṃbhāvya*), unclear (*avyakta*), having another meaning (*anyārtha*), or being excessively defective (*atidoṣavat*); as well as those that are non-pervasive (*avyāpaka*), with inverted words (*vyatyastapada*), with hidden meaning (*nigūḍhārtha*), confused (*ākulavyākhyāgamya*), or lacking essence (*asāra*). Furthermore, that which is spoken by one ignorant of the marks, parts, configuration, number, or conventions [of a script] is "unestablished" (*aprasiddha*), as is that which is spoken in a regional dialect (*adeśabhāṣā*).

"I returned it in my youth; indeed, I did not return it"—this kind of statement, which is contradictory in its preceding and following parts, is what is meant by a "contradictory reply" (*viruddhottara*). Furthermore, when one ought to say, "This was previously requested by me," saying merely, "This was previously by me," and omitting "that," is an "insufficient" reply. When one ought to give a truthful reply consisting of the mere fact that "it was received," stating instead, "He performed that act for me, but I received it long ago," is an "excessive" reply. And when one ought to say, "It must be given by me," saying instead, "It is to be given by me," is likewise [an excessive reply].
"Likewise, in legal proceedings, the wise should recognize that an answer which is ambiguous is [considered] inadmissible."

In the case of "it must be given by me," because of the ambiguity arising from the pun on the vowel *ā* (which can mean both "by me" and "not"), one understands "it is not to be given"; thus, such a response is indeed "doubtful. A reply of the form "the property to be given by us was already given by our great-grandson's grandson" is "impossible. An "unclear" response, however, is one that cannot be easily articulated. That which ends up being merely a recounting of the plaintiff’s bad conduct is "for another purpose. "Exaggerated" is like saying "two hundred" when "one hundred is to be given," or saying "I gave him a thousand along with myself" when it was said "a thousand was given to him."
Half of that which was returned is considered here to be non-pervasive.
As long as the plaintiff has not properly set forth his case,
it is said that he has not stated his claim with its constituent parts arranged in order.
The meaning is that a reply such as "false" (*mithyā*) and so forth, given before the determination of the plaintiff's case, is called a "disjointed word" (*vyastapada*). [Objection:
Would anyone fail to give a lotus (*tāmarasa*) simply because it has not been grasped?
[Response: However, that reply is to be understood as having a hidden meaning (*nigūḍhārtha*) through the threefold judicial procedure (*tryavahārataḥ*).

Because the term *tāmarasa* is not established through universal usage; and because it possesses "crooked speech" (*vakrokti*) and so forth, the meaning is that it is "obscure" (*nigūḍhārtha*). It is "confused in meaning" (*ākulārtha*), like a sentence containing many unrelated word-meanings, such as: "What should always be given by him? Should it be given by me? and so forth. "Accessible only through commentary" (*vyākhyāgamya*) means it is difficult to understand by its own nature. It is "worthless" (*asāravat*), meaning it is purposeless, like an answer concerning the existence of a crow's teeth. It is "incoherent" (*anuttara*), meaning one speaks untruths or falsehoods in a single language while providing many other [irrelevant] replies, as Nārada said:
That which is true in one part of the thesis, but is a reason in another part,
and is false in yet another part, is not a valid rejoinder because of its inconsistency.
The logical reason "because of confusion" (*saṃkarāt*) is employed to indicate that the higher [proof] occurs when there is a confusion of the [lower] ones, and not otherwise.
Furthermore: "In a single legal dispute, there cannot be a means of proof for both parties;
nor can there be establishment for both, nor can there be two means of proof in one [case]."

Thus, according to the statement of Kātyāyana: "In the case of a confusion between *mithyā* (denial) and *kāraṇa* (justification), the burden of proof (*kriyā*) falls upon both the plaintiff and the defendant," because of the traditional legal maxim: "The burden of proof lies with the plaintiff in the case of *mithyā*, and with the defendant in the case of *kāraṇa*. Both of these [burdens] are contradictory in a single lawsuit, as for example: when the charge is, "He took from me a hundred *rūpakas* and gold," the defense is, "The hundred *rūpakas* were not taken, but the gold was taken and has been returned. However, in the case of a confusion between *kāraṇa* and *prāṅnyāya* (prior judgment), the two burdens of proof fall upon the defendant alone.
"In a plea of prior judgment (*prāṅnyāya*) or a plea of confession (*pratyavaskanda*), the defendant shall point out the means of proof (*kriyā*)."

For example: "Gold was returned, but he was defeated in a transaction involving one hundred *rūpakas*. In this case, the prior judgment (*prāṅnyāya*) must be established by means of the decree of victory (*jayapatra*) or by those who witnessed the prior judgment. However, in the case of a plea based on a legal reason (*kāraṇottara*), it must be established by witnesses, scribes, and so forth; thus there is no contradiction. This should be understood to apply likewise when there is a mixture of the three types of replies. For instance, when there is a formal charge that "he took gold, one hundred *rūpakas*, and clothes," and the defendant says: "It is true that gold was taken, which I shall return; however, the hundred *rūpakas* were not taken, and regarding the goods, I was previously defeated according to the prior judgment. The same applies to a mixture of four types of pleas. As for these [pleas], they cannot be considered valid replies simultaneously because each specific constituent part cannot be established without its respective [corresponding evidence]; rather, they constitute replies only in sequence. What is meant is this: where, moreover, a single, unmixed reply is in no way obtainable, there, out of necessity, one should treat each part as a reply and accept a reply for each individual claim in succession. Otherwise, there would be a lack of final determination (*nirṇaya*) in that case. For this very reason it is said: "Because of the mixture, that [reply] is invalid. Once the objection regarding the mixture has been refuted according to the stated method, the reply will indeed be valid; such is the challenge. In a case of mixture, the legal proceeding should first be conducted by adopting the procedure (*kriyā*) pertaining to whichever [part] covers the most extensive subject matter, and afterwards by adopting the procedure for the reply concerning the minor subject matter. Where there is a mixture of a plea of admission (*saṃpratipatti*) and another type of reply, the legal proceeding should be viewed as being conducted by adopting the other reply, since there is an absence of formal procedure (*kriyā*) in a plea of admission. Hārīta, however, states:
If both a false plea and a plea based on a special cause should occur in one case,
or if a true plea occurs along with another [ground], which plea should be accepted therein?
Having said this:
"That answer which concerns a vast subject matter, or wherein the fruit of the action resides, should be known as the *uttara*; otherwise, it is not distinct."
Thus it has been stated.

The implication is that otherwise, the case becomes confused. For this very reason, Nārada says regarding a situation involving multiple defenses that pervade the entire claim: "Whether there be both a denial (*mithyā*) and a plea for a specific cause (*kāraṇa*), the plea based on the cause (*kāraṇottara*) is to be accepted."

This is because the reason (*kāraṇa*) is not otherwise established; the intention is that it is more serious than a falsehood (*mithyā*). Therefore, even when there is a conjunction with another subsequent [reason], the heavier one must be accepted. This is because, in this statement, both the falsehood and the reason serve merely as examples. Furthermore, where the plaintiff and defendant belong to the three higher castes (*traivarṇika*), the legal proceeding must be decided in accordance with the sequence of the castes, taking into account their relative gravity. Thus says Hārīta:

"Where there is a confusion of castes among those belonging to the [four] castes, the legal proceeding shall be decided according to the order beginning with the Brāhmaṇa, taking into account their relative gravity."

With respect to social rank (*gaurava*), the sequence begins with the Brāhmaṇa and so forth. In a dispute between a Brāhmaṇa and a Kṣatriya, the matter to be proven (*sādhya*) may be smaller for the Brāhmaṇa and larger for the Kṣatriya; nevertheless, the meaning of the rule is that the smaller matter to be proven must be accepted out of regard for the dignity of the caste. However, where there is a *saṃkara* (confusion) of replies and they possess equal force—such that the aforementioned reason for the sequence does not apply—even there the reply should be accepted according to the defendant’s preference, because a decision is mandatory. For instance, in a *saṃkara* of *prāṅnyāya* (prior judgment), when witnesses and other evidence capable of proving both are available in documents such as a decree of victory (*jayapatra*), the meaning of the word "according to preference" (*yathāruci*) is that the defendant must stand by one side in the legal decision, and not by both. Similarly, in the *Candrikā*, regarding the *saṃkara* of *pratyavaskanda* (denial) and *prāṅnyāya*, the meaning of the phrase "let the defendant stand according to his preference" (*yathāruci sthīyatām*) should be understood in this same way. Now, if it is argued that *saṃpratipatti* (admission) cannot be a valid reply because it lacks the capacity to refute the plaintiff's claim (*pakṣopamardakatva*), do not say so. Even in the case of admission, since the claim presented as something to be proven (*sādhya*) is shown to be already established, its status as a "matter to be proven" is removed, and thus it constitutes a valid reply. But then, in the case of a *kāraṇamithyottara* (a denial based on a specific cause), the aforementioned logic applies. Suppose one says, pointing directly at the object: "This cow is mine; it was lost at such-and-such a time, but it has been seen in his house. Another, however, says: "That is false; she was already staying in my house before the time he indicated, and she was even born there. This is certainly not a non-reply, as it is capable of refuting the claim. Nor is it a mere *mithyā* (simple denial), because a specific cause (*kāraṇa*) is adduced. Nor is it a pure *kāraṇa* (affirmative plea), because there is no admission of any part of the claim. Therefore, this is a *sakāraṇamithyottara*. In this case, the burden of proof (*kriyā*) lies with the defendant, according to the rule: "In the case of a *kāraṇa*, the burden is on the defendant. Now, why is the burden not on the plaintiff, according to the rule: "In a *mithyā*, the burden is on the first party"? Because that rule refers only to a pure *mithyā* plea, which is not the subject here. If it is asked why the rule "when the defendant pleads *kāraṇa*" does not refer to a pure *kāraṇa* plea, do not say so; for every *kāraṇa* reply is essentially accompanied by a *mithyā* element, and a purely pure *kāraṇa* reply does not exist. In a well-known *kāraṇa* plea, since one part of the asserted matter is admitted, there is a *mithyā* element regarding the other part. For example: "It is true that I received a hundred coins, but I do not owe them because they were given back. Here, there is an admission of one part. But in the present example, there is no admission of even a single part of the asserted matter; this is the distinction. Thus defined, the reply must be provided by the defendant of his own accord.
In that case, the defendant’s reply, following from the application [of the charge],
should be presented after extracting its essential meaning and being free from any designation of faults.

Thus says the Smṛti: "But when one gives [the answer] oneself, and the time for giving the subsequent answer has passed, then— 'When the defendant does not give the answer according to the facts during the first half of the month, he should be made to pay it by means of conciliation and other such methods.'"
"He should be made to pay by the king"—this is the ellipsis [to be supplied].

For it is stated in the Smṛti: "One should give a reply according to the facts; then the king should cause that to be paid. The seven means, beginning with conciliation (*sāma*), have already been explained at the very beginning of this section. Regarding that which cannot be accomplished even by these means, Hārīta says:
But he who, though being urged by various means, does not give an answer, is considered defeated once seven nights have passed; he ought to pay the debt.
Thus concludes the description of the nature of the reply (*uttara*).

Now, following the description of the reply, the method for describing the means of proof (*pramāṇa*) is described: when the written statement of the reply has been thus entered, since the establishment of the thesis depends upon the means of proof, Yājñavalkya [proceeds] in response to the expectation as to who should provide the exposition of those means of proof.
Then the plaintiff should immediately have a document drawn up to prove the matter he has asserted.

Then—immediately after [the defendant's reply], the claimant (*arthin*), who possesses the matter to be proved (*sādhya*), should have it written down "immediately" (*sadyaḥ*), that is, without delay. Regarding the phrase "the matter to be proved": that which is to be established is the *sādhya*; the means by which it is established is the *sādhana*, i.e., the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). By the rule "the claimant should have the proof of the matter asserted written down," since it is the plea of prior judgment (*prāṅnyāya*) alone that constitutes the *sādhya*, it follows that only the plaintiff (*kāraṇavādin*) is the *arthin*, and thus he alone should have it written down. In the case of a plea of denial (*mithyottara*), it has been stated that the plaintiff himself is the *arthin* and he alone should point out the proof; this is the intended meaning. By the inclusion of the term *arthin*, however, in the case of a plea of admission (*saṃpratipattyuttara*), because there is no *sādhya* (matter to be proved), neither of the two—the proponent of the plaint nor the proponent of the reply—is a *arthin*. Consequently, there is no pointing out of proof at all, and it is understood from this alone that the legal proceeding (*vyavahāra*) is concluded. For this very reason, Hārīta says:

"But when a plea of prior judgment or a plea of a legal cause has been stated, the defendant shall point out the proof; however, when there is a plea of denial (*mithyā*), the plaintiff shall do so, but it shall not be so in the case of a plea of admission (*pratipatti*). Thus ends the section on admission. Regarding this, Kātyāyana states a specific rule:
When both have submitted their statements and the determination of the case has begun, he who speaks what is improper therein shall be deprived of that object and his assistance.

[100] For by this very statement, it is understood that in disputes arising from anger, if one speaks with negligence, one is deprived even of the matter at hand. Just as when, at the time of filing a complaint, one declares, "I was struck on the head by him with his foot," but at the time of the trial says, "I was struck by him with his hand or his foot," one is not only punished but is indeed defeated. Regarding this matter, Yājñavalkya gave instruction solely for the purpose of avoiding negligence by both the plaintiff and the defendant.

"Without having fully resolved the charge, one should not bring a counter-charge against him. Here, "charge" (*abhiyoga*) refers to an offense; that is, without having fully resolved—that is, without having cleared—that charge, one should not bring a counter-charge against the accuser, nor should one join him with an offense. Although this counter-charge is of the nature of a rebuttal (*pratyavaskandana*), nevertheless, because its purpose is to subvert the opponent's own charge, it is not subject to the prohibition. This was stated with reference to the defendant (*pratyarthin*); the same author says the following regarding the plaintiff (*arthin*):

"One should not bring forward what has been contested by another, nor what has been stated, nor what has been altered. This means that one plaintiff should not bring a suit against someone who has already been sued and whose case has not yet been resolved. Furthermore, one should not present as "altered"—that is, as having a contradictory nature—whatever was stated at the time of the formal claim (*vedana*). What is meant is this: whatever matter was reported in a certain form at the time of the claim must be written down exactly in that same way at the time of the trial;
it must not be otherwise. Now, [one might ask]:
That which has been stated by the plaintiff in the presence of the defendant shall be committed to writing.

Regarding this, the following has been stated: why then is it said again, "One should not lead a case that has been altered from what was stated" [101]? It is replied: by the rule "as informed by the plaintiff," whatever matter was presented at the time of the formal complaint (*āvedana*) must be written down at the time of the plea (*bhāṣā*) as well. It is stated that in this stage, no other matter [than that previously declared] is permitted. For example, having established at the time of the complaint that "he took a hundred coins (*rūpaka*) on interest," one must not say at the time of the plea in the presence of the defendant, "I took a hundred items (*vastu*) on interest. If that were the case, then even upon moving to another point of the case, because one would have moved to a different matter, the plaintiff would be liable for punishment as a loser of his suit. However, where one states at the time of the complaint, "Having taken a hundred coins on interest, he does not give them back," but then at the time of the plea says, "He forcibly seized a hundred coins," then that constitutes a movement to another point of the case such as an act of violence (*sāhasa*); since this is already covered by the rule "one should not lead a case that has been altered from what was stated," there would be redundancy. This very point has been clarified by Nārada.
"He who, having abandoned his previous argument, takes recourse to another again,
should be known as a person of inferior speech because of his shifting of positions.
Regarding this, he himself states an exception:

"But one may bring a counter-charge in cases of quarrels and acts of violence"—the remainder of the sense is "when a counter-offense is possible. "In quarrels" means in both types of verbal and physical abuse.
There are five kinds of litigants who speak falsely.
Nārada, however, states that there are five kinds of "defeated" litigants:

"One who speaks otherwise, one who hates the legal procedure, one who does not appear, one who fails to provide an answer, and one who absents himself after being summoned— these are recorded as the five types of the defeated."
One who speaks otherwise—that is, one who speaks differently—thus describes the characteristic of the inferior:
"He who, having abandoned his previous position, again takes up another, should be known as an inferior speaker because of his shifting of words; such indeed is that man."

[102] Thus. *Padasaṃkramaṇa* (shifting the ground): having abandoned one of the grounds such as non-payment of debt (*ṛṇādāna*) and so forth, and after first adopting another ground, making the formal statement. And so Kātyāyana says: "If, after having had his case heard, he should abandon it and state something else—that plaintiff has shifted to another ground; therefore, he is defeated."
Having charged another with a matter stated according to the rules of procedure, one should speak;
and if he should speak falsely, one should likewise designate him as defeated.
But a litigant who, having caused a statement to be written, subsequently asserts it to be either deficient or excessive, shall suffer defeat; he does not deserve to maintain his suit.
*Abhiyoga* means the plaint; the meaning is that one who is deficient [in merit] is not entitled to make it.
He states the definition of one who is deficient due to aversion toward the *kriyā*:
"The wise should know that the *kriyā* consists of both the members of the court (*sabhyas*) and the witnesses."
"He who, out of delusion, hates that ritual act is called a hater of rituals. Thus [it is said].
He states the definition of one who does not attend:
"By not attending after being summoned, he is immediately excluded. Thus.

The meaning is that if he does not appear immediately after being summoned, he becomes defeated at that very moment. He defines defeat by way of being unable to provide an answer: "When told 'Speak!', if he does not speak, he deserves immediate imprisonment;
on the second day, one should know that the defeat of that evil-minded man has occurred."

Defeat (*parājaya*) means inferiority (*hīnatā*). However, one who absconds after being summoned (*āhūtavyapavāyī*) is one who, having understood the summons for the purpose of avoiding the legal charge, acts in concealment. Now, it has been stated that "the defeated party (*hīna*) is recorded as being of five kinds" in order to demonstrate that each subsequent one among these is more severely inferior; it is not, however, for the purpose of restriction—that there are only five kinds of defeat—since other varieties are also recorded in tradition. [103] The sequential punishment for the five types of defeated litigants serves to demonstrate the gravity of their respective defeats, which in turn demonstrates the proportionality of their increasing penalties. And so it was said by Kātyāyana:
One who speaks otherwise shall pay five *paṇas*; one who hates the legal proceeding, ten *paṇas*;
one who does not appear, twelve *paṇas*; and one who fails to provide an answer, sixteen *paṇas*.
But one who, having been summoned, absconds, shall be made to pay a fine of twenty *paṇas*.
A different kind of defeated party has been shown by that same author:
"He who, among those for whom the legal proceedings have been announced, should subvert even one [point]."
One should also entice the disputant; when he has been so enticed, one should declare him defeated.
If he causes fear, or division, or intimidation, or obstruction,
he loses his case in the legal proceeding.

The meaning is that by whichever disputant all or some of the factors such as fear are employed during the legal proceeding (*arthavyavahāra*), he is "glorified" (*mahīyate*). As for "terrifying" (*bhīṣaṇam*), this refers to the production of fear through another means; thus, there is no tautology.
After three fortnights, the one who speaks weakly is defeated;
regarding this, Nārada states a specific rule: "By fleeing after three fortnights, or by remaining silent for seven days,"
"One who is contradicted by witnesses is defeated at that very moment, even if he has previously admitted [the claim].
Regarding the specific case of a division among witnesses, the same author says:
"But he who, having designated witnesses, does not litigate with them..."

After thirty nights or three fortnights, his downfall occurs; [104] the word "intentionally" is to be understood as the ellipsis. But if unintentional, then: "In the case of a formal act of censure, having performed the divine rite and determined the period of attendance..."
When no one is present, one should not employ deception therein.
The performance of customary conduct is the determination of legal procedure. In that regard, a distinction has been shown:
"The wise know that the restoration of one who is defeated by the statement of another is possible;
however, for one who is divided from his own statement, no restoration exists."
Manu also says:
"The internal mind is grasped through outward forms, gestures, gait, activity, speech, and changes in the eyes and face."
The word "corrupt" (*duṣṭam*) is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence].
As for the types of treaties (*sandhiprakāra*),
Bṛhaspati, however, has described the various kinds of treaties.
But when the prior and subsequent accounts have been written down regarding the matter at hand,
there may be a reconciliation between the two heated parties, like that of two iron balls.
In that case, there may be a disagreement between both the witnesses and the members of the court;
being discerning, they should effect a reconciliation between the two parties who are wavering.
"Wherever a distinction between the treatise and practice is recognized as authoritative,
there a reconciliation of both is praised by royal decree.
This means that those two wise men should effect a reconciliation before one of the disputants suffers defeat in private.
Regarding the duty of the court when neither party accepts the reconciliation, Bṛhaspati says:
"When it has been properly examined and recorded, and the defendant's reply is found to be faultless..."
Whether it be a defendant or a plaintiff, legal action is held to depend upon proof.

The meaning is that the defendant or the plaintiff should prepare a written statement of evidence (*pramāṇalekhana*) for the sake of establishing the point to be proven (*sādhyasiddhi*). Regarding this very matter, the author of the *Candrikā* and others call it "investigation" (*pratyākalanam*). When the question arises as to what constitutes that evidence, Yājñavalkya says:
"Evidence is declared to be documents, possession, and witnesses;
in the absence of any one of these, any one of the divine ordeals (*divya*) is prescribed. Thus it is said.
Nārada also says: "Worldly and divine means of proof have been declared; however, judicial procedure is said to be of two kinds: human and likewise divine."
Human evidence is said to consist of documents and witnesses, while divine evidence is considered to be the balance-scale and other such ordeals.

The mention of "writing" and "witnesses" is also an elliptical indication for "possession," since possession likewise does not differ from the others in its connection with human agency. The ordeals such as the balance and so forth have been shown by Bṛhaspati:
"The balance, fire, water, poison, and the fifth is the sacred libation (kośa);
rice is declared the sixth, and the heated gold-piece the seventh."
The eighth is said to be the ploughshare, and the ninth is that born of Dharma;
all these divine [weapons] have been pointed out by the Self-Existent One.
The oaths were shown by him as follows:
"Truth, vehicles, weapons, cattle, seeds, and gold; the deities, the feet of the ancestors, and meritorious deeds that have been given."
By the word "and" (*ca*), other acts such as touching the head of a son are also included. [106] These are the varieties of oaths.
"The Seven Sages, as well as Indra and the others, whose wealth is their asceticism, swore an oath with undistracted minds for the sake of the Puṣkara [dispute], for the sake of mutual purification.
Although even those who do not swear may be designated by the term *divya* (ordeals), [this refers specifically to those who do].
"Since they were employed by the wise gods for the sake of the *puṣkara* [lotus] ordeal, and for the sake of mutual purification, they are therefore called 'twofold' (*dviyāni*) by name.
Nevertheless, some maintain that the term "divine" (*divya*) applies to heavy ordeals and "oath" (*śapatha*) to light ones; but that is not correct.
When the performance of legal duties is conducted by the sun (during the day) in villages and cities,
and when witnesses are available, divine means of proof are not to be employed.
In the absence of all human evidence, the decision must be made by divine means alone;
however, when witnesses are available, a wise man should avoid recourse to divine proof.
Since these statements present the divine and human oaths as being of a single syntactical unity, and because it is likewise well-known in the world, however—
oaths corresponding to the nature of the matter are prescribed, such as those involving truth, a balance, and so forth,
in cases where no witness is found among men litigating.
Then one should examine him by means of divine ordeals and various kinds of oaths.

Thus, the distinction between divine and human ordeals mentioned here is not intended to describe their difference per se, but rather to demonstrate that human ordeals are generally applicable in cases involving minor offenses; this is how it should be understood. Kātyāyana and others, however, state:
"If there exists a human ordeal that pervades even a single part [of the proof], that should be accepted by men speaking [in court], and not a divine one, even if it is complete. [107]

When human evidence is available for one part [of the case], the qualification for that part is established by the principle of partial proof (*ekadeśavibhāvitanyāya*). Alternatively, the intention is that the matter may be decided even by a minor oath. If one party should state a human means of proof while the other states a divine one, the king should accept the human means there, and not the divine procedure.
"Where even a very slight human means of proof exists, one should not postulate a divine one.
Therefore, the general rule is that when human means are entirely unavailable, a divine one is used. He himself states an exception to this in certain cases:
"In cases involving violent acts, verbal abuse, or physical assault..."
In matters arising from force, there shall be either witnesses or divine proof.
He (Yājñavalkya) himself states the specific rules regarding the non-payment of debt and other matters:
"In cases of debt and the like, documentary evidence, witnesses, or even a trace of circumstantial proof,
as well as divine ordeals, have been declared as means of proof for subjects out of a desire for their welfare."
In all disputes concerning matters of fact, the lord of men should always reach a decision by means of authoritative evidence, logical reasoning, or even divine proof.
"A written document, witnesses, and possession are remembered as the threefold means of proof;
the wise know inference to be the logical reason, as well as reasoning (tarka).

Thus, the intended meaning is that when a matter is not established by visible means of proof, one must resort to invisible means of proof, and not otherwise. Regarding this, Bṛhaspati states an exception in certain cases:
In the first or the third [stage], the evidence is divine or human; but in the fourth and subsequent stages, there shall be the testimony of witnesses and the document of victory.

Among the four types of replies—*mithyā* (denial), *saṃpratipatti* (admission), *avaskandana* (confession with a counter-claim), and *prāṅnyāya* (prior judgment)—in the first (*mithyā*), in the third (*kāraṇa*), and in the fourth (*prāṅnyāya*), the means of proof (*kriyā*) may be either divine (*daivikī*) or human (*mānuṣī*). In the case of the fourth, the *prāṅnyāya* reply, the decision is reached by relying on either witnesses or a document of victory; that is the literal meaning of "the introduction of divine proof" (*divyāvatāra*). In the case of *saṃpratipatti*, since there is no matter to be proven in the plaint or the reply, this legal proceeding consists of only two parts. Such is the decision regarding a two-part proceeding; and so says Kātyāyana: [The text continues with the verse: "Where the defendant admits the claim, there is no need for witnesses or documents; the judge should immediately pronounce a verdict of victory for the plaintiff. This concludes the section on the determination of the two-part proceeding.
In cases of false testimony, in a counter-attack, and in a plea of prior judgment, that [judgment] is known to have four feet; in cases of admission, it has two feet.

Because there is no instruction regarding the performance of an act in the case of *saṃpratipatti* (admission), legal procedure (*vyavahāra*) is concluded at the very end of the answer. And thus, the intended meaning is that in the cases of *mithyā* (denial) and *kāraṇa* (justification), the ordeal may be either human or divine; however, in the case of *prāṅnyāya* (prior judgment), it must be human, while in the case of *satya* (truthful admission), it never occurs.
