The meaning is that one should act so as to make [the matter] clear, without suspecting any defect in the witnesses. The intention is that witnesses who have been proven to be defective should be excluded [from testimony], but they are not to be punished. As it is said:
"Whether by the defendant or by the plaintiff, when proving a defect in the witnesses, there shall be no separate lawsuit against the witnesses; rather, it is a distinct legal proceeding. [145]

The intention is that the determination of disputes regarding the defects of evidence must be made within the context of the original legal proceeding itself. Nor should it be argued that this is improper because it is unsuitable to decide another legal matter in the midst of a proceeding; for since the determination of disputes over the defects of evidence is a supplement to the original suit, it must be performed right there. Furthermore, because there is no separate result, it does not constitute a distinct legal proceeding. Yājñavalkya states that victory belongs to whichever litigant—plaintiff or defendant—whose witnesses have declared the statement of what was to be proven to be true. This is the result concerning witnesses.
"He whose witnesses declare his claim to be true shall be the victor. So says Bṛhaspati as well:
"Where the matter of the claim is found faultless by the witnesses [having testified accordingly]..."
The *pratijñā* (proposition) is the statement of that which is to be proven (*sādhya*). Yājñavalkya states that for one whose proposition witnesses have declared to be false, there is defeat:
"For him who speaks otherwise [than the truth], defeat is certain.
In certain cases, however, false testimony is permitted.

Now, if it be argued that in the statement of Yājñavalkya—“In a case where the death of those belonging to the [social] orders would result from testimony, one should speak untruth therein”—it is understood that because the members of the orders achieve victory through the witness’s false statement, it is not thereby restricted that victory must come only through speaking the truth; then [we reply]:

It is not so; for since speaking untruth is enjoined therein, there is no fault because of the expiation (*prāyaścitta*). Nor should it be said that speaking untruth is not enjoined here; for in the second half-verse [146], it is recorded as an expiation for the removal of the evil produced by speaking untruth: "To purify that, a *caru* offering to Sarasvatī is to be prepared by the twice-born.
If it is argued that, since speaking untruth is thus enjoined, an expiation for it is inappropriate, [we reply:]...

It is said: here, the opinion of Vijñānayogin (on YDh 2.83cd) is that, by accepting the two halves of the verse—the latter and the former—as a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatā*), the *sārasvata* oblation (*caru*) should be performed according to the meaning of the latter half for the purpose of removing the evil produced by speaking untruth. However, the opinion of Bhagavatpāda is that the *sārasvata* [oblation] is like the *kṣāmavatī* sacrifice; the meaning is this: for the sake of purifying that [sin], for the sake of purification, and for the sake of protecting the guilty—up to this point it is one sentence. Where there is the killing of those belonging to the [social] orders (*varṇin*), there one may speak false testimony for the sake of purifying that [act]; therefore, because it is a sacrifice on account of a specific occasion (*naimittika-kratu*), the *sārasvata* oblation is occasional. Regarding its being occasional, the commentator (*ṭīkākāra*) explains by supplying the word "otherwise" (*anyathā*), so that the phrase "for the sake of purifying that" (*tatpāvanāya*) would not be construed [with the preceding]. The meaning is this: having spoken the truth, the *sārasvata* oblation is occasional. Nor should it be said that once the killing of a living being has occurred after speaking the truth, the *sārasvata* oblation is merely an expiation (*prāyaścitta*) to remove that [sin]. This is because speaking untruth is prescribed [by the text], and the traditional law (*smṛti*) records expiation only for the performance of what is prescribed. On this point, some read and explain this statement differently: "it is offered for the sake of protecting the truth" (*tatvāvanāya nirvāpyate*). "For the sake of protecting the truth" means for the sake of preserving the truth. Even in this case of untruth, the *sārasvata* oblation is indeed occasional. The meaning of "for the sake of protecting the truth" (*tatvāvanāya*) is the protection (*avana*) or preservation of the truth. The intention is that at such a time, the truth will be accomplished only through the speaking of untruth. The dative case is used here simply to denote the action itself (*kriyāgrahaṇamātre*). In a case where some witnesses state the facts truly and others falsely, Manu says: [Manu 8.104: *yatrānṛtena mokṣaḥ syāt satyena caiva bandhanam | anṛtaṃ tatra vaktavyaṃ satyād dhi gurukaṃ bhavet ||* "Where there might be release through untruth and bondage through truth, there untruth should be spoken, for untruth is heavier than truth. [Manu 8.105: *vāgduṣṭaṃ caiva pāpiṣṭhaṃ yaś ca syāt prāṇighātakaḥ | tāv ubhau pataṃtau hi satyānṛte kṣipej jale ||* "The one who speaks wickedly and the most sinful, and he who is a slayer of living beings—these two, falling, one into truth and the other into untruth, he should cast into water. [Manu 8.106: *varaṃ kūpaśatād vāpī varaṃ vāpīśatāt kratuḥ | varaṃ kratuśatāt putraḥ satyam putraśatād varam ||* "A pond is better than a hundred wells; a sacrifice is better than a hundred ponds; a son is better than a hundred sacrifices; truth is better than a hundred sons. [Manu 8.107: *satyena pūyate brahma kṣatraṃ rājanyabandhavaḥ | vaiśyā mānuṣyāḥ śūdrāś ca satyenaivābhipūyante ||* "Brahman is purified by truth; the Kṣatriyas and their kinsmen, the Vaiśyas, and the human Śūdras are likewise purified by truth alone. [Manu 8.108: *satyasyaiva hi loke 'smin sarvaṃ pratiṣṭhitam | tasmāt satyaparaḥ syādd hi yadīcchet paramāṃ gatim ||* "For everything in this world is established upon truth; therefore, one should be devoted to truth if one desires the highest goal. [Manu 8.109: *na svargyaṃ nāpavargyaṃ vā nālaṃ dāsyāya karhicit | yac chilaṃ satyavacane na tac chakyaṃ kadācana ||* "That which is established in the speaking of truth is neither conducive to heaven nor to liberation, nor is it fit for servitude at any time. [Manu 8.110: *na hy asatyād adhikaṃ pāpaṃ na satyād dharmam uttamam | ubhau satyānṛte tyaktvā yac chīlaṃ tan mahāphalam ||* "For there is no sin greater than untruth, and no higher dharma than truth; having abandoned both truth and untruth, that conduct which remains bears great fruit. [Manu 8.111: *anṛtaṃ tu vaded yas tu sākṣye rājani saṃsthitaḥ | sa kṛtvā pāpam apy urvyāṃ naivāsmāl lokād dhīyate ||* "But he who, standing before the king, speaks untruth in testimony, even though he has committed a sin upon the earth, he is not excluded from this world [of merit]. [Manu 8.112: *anṛtaṃ tu vaded yas tu sākṣye rājani saṃsthitaḥ | sa mṛto narakaṃ yāti tiryagyoniṃ ca gacchati ||* "But he who, standing before the king, speaks untruth in testimony, he goes to hell when dead and enters the womb of an animal. [Manu 8.113: *anṛtaṃ tu vaded yas tu sākṣye rājani saṃsthitaḥ | sa jīvann eva śūdratvam āśu gacchati sānvayaḥ ||* "But he who, standing before the king, speaks untruth in testimony, he quickly attains the status of a Śūdra while still alive, along with his lineage. [Manu 8.114: *anṛtaṃ tu vaded yas tu sākṣye rājani saṃsthitaḥ | tasya niṣkṛtir uddiṣṭā dhīmatā manunā svayam ||* "But for him who, standing before the king, speaks untruth in testimony, an expiation has been ordained by the wise Manu himself: [Manu 8.115: *brāhmaṇo daṇḍam arhati rājanyaḥ sāhasaṃ param | vaiśyo 'pi madhyamaṃ daṇḍaṃ śūdro jīvitam eva ca ||* "A Brāhmaṇa deserves a fine; a Kṣatriya, the highest amercement; a Vaiśya, the middle fine; and a Śūdra, even his very life. [Manu 8.116: *anṛtaṃ tu vaded yas tu sākṣye rājani saṃsthitaḥ | tasya daṇḍo vidhātavyaḥ svayaṃ rājñā yathāvidhi ||* "But for him who, standing before the king, speaks untruth in testimony, a punishment must be imposed by the king himself according to the rule. [Manu 8.117: *anṛtaṃ tu vaded yas tu sāk

In the case of a conflict between two sets of witnesses, the king should accept the majority; when the numbers are equal, he should accept those superior in qualities; and when there is a conflict regarding their qualities, he should accept the best among the twice-born. [147]
Nārada also says:
"In the case of a conflict between witnesses, the majority is the authority;
when they are equal in number, those who are pure should be accepted; but when they are equally pure, those who are more pure should be accepted."
"Where a dispute is seen to arise due to similarity between the witnesses,
one should set aside the point to be proven because of the subtlety of the property to be established. Thus,
the witnesses must state exactly what they have seen, neither more nor less.

Kātyāyana says that one must not make [the testimony] less or more than what was asked. When the categories of facts have been specified and the witness has arrived for the trial, if he does not speak in accordance with the syllables [of the questions], that shall not be considered properly stated.

Regarding testimony—when the testimony has been delivered—[the witness must speak] in accordance with the syllables, meaning in conformity with the letters, that is to say, regarding the matter asked. The meaning is that what does not convey the matter asked is "meaningless" (*apārtha*). Likewise, one should not state anything less than or more than what was asked.
Where witnesses declare a matter that is either deficient or excessive, that too should be known as improper. This is the determination regarding witnesses.

Regarding the signs of a false witness, Viṣṇu states: "One should recognize a false witness by a change from his natural state, a loss of color in the face, and incoherent speech. Yājñavalkya describes this alteration of the natural state:
"He moves from one place to another and licks the corners of his mouth."
The forehead of one whose face becomes pale and breaks into a sweat [is a sign of approaching death].
"He is declared to be corrupt in a legal proceeding or as a witness.
[148] This refers to the punishment for a false witness who knows [the truth] but does not speak it.
For that lowest of men who does not give testimony even though he knows [the facts],
is indeed equal to false witnesses in both his sin and his punishment.

He who, although knowing the matter at hand to be perverted, refuses to give testimony out of malice, saying "I am not a witness in this case," should be punished like a false witness; the meaning is that he is equally sinful. Bṛhaspati, however, states a specific rule: "A witness who, being summoned and free from illness, does not come, shall be made to pay the debt and a fine after three fortnights have passed."
And so Manu says:
"If a man fails to give testimony regarding a debt or other matters within three fortnights,
he shall be liable for that entire debt and a fine of one-tenth in every case."
*Agada* means healthy. By the term *daśabandha*, the tenth part is expressed; that fine is to be taken by the king. As for the statement:
"The king must not cause delay in the testimony of witnesses;
at the proper time, a great fault characterized by the obstruction of dharma may arise."
Thus, that [rule] concerns the subject of clear witnesses. Therefore, Kātyāyana says:
"The time for witnesses is to be known as being when the facts have been fully ascertained through evidence;
however, when a document or witnesses are doubtful, one should litigate immediately if they are clear. Thus it is said.
Yājñavalkya, however, states a specific rule regarding false witnesses:
"The punishment for a false witness shall be inflicted individually; likewise, the one who fabricates the falsehood and the witnesses themselves shall be punished."
"The Brāhmaṇa is declared to be banished, his fine being double that of the dispute.

[149] This is its meaning: those who, by means of withholding wealth and so forth, act fraudulently—that is, witnesses who give false testimony—are to be punished separately by the king. However, the Brāhmaṇa is to be banished—meaning he is to be expelled from the kingdom and not fined. This should be understood to apply when a specific motive such as greed is known and when it is not a habitual offense. As Manu says: "Out of greed, he should be fined one thousand; out of delusion, however, the first *sāhasa*."
Indeed, the middle punishment is out of fear, while the first is fourfold due to friendliness.
Ten times more [severe] than desire is the former [karma], but three times more than anger is the latter;
from ignorance it is two hundredfold, but from childishness it is exactly one hundredfold.
This is the time for punishment.

In this context, *lobha* (greed) is the desire for wealth; *moha* (delusion) is knowledge born of error; *bhaya* (fear) is terror; *maitrī* (friendliness) is an excess of affection; *kāma* (lust) is the longing for sexual union with women; *krodha* (anger) is intolerance; *ajñāna* (ignorance) is indistinct knowledge; and *bāliśya* (foolishness) is the non-arising of knowledge. All of these are to be understood as occurring after a period of waiting has been established, such as seven days and so forth, in the case of conflicting testimony from witnesses. If, in the event of a conflict between witnesses, one party—whether the plaintiff or the defendant—does not accept the testimony of the most virtuous witnesses even when they are equal in number, then following the trial, a waiting period must be observed for seven days, fourteen days, twenty-one days, forty-six days, or forty-two days, depending on whether the cause is human or divine. This is according to the author of the *Nibandhana*. On this point, Kātyāyana says:
One should recognize that a witness speaks falsely when, within seven days,
or within fourteen or twenty-one days, disease, fire, or the death of a kinsman occurs.
Or even in the case of forty-six [paṇas], according to the distinctions of substance, genus, and so forth.

[150] "Distinction of substance" means the gradation of substances; "distinction of genus" means the gradation of genera—this is the meaning. And thus Viṣṇu states: "Upon the loss of one hundred [paṇas], there is a waiting period of forty-six days; upon the loss of two hundred, a waiting period of twenty-one days; upon the loss of five hundred, a waiting period of fourteen days; upon the loss of one thousand, a waiting period of seven days. Herein lies the distinction regarding the *paṇa*.

Regarding the number of copper *paṇas* to be counted by numbers such as one hundred and so forth, Bhāruci says they are [copper *paṇas*]; Varadarāja says they are gold *māṣas*. Regarding the prescription of punishment in passages such as "A Brāhmaṇa is to be fined one thousand," Vijñānayogin says that the number one thousand refers to the count of copper *paṇas*; Bhāruci, however, says that the number one thousand refers to the count of gold *māṣas*. In this matter, the determination depends on the region. The distinction regarding the punishment for false witnesses: A righteous king should punish the three castes who give false testimony.
"Having punished him, he should banish [the offender]; however, in the case of a Brāhmaṇa, he should exile him. Thus [it is said].

And this refers to cases of habitual practice, because of the use of the present tense in the word "kurvāṇān" (those who are doing). Having punished the three castes beginning with the Kṣatriya, he should banish them—meaning he should kill them, since the word *pravāsa* is used in the sense of execution in the *Arthaśāstra*, given that this section has the nature of the *Arthaśāstra*. Even there, the banishment should be understood according to the specific context of false testimony as consisting of the cutting off of the lips, the cutting off of the tongue, or the taking away of life. But having punished a Brāhmaṇa, he should exile him—meaning he should expel him from his own kingdom. [151]

Or else, *vivāsana* means the state of being without clothing (*vāsasaḥ rāhityam*), that is, making one naked. Alternatively, *vāsaḥ*—derived from "that in which one dwells" (*vasati asmin*)—means a house; thus, *vivāsayet* means he should cause the house to be destroyed. Even for a Brāhmaṇa, if there is no knowledge of specific motives such as greed and so forth, and if the offense is not habitual, the punishment shall be the fine prescribed for each respective case. However, in the case of habitual repetition, there is both a monetary fine and *vivāsana*. One should not think that a Brāhmaṇa is exempt from monetary fines; for if monetary fines were absent and corporal punishment were prohibited, then even for a minor offense, consequences such as being made naked, the destruction of the house, branding, exile, or total impunity would result.
In the case of a great offense, even for a Brāhmaṇa there is both a monetary fine and corporal punishment; for members of all four castes who do not perform penance,
one should prescribe lawful punishment consisting of both corporal and monetary penalties.
And because of this traditional teaching:
"A Brāhmaṇa who approaches a guarded Brāhmaṇa woman by force shall be fined one thousand [paṇas]."

And because of this traditional teaching (*smaraṇa*): even in that case, the determination of the punishment—namely, banishment, stripping of clothes (*nagnīkaraṇa*), house-breaking, and expulsion from the country—should be understood as depending on factors such as the caste, the specific object, and the nature of the offense. When the specific motive such as greed is unknown, when there is no habitual practice, and when the matter is minor, for false testimony even a Brāhmaṇa receives only a monetary fine (*arthadaṇḍa*), just like a Kṣatriya or others. But in a major matter, there is indeed expulsion from the country. In cases of habitual practice, for all castes, there is a combination of stripping of clothes, house-breaking, expulsion from the country, and a monetary fine. As it was stated by Manu:

"He shall banish him from the kingdom, with all his wealth and unhurt"—this refers to the category of *sāhasa* (violence) under discussion, not to every instance of *sāhasa*. Corporal punishment for a Brāhmaṇa never occurs:
"One must never kill a Brāhmaṇa, even if he is guilty of every possible crime" [MDh 8.380].
And because of Manu’s general statement:
"There exists no greater unrighteousness on earth than the killing of a Brāhmaṇa;
therefore, the king should not even contemplate his killing in his mind" (MDh 8.381).
This purification has been declared for killing a twice-born man unintentionally;
for the intentional killing of a Brāhmaṇa, no atonement is prescribed.

And because of this statement by Yājñavalkya: "Therefore, for all four castes," in this context, the punishment consisting of a fine applies to all four castes. However, the punishment involving both corporal and monetary fines should be understood as applying to the three castes other than the Brāhmaṇa.
Now, it was stated in the second section that there is the *Arthaśāstra*; and in the *Arthaśāstra*, the killing of an *ātatāyin* (an aggressor) is prescribed even for a Brāhmaṇa:
"Whether it be a teacher, or one who is young or old, or a Brāhmaṇa of great learning..."
One should indeed kill an approaching assassin without hesitation.
In the killing of an assassin, no fault whatsoever attaches to the slayer;
whether done in secret or openly, it is fury that meets that fury.
Likewise:
"Even one who has mastered the Vedānta, if he comes as an assassin in battle seeking to kill, one may kill him in return; by that act, one does not become a killer of an embryo."

The term *bhrūṇa* refers to a Brāhmaṇa. The status of being an *ātatāyin* (an aggressor) also applies to a false witness. As Viṣṇu says: "One who violates another’s wife, one who steals another’s field, one with a raised sword, an arsonist, a poisoner, one who steals another’s property, a false witness in major legal cases, and one who makes a false accusation in a major case—these are *ātatāyins*. Here, by the word "another" (*para*), the Brāhmaṇa is meant. [153] Thus: one who violates a Brāhmaṇa’s wife, one who steals a Brāhmaṇa’s field, one who steals a Brāhmaṇa’s wealth, one who accuses a Brāhmaṇa of a mortal sin (*mahāpātaka*), one with a weapon in hand against a Brāhmaṇa, a false witness in a major accusation against a Brāhmaṇa, an arsonist in Brāhmaṇa houses, and a poisoner of a Brāhmaṇa. In this context, the state of being a poisoner refers to one who administers poison through herbs and the like once the poison has been neutralized; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of it constituting a mortal sin (*mahāpātaka*).
One who raises a sword, poison, or fire; likewise one who raises his hand to utter a curse;
one who kills by means of Atharvan rites; and also one who is treacherous toward the king.
"One who violates his wife, one intent on seeking out vulnerabilities,
and others such as these— one should recognize all of them as *ātatāyin*s (assassins).
And therefore:
The incendiary, the poisoner, one with a weapon in hand, the robber of wealth,
and the abductor of land or wife— these six are assassins (ātatāyin).
This should be understood as an illustrative indication (*upalakṣaṇa*).

Regarding the discernment of the relative strength and weakness of the *Dharmaśāstra* and the *Arthaśāstra*, some offer this resolution here: the *Arthaśāstra* intended here is that which is included within the *Dharmaśāstra* itself, not the *Arthaśāstra* composed by Uśanas and others. Consequently, when there is a conflict with the *Dharmaśāstra*, the *Arthaśāstra* is weaker. As it has been stated by Yājñavalkya:
"The established rule is that the Dharmaśāstra is more powerful than the Arthaśāstra.

Although there is no difference in nature between the Arthaśāstra and the Dharmaśāstra insofar as they share the same author, the intention is that the Dharmaśāstra is more powerful because, regarding the subject matter, Dharma is primary while Artha is secondary. Consequently, when there is a conflict between the Dharmaśāstra and the Arthaśāstra, the Arthaśāstra is simply set aside; there is neither a restriction of scope nor an optionality.

That is incorrect; since these two can have the same object, there is no contradiction, and thus an inquiry into their relative strength does not arise. For instance, having begun with: "The twice-born may take up arms when dharma is obstructed," [it continues:]...
One who kills in accordance with the Dharma is not blameworthy when acting for his own protection, in a conflict over sacrificial fees, or to prevent the loss of women, wealth, and so forth.

Having stated that one who kills an *ātatāyin* (an aggressor) with a weapon other than a deceptive one incurs no punishment—whether for protecting oneself, for sacrificial implements such as the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), for in battle, or for the protection of women and Brahmins—this [verse] is spoken as an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*) for that purpose: “Whether it be a teacher, or a child, or an old man,” and so forth. Because of the inclusion of the word “or” (*vā*), which implies that one may kill even teachers and others who are absolutely not to be slain, let alone others, and because the word “even” (*api*) is heard in the phrase “even one who has mastered the Vedāntas,” there is no perception here that teachers and the like are actually subject to being killed. And thus says Sumantu:
"Even in the case of a great offense, there is no corporal punishment for a Brāhmaṇa;
there is no fault in killing an *ātatāyin* (an assailant), except in the case of cows and Brāhmaṇas.

As for what Bhavadeva stated—that the syntactical connection is "there is no fault in killing an *ātatāyin*," and that by the word "cow" (*go*) the place of the cow's horns is meant, and by the word "Brāhmaṇa" (*brāhmaṇa*) a Vedic sentence in the form of a Brāhmaṇa is meant—that must be rejected because it contradicts all the *smṛtis* and involves an artificial interpretation. Furthermore, as for what Aparārka stated:

"One with a raised sword, one with a curse ready on his lips"—regarding this definition of an *ātatāyin* (an aggressor), because of the force of the two terms "one with a raised sword" and "one with a curse ready on his lips," it is agreed by all learned men that even Brahmins who are engaged in killing are *ātatāyins* and may be slain; therefore, [the contrary view] should be rejected.
[155] And the teacher, the expounder, the father, the mother, and the preceptor...
One should not harm a Brahmin, a cow, or any ascetics whatsoever.

And from this statement of Manu, the fault in killing a Brāhmaṇa is recorded in the Smṛti. Therefore, since the prohibition is already established by the general rule, "A Brāhmaṇa must not be killed," this specific statement—"There is no fault whatsoever for the slayer in killing an *ātatāyin* (aggressor)"—is meaningful as a prohibition against harming those who are aggressors.

This statement refers exclusively to persons other than Brāhmaṇas. In the case of a Brāhmaṇa giving false testimony, he should be expelled from his country, expelled from his village, made naked, branded, deprived of his home, and subjected to a monetary fine. It must be understood that it is established by all the *smṛtis* that there is never any corporal punishment for a Brāhmaṇa; enough with this elaboration.
Regarding the manner of questioning witnesses, Manu states the method of interrogating witnesses:
In the presence of the gods and Brahmins, the king, being himself pure, should question the twice-born witnesses in the forenoon,
while they are themselves pure and facing either northward or eastward.
But Nārada says:
Having summoned the witnesses, he should question them individually after restraining them with severe oaths—
those who are all of known conduct and who have knowledge of the matter.

The meaning is that one should question each person individually after making them committed to truth by means of terrifying oaths. Those oaths have been shown by him [the author] himself: "One should cause a Brahmin to swear by his truth regarding a specific object; a Kṣatriya, by his chariot and weapons."

"A Vaiśya by means of cattle, seed, and gold; but a Śūdra by all sins. Therefore, it should be understood that the mention of "the twice-born" (*dvijān*) is intended to indicate witnesses in general, because of the injunction for the cursing of a Śūdra with "by all sins. In this regard, a specific rule has been recorded by Manu:
"One should ask a Brāhmaṇa, 'Speak!'; one should ask a King, 'Speak the truth!'"

Regarding the question for a Vaiśya, since no specific rule is stated, it follows that he would suffer separation from cattle, seed-corn, and gold if he should speak otherwise. However, the manner of questioning a Śūdra has been elaborated by Manu:

"Those who are remembered as slayers of Brahmins, those who are thieves, those who kill women and children, those who betray friends, and those who commit sins—these [would be yours] if you speak falsely."
O Bhadra, whatever merit you have accumulated since birth—
all of that would go to a dog if you were to speak otherwise.
The god Yama Vaivasvata who resides here in your heart—
if you have no dispute with him, then do not go to the Gaṅgā, nor to the Kurus.
Naked, shaven-headed, carrying a skull-bowl, and tormented by hunger and thirst,
he who gives false testimony shall go to the house of his enemy below.
One kills five by lying about cattle, one kills ten by lying about cows;
one kills a hundred by lying about horses, and one kills a thousand by lying about men.
One who speaks falsehood for the sake of gold destroys both the born and the unborn;
one destroys everything by a falsehood regarding land. Do not, therefore, speak a falsehood concerning land.
Having considered all these faults in speaking untruth,
you should speak the truth directly, exactly as it was heard and exactly as it was seen.

"Kurūn" refers to Kurukṣetra. "Añjasā" means with a pure heart. "Those born and those unborn" (jātān ajātān)—the remainder is that this refers to one's own family. And this rule, mentioned in the context of questioning a Śūdra, applies even to twice-born men who subsist on low occupations when not in times of distress, because it is impossible to constantly restrain them by means of a minor oath. For this very reason, Manu says:
"Those who have fallen away from their own duties and subsist on the food of others, yet desire the status of the twice-born—one should treat them like Śūdras."
The word "in testimony" is to be understood as the ellipsis. Regarding this, Kātyāyana states: "Testimony must be given by witnesses standing within the court, and not elsewhere;
this rule applies to all testimonies, except in the case of immovable property."
The meaning is: "except in the case of immovable property.
If there is a killing of living beings, one should cause the witness to testify in the presence of the corpse;
but in its absence, in the presence of a mark [of identification]; one should not cause it to be testified otherwise.
Regarding the "mark," such as a horn or the like;
Bṛhaspati states the manner of giving testimony as follows:
Having removed his sandals and turban, he should raise his right arm;
taking gold, cow dung, and darbha grass, he should speak the truth.

The meaning is that he should raise his right hand and arrange his garment like the *yajñopavīta*. Thus says the Śruti: "He raises the right arm and drapes the left; this is the *yajñopavīta*. And likewise Vasiṣṭha: "A witness who stands facing the east, having been sworn by his own oaths, shall speak the truth after touching gold, cow-dung, and *darbha* grass. [158]
*Ṛta* is truth. Manu has declared his own oaths:
"A witness is purified by truth; *dharma* increases through truth.
Therefore, truth must indeed be spoken by witnesses among all social classes (*varṇas*). Thus it is said.
A man who gives false testimony is bound by the nooses of Varuṇa; rendered helpless, he is led away for a hundred years. Therefore, a witness should speak the truth.
For the self alone is the witness of the self, and the self is likewise the refuge of the self;
do not despise yourself, the supreme witness of men.
"Through a hundred births" means up to the limit of a hundred lifetimes. "Helplessly" is an adverbial modifier of the action. Nārada also says:
"Kubera, Āditya, Varuṇa, Śakra, Vaivasvata, and the other guardians of the world constantly behold [him] with their divine eye."
Bṛhaspati also says:
"A fraudulent juror, a false witness, and a killer of a Brahmin are declared to be equal;
a killer of an embryo and a stealer of wealth are said not to be greater than these."
Vasiṣṭha also says:
"If, however, one should speak a falsehood, it is equivalent to eating impure matter in every respect;
upon death, one enters hell and thereafter goes among the animals."
The meaning is that one who dies goes to hell, joined with the act of eating impure substances.
Vyāsa also [describes] the faults in false testimony:
Witnesses who speak falsely are tormented by the nooses of Varuṇa;
their residence in hell is certain for sixty thousand years.
When a hundred years of these have been completed, a single bond is released;
once that time has passed and the bonds are freed, one is born among the animal wombs.
Regarding false testimony, Vasiṣṭha says:
"He becomes a pig for ten years, an ass for ten years,
a dog for ten years, and a vulture for twenty years."
Likewise, among worms, insects, and moths he remains for forty years;
thereafter, he is born as a deer for ten years, and after that, as a human being.
But when he attains human birth, he may become mute or blind;
moreover, he shall suffer poverty in birth after birth.
Hungry, he begs at the house of an enemy along with his wife;
having understood the faults in falsehood and having understood the excellent qualities in truth.
Therefore, a witness should speak the truth here, even toward an enemy, for it is conducive to one's welfare.

The word "water" (*ap*) should be supplied here; the meaning is that one should speak the truth even when the witness is an enemy. Thus, the purification [of the witness] must be performed by these very words.
Manu states that in certain cases of testimony there is no sin, while in other matters he mentions an exception (*apavāda*).
"Where the death penalty would fall upon a Śūdra, a Vaiśya, a Kṣatriya, or a Brāhmaṇa for telling the truth, there a falsehood should be spoken; for that is superior to the truth.
Thus says Yājñavalkya.
"For where the killing of those belonging to the [four] castes would occur, one may speak untruth as testimony.
Regarding the absence of witnesses, Nārada states that even in disputes such as arson and the like, signs such as a torch in hand perform the function of witnesses.
One with a firebrand in hand is to be known as an arsonist; one with a weapon in hand is a murderer;
and one seized by the hair of another is a simultaneous adulterer.
One who approaches the vicinity of a dam with a spade in hand should be known as a "dam-breaker";
likewise, one who approaches a forest with an axe in hand is proclaimed a "forest-cutter."
"A man who commits assault is to be recognized by visible marks;
for these cases of assault are matters of conviction without witnesses, and thus require careful investigation. Thus says Hārīta.
Someone, having made a mark upon themselves, might out of malice cause harm to another;
in such a case, an investigation is appropriate through logical reasoning, causal evidence, and the connection of facts.
And so Nārada says:
"Even one who is not a thief incurs the status of a thief, and a thief attains the status of a non-thief;
through legal proceedings, Māṇḍavya—who was not a thief—was reduced to the state of a thief."

Therefore, the intention is that examination is necessary. This is the underlying principle: here, only documents such as written records that are characterized by the absence of contradiction (*ākrośābhāva*) enter the path of valid proof, not otherwise. For this very reason, Viṣṇu says: "That which is established is indeed [only] that which is uncontradicted. Bhāruci explains this as follows: "‘Established’ refers to all written records, possession (*bhukti*), and so forth; ‘uncontradicted’ means that it is not established from all sides—it never becomes established. As for what was stated by Nārada:
"The plaintiff shall restrain one who does not abide by the matter to be stated and who departs from that speech, until the appearance for summons. Thus it is said.

This has been explained by the author of the *Candrikā* (p. 33): “When there is a dispute over a doubtful matter, one who is indifferent [to the outcome] should be urged to resolve it; thus, disregarding the statement of the plaintiff that ‘the defendant must be restrained,’ the plaintiff himself should effect restraint (*āsedha*). By royal command, he should block [the defendant] until the conclusion of the judicial proceeding. This describes what is called “restraint of the person” (*svarūpāsedha*). However, that should be understood as referring merely to restraint of the person, insofar as the plaintiff himself effects the restraint through the means of returning property that was seized by the defendant. But Bhāruci says:
The plaintiff, seeking a legal decision, should restrain the defendant who does not abide by the matter to be stated and who evades that speech.

"One should cause the seizure of the object regarding which there is a desire to establish [one's claim]—that is, one should have the king, by royal command, detain the property itself that has been seized and is the object of the desire to establish; in its absence, one should detain the person who seized it or the one who destroyed it. Thus, this statement primarily concerns the seizure of the property (*dravyāsedha*)," so he says. Therefore, the explanation of Bhāruci alone is correct, because it accords with the statement of Viṣṇu.
But is this not improper, since it lacks accordance with the statement of Viṣṇu? For Viṣṇu states: "The fruit of the seizer himself shall be seized."

Not so; for you have failed to understand the intended meaning (*tātparya*) of the Vaiṣṇava statement. Its intended meaning, however, is that the prohibition of the fruit (*phalāsedha*) is stronger than the prohibition of the written document (*likhitāsedha*), because everyone engages in action solely for the sake of the fruit. Since the prohibitions previously made regarding the written document and so forth would be entirely ineffective if the prohibition of the fruit were not enacted, that statement is intended to demonstrate the superiority of the latter. And thus says the Gautama Sūtra: "The prohibition of the fruit is like that of a weaver."

The meaning of this has been explained by the author of the commentary (*nibandhakāra*): here, the suffix *vati* is used in the sense of the accusative; thus, *kauttikaḥ* means a "debt-collector" (*kuttājīvaka*), just as in the case of the "object of restraint" (*āsedhaviṣaya*). In this way, in all cases, the fruit itself is the object of restraint. For example, a debt-collector is to be restrained at the time when he takes possession of the accumulated wealth that exceeds the conventional meaning of the term "debt. [162] Likewise, in all legal proceedings, restraint must be exercised at the moment of taking possession of the fruit. The intended meaning is that at the time of taking possession of the fruit, the fruit itself is the object of restraint, not the underlying substance. The mention of the "debt-collector," however, should be understood as being for the purpose of making known this specific distinction: that in matters of debt, unlike other types of legal proceedings, there are no restraints prior to that time; rather, in the case of debt, the fruit alone is the object of restraint.
The relative strength and weakness of restraint and verbal abuse.

Now, "obstruction" (*āsedha*) means the prevention of a result; that is to say, the depositing of an object that has become the subject of dispute within the reach of neutral persons. When the result is not produced, it is the obstruction of the effort to take possession of it. When there is an effort to destroy the result, it is "obstruction of the essential nature" (*svarūpāsedha*), which is the restraint by royal command—this is *āsedha*. Abuse (*ākrośa*), however, is not like that. Rather, it consists of verbal activity in such forms as: "The fruit must not be enjoyed," "No document must be written," "You must not act as a witness," or "You must come with me for the judicial decision"; otherwise, you will have transgressed the royal command. It is not of the nature of physical action. Therefore, abuse is indeed weaker than obstruction. Consequently, if it is argued that obstruction alone is the seed of legal procedure (*vyavahārabīja*) and not abuse, [we reply: [This is the opponent's objection.]

It is not so; there is a difference in the scope (*viṣaya*) of reviling (*ākrośa*) and restraining (*āsedha*), but no difference in their essential nature (*svarūpa*). An obstruction caused by a weak claimant is designated by the term "reviling," whereas one caused by a powerful person is designated by the term "restraining. Thus says Viṣṇu: "Reviling and restraining are performed by the weak and the powerful [respectively]."

The meaning is as follows: according to the principle that "the king is the strength of the weak," an *āsedha* (seizure/restraint) carried out by royal officers—even if initiated by a weak party—remains an *āsedha* because it is effected by those possessing power, even though it is rooted in an *ākrośa* (an act of verbal abuse). While it is true that the definition of an *ākrośa* is simply an act committed by a weak party, there is this distinction between an *ākrośa* and an *āsedha*: an *ākrośa* draws forth ownership, including its fruits, at a later time following the judicial determination of the law; whereas an *āsedha*, at the very moment of seizure, blocks the fruit itself. On this point, Bhārucyā and others state that only an *āsedha* should be performed by one who is powerful, not an *ākrośa*. Here, the description of the perpetrator of an *ākrośa* has not been elaborated upon because it is obvious. Therefore, when an *āsedha* exists, the *ākrośa* subverts the entire specific evidence through the medium of destroying the legal property characterized by the absence of that [evidence].
An Analysis of the Power of Written Contracts and Documents.

Now, is it not the case that the authority of written documents and the like depends upon the determination of the source (*āgama*)? In the absence of such a source, their authority lacks a firm foundation and thus does not become secure. According to some, there are seven sources; as the *Smṛti* states: "There are seven lawful sources of wealth. However, in the opinion of Gautama and others (GDh 10.39), there are eight sources of wealth: inheritance, purchase, partition, acquisition through occupation, finding, acceptance of gifts, and so forth. In the view of Bhāradvāja, however, because exchange (*parivṛtti*) is also declared to be a form of acquiring wealth, there are nine sources when that is added. Among these, since the meaning determined by a fraudulent transaction (*kuttā*) is not included, and since it is impossible to determine the specific mode of acquisition, it follows that the fraudulent document and the witnesses recorded therein are weak in authority.
The lord of the earth should punish that sinner with the punishment due to a thief, even if he has enjoyed [the property] for many hundreds of years without legal title.

Thus, according to the Smṛti, it is understood that possession (*bhukti*) devoid of traditional title (*āgama*) lacks entry into the category of valid means of proof. As for the equality between possession and title that is perceived from the statement of Bṛhaspati, that is not contradictory, as its purpose is to indicate the weakness of mere possession alone. And so says Bṛhaspati: "One shall not obtain ownership of land by possession alone; one shall obtain ownership through both pure title and possession. [164]
And so Vyāsa says: "Possession is held to have five constituent parts: traditional title, long duration, being free from interruption and opposition, and the presence of the opposing party."

Regarding this, it was stated previously that by saying "enjoyment is held to have five factors," [the author] demonstrates that enjoyment lacks validity even when a single factor is deficient; therefore, since its absence is perceived during the investigation of the source of income, there is a lack of firmness in the evidence that establishes it due to the absence of purity in the root source. To this, it is replied: in some cases, even a technical convention (*paribhāṣā*) pertains specifically to the acquisition of wealth, as for example: "If it is not released, the pledge shall perish once the debt has doubled."

Regarding this, Vijñāneśvara maintains that although the convention based on the doubling of wealth is not enumerated among the means of acquiring property (*vittāgama*), it nevertheless indicates ownership subject to a condition (*sopādhika-svatva*). The author of the *Candrikā*, however, states that the convention regarding the doubling of wealth constitutes a form of exchange (*parivṛtti*), like the barter of sesame for rice, and thus brings about ownership. According to the view of Vijñāneśvara, the convention possesses the power to produce ownership because it is included within verbal gift (*vācika-dāna*); for even in the case of conditional ownership, once the condition ceases, the ownership becomes firm. To illustrate: in a convention such as, "Let so much wealth be given to us from this field, and let the remainder be taken [by you]," or "Having taken this much property, let that debt be cleared, and let the remainder be taken," it is observed that the cessation of one's own ownership over the remaining property extends until the acquisition of ownership by the other party. Alternatively, according to the view of Bhāruci, the convention possesses the power to produce ownership because it culminates in a mental gift (*mānasika-dāna*) supported by the *kuttākāra* calculation method.

If it is argued: "Surely ownership does not arise from mere intention (*saṃkalpa*); rather, ownership ceases through intention. The arising of ownership, however, results only from acquisition (*arjana*), as established by the principle governing the acquisition of wealth; therefore, there is no contradiction in stating that intention is the cause of ownership within this technical definition, which concludes with mental giving."

Not so. This fault would arise only if the mental act alone were the cause for the loss of ownership (*svatva*) in the case of methods for acquiring wealth; but that is not the case. It has been stated that the cause for the loss of ownership is, in some instances, a mental resolve (*saṃkalpa*), and in others, a heinous crime (*mahāpātaka*) and so forth. Furthermore, because this legal topic (*adhikaraṇa*) conforms to worldly practice (*laukikavyavahāra*), and because ownership itself is a worldly matter, one must accept things as they are observed in the world. In worldly transactions such as *kuttā* (fraudulent acquisition), it is the consensus of common people that the mental act alone is the cause of ownership. And this is indeed seen: many scribes (*kāyastha*) are frequently observed taking possession of fields, regions, villages, and the like through fraudulent means (*kuttākāreṇa*), and they are seen to endure the burden of occasional losses. In those cases, ownership over the property—whether it be a village, a field, a region, or other such designated assets—does indeed belong to them. And that title of acquisition (*āgama*) is quite valid.

If it is argued that when goods are received through usury, an increase [of capital] exists, and that those who provide the loan (the *kuttā-pradātṛs*) are seen to appropriate that increase and are designated as *uttama*s, this is not so. For if the moneylender (*kauttika*) were not capable of enduring the burden of loss, then even the *uttama* would not be capable of enduring the decrease of his increase. The well-known status of being a moneylender is rooted in providing enjoyments that are contrary to [the debtor's] milk [i.e., interest], and in not acting otherwise. Therefore, Viṣṇu has stated: "The moneylender is one who endures the burden of loss; the *uttama*, however, is one who endures both the increase and the decrease."

On this point, Bhāruci says: "A *kuttopajīvī* is a *kauttika*. He is one who receives the best of what is given as *kutta*. *Kutta* is defined as the handing over of a collection of household goods, such as houses, fields, gardens, villages, and lands, to any merchant whatsoever for the purpose of obtaining the abundant fruits of those items."

*Saṃdāna* means that it is not a "right gift" (*samyagdāna*), because *kuttā* has the nature of a conditional gift; rather, it is a *saṃdāna*, meaning a bond. Even for the superior party, since no increase is admitted, it is called *kuttā* because it is essentially a bond; thus it is designated as *kuttā*. Some say that *sadāna* means mere relinquishment; however, there is this distinction here: if there is an agreement between these two—the *kauttika* and the superior—stating, "If there is an increase, it must be endured by me as the superior; if there is a decrease, it must be endured by you as the *kauttika*," then, in accordance with that agreement, even when an increase exists, the ownership of the *kauttika* extends only to an increase of one-quarter (*pāda*) according to the words of Viṣṇu.

And likewise Viṣṇu states: "Ownership belongs to the weaver upon an increase of one-quarter [of the debt]. On this point, Bhāruci comments: "Regarding this 'increase,' if it is only a quarter from the weaver, then even with respect to that very increase, the creditor (uttama) [retains] it mentally; however, in the case of other increases or losses, ownership remains dependent on the debtor, not on the weaver. For he records that ownership belongs only to an increase exceeding a quarter. Therefore, the meaning is that when there is an increase of material goods by only a quarter, the creditor's ownership ceases—that is, it reaches the point of being transferred to another."

The intention is as follows: even mental gift (*mānasika-dāna*) consists of renunciation and establishes ownership; such is the Vaiṣṇava doctrine. When Bhāruci says, "Let this *uttama* [creditor] take this accumulation by means of his mind," the Vaiṣṇava position is that ownership arises in whatever amount of accumulated wealth there is for which the *uttama* performs a mental act of renunciation; it cannot be less than that.

On this point, some say: by this very logic, even when there is a reduction in the amount of debt, the creditor must tolerate at most one-quarter [of the original sum]; anything less than that is out of the question, while anything more is optional—such is the intended meaning of Viṣṇu’s statement. Thus concludes the determination of human means of proof;
now follows the description of divine means of proof.
In this regard, Nārada says:
"A king who always administers the five ordeals everywhere according to the prescribed rules rejoices in heaven after death when he has been challenged by a litigant. [167]

There are five divine ordeals—the balance, fire, water, poison, and the sacred libation (kośa). As Yājñavalkya says: "The balance, fire, water, poison, and the sacred libation—they call these divine ordeals for the sake of purification. By this, it is implied that these are the ordeals for those who bring a lawsuit. As Kātyāyana says:

"No one shall employ the accuser in the divine ordeals; the ordeal must be administered to the accused by those expert in divine ordeals. Here, "no one" refers to the presiding judge and others; "those expert in divine ordeals" refers to the judges and so forth. By this, it is implied that this rule applies when the plaintiff and defendant mutually agree to undergo the ordeal. And it has been stated by Yājñavalkya:
"Or, by mutual consent, one may perform [the ritual] while the other carries the head," so it is said.

The *śiras* is the fourth limb of legal procedure, characterized by victory and defeat; by means of it, punishment is indicated. By *rucyā*—that is, through the mutual consent of the plaintiff and the defendant—one or the other—the plaintiff or the defendant—shall undergo the ordeal (*divya*). The "other"—the defendant or the plaintiff—[shall likewise do so]. *Śiras* refers to the head or the monetary fine. *Vartayet* means he shall accept [the responsibility]. Regarding the "five ordeals," this pertains to the subject of major charges (*mahābhiyoga*). As Yājñavalkya says: "These [ordeals] are for major charges. This restricts them to major charges alone and not to others.
"The balance, fire, water, poison, as well as the [divine] vessel (kośa), rice grains, and the seventh, the heated gold coin (taptamāṣaka)—these are the divine ordeals.
This also serves as an illustration for the plough and the sacred law (phāla-dharma). As Bṛhaspati has said:
The balance, fire, water, poison, and the fifth is the sacred libation;
the sixth is said to be rice grains, and the seventh is the heated gold coin.
"The eighth is said to be the balance, and the ninth is remembered as that born of dharma (the sacred libation).
All these divine means have been pointed out by the Self-Existent One.

Now, one might object: "Even in a case of minor accusation, the ordeal by sacred libation is indeed applicable, for there is a traditional legal text stating: 'One should cause the sacred libation to be administered even in a minor case.'"

True; the mention of the ordeal by sacred libation (*kośa*) among the weighing and other ordeals is not intended as a restrictive rule (to apply only to great charges), but rather as an extension to ensure its application in cases of charges brought with firm confidence; otherwise, it would apply only to charges based on mere suspicion.
For those accused on the basis of physical force, one should prescribe ordeals such as the balance and others;
for those suspected of a crime, rice and the ordeal of the sacred libation (kośa) are to be used—of this there is no doubt.

Thus it is from the Smṛti. The phrase "in cases of suspicion" (*śaṅkāsu*) is intended as an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*) for trust (*viśvāsa*) and so forth. As Kātyāyana has said: "In matters of suspicion, trust, making an agreement, and likewise in the partitioning of inheritance, as well as in the performance of a collective action, one should cause the ordeal by sacred libation (*kośa*) to be administered."
In this context, the *kośa* (divine ordeal) is devoid of the head.
One should avoid divine ordeals that lack the head-position;
from the balance (*dhaṭa*) up to poison (*viṣa*), the *kośa* alone is traditionally held to be without a head. Thus it is said.

The phrase "in cases such as suspicion and formal accusation" is to be understood as the remainder [of the sentence]. However, in a formal accusation involving a grave matter (*mahātattva*), even the *kośa* ordeal is to be avoided if the accuser is not positioned at the head; for Yājñavalkya, in the context of the five divine ordeals, has stated: "When the accuser is positioned at the head. Even in cases of grave accusations, there is no requirement for the head to be placed [on the scale] during the five divine ordeals, such as the balance, when held in an assembly other than that of the King and the Chief Justice (*prāḍvivāka*). Both verbal punishment and the penalty of public reproach (*dhigdama*) are recorded in the Smṛtis as being dependent upon Brāhmaṇas.
Both fines and corporal punishment have been declared to be dependent upon the king alone.
Since it has been stated that punishment, which occupies the position of the head of legal procedure (*vyavahāraśiras*), belongs specifically to the royal court of justice, it follows:
[169] Verbal punishment and the censure "fie! are both traditionally held to depend upon the Brahmins;
monetary punishment and corporal punishment are both declared to depend upon the king.

Since it has been stated that the rule regarding the placement of the head (the primary part) of the defendant's legal case applies specifically to the royal court of justice presided over by the judge (*prāḍvivāka*), one must understand that scriptural injunctions such as "one should avoid ordeals that lack a fixed position for the head" apply only to the royal court of the judge and similar assemblies. However, an ordeal born of *dharma* (truth) concerns only a minor subject, because it is appropriate for use in cases of suspicion regarding penance and the like. As Pitāmaha said:
The examination of dharma and adharma concerns men who have committed murder, those who are pleading for mercy, those seeking expiation, and those accused in matters of doubt.
These divine ordeals and oaths should be employed, as appropriate, in disputes concerning the lending of money and similar matters.
Regarding immovable property, when there is an absence of documentary evidence, this is the occasion for a divine ordeal, according to the statement of Pitāmaha:
"In disputes concerning immovable property, one should avoid ordeals.
This should be explained to mean that when there exists evidence such as written documents (*likhita*) or witnesses (*sādhya*), one should avoid ordeals.
Now, it may be argued that in other types of disputes as well, where other means of proof are available, there is simply no occasion for the employment of ordeals.

True; even when the plaintiff has presented witnesses with the characteristics previously described in disputes such as the non-payment of debts (*ṛṇādāna*) and so forth, if the defendant, relying on the support of accepting punishment, resorts to an ordeal (*divya*), then an ordeal may also be employed, because of the possibility of excessive defects in witnesses. This is because an ordeal, by virtue of its freedom from defect, is in fact applicable to all subjects.
As Nārada says:
"In that regard, *dharma* is established in truth, and legal procedure (*vyavahāra*) is established in witnesses."

"In matters to be accomplished by the gods, one should not employ human effort or documentary evidence. This [rule] is intended to mean that in disputes concerning immovable property, even if the defendant relies on an ordeal as a support for his defense, an ordeal should not be accepted when witnesses such as neighbors and other means of proof are available; thus, "one should avoid ordeals in disputes concerning immovable property."

This statement of the Grandfather (Bṛhaspati) is not intended for the absolute exclusion of ordeals; for if there were no documentary evidence, neighbors, and so forth, it would result in the impossibility of a decision in disputes concerning immovable property. As for the verse:
"Where neither a document exists, nor possession, nor witnesses, and where there is no application of an ordeal, the king himself is the authority therein."

Since the non-occurrence of divine ordeals (*divyāvatārābhāva*) is itself the subject matter of disputes concerning immovable property (*sthāvaravivāda*), one should not say that the statement—"the king’s command is the deciding factor therein, for otherwise there would be the contingency of no decision in disputes over immovable property"—is improper. This has already been explained previously as being settled according to the different views of the author of the *Candrikā* and Vijñāniyogi; therefore, it shall not be elaborated upon here. He states the specific time for divine ordeals:
"The specific time for divine ordeals was declared by Pitāmaha."

The examination should take place in the forenoon, and the balance should be prepared in the forenoon; however, by one who desires to ascertain the true nature of dharma, the ordeal by water should be administered at midday.

"The purification by the [divine] vessel (kośa) is prescribed for the forenoon of the day; however, during the latter watch of the night, poison should be administered while it is cool. Thus, because of the general traditional teaching of Nārada—that for those ordeals such as rice, heated coins (taptamāṣa), and so forth, for which no specific time has been mentioned, the forenoon alone is declared the primary period—Hārīta likewise demonstrates this distinction.
The seasons of winter and late winter, as well as the rainy season, are proclaimed to belong to Agni;
whereas autumn and summer consist of water, and the late winter and early spring consist of poison.
Caitra, Mārgaśīrṣa, and likewise Vaiśākha—
these months are common to all and are not in conflict with the divine reckoning.
The balance should always be given as a gift; the scale, however, may be used at all times.

The prohibition of divine ordeals refers to the period of taking the *kośa* (sacred water), serving as an illustration for all oaths; however, because rice and other such ordeals are specifically mentioned, they are applicable at all times. There is a prohibition regarding certain specific times:
"There shall be no purification by cold water, nor shall there be purification by fire during the hot season."
One should not administer poison during the rainy season, nor likewise should one employ a scale in a high wind.
Neither in the afternoon, nor at twilight, nor ever at midday.

"Cold" means the cold season. Now, Bṛhaspati states the rules for administering ordeals according to the caste and other status of the litigants: "In matters such as debts and the like, when there is a mutual dispute..."
It should be given accompanied by the number of substances and so forth, according to the status of the person.
"With respect to the person" means with respect to the caste of the two disputants;
divine [ordeals] according to the distinction of social class (varṇa) are as he himself has stated.
The balance should be administered to a Brāhmaṇa, fire to a Kṣatriya;
water should be administered to a Vaiśya, and poison alone to a Śūdra.
"The treasury of all is declared by the wise to be common. This rule, however, is not absolute. As Kātyāyana says:
"Or rather, every ordeal may be administered to all, except the poison ordeal, in the case of the best of the twice-born. [172]
Regarding this, Yājñavalkya states the specific rule:
"The balance [is for] women, children, the elderly, the blind, the lame, Brāhmaṇas, and the sick;
fire or water [is for] a Śūdra, or seven grains of dill for one who is fit for poison."

"Female" (strī) means merely a woman, regardless of distinctions of caste, age, or condition; "child" refers to one up to sixteen years of age, and likewise "the elderly" refers to those beyond eighty. This [exemption] should be understood to apply to women and others who are observing vows or are extremely distressed, as Pitāmaha stated:
"For those observing vows, for those who are severely afflicted, for those who have been solicited, for ascetics, and for women—the ordeal shall not take place, if one has regard for dharma."
For women, however, poison is not prescribed, nor is water;
one should investigate their inner truth by means of the balance, the holy water (kośa), and other such ordeals.

Thus, because purification is prescribed by means of the balance, the sacred water-vessel (*kośa*), and other methods distinct from poison and water; and because the term "of women" is indicative of children as well, since they are mentioned generally in the phrase "those who observe vows" and so forth; even for Brāhmaṇas and the other castes, there is no rule that the balance and other tests must be used at all times. For it is ordained that purification by the sacred water-vessel (*kośa*) applies to all castes: "Purification by the *kośa* is prescribed for all classes."

"All these [methods] apply to all [castes], except for the Brāhmaṇa, for whom poison [is never permitted]. This is the summary here: during the rainy season, fire alone is [the ordeal] for everyone; but during the winter and the cool season, there is an option between fire and water for the three castes beginning with the Kṣatriya; however, for the Brāhmaṇa, fire alone is used and never poison; during the summer and autumn, water alone is used; and during the common season when many divine ordeals are available together, the rule is that the balance (tulā) and so forth are employed.
Regarding specific types of persons, there is a prohibition against certain divine ordeals;
however, Kātyāyana states a specific exception for ironworkers and others:
"Fire [is not used] for ironworkers, nor water for those who subsist on water."
And one should never administer poison even to those who are experts in the yoga of mantras.
One should not administer rice to those with ulcers or diseases of the mouth;
one should avoid fire for those suffering from leprosy, and water for those afflicted by asthma and coughing.
One should always avoid poison for those with an excess of bile and phlegm,
as well as for those addicted to wine and women, and likewise for gamblers.
"The treasury must not be given by the wise to those who follow the conduct of nihilists," so it is said. Nārada also states:
"To one who has committed a great offense, to one devoid of dharma, to an ungrateful person, or to one whose character is contemptible..."
One should avoid giving a treasury to an atheist or to one who has committed an offense visible to the world.
And thus, fire and the water-vessel (kośa) should be avoided for eunuchs and the like. As Nārada says:
"One should always examine eunuchs, the sick, those devoid of truth, men afflicted on all sides, as well as women, children, the elderly, and the blind, by means of the balance (dhaṭa)."

And this rule is permanent, because it is designated as "always" (*sadā*). Regarding this, that same author [Manu] states a specific exception: "In those legal proceedings where divine ordeals have been strictly prohibited, one should have them performed by one's own kinsmen; Manu says one must not abandon a person accused [of a crime]."
One should not abandon [the ordeal] without having purified it in the manner described; this is the remainder of the sense.
Regarding specific types of ordeals based on the particular number of items, Kātyāyana, however, states a distinction:
Having ascertained the measure of all substances by means of divine knowledge, one should apply it;
having ascertained the number of gold pieces, poison is prescribed in the event of a loss of a hundred.
The meaning here is that, having ascertained the number of gold pieces, one should treat the stolen property as being of the nature of gold and thus determine its numerical value.
In the event of the loss of eighty [gold pieces], one must indeed offer fire;
for a loss of sixty, water should be given; and for a loss of forty, the balance ordeal (dhaṭa).
Upon the loss of twenty or ten [measures], the giving of a treasury-measure (kośa) is prescribed;
or upon the loss of five more than that, rice equal to half of that half [of a treasury-measure] is required.
Upon the destruction of half of that half, however, the heads of sons and wives [are lost];
and upon the destruction of half of that half, worldly activities are said to cease.

In all these cases, the word "destruction" (*vināśa*) indicates denial (*apahnava*), because that alone serves as the basis for introducing the means of proof. By the word "and" (*ca*), oaths prescribed by the Smṛtis are included. As Hārīta says: "For a [debt] of one *niṣka*, there is a declaration of truth; for two *niṣkas*, touching the feet; for less than three, it shall be with a flower; beyond that, the ordeal of the sacred water-vessel (*kośa*)."

Regarding this, the author of the *Candrikā* states that the word "niṣka" here refers to a worldly (secular) *niṣka*, because it is so used in common practice. On this point, Viṣṇu states the specific rule: “The performance of the ordeal (*samayakriyā*) shall be according to what is appropriate. In cases of treason against the king or acts of violence, it may be performed at will. In cases of deposits and theft, gold shall be calculated as the value for all types of property according to their monetary worth. In that regard, for a debt of one *kṛṣṇala* or less, one should administer an oath with *dūrvā* grass. For two *kṛṣṇalas* or less, an oath with sesame seeds. For three *kṛṣṇalas* or less, an oath with silver. For four *kṛṣṇalas* or less, an oath with gold. For five *kṛṣṇalas* or less, an oath with earth turned up by a plough. For half a *suvarṇa* or more, the ordeal of the sacred water-pot (*kośa*) must be given to a Śūdra. Beyond that, the ordeal of the balance, fire, water, or poison shall be administered as appropriate. For a Vaiśya, the performance of the ordeal is as prescribed when the amount is double the half-portion; for a Kṣatriya, when it is triple the half-portion; and for a Brāhmaṇa, when it is quadruple the half-portion. A Brāhmaṇa whose guilt has been previously established should be made to undergo one of the ordeals even for a small matter; but one of well-known good character should not be subjected to them even for a great matter. This statement of Viṣṇu shall be explained in its entirety in accordance with all the *Smṛtis*. “Performance of the ordeal” (*samayakriyā*) means secular procedure. “Earth turned up by a plough” (*sīroddhṛtamahīkara*) means a clod of earth turned up by a ploughshare. Here, the mention of “less than” (*ūna*) is intended to exclude the administration of an ordeal when the amount is greater. On this point, Manu states a specific rule: [Manu 8.114–120] provides further details regarding the application of ordeals based on caste, the nature of the crime, and the character of the accused. The term *samayakriyā* is understood as the conventional or customary ritual act. The phrase *sīroddhṛtamahīkaram* is interpreted as taking a handful of soil raised by a plough. In this context, the inclusion of the word “less” (*ūna*) serves to preclude the use of an ordeal when the sum involved exceeds the specified threshold. Regarding this, Manu declares a particular distinction.
"This number is prescribed for those of low status; for those of middle status, it is remembered as double; but for those of superior status, it is fourfold. This is the rule for all castes."

The number of these [grains] constitutes one *kṛṣṇala*, which is the twentieth part of a conventional *niṣka*. According to another opinion, five *kṛṣṇalas* make a *pala*; in that case, four units of common measure are called a *kṛṣṇala*, and it is well known as a measure equal to a grain of rice (*taṇḍula*). In the two scriptures of Manu and Yājñavalkya, seven measures less two *kākaṇikas* are called a *kṛṣṇala*. Since there are thus three types of *kṛṣṇalas*, it is appropriate to rely upon the *kṛṣṇala* mentioned in the Vaiṣṇava Dharmaśāstra. Here, however, the *kṛṣṇala* consisting of six measures less three *kākiṇikas* is naturally relied upon; the *kṛṣṇala* of Manu is relied upon based on the qualities of the performer and other factors. In that regard, the theft is measured by the amount of property stolen required to complete the count of a *kṛṣṇala*. For the theft of such a *kṛṣṇala*, a Śūdra—having fasted, bathed, and wearing wet clothes—should take *dūrvā* grass in his hand and swear an oath in the presence of the Vedas and Brāhmaṇas. Starting from the second *kṛṣṇala* up to the third, a Śūdra should swear an oath holding sesame seeds in his hand. Starting from the third *kṛṣṇala* up to the fourth, he should swear an oath with silver in his hand. Starting from the fourth *kṛṣṇala* up to the fifth, a Śūdra should swear an oath with gold in his hand. Starting from the fifth *kṛṣṇala* up to the eighth, a Śūdra should swear an oath holding a clod of earth dug up by a plow. [176] Starting from the sixth *kṛṣṇala* up to ten *mānas*, if the Śūdra is of low status, he should swear an oath through his son or his wife. If he is a virtuous Śūdra, for this very matter he should swear an oath by all the sins [of the world]. Even though here...
"But for a Śūdra, [the punishment] shall be all the [penances for] mortal sins (pātaka).
Having seized his sons and wife, one should cause him to touch their heads individually.

Although no specific measure of the substance has been stated, nevertheless, by way of propriety, these two [punishments] ought to range from five *kṛṣṇalas* up to ten *mānas* or *paṇas*. And so Bṛhaspati, having mentioned the [ordeals] beginning with poison and ending with *dharmaja*, said:
"Truth, vehicles, treatises on science, cattle, seeds, and gold;
the feet of gods and Brahmins, and the heads of one's sons and wife—
these are declared to be oaths that are always easy to perform when the matter is true."

Thus, because these [penances] relate to matters of minor significance (*pratyalpārthaviṣayatvāt*), they are determined solely by reflecting on the nature of the circumstances (*pratyayasvarūpaparāmarśanenaiva*). It has been stated that these apply from below fifteen *paṇas* up to above five *kṛṣṇalas*. Starting from ten *paṇas* and up to fifteen *paṇas*, this constitutes the purification of a Śūdra’s transgression. Regarding this very point, it is said that for those who live by the plow—the cultivators—a plowshare (*phāla*) should be given. And so says Bṛhaspati:
"When a hundred [karṣas] have been taken and denied, the purification by ordeal must be administered;
the members of the court must diligently provide a ploughshare for the one who grazes cattle. Thus it is said.

When a Śūdra denies a hundred measures (*māna*), his purification through penance (*dharmaśodhana*) occurs; this is because a hundred measures consists of ten *paṇas*. The meaning is that from fifteen *paṇas* up to five times fifteen *paṇas*, there is reliance on religious penance (*dharmapratyaya*). In this very sense, "the plowshare of one who grazes" refers to a Śūdra farmer, for the Smṛti of Gautama states: "A plowshare should be given to a Śūdra. From fifteen *paṇas* up to thirty *paṇas*, the Śūdra must undergo the ordeal by sacred libation (*kośa*). From thirty *paṇas* up to forty *paṇas*, the Śūdra must undergo the ordeal of eating rice (*taṇḍulabhakṣaṇa*). From forty *paṇas* up to fifty *paṇas*, the Śūdra must undergo the ordeal of drinking poison (*tatpītamāṣa*). And so says Bṛhaspati: [177] *gocārasya phālam*—meaning of a Śūdra farmer. "The plowshare should be given to a Śūdra," according to the Smṛti of Gautama. From fifteen *paṇas* up to thirty *paṇas*, the Śūdra must undergo the ordeal by sacred libation. From thirty *paṇas* up to forty *paṇas*, the Śūdra must undergo the ordeal of eating rice. From forty *paṇas* up to fifty *paṇas*, the Śūdra must undergo the ordeal of drinking poison. Thus says Bṛhaspati.
In a lawsuit involving four hundred [paṇas], the heated māṣaka ordeal must be administered;
for three hundred, rice grains should be given, and for half of that amount, the ordeal of the sacred water (kośa).

Regarding the charge of four hundred: this means in a charge concerning gold weighing four hundred *māṣas*. In that case, the heated *māṣa* ordeal must be administered; since those [four hundred *māṣas*] consist of forty *paṇas*, the meaning is that for a charge of forty *paṇas*, the heated *māṣa* ordeal must be administered to a Śūdra. Regarding "rice grains (*taṇḍula*) are to be given for three hundred," here too, when the gold weighs three hundred *māṣas*—that is, thirty *paṇas*—rice grains are to be given to a Śūdra. Likewise: "And the *kośa* ordeal in half of that" means that when the gold weighs one hundred and fifty *māṣas*—that is, fifteen *paṇas*—the *kośa* ordeal is to be administered to a Śūdra. Similarly, from fifty *paṇas* up to sixty-seven *paṇas*, the balance ordeal (*tulādhāraṇa*) applies to a Śūdra. From sixty-seven *paṇas* up to seventy-five *paṇas*, the water ordeal (*jalapratyaya*) applies to a Śūdra. From seventy-five *paṇas* up to ninety-nine *paṇas*, the axe ordeal (*paraśu*) applies to a Śūdra. From one hundred *paṇas* upwards, the Śūdra must undergo the ordeal of consuming poison (*viṣabhakṣaṇa*). And so says Bṛhaspati:
When a thousand [palas] have been stolen, poison is administered;
when three-quarters are stolen, fire; when two-quarters are stolen, water; and when half is stolen, the balance (dhaṭa) should always be employed.

For a Śūdra, when the gold amounts to one thousand *mānas*—equivalent to one hundred *paṇas*—the ordeal consists of consuming poison. When it is reduced by a fourth part of a thousand *mānas*, amounting to seven hundred and fifty *paṇas* (one hundred and seventy-five *mānas*), the Śūdra must undergo the ordeal of holding a heated axe. Likewise, when the gold is reduced by a third part of a thousand *mānas*, amounting to sixty-seven *paṇas*, the Śūdra undergoes the ordeal of water. When it is half of a thousand *mānas*, amounting to fifty *paṇas*, the Śūdra must mount the scale; such is the meaning.

Now, one might ask: in passages such as "a thousand poisons," since numbers like "thousand" are things to be counted (*saṃkhyeya*), how is it determined that only gold weighed in the same measure as rice (*taṇḍula*) is to be understood?
It is said in reply:
"Having understood the measure of all substances, one should determine the cause."
One should likewise employ a divine [image] endowed with the proper measurements of gold.
Poison is prescribed for a fine of one hundred [paṇas],
the ordeal of water for ninety-seven and a half, and the ordeal of the balance for fifty.
The gift of a treasury, or half of that, or ten, five, or seven [measures];
half of that should be known as rice, and half of that as a heated masha-coin.
Thus says Kātyāyana. And likewise:
"Having ascertained the quantity of gold, poison is prescribed for a *śatamāna* weight;
but for a loss of eighty [māṣas], fire is prescribed as the means of proof."
The fire-eater (the ordeal by fire) is for debts up to one hundred;
for destruction [of the debt] at sixty, water should be administered; at forty, the balance ordeal;
and at thirty, Bṛhaspati says that the ordeal of the sacred libation (kośa) should be given there.
Or, upon the destruction of one and a half *pañca* measures, there shall be rice for half of that amount.

Thus says Vṛddha-Manu. Since poison is prescribed for the loss of a hundred in these two statements of Kātyāyana and Vṛddha-Manu, whereas in the statement of Bṛhaspati poison is prescribed for the loss of a thousand, it is evident that there is a great contradiction between them. To resolve this contradiction, one should interpret the statement of Bṛhaspati in accordance with the other two by applying the maxim of the majority (*bhūyasāṃnyāya*). This being the case, since in the Dharmaśāstras, when a mere number is specified in the prescription of punishments and the like, *paṇas* are generally understood as the objects to be counted because they are established as the standard unit for legal transactions, so too here, in the statements of Kātyāyana and Vṛddha-Manu, *paṇas* alone are taken as the objects denoted by the numbers such as "hundred" and so forth. Consequently, regarding the numbers such as "thousand" in the statement of Bṛhaspati, if the objects to be counted are taken to be gold measured by *mānas* of rice—as seen in such texts as "A *māna* of rice shall be used; ten *mānas* are declared to be a *paṇa*"—then there is no contradiction between the "hundred" and the "thousand. As for the statement of Yājñavalkya as well...
One should not take [a deposit] for less than one thousand [paṇas], nor [deal with] poison, nor likewise a scale.

Here, the word "thousand" (sahasra) is intended as an indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) of values slightly less than three-quarters or half [of a thousand]; thus there is no contradiction. In this context, the word "plowshare" (*phāla*) refers to an axe (*paraśu*), since it has been shown that the primary sense of the word "plowshare" pertains to objects of small value. As for what was stated here by Vṛddha-Manu:
"But in the case of loss [of an object] valued at eighty [paṇas] or more, ordeal by fire is prescribed."
And as it was stated by Kātyāyana: "Poison is administered for [a fine of] one hundred; the fire-ordeal is prescribed for ninety-five;
water for seventy-five; and the balance is traditionally ordained for fifty."

From these two statements, it is understood as follows: starting from seventy-five and up to eighty, fire and water are obtained; likewise, starting from sixty and up to sixty-seven locations, for a preeminent man accompanied by a son, there arises a light conviction [of innocence] upon obtaining the water-jar. For one without a son, however, there arises a heavy conviction [of guilt]; thus states Varadarāja.
