Furthermore, regarding the rule "half of that amount rice should be given, and half of that a heated māsaka," this prescription of the *taptamāṣa* (heated gold) for a minor matter concerns cases where there is suspicion of theft and the like; thus, there is no contradiction.
Where there is a denial of what was given, proof must be established;
in cases of theft or violence, one should cause an ordeal to be administered even for a very small matter.

Thus, according to the statement of Kātyāyana. In this manner, there exist Smṛti texts that set forth meanings contrary to the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) here; one should keep in mind that the resolution of such contradictions must be achieved by postulating a systematic arrangement (*vyavasthā*) for those very texts. Regarding the passage beginning with "for a Brāhmaṇa, in the future time," the meaning is as follows: in matters concerning future events, even a Brāhmaṇa may undergo the ordeal of the balance (*kośa*). The phrase "for a Śūdra" means that the previously mentioned measures of wealth apply specifically to the case of a Śūdra. It should be understood that in all the aforementioned cases, the performance of an oath (*śapatha*) is required for a Vaiśya when the amount involved is double [the standard]; for a Rājanya (Kṣatriya) when it is triple; and for a Brāhmaṇa when it is fourfold. As for that which was stated by Bṛhaspati:
"This number is prescribed for the low; for the middling, it is remembered as double; and for the superior, it is fourfold—this is how it should be determined by examiners.

This statement, however, is indicative of the fact that for those inferior to the superior and superior to the middling, a threefold increase may also be established, in accordance with the words of Viṣṇu. By this very interpretation, the statement of Manu, "This number is for the low," and so forth, is also explained. For those even lower than a Śūdra, the ordeals should be administered exactly as they are for a Śūdra.

"Indeed, all those born of degradation (apadhvaṃsaja) are declared to share the same dharma as Śūdras," according to the statement of Manu. Kātyāyana states that even for certain Brāhmaṇas, the ordeal must be administered exactly as for a Śūdra: "Cowherds, merchants, artisans, and actors..."
One should treat even Brahmins who are servants or usurers as one would a Śūdra.

This is what is meant: for a Śūdra, the oath is by means of his children, wife, and so forth; for a Vaiśya, the oath is by means of cattle, seed, and gold; for a Kṣatriya, by means of vehicles and weapons; and for a Brāhmaṇa, by means of a truthful statement. Therefore, the oaths prescribed for the conduct of a Brāhmaṇa are to be employed [for him]. Regarding this, the elders dispute: some maintain that although the number of *paṇas* is specified in the ordeals, because in common usage the term *paṇa* refers even to four *kākaṇikas*, and because it is well-known among grammarians that a *kākaṇika* is a fourth part of a *paṇa*, the *suvarṇa-paṇa* consisting of four *kākaṇikas* alone is what is counted in numbers such as one thousand and so on. Others, however, hold that the number mentioned in all ordeals refers to copper *kākaṇikas*. Still others—
"Ten *māṣas* should be the measure of a *taṇḍula*; this is recorded as a *daśamāna*, which is known as a *paṇa*.
Based on this scriptural statement, some maintain that a *paṇa* consists of exactly ten *māṣas*. Others hold that "one-twentieth of a *kārṣāpaṇa* should be understood as a *māṣa*."
A kākaṇī is proclaimed to be one-fourth part of a māṣa.
Thus, from the words of Auśanasa: "The wise say that a *māṣa* consists of four *kākaṇīs*;
twenty of those [māṣas] constitute what is called the primary *paṇa*."
Based on the statement of Bhāradvāja,

"A māṣa is declared to be the twentieth part of a paṇa," and from the traditional teaching (smaraṇa) of Kātyāyana, "Twenty māṣas constitute a paṇa," it is held that this number applies to the ordeals (divya). However, this is without substance.

"A *paṇa* is declared to consist of twenty *māṣas*, except in the case of ordeals (*divya*)," according to this statement by Kātyāyana; for it prohibits the use of a *paṇa* consisting of twenty *māṣas* in ordeals. Likewise, from the Smṛti: "Having ascertained the quantity of gold"—meaning, "having determined the measure of all goods, one should calculate the amount of gold."
For all categories of goods, one should determine the price in gold.

Because of such Smṛti texts as these, it is understood that only gold (suvarṇa) is to be counted; and since there is no statement authorizing the copper kārṣāpaṇa to be counted in ordeals (divya), it is stated that only gold paṇas are to be counted in ordeals. As for the claim made by the author of the Candrikā that numbers such as one thousand refer to the counting of the worldly niṣka—that must be rejected, because according to the reasoning already stated, it is logical that numbers such as one thousand refer only to the paṇa, and because there is no scriptural statement establishing the niṣka.

Is it not the case that eight *kākaṇikās* are denoted by the word "grain" (*taṇḍula*), and that very same thing is also denoted by the word "measure" (*māna*)? For in that section concerning punishments, there is the statement: "But for damage to standing crops, one should pay eight *māṣas* for a buffalo and one *kākiṇī*."

"One should cause [the offender] to pay a quarter-pana for a cow, and likewise two quarters for a great cow"—from this statement, since it is understood that the words *pāda* (quarter) and *māṣa* have the same meaning as two quarters of a *paṇa*, it follows that a *paṇa* consists of sixteen *māṣas*. And so it is stated in the *Caraka*:
"That which has arisen from the rays of the sun is called a *trasareṇu*."
Eight *trasareṇus* are proclaimed to be one *likṣā*.
Three of those are declared to be a mustard seed (sarṣapa), and that is remembered as a kākini;
eight kākini are proclaimed to be a grain of rice (taṇḍula).

A *taṇḍula* is declared to be a *mānaka*, and a *māṣaka* is proclaimed [to be four of those]. Whatever substance is referred to by the word "measure" (*māna*) in the *Smṛtis*, that very same thing is referred to by the word "measure" in medical science (*vaidyaka*). Two of those are declared to be a *kṛṣṇala*, and two *kṛṣṇalas* are a *maṇḍikā*.
"The words *asti* and *kāpaṇa* are proclaimed as synonyms.
From this, it is understood that the *paṇa* consists of sixteen [māṣas]. Likewise, in the Vaikhānasa-saṃhitā it is said:
"The *māna* should be the measure of a single grain of rice; eight *māṣas* are recorded as a *paṇa*."

In that regard, it is true that eight *kākiṇīs* alone are designated by the words *māṣa* or *taṇḍula*, such that a *paṇa* consists of sixteen *māṣas*. However, whether a *paṇa* consisting of sixteen *māṣas* or one consisting of ten *māṣas* is taken as the unit of calculation depends on the following rule: if the accused (*śodhya*) possesses merit, a *paṇa* consisting of sixteen *māṣas* is taken as the unit; if the accused lacks merit, this *paṇa* consisting of ten *māṣas* is taken as the unit of calculation. Kātyāyana states the rules for ordeals (*divya*) according to the rules for accusations (*abhiśāpa*).
According to the specific nature of the offense, one should assign divine stations for men who have committed great sins (mahāpātakin) and been accused at the abode of Indra;
for those intent on treason against the king, one should assign them at the king’s gate.
For those born of inverse unions, the ordeal should be administered at a crossroads;
for other matters, however, the wise declare it should take place in the midst of the assembly hall.

In other matters—whether they be minor matters or even major ones—for the superior classes, oaths beginning with truth and ending with the person (satyādipuruṣāntāḥ) alone are prescribed. By the mention of "divine ordeal" (*divya*) in the phrase "the divine ordeal shall be administered," it should be understood that these include all ordeals from the balance (*ghaṭa*) to poison (*viṣa*). The term "Indra’s abode" (*indrasthāna*) indicates a temple of a well-known deity, as Nārada says: "The assembly hall, the palace gate, a deity, and a crossroads.
These divine ordeals must be administered in the very presence of the people. As Pitāmaha says:
The king, or his authorized official,
shall cause the ordeal to be administered directly before learned Brāhmaṇas as well as before the subjects.
*Prakṛti* means subjects; *adhikṛta* means a judge (*prāḍvivāka*). *Pratyakṣa* means that which has come before the eyes. Regarding this, Hārīta states a specific rule:
"When wealth has been stolen by thieves or even when it has been seized [by force], the owner himself shall clear up both its quantity and its nature by means of an oath."

When property has not been stolen by thieves, the owner shall establish the quantity and nature of that property—whether it be of large or small measure—by means of an oath alone, disregarding the claims of the police officers; this is the meaning. Thus ends the *Mātṛkā* applicable to all ordeals, and the method for the preparation of ordeals.

Now, the method for divine ordeals is described. Regarding this, Prajāpati says: "In divine ordeals, the presiding judge (prādvivāka) shall cause all matters to be manifested, just as the Adhvaryu priest does in sacrifices, while fasting by the king's command."
Having cut down a tree suitable for sacrifice, like a sacrificial post (yūpa), according to the prescribed mantras,
and having paid homage to the guardians of the world, the wise should construct the scale.

In this context, because of the mention of the *prāḍvivāka* (the presiding judge), the balance is to be used only in a court appointed by the king, and not in village or other local assemblies, as the *prāḍvivāka* is absent there. The phrase "having fasted" (*sopavāsa*) is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the previously mentioned observances. The syntactical connection is that the balance is to be employed by the king’s command. "Having cut" means having split [the wood]. Regarding the phrase "preceded by a mantra," he states the mantra: "O gentle one, you belong to the forest trees" (*saumyo vānaspatyaḥ*). "Gentle" (*saumya*) means having Soma as its deity; the mantra begins with "Soma [gave] the cow," and so forth. "Belonging to the forest trees" (*vānaspatya*) means having the Vanaspati as its deity; the mantra begins with "O Vanaspati, grow with a hundred shoots," and so forth. Viṣṇu states: "The balance must be made straight, from the *khadira* tree or from the *tinduka* tree. On this point, Prajāpati states a specific rule:
In that case, one should have [the staff] made of khadira wood, free from wounds and devoid of white [sap].
"White" refers to resin (*niryāsa*).
In its absence, however, one may use śiṃśapā or sāla wood, provided it is without hollows.
One should construct such chambers for the purpose of the balance.
The balance-beam should be made four cubits long, and its two supports should likewise be of that same measure;
the distance between them, however, should be two cubits or indeed one and a half cubits.
And likewise, the two side-arches of the gateway should always be made ten finger-breadths higher than the balance-beam.
"The construction of the balance-beam [185]:
two supports should be made from clay, facing downwards from the two arches, connected by a cord, and touching the top of the balance-beam. Thus it is said.

In this context, the felling of trees is for the sake of the scale, including all its ancillary parts (*saparikarāyās tulāyāḥ*). Therefore, it should be understood that the felling of those trees must also be performed for the sake of the pillar-stumps (*pādastambha*) [that support the scale]. By the statement, "The scale should be made four cubits long," the measurement of the scale together with its ancillary parts is stated. The phrase "of such a kind" (*tathāvidhau*) means measuring four cubits. The term "feet" (*pādau*) refers to the two pillars intended to support the wooden frame of the scale. These should be made to measure four cubits, rising above the two [cubits] used for the main body. However, it is taught that the two rings (*kaṭaka*) should be buried two cubits deep.

"The measure of those two is declared to be six cubits according to the standard. Thus, the measure of the axle is established by implication through the description of the distance between them; therefore, it should be understood that the axle-shaft must be made such that it extends outward from the socket attached to the pillar-base, being more than two and a half cubits long, rather than merely two cubits. Furthermore, a cubit consists of twenty-four finger-breadths (*aṅgula*).
"Eight horizontal barley-corns, or three vertical grains of rice."
The measure of a finger has been stated; a span (vitasti) consists of twelve fingers.

According to the Smṛti, "two spans (vitasti) make one cubit (hasta). However, since no specific thickness for the beam (tulā) is prescribed in the traditional texts, it should be made with such thickness as ensures its firmness. Alternatively, the specific thickness is to be understood from established custom. With this very intention, Pitāmaha stated:
"The balance-beam should be made four cubits long, firm, and likewise straight;
and rings should be carefully attached at three places."

"Rings" (kaṭakāni) are iron loops; they are to be placed at the two ends and in the middle. The distinction is that they are for supporting the suspension strings at the two ends, and for supporting the beam of the scale in the middle. As Pitāmaha has said:
"The knower of Dharma, having grasped it in the middle with an iron foot, should join the well-constructed scale so that it extends from east to west."
"Extending eastward and westward"—meaning long from the east to the west.
"The balance-beam should always be made motionless, facing east, in a clean place;
having attached two scales on both sides."
One should arrange the darbha grass with their tips pointing eastward upon the two scales; this is the settled rule.
One should place the persons to be weighed on one scale and auspicious earth on the other.
But if the reading is *kartuḥ*, the meaning is "the agent"—that is, the accused.
One should fill the *piṭaka* (basket) therein with bricks, stones, earth, and dust;

here, it should be understood that there is an option (*vikalpa*) among clay, bricks, stones, dust, and so forth. And this is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) for beans as well, because of the statement in another Smṛti: "Or one should fill the *vikaṭa* with beans. *Vikaṭa* refers to the vessel contained within the swing-balance (*śikya*).
Examiners should be appointed who are experts in weights and measures,
as well as merchants, goldsmiths, and likewise bell-metal workers.
The balance-beam must always be made by experts to be perfectly level;
and water must be poured upon the beam by the learned.
That balance on which water does not float is to be known as even;
one should always cause the balance to be made adorned with banners and flags.
Having first weighed the man, he should then cause him to descend.
Having thus prepared the balance according to the prescribed method, what should the judge do? To this he says:
"Then the judge, facing east and with palms joined in reverence, should speak."
Come, come, Blessed One; enter into this divine Dharma.
Having invoked Dharma into the balance along with the world-protectors, the Vasus, Ādityas, and the hosts of Maruts, one should subsequently assign the limbs [of the deity].
Having first established Indra in the east, likewise Yama, the Lord of the Dead, in the south;
Varuṇa in the western quarter, and Kubera in the north.
And one should place the world-protectors, beginning with Agni, in the corner regions:
Indra is yellow, Yama is dark, and Varuṇa has the luster of crystal.
Kubera has a golden luster, and Agni likewise has a golden luster;
similarly, Nirṛti appears dark-hued, and Vāyu appears smoky.
Īśāna, however, should be red; thus one should meditate upon these in sequence.
On the right side of Indra, the wise practitioner should cause the Vasus to be conveyed [there].
Dhara, Dhruva, Soma, Āpa, Anila, Anala,
Pratyūṣa, and Prabhāsa are proclaimed as the eight Vasus.
Between Deveśa and Īśāna is the path of the Ādityas;
namely Dhātṛ, Aryaman, Mitra, Varuṇa, Aṃśa, and Bhaga.
Indra, Vivasvat, Pūṣan, and Parjanya is recorded as the tenth;
after him Tvaṣṭṛ, then Viṣṇu, who, though born last, is not the least.

Thus these twelve Ādityas have been proclaimed by their names. Here, the terms *ajaghanya* ("not inferior") and *jaghanyaja* ("born later") are qualifiers of Tvaṣṭṛ and Viṣṇu respectively; therefore, there is no excess in the number. To the western part of Agni, however, the abode of the Rudras is traditionally taught.
And Vīrabhadra, Śambhu, and the highly renowned Vāgīśa.
Ajaikapād, Ahirbudhnya, Pinākin, and the unconquered Aparājita; Bhuvanādhīśvara and Kalipā as well, O lord of the people.
Sthāṇu and the blessed Bhaga are remembered as the eleven Rudras;
one should designate the station of the Mothers between Prajeśa and Rakaso.
Brāhmī, Māheśvarī, Kaumārī,
Vaiṣṇavī, Vārāhī, Māhendrī, and Cāmuṇḍā, surrounded by their hosts.
They know the abode of Gaṇeśa to be in the northern part of Nirṛti;
the station of the Maruts is said to be in the northern part of Varuṇa.
[The names of the Maruts are: Gagana, Sparśana, Vāyu, Anila, and likewise Māruta.
Prāṇa, Prāṇeśa, and Jīva, along with the eight Maruts, are proclaimed [as the vital breaths].
But in another Smṛti it is said: "Āvaha, Vivaha, Udvaha, Saṃvaha,
Nivaha, Adhivaha, Pravaha, and likewise Abhivaha."
There is an option regarding these two.
A wise person should invoke Durgā in the northern part of the balance.
It is known that the worship of these deities is performed by their own names.
Having given ornaments and garments for the sake of Dharma, one should offer the arghya and other items in due order.

"Ending with ornaments" (*bhūṣāvasānam*) means up to the ornaments. This is the summary here: having invoked Dharma into the balance with the mantra "Come, come," and having offered to the invoked Dharma the guest-water (*arghya*), water for the feet (*pādya*), water for sipping (*ācamanīya*), the bath, clothing, water for sipping, the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*), water for sipping, and ornaments ending with genuine gold; and having performed the worship—beginning with the guest-water and ending with the ornaments—for Indra and the others down to Durgā according to the sequence of individual items (*padārthānusamaya*); one should then offer to both [Dharma and the deities] perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, food offerings (*naivedya*), and so forth. Regarding the balance-worship (*dhaṭapūjā*), the flowers and perfumes should be red. As Nārada said:
"One should offer red flowers, perfumes, incense, lamps, unbroken rice, and so forth;
one should first worship the balance (dhaṭa) and likewise honor the remaining deities.
Thus, the worship of Indra and the others may be performed with red flowers or other colors, as no specific distinction is seen. All of this should be carried out in the forenoon.
"The administration of all divine ordeals is proclaimed for the forenoon," according to the statement of Nārada. And Prajāpati says that the presiding judge (*prāḍvivāka*) should perform this:
"Then the presiding judge shall be a Brahmin who has reached the further shore of the Vedas and Vedānta."
Endowed with learning and virtuous conduct, his mind is tranquil and free from envy.
True to his word, pure, and skillful, he was devoted to the welfare of all living beings;
having fasted and dressed in clean garments, he had set out in pursuit of his beloved.
One should perform the worship of all the deities according to the prescribed rules;
likewise, a fire sacrifice (homa) should be performed in the four directions by those who have mastered the Vedas.
With clarified butter, sacrificial oblation, and fuel-sticks as the means for the fire-oblation.
"One should contemplate with the Sāvitrī, the Praṇava, and likewise with that which ends in Svāhā.

Thus spoke Vijñānayogin regarding the method of the fire-oblation (*homa*): "The four officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), having recited the Gāyatrī preceded by the Praṇava in the four directions over a common fire (*laukikāgni*), and then having recited the Praṇava ending with the utterance of *svāhā*, should offer one hundred and eight fuel-sticks (*samidh*), clarified butter (*ājya*), and sacrificial porridge (*caru*) for each.
And whatever matter one may be intent upon, having written it upon a leaf...
"Accompanied by this mantra, that [document] should be placed upon the head.

Thus, having performed the worship of the deity ending with the fire-oblation (*homa*), one should subsequently write the matter under dispute along with the mantra on a leaf and place that leaf upon the head of the person to be purified; this is the meaning. As for the mantra:
"The sun and the moon, fire and wind, heaven, earth, water, the heart, and Yama;
day and night, both twilights, and Dharma—these know the conduct of a man.
As for that which was said by Prajāpati:
"One should employ this entire ritual procedure for the mantra in all divine ordeals;
likewise, one should arrange the invocation of the divine [deities].

This is the meaning: it should be understood that the section of the performance beginning with the invocation of Dharma and ending with the placing of the leaf upon the head has been stated as common to all divine ordeals. Immediately thereafter, the judge, having addressed the balance, shall cause the person to be purified to ascend it again.
Then, having secured him with pledges, one should place the man back [on the wheel];
having placed a leaf upon his head in a windless place free from rain.

Oaths are equal [in weight]. And those oaths have been shown by him [Manu] himself: "Whatever worlds belong to the slayer of a Brahmin, and whatever worlds belong to false witnesses—those same worlds belong to the one who holds the scales falsely. Thus it is said.
Furthermore, after the mounting has been completed, Nārada says:
"When that very target has been made, the twice-born shall say:
'O Balance, you have been ordained by Brahmā for the purpose of testing the wicked-souled.'"
Because you are the embodiment of Dharma through the letter *dha*, and because you hold and contemplate the crooked man through the letter *ṭa*,
you are therefore called *Dhaṭa*.
You know the sins and the good deeds of all living beings;
you alone, O God, know those things which human beings do not perceive.
"This man, accused in a legal proceeding, desires purification;
therefore, you ought to deliver him from this doubt in accordance with the Dharma.
Immediately thereafter, the person to be purified should address the balance, as Yājñavalkya has said:
Not separated from those who know the rules for weighing with a balance, he rests upon the scale;
having been made equal by the counterweights and having drawn a line, he is then lowered.
The consecration of the balance: O Balance, you are the abode of truth, fashioned of old by the gods;
therefore, speak the truth, O auspicious one, and release me from my doubt.
"If I am a doer of evil deeds, then lead me downward;
if I am pure, lead me upward"—with these words, one should consecrate the scale.
Regarding this, Nārada says:
"Having firmly attached two balances to the hooks of the beam,
one should place a man on one scale and a stone on the other."
Regarding the two *dhaṭas* (balance-beams) resembling the horns of a crab— two iron rings attached at both ends—
one should place a person on the northern side and a stone on the southern side.
Having again mounted the balance-beam with the leaf-plate positioned upon its head, one should keep it in that very state for five *vināḍīs*.
Regarding the definition of the *vināḍī* and other units:
"Five *vināḍīs* are to be known and examined by those skilled in time.
Thus, the duration of the pronunciation of ten long syllables (*gurvakṣara*) is one *prāṇa*, and six *prāṇas* constitute one *vināḍī*; this is also stated in the *Jyotiḥśāstra*.
"Ten long syllables constitute one *prāṇa*; six *prāṇas* make one *vināḍikā*;
sixty of those make a *ghaṭikā*, and sixty of those are called a day.
By this [definition], one who is conversant with the science of astrology (*jyotiḥśāstra*) should be appointed as a single expert among those skilled in weighing.
[192] Prajāpati has stated the manner of determining purity and impurity, as well as the method for deciding between purity and impurity, regarding the balance scale.
If, when weighed, he increases in weight, he is pure; of this there is no doubt.
But if he remains equal or decreases in weight, that man would not be pure.

As for that which was stated by Pitāmaha—"One who is declining would not be pure; among these, however, one who is equal is pure"—that is intended as a citation of another opinion for the sake of honor, and not for the purpose of providing an option. It is the same elsewhere.

"In the case of the snapping of the whip, the breaking of the balance-beam, likewise for the *dhaṭa* and the *karkaṭa*, as well as the breaking of the rope or the failure of the axle— one should declare [the result] to be impure. Nevertheless, when the cause of the breaking is visible and not due to the power of the unseen (*adṛṣṭa*), then, having performed a propitiatory rite (*samādhāna*), one should perform the weighing again.
"And if the sling or other parts are cut or broken, one should have the man weighed again"—such is the statement from another Smṛti. For this very reason, Bṛhaspati says:
"If a person appointed to the balance, when weighed, is found to have lost weight, he shall suffer defeat."
But when they are equal, the one that has increased further shall be the victor.
In the event of the breaking of the sling or the snapping of the rope, the king shall provide a new sling;
the witnesses shall be eminent Brāhmaṇas who speak according to what they have actually seen.
The king should appoint kinsmen who are pure and free from greed;
the determination of purity or impurity must be understood according to their testimony.
"The sacrificial fee must be given to the officiating priests," said the Grandfather (Brahmā).
"One should satisfy the officiating priests, family priests, and teachers with sacrificial fees.
Having caused this to be done, the king, having enjoyed delightful pleasures, [should proceed].
He attains great fame and is fit for becoming one with Brahman.
[193] The Method for Guarding the Balance: Pitāmaha states the method for guarding the balance.
One should cause a spacious, elevated, and bright weighing-hall to be constructed,
situated where it cannot be disturbed by dogs, outcasts, or crows.
In those very directions, one should install the world-protectors and the others;
one should worship them at the three junctions of the day with perfumes, garlands, and ointments.
"The king should cause [the hall] to be kept non-empty, provided with door-panels and seeds, guarded by attendants, and supplied with clay, water, and fire.

Here, "seeds" refers to barley, rice, and so forth. Vijñānayogin, however, states: "When he wishes to place the balance (dhaṭa) in that very manner as described, then he should construct a hall equipped with doors and other such features for the purpose of preventing interference from dogs, crows, and the like."
Thus ends the procedure for the ordeal by balance;
now follows the procedure for fire;
next, the procedure for fire is being described.
I shall proclaim the ritual procedure for the fire as enjoined by each respective Vedic branch;
one should cause eight mandalas to be made in front, and likewise a ninth.
The first mandala is of Agni; the second is known as that of Varuṇa;
the third has Vāyu as its deity; and the fourth has Yama as its deity.
The fifth mandala is said by the wise to have Indra as its deity;
the sixth is called Kaubera, and the seventh has Soma as its deity.
The eighth is that of Āditya, and the ninth is that of all the deities;
those who know the scriptures understand these to be the eight maṇḍalas.
These nine mandalas should be prepared with cow dung in a location designated as a shrine for renowned deities and the like, ending toward the east. Regarding this, Hārīta says:
"The calculation of the area of the ground is said to be two hundred and fifty-six finger-breadths when measured by eight mandalas."
The mandala is to be known as sixteen finger-breadths (aṅgulas) in extent, and the interval between mandalas is likewise.

The measurement of a finger-breadth has been demonstrated in the section on the balance (tulā). Pitāmaha has also stated: "They say the mandala is thirty-two finger-breadths, and so is the interval between mandalas."
Thus, with eight mandalas, there are two hundred finger-breadths.
The measurement of the ground should be calculated as fifty-six [units]; the maṇḍala should be constructed according to its dimensions so that it is equal in size to the [central] square.

In that context, the ninth mandala has an immeasurable number of finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) as its measure. Excluding that, by means of eight *saṇḍalas* and eight intervals, each measuring sixteen finger-breadths, a total of two hundred and fifty-six finger-breadths is obtained. Even there, only seven mandalas are to be traversed. How so? Because one stands at the first and casts [the stone] into the ninth.
Now, it is said: "They declare a mandala and the interval between mandalas to be thirty-two finger-breadths."
Thus, with eight mandalas, there are two hundred finger-breadths.
If it is asked how the statement of Nārada— that [the earth] exceeds forty finger-breadths in measurement— can be so:

It is said: that refers to the intention of proceeding from the mandala of abiding to another mandala to be traversed. This is the meaning: starting from the mandala of abiding, which measures sixteen *aṅgulas*, each subsequent other mandala—beginning with the second—is thirty-two *aṅgulas* long, including the intervening space. Thus, the mandala of abiding is sixteen *aṅgulas*, and the seven mandalas to be traversed, together with their intervening spaces, are forty *aṅgulas*. Therefore, by means of these eight mandalas, there are two hundred and forty *aṅgulas* of ground. Here, when the common rules mentioned in the *Dviyamṛtṛka* have been performed, and the ritual procedure ending with the head-leaf as described in the *Tulāprakaraṇa* has been completed, Prajāpati states a specific rule regarding the rite of fire (*agnividhi*).
In the western mandala, the pure person to be purified should stand facing east with palms joined.
"Should stand" refers to the one being purified. He states the method of purification:
"The examiners should observe any wounds or other marks on the hands of that [person] who is undergoing the ordeal."
The *lakṣaṇa*—that is, the mark—is as Nārada has stated:

"In all cases of hand wounds, one should make 'swan's foot' marks. This means that one should brand with the shape of a swan's foot at the sites of scars using lac juice and other substances. When it is asked what follows from this, Yājñavalkya says:
Having observed that the hands have been rubbed with rice grains,
one should then place seven leaves of the *aśvattha* tree upon them and wrap them in bright white cloths.
One should wrap the hands with seven white threads of cotton.

Thus, according to the words of Nārada, one should place seven *aśvattha* leaves on top, along with seven *śamī* leaves, seven *dūrvā* leaves, curds, and unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*). Likewise, Pitāmaha says: "Seven *pippala* leaves, *śamī* leaves, and unbroken rice grains;
seven leaves of *dūrvā*, and likewise unbroken rice grains mixed with curds."
The word "should place" (*vinyaset*) is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence]. One should also place flowers. And so says Pitāmaha:
"One should place seven *pippala* leaves, unbroken grains (*akṣata*), flowers, and curd there in the hands, likewise encircled by a thread."
*Sumanas* refers to flowers. As for that which was stated by Hārīta:
"If one carries heated iron, shielded from the hands by seven *arka* leaves, he is purified if he is not burned by the time he reaches the seventh step."

[196] Thus it is said; however, in the absence of *aśvattha* leaves, this should be understood as referring to *arka* leaves, because the primary status of *aśvattha* leaves is established by the statement praising them for the Grandfather (Brahmā):
"Fire is born from the *pippala*; the *pippala* is remembered as the king of trees.
Therefore, a wise man should place its leaves in his two hands."

Thus says Vijñānayogin. Others, however, say that this passage is intended to mean that there is no inclusion of *śamī* leaves and the like within the category of *arka* leaves. On this point, Prajāpati states:
"One should fashion a round [ball] made of iron, eight finger-breadths in size and devoid of sharp edges;
one should heat this ball, which is prescribed to weigh fifty palas, in the fire."
On this point Vyāsa says:
"Then, wearing wet clothes and remaining pure, he should stand facing east with his fingers and limbs extended, having placed a leaf upon his head."
One who is a blacksmith by birth, skilled in the work of fire,
and experienced in other practical applications— by him one should cause the iron to be placed in the fire.
Furthermore, having bathed a red-hot iron ball, glowing like fire and emitting sparks,
weighing fifty palas, the twice-born man, purified, [should proceed].

"One should address the one undergoing the third heating while placing truth before him. By the phrase "and this practice is seen elsewhere," the author of the *Candrikā* maintains that these statements—beginning with "one undergoing the third heating"—are restatements of matters established by logic; for he argues that just as in the world, when iron is heated until red-hot and then plunged into water, it is subsequently heated again to accomplish its intended purpose, so too should it be done here. Regarding the term "placing truth before him" (*satyapuraskṛta*), Pitāmaha describes its nature:
Listen to this law of Manu, which is presided over by the world-protectors.
O Agni, you are the supreme purifier and the mouth of all the gods.
O Agni, dwelling within the hearts of all beings, you know their every action.
On this point, Yājñavalkya says:
"When he has spoken thus, one should place a ball of iron weighing fifty palas and heated to the color of fire upon both his hands."
Of him—the agent—in this very manner:
"O Agni, you move within all the gods like a witness;
you alone, O god, know those things which human beings do not know."
"This man, accused in a legal dispute, seeks purification;
since you indeed purify sin, you are therefore called Pāvaka (the Purifier)."
"O Purifier, reveal yourself among the wicked and become radiant;
or else, O Consumer of Oblations, become cool through your pure nature.
On this point, Vyāsa says:
"By this truth, this man sustains you;
O Consumer of Oblations, become cool toward him whose word is true, but burn the hands of this deceitful sinner who speaks falsehood. Thus [he said].
Prajāpati has stated the subsequent duty:
having caused the accused to hear this mantra written upon the leaf according to the facts, one should place it upon his head in this manner, following the proper sequence.
Manu states the method of the ritual placement (nyāsa):
"Having said this, he should place into his hands a ball of fire that is well-heated, unbent, and drawn from a fire with sparks."
The meaning is that it is not bent, its surface is not depressed, and it remains in its natural state.
"Having firmly grasped with tongs, [it should be] like the brilliance of a network of lightning" (verse 198).
It is held upright so that it does not melt; thus it is called *anuddhṛta* (not drawn out). Then Yama states the procedure for purification:
Having taken them with both hands and standing near the judge,
he should then walk seven steps in a straight line toward another spot.
"In one"—that is, in the first [or western] mandala. "Straight-going" means one whose path is not crooked.
"Unperturbed," he should walk slowly and without anger toward the fire.
As Yājñavalkya has said:
"Taking that, he should walk slowly for exactly seven circles.

Here, "he" refers to the man. "That" refers to the heated iron ball. By the use of the particle *eva* ("exactly"), [the text] indicates that the placement of the foot must be upon the circles themselves; furthermore, Pitāmaha shows that one must not overstep the circles nor place the foot short of them:
"One should not overstep a circle, nor should one place the foot before it."
Having reached the eighth circle, the man should then cast the fire;
however, he who causes it to fall in between should be punished, and he must demonstrate his innocence.
One should cause that fire to be carried away again; this rule has been firmly established.
Yājñavalkya states the consecration of the performer standing within the first mandala:
"O Agni, Purifier, you move within all beings;
you are the witness of my merits and sins; O Sage, speak the truth for me."

"Speak the truth; show [it]"—this is the meaning. Herein is the procedure: having cast a well-heated iron ball into water for the purpose of purifying the metal, and having heated it again and cast it into water a second time, one should take hold of it with tongs during the third heating and, bringing it back, recite the consecration mantra: "O Fire, [you who are] among all beings... At this juncture, the judge (prāḍvivāka), having established a common fire in the southern region of the circle, should offer one hundred and eight oblations of clarified butter into it with the mantra "To Agni Pāvaka... According to the author of the *Candrikā*, the heating of the iron ball takes place in this very fire. As for what should be done after standing in the eighth circle and performing the abandonment of the fire in the ninth, Yājñavalkya says: [he should proceed].
Having released the fire and having crushed the grains of rice, he shall obtain purification and be exempt from punishment;
regarding this, Kātyāyana states a specific rule: "If the accused does not stumble, he is not burned at a spot other than the original place."
The gods know him to be unburnt; one should cause him to undergo [the ordeal] once again.
"Other than the place"—the meaning is "other than with the two hands. But Prajāpati says:
"If the rice-ball falls in between, or if there is doubt, it should be performed again. But if it has been stolen, one should later crush grains of rice or barley."

When, while walking, the ball falls within the interval—specifically before the eighth circle—and after the rice and barley have been crushed, a doubt arises because there is no determination as to whether he is liable to punishment or not, then [the test] should be performed again. Even in the second application, when a doubt arises, it follows by logic that the ordeal should be held again, even in the absence of an explicit statement such as "one should take [the test] repeatedly. As Vijñānayogī said: "The phrase 'one should take [it] repeatedly' is stated as being implied by the sense" (on YDh 2.107cd). In this case, a certificate of purification (*viśuddhipatra*) should be given by the king to one who is pure; for one who is impure, there is only expulsion preceded by punishment. Regarding this, Nārada says:
"By this method, it should always be worn like fire,
except during the summer, at midday, or at other very cold times. Here,
"like fire" refers to a red-hot iron ball.
Thus ends the procedure for fire; now the procedure for water.

Now the procedure for the water ordeal (*jalavidhi*) is described. Regarding this, the *Candrikā* states that both the water ordeal and the poison ordeal (*viṣavidhi*) have been set forth. As the author of the *Candrikā* has said: "[200] Since the performance of the water and poison ordeals has declined, their procedures will not be explained; instead, the procedure for the *kośa* ordeal is now stated. This is because in certain regions such as Utkala and others, the water ordeal alone is practiced as authoritative, whereas in certain regions such as Śūrasena and Magadha, the poison ordeal alone is accepted as authoritative. Therefore, the procedure for the water ordeal is stated here according to its sequential order. In this regard, Prajāpati says:
Now I shall proclaim the ancient, righteous procedure for the ordeal by water,
which was ordained by Brahmā himself for the purpose of testing truth and falsehood (or good and evil).
"One should indeed worship the arrows with devotion, as well as the Vaiṣṇava bow;
one should adorn them with flowers and incense, and then commence the ritual.
On this point, Kātyāyana says:
For the sake of purification, one should fashion arrows with tips not made of iron;
they may also be made from bamboo stalks, and the shooter, being very firm, should discharge them.
The thrower must be a Kṣatriya— or indeed, it is said that the thrower may even be a non-Brāhmaṇa—
provided he is of gentle heart, peaceful, and has observed a fast; then he should cast [the arrow].

Thus, from the words of Pitāmaha. On this point, Nārada says: "A cruel bow is known to be seven hundred [inches], a middling one six hundred, and a mild one five hundred; this is to be understood as the rule for bows."

"Seven hundred" means one hundred and seven finger-breadths; the meaning is that [the distance] is cruel. Likewise for six hundred or five hundred. However, with a medium bow, the wise man should discharge three arrows, having set the target at one hundred and fifty cubits.
But there would be a fault in shooting arrows that are either too short or too long.
[201] Thus:
Having discharged three arrows with a bow that is not too fierce,
one should perform the ritual immersion in water whenever suspicion is perceived.

The meaning is that he against whom suspicion is known is the one to be accused. For the purpose of indicating the mark (*lakṣa*), an archway (*toraṇa*) should be constructed. Thus he [Nārada] himself says: "An archway should be made there for the junction of the marked object and the mark.

The "junction of the marked object and the mark" (*lakṣyalakṣaṇayoḥ saṃdhiḥ*) means their meeting point—that is to say, their thorough identification. And that archway should be built near the place of immersion on level ground, raised to the height of the ear of the person to be purified. As Nārada says:
"Having gone to that body of water, one should erect a gateway on the bank;
however, one should perform the ritual actions on a level and pure portion of ground.
Regarding this, Nārada says:
A Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, or a Vaiśya, free from passion and hatred,
should place a man in water reaching up to the navel, as if he were a pillar standing on dry land.
One who is under a curse should submerge himself while grasping the thighs of that [woman].
Regarding this, Yājñavalkya says:
"O Varuṇa, protect me by means of truth," having thus invoked the water.
"Standing in water reaching up to the navel, one should enter the water after grasping the thighs.

Here, *kaṃ* means water. "Protect me with truth, O Varuṇa"—this is the consecration (*abhimantraṇa*) by means of the mantra; "one should enter the water" means one should immerse oneself. And this [is required] when there is worship of Varuṇa. As Nārada says:
"With fragrant perfumes and garlands, and with honey, milk, clarified butter, and so forth..."
One should first perform worship to Varuṇa with a concentrated mind.

[202] Thus it is said. Likewise, when all the common rites for divine ordeals are present—beginning with the invocation of Dharma (*dharmāvāhana*) and including the worship of all the deities, the fire-oblation (*homa*), the recitation of mantras, and ending with the placement of the written pledge (*pratijñāpatra*) upon the head—and furthermore:
"O Water, you are the life-force of living beings, the primordial cause of creation, and you are declared to be the cause of purification for substances as well as for embodied beings."
"Therefore, reveal yourself for the examination of the auspicious and the inauspicious.

Thus, when the presiding judge has performed the consecration of the water with mantras, the person undergoing purification should pray to the water, saying: "O Varuṇa, protect me by means of truth. On this point, Prajāpati says:
"In water free from grass and aquatic weeds, and devoid of leeches and fish..."
One should immerse oneself in water that reaches up to the navel, neither in water that is too deep nor in water that is too shallow.
One should always enter water that is pure and free from waves and mud; one should avoid water that has been drawn out and that found in rivers with swift currents.

"Extracted"—meaning drawn out by means of a water-wheel (*dhaṭa*) and other such devices. By this, it is implied that the water which is free from defects in rivers of little current, as well as in lakes, ponds, reservoirs, and the like, is "purifying. As it is said: "The king should first place a man in the water like a pillar, leaning upon which men desiring purification may immerse themselves."
Regarding this, a specific rule is stated in another Smṛti:

"He should stand in water facing the east, grasping a pillar of Dharma. On this point, Śaṅkha and Likhita state: "Standing in water reaching the navel, he should stand facing the east, leaning against a pillar of Dharma made from a sacrificial tree. Regarding "his thighs"—meaning the thighs of the man desired [as witness]. A "man desired" is one possessing the characteristics previously mentioned. Nārada states a further distinction in this regard:
"A wise man should not discharge arrows when a strong wind from the Maruts is blowing,
nor on uneven ground, nor where it is crowded with trees and thickets.
Thus says the Grandfather (Brahmā) in this regard.
The movement and immersion of both the goer and the maker are equal;
however, the victorious man, being swift, should proceed to the base of the arch from the position of the target.
When he had gone, the second man also, taking up an arrow, would go with speed to the foot of the tree; then that man departed.
But when the arrow-retriever, having entered the water, does not clearly see [the arrow] situated within the water, then one should declare him impure.
Otherwise, it would not be pure even upon the observation of a single factor,
because of its remaining in one place or moving elsewhere from where it was previously established.
The phrase "even of a single limb" refers to the ears and so forth.
One whose head alone is seen, but neither the ears nor the nose,
when entering the water, should be declared pure.
Thus, because of this specific statement, Nārada declares the determination of the nature of victory here:
"Of the fifty *yāvaka* measures, whichever two should be in excess in the water,
those two are to be employed there in the act of bringing forth the arrows."

The procedure for this is as follows: The presiding judge (prāḍvivāka), having erected a gateway (toraṇa) near a body of water and having placed the target at the prescribed distance, shall worship the bow and arrows near the gateway. Having invoked and worshipped Varuṇa in the body of water, and having honored the deities beginning with Dharma on its bank with the rites of invocation and other offerings, he shall bind the written pledge to the head of the person undergoing purification. The presiding judge himself, having consecrated the water with the mantra beginning, "O Water, you are the life-breath of living beings," and after the person undergoing purification has consecrated the water with the mantra beginning with "By Truth," he shall cause the defendant to go toward a strong man standing waist-deep in the water, or toward a pillar of Dharma (dharmasthūṇā). Immediately thereafter, when three arrows have been released, one swift man runs to the spot where the middle arrow falls, takes it, and stands right there. Another swift man stands at the base of the gateway, at the place from which the arrows were shot. While these two are thus stationed, at the third clap of hands, the defendant plunges into the water. At that very same moment, the man standing at the base of the gateway also runs even more swiftly to the spot where the middle arrow fell. When the man who took the arrow arrives there, he runs back even more swiftly to the base of the gateway; if he does not see the defendant within the water upon reaching it, then the defendant is purified. Having fixed the target at a distance of one hundred and fifty cubits, the two swift men must run to and pursue the target up to the gateway. Some maintain that this specific distance is primary, because a fault is heard of if the distance is less or more than one hundred and fifty cubits. Others hold that the requirement for the worship of the bow, arrows, and so forth implies that this is for the purpose of a restrictive rule (niyama).
Thus ends the ritual for water;
now follows the ritual for poison. Regarding that, Prajāpati says:
I shall now declare the procedure for poison as enjoined by the experts;
it should be administered to the accused, and it is given in a dose the size of a barley grain.
Seven barley-grains, or else six in number,
of the poison from the horned *vatsanābha* and of the golden (*haima*) poison should be administered.
One should avoid all poisons that have been administered, those that are decomposed, as well as those that are artificial, and all those produced from the earth.
But Nārada says:
"One should carefully avoid that which is fallen, as well as that which is practiced, fumigated, mixed, kālakūṭa, and alābhu poison. Thus it is said.
"Conduct—having examined what remains after his conduct [has been observed];
and the king should also examine the medicinal herbs and gems that remove poison through the application of mantras, as well as those residing within the body of the practitioner. Thus it is said.
The establishment of the numbers seven and so forth should be understood according to the distinction of seasons. Thus Nārada says:
"In the rainy season, [the shadow] is the measure of four barley-corns; in summer, it is recorded as five barley-corns;
in winter, seven barley-corns; and in autumn, it is even smaller than that."
"For one who has fasted, he should indeed give [the food] in the presence of the deity and a Brāhmaṇa.

The term "small" means six barley-corns (*yava*). This is because the word "thence" (*tataḥ*) refers back to the number seven. By the word "hemanta" (winter), the *śiśira* (cool season) is also included; for *hemanta* and *śiśira* are generally heard together as a compound, as in the formula "I gratify the seasons Hemanta-Śiśira," and so forth. Vijñāneśvara states: "Since spring (*vasanta*) is common to all ordeals, there too there are seven barley-corns. As for the measurement of a barley-corn:
That subtle particle of dust which is seen when the sun shines through a lattice opening is declared to be the first among measurements, known as a *rasareṇu*.
Eight *trasareṇu*s should be known as one *likṣā* in terms of measurement;
three of those [likṣās] are a *rājasarṣapa*, and three of those are a *gaurasarṣapa*.

"Six *yava*s make a medium-sized mustard seed (*sarṣapa*); three *yava*s are known as a *kṛṣṇala*; five *kṛṣṇala*s make a *māṣa*, and sixteen of those make a *suvarṇa*. Thus it is said. Hārīta has stated another distinction:
"In the forenoon, in a cool place, the poison soaked in ghee should be administered.

[206] Here, the word "forenoon" (pūrvāhṇa) is intended as an exclusive specification (parisaṃkhyā), meaning that one who knows the Dharma should not administer it in the afternoon, nor at midday, nor at twilight.
Thus, because of the traditional rule prohibiting [the administration of poison] at other times: "Ghee should be taken as thirty times the amount of the poison;
for poison should indeed be administered to embodied beings in the forenoon in a cool place, finely mixed with ghee, and the ghee should be endowed with thirty times [the quantity of] the poison."
Thus, according to the traditional teaching of Kātyāyana, the sequence of the procedure was stated by Pitāmaha:
"Poison should be administered to one who has fasted in the presence of Brāhmaṇas,
after having worshipped Maheśvara with offerings of boiled rice and mantras."
"In the presence of the deities, while standing facing south, a Brahmin, composed in mind, should give [the gift] while facing north or east. Thus it is said.

Thus, the summary here is as follows: The judge, having fasted, shall worship Mahādeva with the sixteen types of offerings (*ṣoḍaśopacāra*). Having placed before Him either the *śārṅga* poison or Himalayan (*haimavata*) poison soaked in clarified butter (*ghṛta*), he shall perform the entire procedure for the ordeal (*divyamātṛkā*), beginning with the invocation of Dharma and ending with the placing of the leaf upon the scales. Then, having consecrated the poison with mantras, while facing east or north himself, he gives the poison to the person to be tested, who faces south. The sequence is that the person to be tested, having consecrated the poison with mantras, shall consume it.
