O Poison, you were created by Brahmā for the purpose of testing the wicked-minded;
reveal yourself to the sinful, but become nectar for those who are pure.
"O Poison, you are indeed proclaimed by Brahmā to be the very form of death.
Protect this man from sin; by truth, become nectar for him. Thus [ends the mantra]. Now, the mantra for the consecration of the poison by the person undergoing purification is as follows:
O Poison, you are the son of Brahmā, established in truth and righteousness;
protect us from this curse, and by virtue of that truth, become nectar for me.

[207] Thus. Regarding this, Pitāmaha states that the person undergoing purification must be protected from deceivers and the like: "The king should have the one performing the ordeal guarded by his own men for three nights or five nights, out of fear of deceivers and the like."
Likewise, he [the same author] says that even poison must be protected:
"The Śārṅga from the Himalayas is recommended, endowed with fragrance, color, and taste; it should be unadulterated, not confounded, and not treated with mantras. Thus.
The meaning is that he must be protected in such a way that he becomes characterized by the aforementioned qualities.

As it is said: "But when, having consumed [the medicine], he is restored to health, free from fainting and vomiting, and remains without abnormal symptoms at the end of the day, one should designate him as pure."
And this waiting for the time at the end of the day is merely indicative of the duration it takes for the poison to be digested; it is not a restrictive rule. Accordingly, Yājñavalkya states:
"Having spoken thus, one should consume the Śārṅga poison born of the snowy mountains.
One whose body digests it without [adverse] effects should be declared pure."

When poison has been administered in an excessive dose, one should wait for a period measured by five hundred claps of hands (pañca-tāla-śata) and only thereafter perform medical treatment; thus says the Grandfather (Brahmā):
"When one remains free from any adverse reaction for a time of five hundred tālas, then one becomes purified; only then should one administer medical treatment."

Regarding this, the Vijñānayogin stated: "When poison has been drunk, one must wait for as long as five hundred claps of hands; thereafter, one should administer treatment. Having thus specified the primary period of observation, he added: "The statement regarding purity—'if there are no adverse symptoms at the end of the day,' and so forth—refers only to cases of very small doses. This is weak. For it is said: "One should consume *śārṅga* poison from the snowy mountains. If it is digested without its characteristic effects, one should declare that person to be pure."
Thus, in the statement of Yājñavalkya regarding the digestion of poison:
"When he has become completely purified, then one should administer medical treatment."

Otherwise, even the instruction on medical treatment (*cikitsā*) in the words of Pitāmaha would be contradicted. Therefore, the statement prescribing medical treatment must be understood as referring to cases where the poison has been administered in excessive quantity, by way of waiting for a period of time measured by five hundred hand-claps. Thus, the system of subject-matter (*viṣayavyavasthā*) stated by us alone is correct. As for what Vijñānayogin stated—that "the so-called 'poison-impulse' (*viṣavega*) is the movement of one constituent element (*dhātu*) into another" (on YDh 2.111)—that should be understood as intended in a general sense (*prāyika*), because such a nature is impossible in the case of the very first impulse of the poison. Consequently, it should be understood that Vijñānayogin intended to say merely that the "impulse" (*vega*) is the transition of the poison through the constituent elements (*dhātusaṃkrāma*). [The constituents are: "skin, blood, flesh, fat, bone, marrow, and semen are the constituent elements."

In this manner, a certificate of purity should be granted by the king to one who is pure; for the other, punishment and so forth must be administered. Thus ends the procedure for the ordeal by poison.
Now follows the procedure for the ordeal by sacred libation (*kośa*).

The judge, having observed a fast, shall bathe fierce deities such as Durgā, Āditya, and others, and collect that water in a copper vessel or similar container. Having worshipped those deities with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, he shall lead the bathing water to the place of ordeal. Then, having performed the common procedure for all ordeals—beginning with the invocation of Dharma (Dharmāvāhana) and ending with the placing of the document upon the head—he shall have the person to be purified face eastward and, while standing within a circle smeared with cow-dung, cause him to drink three handfuls (prasṛti) of water from what was previously collected. Thus says Pitāmaha:
Having made the practitioner face the east, one should have him drink three handfuls [of the substance],
provided he has bathed according to the previously mentioned procedure, is wearing wet clothes, and is pure.

"By what was stated previously"—that is, by what has been said regarding the procedure common to all ordeals. "The one performing the ordeal"—the person undergoing the divine test. And so says Yājñavalkya:
"Having worshipped the fierce deities, one should fetch the water from their bathing;
having made [the defendant] hear the charge, one should have him drink three handfuls (prasṛti) of that water. Thus it is said.
But Nārada says:
"Having summoned him who has been cursed and placed within the circle,
and having made him face the sun, one should have him drink three handfuls [of water]."
Hārīta, however, states: "One should make the person drink [the liquid] on ground smeared with cow-dung after he has been purified.
Yājñavalkya, for his part, describes the method of purification.
"If a terrible calamity caused by kings or fate befalls us within fourteen days [of the ordeal], he is pure; of this there is no doubt.
Thus [it is said]. Furthermore, Nārada states that beyond that limit there is no fault.
“If, after two weeks have passed, a great abnormality should occur, he should not be subjected [to the ordeal] by a wise man, because the appointed time has elapsed.

This refers to the subject of major ordeals (*mahābhiyoga*), since it is stated following the introductory remark: “In major ordeals, these [ordeals] are used. Other time limits for minor matters were stated by Pitāmaha, as they pertain to small-scale cases, according to the traditional law (*smṛti*): “But in a minor case, one should cause [the defendant] to undergo the *kośa* ordeal.”

“Whether after three nights, seven nights, ten days, or fourteen days, he in whom a deformity (*vaikṛta*) is observed is declared a wrongdoer. Since the phrase “fourteen days” has the same meaning as the statement of Yājñavalkya, this refers to the subject of a major accusation (*mahābhiyoga*). This very point was stated by Vijñānayogin: “The period of three nights and so forth should be established by dividing the object mentioned in the case of a major accusation into three parts, starting from the lower value of the property. Pitāmaha states the ordeals pertaining to the divine (*daivika*):
Consumption, diarrhea, eruptive boils, affliction of the wind and bones,
eye disease, water-related ailments, and likewise insanity arise.
"Headaches and the breaking of arms—these are the diseases of men caused by fate.
Regarding "royal [affliction]" (*rājakam*), it refers to royal punishment. As Viṣṇu has said:
"If one should see [the effects] within fourteen days, or likewise within twenty-one days..."
Sickness, fire, the death of kinsmen, or even royal punishment—these are the obstacles.
One should know that to be impure, and pure by the opposite;
the term "royal punishment" (rājadaṇḍa) indicates both the loss of wealth and the depletion of assets.
Illness, fire, the death of a kinsman, the loss of wealth, and the depletion of assets [are signs of impurity].

Thus it is stated by Nārada. The author of the *Candrikā* explains: "The word 'wealth' (*artha*) refers to sons and so forth. For this very reason, Pitāmaha declared that when a misfortune occurs to anyone whatsoever among all one's own people, that person suffers;
yet he did not mean that it is only for that single individual, but rather that if such a thing happens to everyone [in the family], then:
"Disease, fire, or the death of a kinsman—that indeed is the cause of its [the inheritance’s] distribution."
A distinction has been stated by the Grandfather:
"One should have that man drink [the water] belonging to whichever deity he is devoted to;
but if there is equality among the deities, one should have him drink [the water] of Āditya."
One should make thieves and those who subsist by weapons drink that water of Durgā;
however, one should not make a Brāhmaṇa drink that water of the Sun.
One should bathe the trident of Durgā and the orb of the Sun;

for the other deities, however, one should bathe their weapons. [211] The summary here is as follows: The judge, having consecrated the water for the ablution of the fierce deity with the mantra “O Water, you are the life-breath of living beings,” as stated in the section on the ordeal by water, should then have the person undergoing purification drink three handfuls of that consecrated water after reciting the mantra: “O Varuṇa, protect me by means of truth. The term “having caused to hear” (saṃśrāvya) refers to the recitation of both mantras. For this very reason, Nārada says:
Having turned [the person] toward the sun and caused them to hear [the oath], one should make them drink water;
so too Yājñavalkya says: "Having caused them to hear [the oath], one should therefore make them drink three handfuls (prasṛti) of that water."

When it is asked, "What should be made to hear? [the answer is]: "Not that which gives pain. And one should cause the sinner to hear [of the sin], and cause the protector to drink three handfuls [of water]. Here, *enaḥ* means sin (*pāpman*). And so says Viṣṇu:
A person who deceives becomes a deceiver through greed, being one of evil intellect.
Also in another Smṛti:
"By acting according to his own whims, having drunk from the treasury, he would deceive."
He is born poor, diseased, and deluded for seven lifetimes.

Thus, having heard this, the one to be cleared (*śodhya*) should say: "This was not done by me. And so Viṣṇu states: "Having worshipped the fierce deities (*ugradeva*), he should drink three handfuls (*prasṛti*) of the water used for their ablutions; facing the deity, he should declare: 'This was not done by me. When this has been performed and no symptoms of distress appear at the times previously mentioned, he becomes pure. Otherwise, it should be understood that there is punishment.
Thus ends the procedure for the vessel;
now follows the procedure for the rice, regarding which Bṛhaspati says:
Fasting during a solar eclipse, one who is pure should eat rice grains;
there shall be purification if the vomit is white, but if it is mixed with blood, it causes defilement.

In this context, the meaning of the word "ca" (and) is that one incurs fault even from mere attachment [to the ordeal]. Here, having performed the invocation of the common divine attributes, the oblation, the placing of the leaf upon the head, and so forth, the person undergoing purification, while still wearing wet clothes, must consume the rice. Moreover, this is to be done only in cases of an accusation of theft, as Pitāmaha has stated:
"I shall proclaim the rule for the consumption of rice as enjoined;
rice is to be administered in cases of theft, and not in any other—this is the settled rule."
Being pure, one should wash bright rice grains— either *śāli* rice or any other kind— place them in an earthen vessel, and set it before the Sun.
One should cause the accused, who has bathed, is facing eastward, and has had his hair tied with a leaf, to remain overnight there mixed with the bathing water.
Having eaten rice grains, one should then spit them out into a leaf;
it should be from a *pippala* tree, and in its absence, from a *bhūrja* tree indeed, and not from any other.
"If blood is seen, and the jaw and palate waste away, and his body trembles—one should declare him impure. Thus it is said.

Regarding the word *bhakṣayitvā*: the causative suffix (*ṇic*) in the root *bhakṣ* is used in its own sense (*svārthe*), with the causal marker (*hetu-māṇṇic*) implied. Otherwise, since the words "having caused to eat" (*nirdiśet*) and "having eaten" (*bhakṣayitvā*) would be understood as having the same meaning, the act of eating would belong to the judge alone and not to the person undergoing purification; thus, the causative suffix is indeed appropriate. The phrase "of the Sun" (*ādityasya*) refers to the image-form of the Sun, because of the natural force of the statement that one should perform the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsana*) there at night. The term "therein" (*tatratya*) means in the temple of the Sun. The prohibition of grains other than *śāli* rice, however, serves an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*). On this point, the author of the *Candrikā* says: [213]

“The decision is that rice [for ordeal] is to be administered in cases of theft, but not in any other case. Here, “in any other case” means in disputes concerning one of the two parties in a charge of adultery with a woman, and not in disputes over wealth. However, in disputes over wealth, rice is to be administered even in cases other than theft, because Kātyāyana stated, “Rice is for half of that half. Nor should it be argued that this statement refers exclusively to the subject of theft, for that would result in a contradiction with the introductory phrase, “where there is a denial of what was given. Thus he says.
This is the procedure for the rice ordeal (*taṇḍulavidhi*).
Now follows the procedure for the heated gold-coin ordeal;
regarding this, Pitāmaha says:
"I shall describe the auspicious procedure for extracting the heated gold-coin."
One should have a vessel made of iron or copper, measuring sixteen finger-breadths.
One should fill a circular mandala made of clay, measuring four finger-breadths in size,
with twenty palas of ghee and oil.

Having taken cow’s ghee, one who is pure should heat it over the fire. A *maṇḍala*—meaning circular or round—should be filled with either ghee or oil; this is one alternative. Or, having filled it with cow’s ghee and established a common fire in a sacred place, one should heat it there. While the heating is taking place in either of these two cases, one should perform the general procedure common to all ordeals, beginning with the invocation of Dharma and ending with the placing of the leaf upon the head of the person to be tested. Regarding the case of filling it with ghee or oil, a specific rule has been stated by Pitāmaha:
Then, one should cast a gold māṣaka coin into that well-heated [liquid];
thereafter, one should extract the heated māṣaka using the combination of the thumb and finger.
"In that"—meaning, in a vessel filled with ghee and oil—he who does not shake his fingertips, nor does a blister arise;
let him be pure by the Dharma, his fingers on the hand remaining unchanged. [214]

In this regard, because of the statement "one should lift it out" (*uddharet*), there is merely the lifting [of the vessel] from the fire, not its casting outside. Regarding the alternative of filling it with cow’s ghee, a specific rule has been stated by Pitāmaha:
"Having taken cow’s ghee in a vessel made of gold, silver, copper, iron, or even clay, one who is pure should heat it over the fire."
One should place therein a beautifully adorned ring made of gold, silver, copper, or iron, which has been washed once with water.
In a place rich with swirling ripples and waves, where the touch of a fingernail cannot be perceived,
one should examine the vessel for the sacrificial pap (caru) using a moist leaf to detect whether it makes a sound.
Then, one should consecrate that [ghee] once with this mantra:
"O ghee, you are the supreme purifier, the nectar in sacrificial rites."
"O Purifier, you who are cool as snow, become hot toward the sinner.
"Toward the sinner" means toward one of evil deeds; "toward the pure" means toward the purified one. Prajāpati stated the subsequent duty:
"Then, having fasted, bathed, and arrived wearing wet clothes..."
One should cause that seal-ring to be grasped, likewise placed within clarified butter.
"Then the examiners should examine its ring finger;
he on whose [finger] there are no eruptions is pure, otherwise he is impure.
Because of the statement "they should examine the ring finger," the extraction of the ring must be performed with that very finger. Here is the sequence of the ritual procedure:

Having performed the procedure common to all ordeals, beginning with the invocation of Dharma (*dharmāvāhana*) and ending with the leaf upon the head, the judge (*prāḍvivāka*), having consecrated either oil or cow’s ghee with the mantra "Burn, O Purifier" (*daha pāvaka*), and having consecrated the fire with the mantra "O Agni, you are the witness of all beings" (*tvam agne sarvabhūtānām*), should have the examiner examine the ring or the heated bean at the conclusion of their removal from the hand of the person undergoing purification. The distinction is that in the case of removing the heated bean, the joints of the fingers are examined, whereas in the case of removing the ring, only the forefinger (*pradeśinī*) is examined.
Thus ends the procedure for the heated gold test (*taptamāṣa*).
Now follows the procedure for the ploughshare test (*phāla*); the procedure for the ploughshare test is now being described. Regarding this, Bṛhaspati says:
An iron ploughshare made of twelve palas is prescribed;
it should be eight aṅgulas long and four aṅgulas wide.
One should lick that water, which has the color of fire, once with the tongue;
if one is not burned, one becomes pure, but otherwise one is degraded.

Regarding this, the author of the *Candrikā* maintains that the mention of the "thief" (*cora*) is intended as an illustration for the person undergoing the ordeal (*śodhya*). However, Vijñāneśvara, Varadarāja, and others state that the procedure for the plough (*phāla*) applies only to the thief and not to other persons undergoing the ordeal. Let the learned among us discern the truth in this matter. The sequence of the ritual procedure (*paryogakrama*) therein is as follows: having placed the plough of the specified dimensions upon the fire established in the place of ordeal, one should perform everything—beginning with the invocation of Dharma (*dharmāvāhana*) and ending with the placing of the leaf upon the head of the person undergoing the ordeal—once the rites common to all ordeals have been performed. This is the procedure for the plough. Now, the procedure for the sacred balance (*dharma*).
On this point, the Grandfather [Brahmā] says:
"Now I shall fully explain the examination of dharma and adharma.
One should have dharma made of silver, and adharma of lead or tin."
Some say it is iron mixed with lead; others say it is either lead or iron.
Regarding "of the slayers" and "of those seeking expiation for men who are petitioning":
"of the slayers" refers to cases of violent assault (*sāhasa*); "of those seeking expiation" refers to cases of grievous sin (*pātaka*). Bṛhaspati states another alternative:
"One should write down Dharma and Adharma on birch-bark, using white and black [pigments]."
Having sprinkled it with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), one should worship it with perfumes and garlands.
Dharma is represented by white flowers, while Adharma is the wearer of black flowers;
having prepared them in this manner and smeared them, one should cause those [flowers] to be placed upon the two lumps.
Then, two equal-sized balls should be made from either cow dung or clay;
they should be placed in an undamaged earthen vessel and remain unobserved.
In a clean place that has been smeared [with cow dung], in the presence of the gods and Brahmins,
he should then worship the gods and the world-protectors as before.
First, having performed the invocation of the Dharma, one should write out the written pledge:
"If I am free from sin, may the Dharma come into my hand.
Thus the accused person should recite the mantra.
"One accused [of a crime] should take one of those two without delay;
if he takes the *dharma*, he shall be purified, but if he takes the *adharma*, he is defeated.
Thus a specific rule was stated by Prajāpati.
Upon the two garments, Dharma and Adharma should be written, white and black respectively,
along with the mantras for recitation, fire-offerings, and so forth, together with the Gāyatrī.
Having addressed [the deity], one should worship with perfumes and white and black flowers;
then, having sprinkled them with the five products of the cow, they should be enclosed within lumps of clay.
Having made two lumps of clay equal in size, they should be placed so as to be unobserved;
then, one should take up one lump from the pot without delay.
If the law is upheld, there shall be purity, and it shall be honored by the investigators;
but if injustice is upheld, the offender shall be punished and even banished.
Thus is the rule of Dharma;
those are the divine [teachings].
Now, as for oaths, they have already been mentioned previously as having been declared by Manu and others. Nevertheless, they are stated here again for the sake of clarity. As Viṣṇu has said:
"For one niṣka, there is the swearing of truth; for two niṣkas, touching the feet."
The flower-head is below the triad; the gift of the sheath is beyond that.
One should cause a Brahmin to swear by truth; a Kṣatriya, by his vehicles and weapons; a Vaiśya, by cattle, grain, and gold; and a Śūdra, by all [of these] and by divisive acts.
And so forth. In this regard, the purification through ordeal (*śuddhivibhāvanā*) has been stated by Manu:
"He who does not meet with misfortune quickly is to be known as pure by means of oaths."

*Ārti* means pain or affliction, as expressed in the phrase, "that which [arises] from kings or the gods. Furthermore, the restriction regarding time—from three nights onwards—should be understood by considering the relative gravity or lightness of the period involved. Although oaths (*śapatha*) are also denoted by the term *divya* (ordeals), they are designated separately from the balance-scale (*dhaṭa*) and other immediate causes in the legal codes (*smṛtis*), because they serve as the basis for a decision at a later time; this distinction is made according to the maxim of the "Brahmin and the Wanderer" (*brāhmaṇaparivrājaka-nyāya*). Regarding this, Hārīta states a specific rule:
"The rules for the *kośa* (water ordeal) and the *taṇḍula* (rice ordeal), as well as those arising from *dharma*..."
One should employ oaths concerning one's sons, wife, and so forth at all times.

Now, it was stated that written documents and the like, when qualified by the absence of abuse, attain the status of valid evidence (*pramāṇa*). That is not tenable, because there is no certainty that the absence of abuse can always be established through witnesses. If it were to be established solely by means of divine ordeal (*divya*), then human evidence would have no scope there; for instance: the absence of abuse is not something to be established by witnesses. This is because an abuse committed by someone at some time in any manner whatsoever cannot be determined in every respect by those with physical eyes who are devoid of divine knowledge. Rather, Devadatta himself, as the plaintiff, knows the absence of restraint (*āsedha*) on his own part, having resolved that he is not to be restrained anywhere, at any time, or in any way by anyone. Likewise, the defendant, having been properly informed that he is to be restrained in every respect, correctly knows the restraint imposed upon him.
[Objection: Surely, an injunction (*āsedha*) must be supported by witnesses. Since such witnesses are absent, the absence of the injunction can indeed be properly established.
[Reply: Not so. For the status of a witness for an absence is never observed anywhere. [Objection:

Surely, the absence of the injunction can be proven through the very means of knowledge that is non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*). Since logical marks (*liṅga*) are supportive of the means of knowledge consisting of non-apprehension, the cognition of the absence of the injunction is indeed authoritative.

If this is argued, we say no. Through the non-perception of witnesses, only the absence of witnesses can be known, not the absence of a prohibition, because there is no lack of a common locus [between them].
If it is objected: "The absence of witnesses is determined by the non-perception of witnesses; by that absence of witnesses, the absence of a prohibition can then be determined," [we reply:]...

True. In cases where a prohibition (*āsedha*) is accompanied by witnesses, let there be validity for the means of proving the absence of such a prohibition. However, in cases where a prohibition is without witnesses, the previously stated position alone remains; thus, there is no contradiction whatsoever. Furthermore, the well-known status of prohibitions as being "with witnesses" is intended in a general sense. In the world, prohibitions exist both with and without witnesses, as is observed in worldly transactions. If one were to determine the absence of a prohibition solely on the basis of the absence of witnesses who could prove it, then—given that "the truth of Dharma is hidden in a cave and only the Lord knows it"—there would be a violation of Dharma which has witnesses.

Now, one might object: "Since it is impossible to bring forth even a few specific defects in the intentions of all those possessing human bodies—whether in the case of witnesses, writers, and the like, or even the original owner—during a formal legal proceeding that is accompanied by witnesses and is authoritative, divine proof (*divya*) alone must be employed everywhere. Therefore, human means of knowledge (*mānuṣapramāṇa*) would be rendered without scope. If this is argued:

Not so. Even when human means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) are present and perfectly pure, the judges—the members of the court and the presiding judge—must bring about a decision by first inducing a weakening of their foundation through the exposure of defects in their disposition, and then by employing divine means; thus the lawsuit must be rendered "with a reply" (*sottara*) and a judgment rendered with firm support. For this very reason, Pitāmaha stated: "A lawsuit is considered to be of two kinds: with a reply (*sottara*) and without a reply (*anuttara*). [219]

Nārada explains this as follows: "Legal procedure (vyavahāra) is divided into two types, with and without a wager (sapaṇa and apaṇa). The word "two-fold" is to be understood as the ellipsis. Consequently, it should be noted that when one resorts to an ordeal (*divya*) by exposing a defect in intention (*āśaya-doṣa*) in order to invalidate human means of proof (*mānuṣa-pramāṇa*), one must necessarily undergo the ordeal after having placed a wager (*paṇabandha*) to support the legal proceeding.
Regarding the function of the decision (*nirṇaya-kṛtya*) here, the author of the *Saṃgraha* states the function of the decision:
Having examined the legal proceedings established according to the principles of his own school of thought,
the king shall determine victory and defeat based on the facts.
He who accomplishes his purpose by means of any one of the aforementioned methods, having achieved a result consistent with the words and letters [of the plaint], is proclaimed the victor.
"He who fails to prove his case after having attempted to prove it, or who proves a contrary matter for himself,
or he in whom a defect in the evidence is perceived, is the one who suffers defeat. Thus says Vyāsa.
The king should punish the defeated party and cause honor to be bestowed upon the victor.
This honor should be rendered with perfumes, garlands, garments, and so forth;
he should cause the victor to receive honor through perfumes, garlands, clothing, and the like.
Thus says the Smṛti. As for that which was stated by Kātyāyana:
"One who is pure should be made to pay fifty [paṇas]; one who is impure shall be subject to punishment."

As for that which was stated by Viṣṇu: “When these [ordeals] are employed to determine divine victory, one who is pure shall be fined half a hundred; one who is impure shall be subject to punishment,” this prescription of punishment for the pure applies only in the case of a lawsuit involving a wager (*sapaṇavyavahāra*). For immediately thereafter, Viṣṇu states: “In a lawsuit involving a wager, there is punishment for the one who is pure. It follows from the context that such punishment is a monetary fine (*arthadaṇḍa*). Kātyāyana describes the types of punishment for the impure:
“In the case of poison, water, fire, the balance, the sacred vessel (*kośa*), and rice...”
And in the ordeals of the heated ball and the ordeal by balance, one should prescribe punishment in due order.

"One thousand, six hundred, as well as five hundred, and likewise four, three, two, and one; in this manner, one should prescribe a lesser penalty for a lesser offense. Thus [it is said]. Vijñāneśvara (on Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 2.113) states: "This penalty is also to be combined with the penalty stated in the rule: 'If the defendant denies [the debt] and it is proven, he shall pay [the fine]'. Bhāruci holds that the status of being the object of the count of thousands and so forth applies only to *paṇas*.
Kātyāyana states the duty to be performed immediately after the conclusion of the trial:
"The king, having first honored the plaintiff, should join him with his proven claim and give him a written document bearing his own signature."

A written document is called a *jayapatra* (document of victory). Whatever is to be stated regarding a *jayapatra* has been explained in its entirety within the rules for drafting documents (*lekhyavidhi*); that should be consulted therein.
Thus [ends the section on] the illustrious Vīragajapati, Lord of Gauḍa, Lord of the nine crores of Karṇāṭakas and Luburigas, Sovereign of Jamunāpura, Protector and Refuge of Huśanasāhi Suratrāṇa.

In the *Sarasvatīvilāsa*, a compendium of law (*smṛtisaṃgraha*) composed by the great king Śrī Pratāparudra Mahādeva— the supreme sovereign of kings of kings, whose son was the illustrious Durgāvarpa, and whose conduct was most holy.
The Third Chapter (Ullāsa) in the Section on Legal Procedure, titled "The Determination of Means of Proof" [Is this the Fourth Chapter?
The Fifth Chapter: Now, the Eighteen Subjects.

Now, in all the *Smṛtis*, immediately after the determination of the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*), there follows the determination of the eighteen subjects (*pada*). Since it is logical that the determination of the objects of knowledge (*prameya*) should follow the determination of the means of valid knowledge, the object of knowledge known as the eighteen subjects is determined immediately thereafter.
Non-payment of debts.

In this context, since legal procedure (*vyavahāra*) is defined primarily through the settlement of debt-recovery (*ṛṇādāna*), which is established by all means of proof—both human and divine—it is first examined as the first subject of dispute according to the order of enumeration. For this very reason, it is said: "Of these, the first is debt-recovery. Here, the rules for debt-recovery are sevenfold. Regarding the debtor (*adhamarṇa*), there are five types of rules: such a debt is payable; such a debt is not payable; it must be paid by this specific person authorized to pay; it must be paid at this specific time; and it must be paid in this specific manner. Regarding the creditor (*uttamarṇa*), however, the rules are twofold: the rule for giving [the loan] and the rule for taking [the repayment]. As stated by Nārada:
"Debt that is to be paid and that which is not to be paid, by whom, where, and when it occurs,
as well as the rules for giving and receiving— this is known as the procedure for the recovery of debt. Regarding this,
since the other matters are preceded by the payment of debt, Yājñavalkya first states the manner of that payment:
The interest shall be one-eightieth part [of the principal] month by month when there is security;
otherwise, according to the order of the castes, it shall be three, four, or five percent.

That which is pledged by a debtor to a creditor for the sake of gaining trust is here called *ādhi*, meaning a pledge. In a transaction involving a pledge, the lawful interest on the lent sum shall be one-eightieth part. Thus, for twenty-five *paṇas*, the monthly interest is one-quarter of a *paṇa*. And so says Manu:
"Hear now the interest prescribed by the words of Vasiṣṭha regarding usury:
five *māṣas* on twenty [silver *kārṣāpaṇas*]; in this way, the law is not violated. [222]
And so Gautama says:
"Interest on a loan shall be lawful at the rate of five māṣas for every twenty [units of currency]."

If ten *māṣas* constitute a *paṇa*, then one *māṣa* is the twentieth part of a *paṇa*. Half of that becomes a *taṇḍula*. If twenty *māṣas* constitute a *paṇa*, it amounts to the measure of a *taṇḍula*. If a *paṇa* consists of sixteen *māṣas*, then for each *paṇa*, a tenfold rate should be calculated. Otherwise—meaning in a transaction without a pledge—for the four castes, beginning with the Brāhmaṇa, the lawful interest is two, four, and five percent respectively. When a Brāhmaṇa is the debtor, the interest is two percent; when a Kṣatriya is the debtor, three percent; when a Vaiśya is the debtor, four percent; and when a Śūdra is the debtor, five percent. This occurs month by month. It is called "two, four, and five percent" because an interest of two, four, or five [per cent] is given in this case. What is meant is this: in all cases involving persons of the same caste, three percent is indeed the proper rate. Thus, for a Kṣatriya, if a Kṣatriya is the debtor, the interest is two percent; if a Vaiśya is the debtor, three percent; and if a Śūdra is the debtor, four percent. Likewise, for a Vaiśya, if a Vaiśya is the debtor, the interest is two percent; if a Śūdra is the debtor, three percent. And likewise, for a Śūdra, if a Śūdra is the debtor, the interest is two percent. Immediately following [the same caste], three percent is lawful; at one degree of separation, four percent is lawful. And so says Manu:
"One may take interest of two, three, four, five, and likewise one hundred [per cent] per month, according to the sequence of the social classes (varṇas).
On this point, Bṛhaspati says:
Growth is said to be fourfold by some, proclaimed as fivefold by others, and fully described as sixfold by yet others; understand them according to their true nature.
The bodily [interest], the periodic, and likewise the wheel-increasing;
then the stipulated, the crest-increasing, and similarly the profit from enjoyment.
[223] He himself explains the essential nature of the bodily and other types [of interest]:

Interest is of four kinds: that which is connected with labor (kāyikā), that which is received monthly (māsagrāhyā), that which is periodic (kālikā), and compound interest (cakravṛddhi); the last is also called *kāritā*, being that which is stipulated by the debtor himself.
That interest which is collected daily is known as *śikhāvṛddhi* (top-knot interest);
it increases constantly like a top-knot and ceases only upon the cutting off of the head.
"When the principal is paid, this interest is likewise remembered as *śikhāvṛddhi* (interest like the growth of a crest).

Satisfaction from the house and the acquisition of enjoyment from the field are proclaimed as the fruit. By the phrase "satisfaction from the house," satisfaction arising from the home due to one's residence is meant. And by "the fruit from the field," the acquisition of enjoyment consisting of grain and other produce resulting from the field is intended. By the phrase "it is taken every day," profit is shown through the taking of interest characterized by the number of days agreed upon. And so says Kātyāyana:
That interest which one pays at every period of time, having cleared off only the principal with absolute certainty, is known as *śikhāvṛddhi*.

Interest that is made by the debtor himself at his own will is "caused" (*kāritā*). The suffix *ṇic* is used here in the sense of the agent’s own purpose (*svārthe*). For this very reason, the author of the *Candrikā* maintains that interest caused by the instigation of another is strictly prohibited. Thus says Kātyāyana:
"But that interest which is stipulated by the debtor as excessive, being always caused [by him] during a time of distress, must be paid."

"In no way should interest that has been stipulated otherwise be paid. This is the essential point here: interest is of two kinds, namely, *kṛtā* (contracted) and *kāritā* (stipulated). *Kṛtā* is contracted by both the creditor and the debtor; it is of six types due to the divisions of corporeal and non-corporeal. *Kāritā*, however, is that which is contracted during times of distress, or even in times of no distress, by neutral intermediaries other than the creditor and the debtor. Thus, among these two types of stipulated interest, that which is contracted in times of no distress is prohibited—meaning it is unrighteous (*adharmyā*) and should not be accepted.

They say there are four types of interest: bodily, that which consists of the increase of wealth, that which is caused, and that which is of the nature of a crest; while the fifth is called wheel-interest.

This should be understood as the intended meaning of the statement by Bṛhaspati. *Cakravṛddhi* (compound interest) is the interest that accrues again every month on the basis of the principal itself. *Kālikā* is the interest obtainable every month—that which is received monthly. *Kāyikā* is that where the very physical labor, such as driving, milking, and so forth, regarding horses, buffaloes, female slaves, and the like, is calculated as the interest. Regarding animals and other property lent for the purpose of interest, Yājñavalkya states: "The offspring [is the interest] of cattle and women. Here, "women" refers to female slaves. In the absence of offspring, however, the profit consists of the fattening or non-destruction of the lent cattle and other property; this means [the profit belongs] to those who desire milk or those who desire service. He (Yājñavalkya) himself states another measure of interest per month for a specific type of debtor:
Those who travel through forests shall pay one hundred [paṇas], while those who travel by sea shall pay one hundred and twenty;
or they may all pay the interest agreed upon by themselves, regardless of their respective castes.

Those who go to the wilderness (*kāntāra*) are "wilderness-goers" (*kāntāragāḥ*). Those who go to the ocean are "ocean-goers" (*sāmudrāḥ*). For them, a hundred increased by ten or a hundred increased by twenty is lawful (*dharmya*), with the phrase "month by month" being supplied from the context. Regarding interest that has been stipulated (*kāritā*), all [castes], beginning with the Brāhmaṇas, [are subject to this]. This is the meaning: the creditor may take a hundred increased by ten from those traveling through the wilderness, and a hundred increased by twenty from those traveling across the ocean, because there is even the suspicion of the principal being lost. In some cases, interest arises even when it has not been stipulated. As Nārada says:
Interest on gifts made out of affection shall never accrue if they have not been requested;
however, even if unrequested, after half a year has passed, it increases twofold.
"Unrequested" means not formally agreed upon. On this point, Viṣṇu says:
He who, having previously taken a loan, says "I will repay it at the same rate," but later fails to pay due to greed, shall then incur interest.
"Equally" means "immediately"—that is to say, without having accrued interest. But Kātyāyana states a specific rule:
"If one who has taken goods departs for another region without paying the price, that wealth shall accrue interest after the lapse of three seasons."
This refers to objects that have not been specifically requested:
"If one who has taken a loan should depart for another region without returning it,
after the lapse of one year, that wealth shall accrue interest."
Furthermore, if one who remains in his own country should not give back a loan even when asked for it, the king shall cause him to pay interest starting from the time of the request:
"But if one staying in his own country should not give when asked at any time,
the king shall force him to pay that interest, even if he is unwilling."

Thus it is stated in the Smṛti. In this context, the measure of interest is established by such statements as, "The interest shall be one-eightieth part," and so forth. As Manu says: "An interest rate higher than the legal maximum, or exceeding it, is not valid;
they call that the domain of usury, for [the lender] deserves only five percent per hundred."

The phrase "they call it usury" prohibits interest exceeding the scriptures. The practice among worldly people of taking interest according to what is prescribed in the scriptures is called "following the established rule. Therefore, interest exceeding that is not valid. For this very reason, Viṣṇu states: "One may pay interest even if it was not previously agreed upon, provided it is as prescribed when a year has elapsed. The phrase "as prescribed" implies "as stated in the Dharmaśāstra. It does not mean interest "stated" by the defendant, the mediator, or the plaintiff; for in this context, a measure dependent on the acceptance of an unrighteous rate is impossible. Since any other measure conceived by human intellect would be outside the scope of the scriptures and thus improper, the essential point is that only the measure declared in the scriptures is to be accepted. A specific distinction is stated in another Smṛti:
"What is given out of affection does not increase until it is requested;
but when it is requested and not given, it increases by five percent per month.
Thus [it is said]. Nārada states an exception to this rule regarding interest that accrues without being requested:
Where a wager, wages, a deposit, or a fine has been stipulated, the stakes in gambling and gifts given in vain increase; they do not increase when they are not intended to be increased.

A gift made in vain is that which is given to actors and the like. A stake at dice is a wager related to dice. Saṃvarta also says: "Interest shall not be charged on a woman’s property, on profit, on a deposit, or on a doubtful matter, nor on a suretyship, unless it has been expressly agreed upon."

By stating "made by oneself" (*svayaṃkṛtā*), he shows that interest is also to be paid on women's property and the like when it has been made. By stating "as it was deposited" (*yathāsthita*) in the case of a deposit, he shows that interest accrues when there is a change from its original state, such as by the substitution of another object. Kātyāyana also says: "In the case of skins, grain, gambling debts, the price of merchandise, and the bride-price, there shall never be interest; nor in the case of those [debts] incurred through suretyship."

Therefore, by stating "at all times," he shows that even when there is a request for repayment and so forth, interest does not cease to accrue. However, Gautama has stated a specific exception: "A pledge that is being used does not increase. Here, "used" refers to items such as clothing or ornaments; this is what is meant by a "pledge being used. Yājñavalkya also says:
"Interest does not accrue beyond that point on one's own wealth that is lent but not accepted, or on that which is deposited with a neutral third party."

[227] Thus, Nārada states the limit for the cessation of interest: "This rule regarding the accumulation of interest on debts is remembered as the universal one; however, there is another established by local custom where the debt remains."
In one region it remains double, in another triple, and likewise in yet another fourfold;
similarly, in other regions it remains eightfold.

That debt which is to be paid increases in some regions twofold, in some threefold, and in others fourfold. Bṛhaspati states the regulation for interest according to the specific nature of the substance lent:
"Interest on gold is twofold; on clothes and base metals, it is threefold;
on grain, it is declared to be fourfold; and on beasts of burden and wool, it is tenfold."
In vegetables, the fivefold increase is stated; in seeds, it is established as sixfold;
and in salt, fats, and liquors, an eightfold increase is traditionally taught.
In the case of molasses and honey, it is stated that when they are employed [as interest], the rate is for a long period.

*Kupya* refers to tin and lead. *Śada* refers to produce grown in a field. Although grain is also produce grown in a field, nevertheless, by the maxim of "the cow and the bull" (*gobalīvardanyāya*), the word *śada* is used here to denote flowers, fruits, and so forth grown in a field. *Lava* refers to wool from sheep, chowries, and the like. Just as with vegetables, the interest on cotton is also sixfold. And thus Vyāsa says:
"A sixfold increase is prescribed for vegetables, cotton, and seeds."
For oil as well, there is an eightfold increase, just like for liquor. Kātyāyana also states:
"For all kinds of oils, for liquors, and for clarified butters—as well as for molasses and salt—an eightfold increase is to be known."

As for the statement of Viṣṇu, "Grain, liquids, and so forth are threefold," that is not in conflict with the previously mentioned rule that grain is fourfold; for it may be established by mutual agreement or by considering regional differences. Liquids are explained by the same rule as grain. Regarding the other Smṛti text stating "flowers and fruits," that refers to those regions where it is settled that they should be returned threefold, or it refers to the case of an indigent debtor. For liquor and similar items, there is only a doubling, just like gold, as Kātyāyana has stated:
"For gems, pearls, corals, and that which is fashioned from gold,
the increase remains threefold.
Regarding this, Manu says:

Interest on a loan, when established once, does not exceed doubling [the principal]. That which is given in small measure with the thought, "I shall take more," is called *kusīda*. By virtue of its association [with the term], it is intended here specifically as gold. "Established once" (*sakṛd āhitā*) means not transferred to another person; or rather, it means that when the principal is made to include the interest, the total does not exceed double that such principal. In this way, even for tripling and so forth, the interest established once does not exceed that limit. On this point, Vijñānayogin [comments]: * *Kusīda* is that small amount given with the intention: "I will take more. * Because of its mention alongside [the term for gold], it is understood to refer specifically to gold. * "Established once" means not passed on to another person; or, it means that together with the principal plus interest, the total does not go beyond being double. * Likewise, even in cases of tripling and so on, the interest established once does not exceed that limit. * Regarding this, Vijñānayogin says: [YDh 2.39cd]...
