Interest on a loan, once stipulated, shall not exceed double the principal.

Thus [it is said]. There is also a reading *sakṛd āhṛtā*; [this refers to] capital (*kusīda*) employed for the purpose of accumulation—that is, interest (*vṛddhi*). It does not exceed—that is, it does not go beyond—doubling (*dvaiguṇya*). If it is *sakṛd āhitā*—that is, if it has been set in motion once—then [the rule holds]; however, if another transaction is made by transferring it to another person and so forth, it exceeds doubling. Regarding the reading *sakṛd āhṛtā*, he says it should be explained as follows: "If it is collected little by little from the debtor day by day, month by month, or year by year, it does not exceed doubling. And so Gautama says: "In a long-standing loan, there is doubling of the principal. By the use of the singular number in "of the loan" (*prayogasya*), the intention is that exceeding doubling occurs when another transaction is made; by the mention of "long-standing" (*cirasthāne*), the non-exceeding of doubling is shown when interest is taken little by little.
An exception regarding the cessation of interest; in some cases, there is an exception regarding the cessation of interest. As Bṛhaspati said:
"In the case of grass, wood, bricks, thread, leaven, leather, bone, and armor..."
And the growth of seeds, flowers, and fruits does not cease.

*Carman* refers to a shield, which wards off arrows and the like; *varman* refers to armor. However, the non-cessation of the increase on flowers and fruits should be understood to apply to the case of an extremely insolvent debtor at the time of repayment; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of contradicting the previously cited statements. Viṣṇu also states: "The interest on yeast, cotton, leather, armor, weapons, bricks, and charcoal is inexhaustible. Here, the contradiction with the statement prescribing a sixfold rate for cotton should be resolved as before. Vasiṣṭha also says: "Likewise for ivory, leather, bone, horn, and earthenware..."
The increase of these, as well as of flowers, roots, and fruits, is inexhaustible.
Manu, however, in some places states a prohibition:
"One should not take interest that is excessive, nor that which is not seen.
"Not seen" means that which is not prescribed in the treatises on Dharma, such as the sixty percent [rate] and so forth; this is the meaning.
Some explain this term *adṛṣṭām* differently:
"The increase for gold, grain, and cloth is two, three, or fourfold;
the increase for ghee is eightfold, and for copper and other metals, it is fourfold."
The interest on oils shall be sixfold; for women and cattle, it is their offspring;
for precious metals, it shall be fourfold; and for cotton, it is fourfold.
The increase of woods such as sandalwood and the like becomes eightfold;
thus the rule for increase has been declared, and there is no increase beyond that.
"There is no increase of an increase"—this is the instruction of the Dharma-kāra;
nor does an increase ever depend upon anything else, nor does an increase [itself] ever [depend on another].

In this context, because the scriptures prohibit interest upon interest (compound interest), such interest is considered "unseen" (*adṛṣṭa*) by the scriptures. Here, the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) in the phrase "sandalwood etc. indicates fragrance in general. By the word "etcetera" in "copper etc.," items other than gold and silver are included. The word "storehouse" (*kośa*) indicates grain. By the mention of the word "cotton" (*kārpāsa*), rice and similar items are indicated. The rule regarding grain being threefold or fivefold has already been stated previously. The meaning of the phrase "not for more than a year" (*nātisāṃvatsarīm*) is as follows: the interest previously mentioned—namely, that one may take five percent per month from a *śūdra* debtor—may, if accepted under some circumstance, be taken from a *brāhmaṇa* debtor for the duration of one year, but not beyond that.

Others, however, maintain that because the rule for taking interest is based on doubling the principal, there is no fault in taking interest even after a year; thus, if one desires prosperity, one should not discharge—that is, one should not take back—the interest that accrues beyond a year. This interpretation is intended by the author of the *Candrikā* and others, whereas the first view is intended by Aparārka and others.
One may accept whichever one prefers according to one's inclination. On this point, Viṣṇu says: "Theft [is incurred] regarding the property of a Brāhmaṇa, as well as in the case of gold ornaments."
Thereafter, he should give that [gift] to him, increased by elevenfold.
This meaning applies to the theft of property other than gold belonging to a Brāhmaṇa, as well as to the theft of gold belonging to a Kṣatriya. And so says Pitāmaha:
"Stolen gems and gold [belonging to a Brāhmaṇa] shall immediately incur a fine twelvefold;
and silver and the like, being the property of a Brāhmaṇa, shall immediately incur eleven times the value."
Kātyāyana states: "Base metals are considered fivefold [in value], and land is likewise considered eightfold;
because of the statement 'immediately,' it is to be paid immediately."
But Bṛhaspati has stated the specific rule:
"The creditor may collect interest on the crest, bodily labor, and likewise a share of profits,
only so long as the principal has not been cleared."
[231] The nature of the *śikhāvṛddhi* and the others has already been explained previously.
The meaning is that it has neither been cleared nor returned by the debtor. For this very reason, Yājñavalkya says:
"But the pledge shall be used until it is returned.
Regarding this, Hārīta states:
One should maintain the bond exactly as it has been established;
otherwise, through its violation, either the profit or the principal itself will be lost.

For example—just as it was established by the debtor, either as something to be guarded (*gopya*) or as something to be used (*bhogya*), such as a pledge (*ādhi*)—in that very same manner, the creditor shall preserve the guarded pledge as something to be guarded, and the usable pledge as something to be used. Otherwise, if the guarded pledge is used as something to be used, or the usable pledge is preserved as something to be guarded, then due to the violation of the agreement, the interest (*lābha*) is lost, or the principal capital (*mūla*) is lost; this is the meaning. And thus says Yājñavalkya: "In the case of using a guarded pledge, there is no interest. The word "by force" (*balāt*) is to be supplied after "in the case of using. And likewise says Manu.

"A pledge must not be used by force; one who uses it shall forfeit the interest. This is the meaning: because one who forcibly enjoys a pledge for safekeeping (*gopyādhi*) commits a grave offense by violating the pledger's prohibition against its use, even a small amount of such enjoyment may cause the total loss [of the debt]. However, for one who enjoys it excessively through sheer force, there is a forfeiture of the principal itself. In the statement of Hārīta, "or the principal," the word "or" (*vā*) serves to indicate an alternative. And likewise, Manu says:
"He who, being clever, enjoys a pledge without the permission of the owner..."
Therefore, an increase must be declared as the compensation for that enjoyment.

In the case of a pledge for use (*bhogyādhi*), however, when it is maintained as an object of enjoyment, there is only the loss of the profit (*lābha*); for by the mere lapse of the agreed time, the position that the principal itself is lost does not apply. Nor should it be argued that because there is no interest (*vṛddhi*) in a pledge for use, the position regarding the loss of profit also does not apply; for enjoyment itself constitutes profit. Alternatively, where the pledgor initially agrees to both the use and the payment of interest on the pledge, it should be understood that the interest has been realized. For this very reason, Yājñavalkya says: "There is no interest on a pledge for custody (*gopyādhi*) when it is used, nor even when it is beneficial, if it is lost."
What is lost or destroyed shall not be made good, except in cases caused by fate or the king.

Interest does not accrue on the use of a pledge consisting of copper vessels and the like belonging to a *gopī* (cowherd woman). Likewise, in the case of a beneficial pledge (*sopakāra*)—such as a bull or similar animal that provides a service—if the pledge is lost while interest is still due, the connection is that "no interest [accrues] once it has been rendered incapable of use. "Lost" (*naṣṭa*) means having undergone a transformation through damage such as breaking or piercing; having restored it to its former state, it must be returned. If interest has accrued, the interest must also be relinquished. "Destroyed" (*vinaṣṭa*) means having reached total ruin; that too must be returned by way of its value and so forth. Upon its delivery, if he receives the value together with the interest, then there is a loss of the value [of the original pledge].

"In the event of destruction, there shall be loss of the principal, except for that caused by fate or the king"—so says the statement of Nārada. "Fate" refers to fire, water, calamities of the locality, and so forth. Except for destruction caused by fate or the king, and excluding destruction caused by the debtor's own fault, the value must be paid with interest, or the collateral (adhi) must be returned by the debtor. As it has been said: "When a field has been swept away by a river, or when it has been confiscated by the king..."
"Another pledge must then be given, or the wealth must be paid to the creditor.
And likewise Nārada says:
"If, in some case, there should be a loss of the principal of the pledge caused by fate or by the king..."
"But the object [of the pledge] itself must be returned by the debtor; however, in case of inability [to repay], it shall be [returned] through enjoyment.
This means that whatever the value of the enjoyment is each year, that much must be paid as interest. Bhāradvāja, however, states a specific rule:
"The debtor who, for the sake of a purchase, should secretly use the pledge or employ it with force..."
Having paid triple the fine, he may again become a creditor.
On this point Vyāsa says:
"If a pledge consisting of gold or other valuables should be lost due to the fault of the borrower, [he must pay its value]."
Having cleared the debt along with the interest, the creditor shall cause the debtor to pay its principal value.
On this point, Bhāradvāja says: If,
at the time of entering into a loan, the creditor out of delusion does not accept it,
there is no enjoyment [of interest] from that point forward, nor does he cause that capital to increase.
One should not consider an excess of enjoyment or a decrease in the pledge;
rather, as long as it is recorded in the document, so long must it indeed be enjoyed.
And therefore:
"If even when being guarded, a pledge becomes worthless over time, another pledge must be provided, or else the wealth must be paid to the creditor. Thus it is said.
In this manner, the subject of movable property is to be understood. Therefore, Bṛhaspati said:
"A pledge (ādhi) is defined as a bond (bandha), and it is declared to be of four kinds:
movable and immovable, as well as to be kept (gopya) or to be enjoyed (bhogya)."
This is the meaning: a pledge (ādhi) is of two kinds—immovable and movable. For this very reason, Nārada said:
"A pledge is declared to be of two kinds, namely movable and immovable;
and that [pledge] is also declared to be of two kinds: to be kept (gopya) and to be used (bhogya)."

In this context, the usufructuary mortgage (*bhogyādhi*) is of two kinds: the usufructuary mortgage with a condition (*sapratyaya-bhogyādhi*) and the usufructuary mortgage without a condition (*apratyaya-bhogyādhi*). That which is for the purpose of clearing the principal along with interest is called a usufructuary mortgage with a condition; that which is for the purpose of clearing the interest alone is called a usufructuary mortgage without a condition. Regarding the usufructuary mortgage with a condition, Vyāsa says: "Having agreed upon a certain rate of interest and having actually received the property, [one says]:
'Enjoy my field for the sake of interest; the surplus shall be the destruction of the principal.'"
If there should be an increase in interest due to such conditions, the repayment shall be double.

The meaning of the statement is that a pledge which is intended for the repayment of the principal along with interest is called a *sapratyaya-bhogyādhi* (a pledge for enjoyment with confidence). Now, Kātyāyana describes the *apratyaya-bhogyādhi* (a pledge for enjoyment without confidence):
"If, having received goods for the sake of interest, one gives property suitable for use—whether movable or immovable—that is called a *bhogyādhi*."
Having paid a price exceeding that [original value], one may recover one's own field or property from [the other] field.

For the purpose of clearing off the principal amount of interest, the debtor, having paid the price obtained from the creditor in the case of a pledge for use (*bhogyādhi*), shall recover his own field and so forth. This is the intended meaning of the statement regarding the "pledge for use without trust" (*apratyayabhogyādhi*). On this point, Bharadvāja says:
"But in the case of a pledge with trust (*pratyayādhi*), the interest that was previously recorded must be enjoyed [by the creditor]."
One should eat only as much as is necessary; such is the settled conclusion of the scriptures.
Whatever additional amount is due there for interest, that must be given back to the debtor;
however, whatever is deficient up to the total of the interest, he should complete that deficiency in the debt.

Regarding a pledge for use that is accompanied by interest, at the time of redemption, one should pay what is insufficient toward the principal plus interest; if there is an excess, one should take it back—this is the intended meaning of the statement. On this point, Yama says:
"In the month of Vaiśākha and others, the redemption of a pledge for use should take place on the full moon of Āṣāḍha.
Whatever is deficient due to the fault of the creditor, this [excess] shall serve to complete it."
Interest on a low loan increases according to the "wheel-interest" rate;
for all those who are under obligation, there is in reality no repayment of the enjoyment [of the object] by force.
If one enjoys [the pledge] by force or at the wrong time, the fine is threefold as compensation; so says Bharadvāja.
If one pledges a pledge without the owner's permission, [he shall pay a fine].
[235] But he would be inferior to one who possesses his own wealth; in times of distress, he acts as before.

"In times of distress" means during a period of calamity, as before—the meaning is that one's own property is lost. In the case of a pledge involving a female slave and so forth, the wages [are forfeited]; in the case of a pledge involving a cart and so forth, the loss of the draft animals and so on [is forfeited]. However, in the case of a pledge involving a female slave, the rice and other products resulting from her employment in threshing and so forth are not lost; thus says Kātyāyana: "If one should compel a pledgee to perform work against his will or without his permission, the enjoyer shall be made to pay the fruit of that labor, or he shall not receive interest."
It should be understood that this occurs "in accordance with the [nature of the] act. The phrase "he shall be made to pay" implies that he is to pay it to the owner of the pledge through the king.
However, one who torments or threatens with words, punishment, or physical acts a person performing work on a pledge shall not incur the first amercement.

By the use of the present participle *kurvāṇam* here, it is indicated that even one who causes pain or intimidation while performing the act of pledging does not incur punishment. "If one should forcibly cause an unwilling person to enter into a pledge that has not been granted, he shall incur the first *sāhasa* fine; the creditor shall also forfeit the pledge."

"Anisṛṣṭam" means "not formally deposited. The essential meaning is that if one forcibly enjoys even a small amount of a secret pledge (*gopyādhi*) that has not been formally deposited, the penalty for the enjoyer shall be the total loss of the principal. However, if the enjoyment was carried out through fraud, the loss of the principal is proportionate to the enjoyment. Otherwise, the author of the *Candrikā* notes that the act of forcible seizure would become meaningless; thus, Hārīta states the rule for the protection of the pledge: "One should protect the pledge exactly as it was deposited."

The meaning is that after the pledge has been accepted, the creditor must protect the pledge with diligence until its return, so that no loss, depreciation, alteration, deterioration, or change into another object occurs during that interval. Even if the pledge, despite being thus protected, should be destroyed by the force of fate or other such causes, there is no fault on the part of the creditor; as that same author states:
"But in the event of destruction by fate or the king, there is never any fault on the part of the creditor.
Regarding this, Kātyāyana states a specific rule:

"If, through the fault of the creditor, the pledge should be lost or destroyed, he shall be made to provide another pledge; thus the debtor is released from the debt. This means that if the loss of the pledge occurs other than through the fault of the creditor, the debtor is released from the debt. Consequently, the debtor must be compelled by the king to pay the creditor an equivalent amount of wealth, either as an additional pledge or in cash. Regarding the realization of the pledge, Nārada says:
A pledge is declared to be of two kinds: immovable and movable;
the fulfillment of its purpose occurs through both, provided there is enjoyment [of the object], and not otherwise.

"Success" (*siddhi*) means success through formal assignment (*ādhitasiddhi*). "Otherwise" means by the mere acceptance of the creditor for what has been designated by the debtor, even without [the transfer of] possession; such is the meaning. And so says Kātyāyana:
"When a field or a house is marked with boundary signs, and villages and the like are recorded [in writing], then one attains success."

By this, it is indicated that being recorded in writing (*lekhyārūḍhatva*) is also a cause for establishing a pledge (*ādhi*). However, the primary purpose is indeed possession (*bhoga*). And so says Viṣṇu: "When two men dispute over a pledge deposited between them, victory belongs to the one whose possession has been established without force."
Regarding the existence of possession by both parties, Bṛhaspati says:
"When a single field has been mortgaged to two people at the same time, it shall belong to the one who first takes possession; for him, it attains validity."

And this should be understood to apply when both [pledges] are recorded on a document. As Vasiṣṭha has said: "When documents have been executed at the same time by the creditor, that pledge which has been possessed first is the stronger."

The intention is that, in the case of a pledge for enjoyment (*bhogyādhi*), priority based on being the primary cause of enjoyment is logically established as having greater force. However, when there is no distinction regarding the enjoyment— namely, if both [creditors] arrive desiring to enjoy it on the same day— the decision is that the pledge must be enjoyed by them equally after dividing it.

The singular form "by him" (*tena*) is an indication for the dual; the meaning is "by both. Alternatively, "by him" (*tena*) is a particle used in the sense of "then" (*tarhi*). Kātyāyana states the specific rule regarding objects of enjoyment and the like: "If one should make a single pledge (*ādhi*) for two [creditors], who among them would be the owner?
Of those two, that which was made first is to be accepted; the one who makes it [later] incurs the punishment of a thief."
"Previously established" means established previously by means of possession (*upādāna*) and so forth. Regarding simultaneity in possession and the like, Bṛhaspati says:

"Between two [claims] that have arisen at the same time, both shall be equal. "Of those that have arisen"—the ellipsis is "to perform possession and the like. Kātyāyana states that in the case of a secret pledge (*gopyādhi*), the written document alone is the stronger proof.
Just as the acts of mortgaging, selling, or giving away are established by means of documents and witnesses,
so too a document that contradicts a single prior transaction is considered fraudulent in that case.

"Written" means that which is produced by writing. "The one involving seizure is stronger. Even though there is no difference in their being established by writing, he (Kātyāyana) himself states the distinction between their relative strength:
"That which is not specified and that which is specified, and that which is written in one place and that which is written separately—the latter is superior," so said Kātyāyana.

That wealth whose specific nature has been determined at the time of the pledge is called "specified" (*nirdiṣṭa*); that which is the opposite of this is called "unspecified" (*anirdiṣṭa*). Even though there is a similarity in being specified at the time of the pledge, he [the author] says the same thing:
"But when one has designated his entire property, yet later takes back what is marked by name, how could that [latter] be more powerful than the marked [former]? (YDh 2.61)

For this very reason, Yājñavalkya said: "In the case of a pledge, a gift, and a purchase, the prior one is indeed more powerful. This means that among these three—pledge and so forth—the earlier transaction alone is legally valid. Otherwise, if one makes a field a pledge for one person and then takes whatever is required as a pledge from another for the same field, it belongs to the former alone, and not to the latter. The same applies to gifts and purchases.

If it is argued that since the fire has already been established at that time, it lacks the status of being one's own property (*asvatva*), and thus a re-establishment (*punar-ādhāna*) is impossible; and likewise, since it has already been given or purchased, the acts of giving or buying are not tenable, and therefore this statement is purposeless—then [we reply]:

It is said: "Vijñāneśvara states that this statement—that when someone, out of greed or delusion, performs a pledge (*ādhāna*) or other such acts despite the lack of ownership, the prior [right] prevails—is rooted in *nyāya* (logical principle) and is therefore not to be challenged. Even though ownership does not cease by the mere act of pledging, it is nonetheless obstructed. Consequently, a pledge or sale made by one whose ownership is thus obstructed is weak and is indeed sublated, because it is as invalid as if it were made by another. The same applies to gifting and purchase. It was with this intention that Vasiṣṭha also [spoke].
If one who has previously deposited [an object] sells it again, which of these two would be stronger? The prior [claim] is more powerful.

Therefore, in the phrase "purchased for a pledge" (*adhau parikrītaḥ*), the word *ādhaiau* is used in the locative case of scope (*viṣaya-saptamī*). Regarding the consideration of the relative strength between the acceptance of a pledge and a purchase, the opinion of some is that the former is weaker. He [Yājñavalkya] himself states this even when the acceptance of a pledge and a purchase occur simultaneously: "When a gift, a pledge, and a sale are all made on the same day, how should one deliberate in the event of a conflict among these three?"
[239] “All three should divide that wealth according to their shares;
for both, the acceptance [of the gift] is by way of division in accordance with the transaction.
Here, the word *kraya* signifies wealth (*dhana*), because the instrumental derivation (*karaṇa-vyutpatti*) is adopted. And so says Bṛhaspati:
If the sale, the ownership, and the receipt have all been completed on a single day,
how should the investigation proceed when there is doubt regarding all three?
"For they would indeed divide the three means of valid cognition according to their respective portions;
and both [the speaker and the listener] should receive them in three parts, in accordance with the object.
In the reading "pratigraha," the word "is accomplished" (*niṣpadyate*) is to be supplied as the ellipsis.
If a pledge is not released when the debt has doubled, it shall perish at the lapse of time; however, a pledge for the enjoyment of its fruit does not perish.

In this context, "loss of the pledge" (*ādhipraṇāśa*) means that the debtor relinquishes his connection to the pledge and it comes under the ownership of the creditor. This is what is meant: when the lent property has doubled in value over time through the interest accrued by the creditor's own effort, if the pledge is not released by the debtor through the repayment of the principal, then it is lost—it ceases to be the property of the debtor and becomes the property of the money-lender. The same applies to a pledge for a fixed period (*kālakṛta*). The term *kālakṛta* means "one for which a time limit has been set"; the word *kāla* is placed first in the compound according to the rule governing words beginning with *āhitāgni*. Such a pledge is lost when the determined time arrives. Regarding a pledge to be enjoyed for its produce (*phalabhogya*)—that is, one whose enjoyment consists of its fruit, such as a field or a grove—it is never lost. For it has been stated that a pledge for a fixed period that is not to be enjoyed is lost upon the lapse of that time, as in the verse: "A pledge for a fixed period is lost when the time expires. Thus, the absence of loss for a non-fixed-period pledge that is to be enjoyed is established by the principle of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*), meaning that the phrase "the pledge shall be lost" refers specifically to a pledge for a fixed period that is merely to be kept (*gopyādhi*). When loss occurs through the sequence of doubling the principal or the lapse of the determined time, a waiting period of fourteen days must be observed.
When gold has doubled and the time limit fixed by the agreement has expired,
the creditor becomes the owner of the pledge after waiting for two weeks.

"By giving that amount of money in the interim, the debtor shall obtain release from the pledge"—from this statement of Bṛhaspati, it is intended here that "money" refers to the value including interest. As Vyāsa has said:
"The debtor should redeem the pledge for custody once it has doubled in value."

"Beyond double"—the meaning is: when the profit on the lent capital has ceased. "He should redeem"—the remainder is that this is done by paying the principal along with interest. Even within the period prior to the cessation of profit, if the money is paid back together with interest, the recovery of the pledge is established by the logic of the "stick and the cake" (*daṇḍāpūpa-nyāya*).
Therefore, having paid the money within that interval, the debtor may recover the pledge:
"The debtor should redeem the pledgeable collateral beyond [the doubling of] the amount."

It should not be said that the explanation of these two statements—that the pledge must be released immediately after the debt has doubled, and that only the doubled principal itself is to be paid in the interim, rather than being paid before the doubling occurs despite the interest accrued over time—is incorrect because it contradicts the interpretations of the authors of the *Candrikā* and *Kulārka*. Since this very explanation follows the opinion of Bhāruci, it is the correct one. In the case of an immovable pledge, the doubling of the debt is the cause for its forfeiture (*gopya*). However, the creditor lent the money for half the value of the pledgeable property, not for the sake of interest. Therefore, whenever the lent amount is repaid, only the doubled principal itself must be returned. There is no acquisition of ownership by another [the creditor] until after the debt has doubled.

"The creditor becomes the owner of the pledge after waiting for two weeks. Thus, the creditor's ownership of the pledge occurs precisely after fourteen days; therefore, ownership of the pledge does not arise immediately after the doubling of the debt. Consequently, even before the doubling, the debtor must pay exactly the doubled amount—this is the established doctrine of Bhāruci. Hence, it should be understood that the opinion of the author of the *Candrikā* and others is incorrect. Having paid the principal alone, the debtor shall obtain the pledge at the end of the period for which it was held as usufruct.
"Having reached the limit of the maximum period, one should release the pledged object that was to be enjoyed.

Here, "āhitam" means "pledged" (*ādhīkṛtam*). And this refers to immovable property. Regarding movable items such as clothing and the like, which are to be enjoyed in their own form, there is no fixed limitation of time. On this point, Bṛhaspati says:
"When a debtor, having paid the principal amount of money, requests the release of the pledge..."
At that very moment it must be released by him; otherwise, the owner incurs guilt.

In this regard, there is a fault—the fault of theft. Due to the separation of place and time, even the creditor’s family must relinquish that object when the creditor is absent. When the one who commissioned the transaction is present, one should obtain the pledge after depositing the wealth in its original form. "Having deposited" means having given it. Bṛhaspati states a specific rule regarding what has been stipulated:
When the debtor, having reproached him, gives the field back to the creditor,
it is certain that it must be released by you for the sake of a peaceful settlement.

"When the principal together with interest has been entered [into the account], you must deliver it to me"—having thus stipulated "this shall be yours" and so forth at the time of taking the loan, if one should provide a pledge such as a field; the meaning is that the acquisition of the pledge occurs according to the previously mentioned rule. Yājñavalkya states that the acquisition of the pledge is established even after the cessation of the accrual of profit by means of this very stipulation:
"But when the debt has become doubled upon the pledge, then indeed..."
The pledge shall be released once the debt, having been doubled, has been paid from the income derived from it.

On this point, Viṣṇu states: "That immovable property which was given solely for the purpose of securing the repayment of the borrowed money must be returned when that borrowed money has been repaid. Worldly people call such a pledge a *kṣayādhi* (perishing pledge). Some refer to this very type as a *paribhāṣitādhi* (defined pledge), while others call it a *saṃvidādhi* (contractual pledge).

If it is argued that "the forfeiture of the pledge would be untenable, because for the debtor there is an absence of causes such as giving or selling which would terminate his ownership, and for the creditor there is an absence of causes such as acceptance or succession which would establish his own ownership," then:

"Not so," says Vijñāneśvara. "In common worldly practice, it is well known that the act of pledging (*ādhīkaraṇa*) alone is the cause for the cessation of ownership with its conditions, and the acceptance of the pledge (*ādhisvīkāra*) is the cause for the acquisition of ownership with its conditions. Here, when the doubling of the debt and the arrival of the stipulated time have occurred, there is an absolute cessation of the substance; by this statement, the debtor's ownership ceases absolutely and the creditor's absolute ownership arises. The author of the *Candrikā* (Vya. p. 142), however, states: "Although in common worldly practice the doubling of the debt and the passing of the limiting time are not generally recognized as causes for the destruction of ownership, nevertheless, such recognition exists in the case of the exchange of goods. This is because, due to the prohibition against selling sesame seeds, even when no sale is made, one observes the cessation of ownership over the sesame seeds through exchange. Therefore, in this case as well, since a time-limit has been fixed and the creditor and debtor have reached an agreement on the exchange at the very time of the transaction—thinking, 'If I do not pay within this much time, the pledge itself shall belong to you to discharge my debt'—it is indeed logical that the destruction of ownership occurs at the limiting time."

The underlying intention is as follows: according to the view of Vijñāneśvara, there is here a literal destruction of one’s own ownership and the acquisition of another’s ownership. According to the view of the author of the *Candrikā*, it is the position of the Naiyāyikas; for, in the absence of purchase, acceptance, or other such means, ownership is acquired by the creditor through exchange or pledge, as established by the principle that this applies to the one who exchanges sesame seeds, just as in the case of rice and other grains.

Others, however, say: "By virtue of a technical convention (*paribhāṣā*), there will be a subsequent sale (*krayāntādhi*) of that which has been doubled in value as its price; thus, it is a sale with a condition (*sopādhikakraya*). Since ownership (*svatva*) is a worldly matter, it is not logical for it to be based on a scriptural injunction. As for the fact that exchange (*vinimaya*) brings about ownership, this is because statements such as "One becomes an owner through inheritance, purchase, partition, acquisition, or finding" are intended as restrictive rules (*niyamapara*); therefore, it is a subsequent sale by technical convention. This is the opinion of Bhāruci, Aparārka, and others, who hold that [ownership arises] either at the conclusion of a sale or at the conclusion of a verbal gift (*vācikadāna*).

This is the intended meaning: at the stage of a pledge (*ādhi*), an exchange (*vinimaya*) is simply not possible. By virtue of convention (*paribhāṣā*), at times such as the Festival of Lights (*dīpotsava*), one says, "I shall certainly give this; otherwise, this pledge shall remain yours. In that case, by the convention itself, the wealth is perceived as a saleable object subject to a condition (*sopādhika-kraya-dravya*). Alternatively, even in the rule "In time, that which is made for a time [as a pledge] shall perish," the destruction of the pledge is understood precisely through convention. Therefore, what is called "convention" is a verbal gift (*vācanika-dāna*); thus, it is the gift alone that brings about ownership (*svatva*). Consequently, because it culminates in a gift, the pledge brings about ownership. With this very intention, Vijñānayogin stated: "Ownership arises from verbal statement" (*vacanāt svatvam*). "Verbal statement" means convention—that is to say, a verbal gift. Otherwise—[if it were a sale], in the case of immovable property or a visible pledge (*sthāvara-dṛśya-ādhi*), [the rule would apply].

"By the very same principle as the prohibition against kinsmen, the prohibition against a pledge (ādhi) is intended. According to this principle which will be stated later, prohibitions regarding pledges from among one's kinsmen would not apply; yet such is not possible. A "pledge" (ādhi) is a collateral security. Since a prohibition—such as "the debt must neither be paid nor accepted"—is possible in the case of giving or receiving a loan, there are no prohibitions regarding pledges from among kinsmen in the case of a visible pledge (dṛśyādhi), and those [prohibitions] certainly do not apply. Therefore, the view that it is only in the case of a verbal gift (vacanikadāna) that [the rules] properly apply is correct. Prajāpati describes the nature of a subsequent pledge (anvādhi): [The text continues with the definition of *anvādhi*: "A subsequent pledge is that which is given after first depositing another pledge for the sake of the same purpose, by one who has already received a loan. If a creditor should cause another person to take a pledge by means of that very same wealth, he must first have a written document of pledge executed and then hand it over to him. Thus it is said.

"Whatever wealth has been lent to the owner of the pledge, he may transfer that same amount of wealth to another creditor as a pledge, but not for more than that," says the author of the *Candrikā* (Vya. p. 143). Viṣṇu also states that a pledge for custody (*gopyādhi*) can become a pledge for use (*bhogyādhi*): "[244] Even a pledge by convention (*pāribhāṣika*) may become a pledge for use. The word "even" (*api*) includes time and other such factors. "By convention" (*pāribhāṣika*) means obtained through a specific agreement. For example: "This pledge shall be used until the day it is not released when the debt lent to you has doubled"—this is a pledge for use that was originally for custody (*gopya-bhogyādhi*). Or: "If the principal lent at the time of a festival like Dīpotsava is not paid back, then from that point forward, starting from the date the loan was made, this pledge shall be for use"—this is a pledge for use determined by time (*kāla-kṛta-bhogyādhi*). By the term "by convention," it is indicated that even a pledge for use may become a pledge by time. For example: "Let this pledge for use be enjoyed until the time of the Dīpotsava festival for the sake of interest on the money lent; if we do not pay the principal then, then this pledge shall belong to you"—this is a pledge for use by time (*bhogya-kālādhi*). Gautama also speaks of a pledge for use becoming a pledge for custody: "A pledge for use may also become a pledge for custody because of the conventional nature of the transaction. "Conventional nature" (*pāribhāṣikatva*) means being based on a specific agreement. Furthermore: "Let this pledge for use be enjoyed for the sake of interest on the money lent until the time of the Dīpotsava; if the money lent is not paid then, let it not be used from the Dīpotsava onwards. After that, if the money lent has doubled with interest and we do not pay it, then this pledge shall be yours. A subsequent pledge (*anvādhi*) should be understood in the same way. A partial pledge (*khaṇḍādhi*) is the pledging of an amount of wealth—whether for one month, two months, or until the time of Dīpotsava—as the principal, based on whatever interest has accrued according to convention. Regarding this, Viṣṇu states a distinction: "In some cases, it ends with a transaction (*kriyānta*). This is the meaning: this aforementioned pledge, depending on the specific case, "ends with a transaction" if the double amount of goods is not paid at the time of Dīpotsava or similar occasions; in such a case, "this pledge is sold for that double amount of goods. A pledge for use that ends with a transaction is also one that ends with a transaction. For example: "Let this pledge be enjoyed for the sake of interest; if the principal is not paid at the time of Dīpotsava, then this pledge itself is sold for the value of the principal. In these cases, such as those ending with a sale or involving a mixture of types, the rules regarding sales apply because they end with a sale due to the force of the convention.
In the forenoon, in the midst of the village, and in the presence of kinsmen and neighbors,
one acquires the earth through the gift of gold and water by means of these six [acts].

Such dharma exists only when [the debtor] is alive; therefore, by the logic to be stated later—namely, "by means of the relatives and so forth"—one must act with the consent of the relatives and others. However, if the debtor should die or suffer some calamity before the seizure of the property that was pledged as security for a loan while the debt remains unpaid, then what should be done? To this, Bṛhaspati says:
"When the gold has doubled, if the debtor has died or disappeared, one should take possession of his property and sell it in the presence of witnesses."
"Or one should guard it for ten days in the assembly of people after its price has been paid; thereafter,
having received another [item] commensurate with the debt, one should relinquish the former," so says Kātyāyana.
But where there is no depositor, the creditor shall report the pledge to the king;
then, having made it public, the creditor may sell it.
Having taken the amount together with the interest, he should then hand over the remainder to the king.

The phrase "he shall hand it over to the king" refers to a situation where relatives (*jñāti*) and others who are nearby are absent; for when they are present, it is only logical that the handover should take place with them. This is the underlying intention: the injunction ending with the handover to relatives and so forth applies only to cases involving high-value items and the like, because the mention of "anger" and "handing over" is connected specifically to those cases. However, in the case of an item of equal value, the seller himself should take it back in the presence of witnesses. In the case of a low-value item, the seller may take it back after having accepted it; if the debtor later comes to the person authorized to pay the remainder of the debt, he may then take it from him. But if he does not come, the rule "let it be lost" and so forth should be applied accordingly. However, when one has taken a loan without regard for the merit (*sukṛta*) of the pledgor, even though the doubling of the interest has occurred, the principal plus interest (*śāntalābha*) does not increase further. Furthermore, if the creditor, thinking that he cannot perform another pledge or sale of the pledged item, intentionally delays the repayment of the debt; or if, due to his own integrity, the creditor accepts only the original pledge and the debtor of lower caste does not pay the money—then Yājñavalkya states that the king shall compel him to pay.
"He shall cause that debt to be paid with interest, secured by a *caritrabandhaka*.

Here, *caritrabandhaka* means a pledge consisting of *caritra*. By the word *caritra*, the *apūrva* (unseen spiritual merit) produced by bathing in the Gaṅgā, performing the *agnihotra*, and so forth, is denoted. In a case where wealth has been acquired by making that very merit a pledge, that same wealth must be paid back when it has doubled; there is no forfeiture of the pledge. Regarding this matter of pledges, Kātyāyana says:
"If a creditor enjoys a pledge from a debtor on the basis of a fraudulent document..."
The king, having caused the money to be paid, shall destroy the pledge-deed.

For the purpose of securing the substance or the enjoyment [of the debt], one should also consider the possibility of profit or loss. It has been stated that upon the payment of the money, one should take a pledge (*bandha*) or a surety (*lagnaka*). Having described the nature of the pledge therein, he now states the nature of the surety: "Scholars have observed in the scriptures that there are four kinds of sureties: for appearance, for trial, for payment, and likewise for the delivery of the debtor's property."

*Pratyaya* means trust. *Dāna* is the handing over of property for the purpose of discharging a debt. *Ṛṇidravya* is the property of the debtor; its *arpaṇa* is the handing over of household utensils and the like.
Bṛhaspati states the nature of these four types:
"One says, 'I shall show it,' while another, being honest, has said, 'Here it is. [247]
"I am the giver; I bestow this wealth," said another.

One is the *darśana-pratibhū* (surety for appearance). Thinking, "I shall produce him when he attempts to flee," he offers his surety and says: "Another is the *pratyaya* (surety for confidence), a specific type of surety who is honest and non-deceptive; he says, 'Give him the money on my guarantee. This is the surety for payment (*dāna-pratibhū*), who says, 'If he does not pay the wealth received, then I shall pay it back with interest. Another is the surety for the delivery of the debtor's property (*ṛṇidravyārpaṇa-pratibhū*), who says, 'When he does not pay the wealth received, then I shall deliver it on his behalf. This is precisely the distinction between the surety for the debtor and the surety for payment. Where there will be a lapse of time before evidence—whether seen or unseen—is produced for the determination of a lawsuit, there too a surety must be appointed for that evidence. A surety must also be appointed for the sake of confidence regarding a slave and so forth, or when there is suspicion of theft and the like. As Kātyāyana has said:
In disputes concerning service by slaves, trust, and oaths,
one should cause a surety to be taken accordingly, or the reverse as appropriate.

In the opposite case—that is, regarding a reversal of the effect—one should act according to what is appropriate, as far as possible. A *lagnaka* is a guarantor (*pratibhū*). On this point, Kātyāyana states: "But the guarantor for appearance who produces [the person] at the appointed time—if he should produce him there, the guarantor shall be released."

Manu says regarding non-appearance: "If a man stands as a surety for the appearance of another here, and fails to produce him, he shall pay that person's debt along with the interest to the men. [2.52]

"In this case, the debt is with interest," because of the legal tradition (*smṛti*) stating: "In the case of what is to be paid by the son of a surety, it is without interest. But Kātyāyana states a specific rule:
"For the purpose of searching for what has been lost, however, [the surety] should be made to pay for a maximum of three fortnights;
if he should produce [the debtor] there, the surety must be released."
"Even when the time has passed, if the surety does not produce this [document], he shall be made to pay that amount; such is the rule prescribed regarding debt.
Here, the phrase "three fortnights" (*pakṣatrayam*) is intended as an illustration for the limiting period. As Bṛhaspati said:
The creditor shall grant time to the surety for the recovery of lost property,
whether it be one fortnight, one month, or even one and a half months, according to the circumstances of the case.

Therefore, this statement is for the purpose of establishing a rule that [the debt] must be paid after three fortnights have passed. A surety for the delivery of the property of the debtor shall pay the wealth that is the subject of the dispute when the proof [of the debt] is established; he shall deliver that property when the debtor fails to perform his obligation. A surety for safety (*abhaya-pratibhū*) shall provide a remedy when danger arises. A surety for proof (*pramāṇa-pratibhū*) shall pay the wealth that is the subject of the dispute when the proof is established. If a slave or similar person has been carried off and is not recovered, a surety for confidence (*viśvāsa-pratibhū*) shall pay by way of compensation; such rules are to be applied in various cases accordingly.

Where a guarantor for appearance (*darśana-pratibhū*) or a guarantor for confidence (*prātyayika*) has died, their sons shall not pay the debt; however, those who stand as sureties for payment (*dāna*) must pay it.

When a guarantor for appearance (*darśana-pratibhū*) or a guarantor for trust (*prātyayika-pratibhū*) has passed away, their sons shall not pay the debt incurred by the guarantee. However, the sons of one who was a guarantor standing for payment (*dānāya sthitaḥ pratibhūḥ*) shall pay it. By the word "sons," it should be understood that the prohibition against paying interest implies a prohibition against paying the principal. "A grandson shall pay a grandfather’s debt incurred through a guarantee; a son shall pay his own father’s debt equally. But the grandson of that [son] need not pay—this is the settled rule. (YDh 2.51)

According to this statement of Vyāsa: a grandson shall pay an ancestral debt incurred by his grandfather, excluding that which arose from suretyship, in equal measure—meaning he should pay exactly as much as was borrowed, and no interest. Likewise, a son shall also pay an equal amount for a paternal debt incurred through suretyship. The meaning of the text is that the sons of these two—the grandson and the son—and their respective sons (the great-grandson and the great-great-grandson), being those who have received wealth in succession, must be made to pay the debt incurred through suretyship. When the debtor is destitute of wealth and a consumer [of the funds], the surety is declared to be one who possesses wealth; in such a case, the son of that surety must pay only the principal, not the interest.
If the debtor is destitute of wealth while the surety possesses wealth, the principal alone shall be paid by him;
he is not liable to pay interest.

In a case where one who acts as a surety for appearance (*darśana-pratibhū*) or a surety for confidence (*pratyaya-pratibhū*) has become a surety after taking sufficient collateral (*bandhaka*), his sons must also pay the debt incurred through that suretyship from that very collateral. As it is said: "Where one stands as a surety for appearance after having taken collateral, the son shall be made to pay that debt from that wealth even without the father."

The mention of "seeing" (darśana) is also indicative of the "testimony" (pratyaya). [This applies] when the father is deceased or has gone to a distant land, even in the absence of the paternal uncle. On this point, Bṛhaspati says:
"But if the first two [sureties] fail, they must pay the wealth reported at that time;
however, if there is a discrepancy, the latter two must pay, and in their absence, their sons likewise."

The first two are guarantors for appearance (*darśana-pratyaya-pratibhū*). When these two types of guarantor statements—such as "I will produce him" or "He is a virtuous man"—are false, they fail. The latter two are guarantors for payment (*dāna-dvayārpaṇa-pratibhū*). In the case of non-payment (*avaṃvāda*)—that is, when the debtor does not apply himself to the repayment of the debt due to deceit or other reasons—they fail. "In their absence" means when the latter two have gone abroad or have died. As Manu says:
"But the debtor shall pay the debt to the creditor if the nature of the transaction is known."
Afterwards, when the surety has died, by what means should one seek to recover [the debt]?
But if the man for whom the wealth was designated is a surety possessing sufficient wealth, he shall pay that from his own property; such is the settled rule regarding one who was "designated."

One who has "fully assigned his wealth" (*nirādiṣṭadhana*) is one whose wealth has been completely surrendered as a form of kinship. "Sufficiently wealthy" (*alaṃdhana*) means possessing adequate wealth. In this context, by the term *pratibhū* (surety), the son of a surety for appearance (*darśanapratibhū*) is indicated; otherwise, the statement that "if the surety dies later" would be contradicted—this is the consensus of many commentators. Regarding the case of multiple sureties, Yājñavalkya states the specific rule: "If there are many sureties, they should pay the debt according to their respective shares; however, among those who have relied upon a single [joint] liability, the creditor may collect as he pleases."

If there are two or many sureties for a single transaction, they shall pay that debt by dividing it according to their respective shares. Regarding those who have resorted to a single shadow (*ekacchāyāśrita*): the "shadow" is the similarity to the debtor; those who have resorted to it—just as the debtor stands ready to pay the entire amount, so too each of the payment-sureties stands ready to pay the entire amount. Likewise, in the case of a surety for appearance (*darśana*) or for trust (*pratyaya*), the creditor (*uttamarṇa*) may act according to his own will or desire. Consequently, among those who have resorted to a single shadow, whichever one the creditor requests for his own purpose—considering wealth and other factors—that person alone shall pay the whole, not merely a portion. Among those who have resorted to a single shadow, if someone has gone to another country and his son is present, then at the creditor’s wish, the son shall be made to pay him. But if someone has died, the son shall be made to pay his father’s debt along with interest. As Kātyāyana said:
Among those who have entered under a single roof, he who is seen there shall be made to pay;
if the owner is absent, his son shall pay the entire paternal share, but if the father is dead, the son himself shall pay it.
[251] Thus it is said. Regarding this, Hārīta states the specific rule:
"When a suretyship has been lost, all the sureties shall be made to pay."

This is the meaning: when the four types of suretyship (*prātibhāvya*) have proven false, the sureties must be made to pay that wealth to the creditor by the king; since this point has already been stated previously, it is not elaborated upon here. Thus, the summary here is as follows: at the time of taking a loan, a pledge (*bandhaka*) or a surety (*lagnaka*) should be established for the sake of confidence. In this regard, a pledge is of two kinds: a pledge to be kept in custody (*gopyādhi*) and a pledge to be used (*bhogyādhi*). Among these, the pledge to be used is of two kinds: that which is based on doubling the principal (*dvaiguṇya*) and that which is determined by time (*kālakṛta*). The time-determined one is further of two kinds: with interest (*savṛddhika*) and without interest (*avṛddhika*). The pledge to be used, however, is of four kinds: with consent (*sapratyaya*), without consent (*apratyaya*), a pledge subject to loss (*kṣayādhi*), and a secondary pledge (*anvādhi*). In that context, if a pledge to be kept in custody is used, there is no interest; if it is excessively used, the principal is lost. Even if the value is insufficient to cover the debt, the principal is indeed lost, and the debtor must pay the remainder. Having taken up to double the amount, the remainder should be paid to the debtor; if the debtor is absent, it should be paid to his kinsmen. After the amount has doubled, the pledge must be released. In the case of a pledge subject to loss, once the money has doubled and the value of the pledge has been recovered through its use, that pledge must be released. In the two types of time-determined pledges, the pledge must be released when the stipulated time arrives. In the case of a pledge to be used, if it is excessively used, one should cause the debtor to pay money according to the extent of the use. A secondary pledge (*anvādhi*), however, belongs only to one who has received an equal amount of capital; it does not hold if the amount exceeds that. If everything is contractual (*pāribhāṣika*), it certainly holds. As for a pledge to be kept in custody during a legal dispute, the opinion that the pledge holds only until the time of the trial because it is contractual has been refuted below. (Regarding *saṃkarādayas*, etc., they are established by convention alone. A surety for confidence (*viśvāsa-pratibhū*) must be made to pay the money if the confidence is betrayed. But a surety for appearance (*darśana-pratibhū*) must be made to pay the money in the absence of the person for whom he stood surety. If both have gone to another country or are dead, their son must pay only the principal. If the debtor becomes ruined or poor, the surety for payment must pay the money with interest; in his absence, even the son must pay with interest—this is the general rule. Regarding this procedure for the taking back and giving of loans, Bṛhaspati says: *(Note: The provided text ends mid-sentence regarding Bṛhaspati’s verse.)*

A debt contracted at a time other than the improper hour must be paid upon request; when the term has expired, it must be repaid with the agreed interest, and in the absence of the father, it must be paid by the sons.

"Aprakālam" means not at an improper time, that is to say, not after a long period of time. "Kṛtam" refers to a debt contracted with a specific condition, such as "it must be repaid during the festival of lamps. The meaning is this: a long-term debt is to be paid immediately upon request; a debt contracted with a condition is to be paid when that deadline arrives; and a debt for interest is to be paid once the profit has been settled. Even in the absence of the debtor, his sons must likewise pay it, for otherwise a fault is recorded in the legal tradition: "If an ascetic or an *agnihotra*-performer dies while still indebted..."
"Austerity and the *agnihotra* sacrifice—all that belongs to the wealthy man.
By this, the meaning is that the repayment of the debt must necessarily be performed. In that regard, it must be done with witnesses. As Yājñavalkya said:
"Whatever [debt] there may be, it should be accompanied by witnesses; that [debt] must be paid with witnesses."

Because of the general statement, it follows that in the absence of the previous witness, the debt must be paid in the presence of another witness. Regarding this, Pitāmaha states a specific rule: "Undivided kinsmen shall pay a debt incurred by a father or a mother;
in their absence, even those who are divided [shall pay], but not one for whom the debt was promised by him."
Varadarāja states that in the absence of property belonging to the mother or father or their relatives, what was promised by them need not be paid. Vyāsa, however, says:

"The grandson shall pay the grandfather’s debt, and the son shall pay what arose from a guarantee; the two grandsons of those [debtors] shall pay an equal amount, but it is settled that their sons are not to be made to pay. [253]

The *Pradīpa* states that even a grandson must pay a debt incurred through a guarantee (*prātibhāvya*). Furthermore: "If a debt has been contracted for the sake of the family by one who is undivided [from his kin], the heirs shall pay it when the head of the household has died or gone abroad."
Nārada says: Whatever debt has been contracted by an undivided paternal uncle or brother,
or by the mother for the sake of the family, the heirs shall pay that entire amount.
Bṛhaspati: Whatever property of the father has been taken by brothers, sons, slaves, pupils, or dependents for the sake of the family, the householder ought to pay that.
Kātyāyana states: That which was done for the marriage of a maiden, that which was performed for funeral rites,
and whatever was done by the family— all this must be paid.
On this point, Manu says: "He who, being unable to pay the debt, wishes to make a new transaction, shall,
after paying the interest that has accrued, renew the bond."

"Renewal (*parivartyate*)" means that one should again perform the act of writing [the document] marked with the current year and so forth. Regarding this as well, he (Yājñavalkya) states a specific rule: "Without having shown the gold [as collateral], one may renew the bond right there;
one ought to pay as much interest as has accrued."

By the word *hiraṇya* (gold/wealth), "conquered interest" (*nirjitā vṛddhi*) is meant; that is to say, interest that has been won over but not yet paid. Regarding this very point, it is said: "One should convert even a previously executed document"—the meaning is that one should treat the interest as the principal amount. Having given a small amount according to one's ability, one should obtain from the creditor a document known as an *upagata*. This must certainly be granted by the creditor as well: "The creditor shall give the *upagata*, marked with his own hand."

Thus says the *Smṛti*. And this position is to be understood as applicable when there is no son [to pay the debt]. Likewise, Viṣṇu states: "In the case of partial repayment and in the absence of the document, the creditor shall deliver his own written record. The words "to the debtor" (*ṛṇikāya*) are to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence. But when the document exists, the amount of wealth already returned should be recorded on the back of the document, and the remaining debt should be cleared away. This is the meaning: the "remaining" refers to the amount of wealth still owed out of what was borrowed. When one is unable to repay the entire amount, but has given something according to one's capacity, this is for the sake of clearing the account—that is, for the sake of a formal acknowledgment. It follows that when the entire wealth is paid, the document should be torn up. That very point has been clarified by Nārada.

"Having taken what has been brought forward, the creditor shall give it to the debtor with interest (*udaya*). Regarding this: "with interest" means for the sake of interest; "having taken what has been brought forward" means having accepted the agreement regarding the object, or having received a written receipt (*upagata-patra*) on the back of the document; "he shall give to the debtor" is the meaning. Some consider this statement to refer to the substance that must be accepted by convention every day or every month. Others, however, hold that "interest" refers to the wealth acquired by the debtor, which the creditor may take and compel the debtor to deliver through force—even by binding one who is unable to pay the debt and making them perform labor under his control.

Thus, because of the traditional teaching (smaraṇa) of Kātyāyana: "But one who is unfit for performing work should be kept in a prison; however, there shall be no entry into a prison for a Brāhmaṇa unless he is incapable [of working]. And therefore, even one of equal caste who has become impoverished should be made to perform appropriate labor. The mention of the Brāhmaṇa is an indicative mark (upalakṣaṇa) for those of superior caste; consequently, even a Kṣatriya or others who have become impoverished should be made to pay gradually to a Vaiśya or others. This very point has been clarified by Manu:
A creditor may even take action against a debtor, provided he is of equal or lower caste;
however, one who is of superior caste should repay the debt gradually.
[255] Thus it is said. Regarding this, Kātyāyana states the specific rule:
"But when there is a concurrence of multiple debts, whichever debt is the oldest shall be paid first;
after that, one may pay the king, and thereafter the debt to a Śrotriya."

In this context, a *śrotriya* is one who possesses merely the status of a Brāhmaṇa, and not necessarily one distinguished by learning or Vedic study; for the term *śrotriya* is employed here with reference to a superior caste relative to the king and others. The sequence of castes as traditionally established should be understood here, because the Brāhmaṇa is to be favored due to his venerability. Likewise, when a Kṣatriya and a Vaiśya, or a Vaiśya and a Śūdra, appear simultaneously, the debt should be paid according to the order of the castes, since each preceding one is more excellent and thus more worthy of favor. It should be understood that when the discharge of the debt is carried out in this order, the rule beginning with "one of low caste who is impoverished" (*hīnajātiṃ parīkṣīṇam*) is to be kept in mind. On this point, Kātyāyana says:
Where it is written on a single day, one should treat the debt as equal;
otherwise, however, the taking, the characteristics, and the profit follow their respective order.
Otherwise—that is to say, by reason of the difference in days apart from one day and so forth—is the meaning. Regarding this, he (Yājñavalkya) himself states an exception in a certain case:
"If a person should prove that a commodity was purchased with a specific object, then that object must be returned by the debtor alone; in that matter, it cannot be otherwise."
On this point, Bṛhaspati says:
"A debt incurred that is not time-barred must be paid to one who requests it;
when the term has expired, it must be paid with interest ceased, and in the absence of the father, it must be paid by the sons."
And so Nārada says:
"Fathers desire sons for the sake of their own interest, thinking,
'He will liberate me from my creditors and my debtors.'"
Therefore, once a son is born, he should strive with effort to liberate his father from debt so that he does not fall into hell, even at the cost of setting aside his own interests.

[256] Thus it is said. Regarding this, the discharge of debt has been stated: "A Brāhmaṇa, being born, is indeed born burdened with three debts," as declared by the Śruti; the status of the debtor has already been explained previously. On this point, Kātyāyana says: "But when the father has passed away, [the son] who has not yet attained legal capacity may, at the proper time, pay according to the rule; otherwise, they shall dwell in hell."

He (Yājñavalkya) himself states that even while the father is still alive, if he is unable to repay the debt incurred by the father, the sons must pay it: "Even if the father is present, if he is afflicted by disease or has gone abroad from his own country,
the debt incurred by the father must be paid by the sons after twenty years."
Regarding the phrase "from twenty years"—the *Candrikā* states that the remainder of the passage means "starting from [the time of] departure from exile" and so forth. Bṛhaspati, however, says:
"When present, the debt of a father must be paid by the sons, provided it is proven;
[but not by those who are] born blind, outcaste, insane, or afflicted with consumption, leprosy, and similar diseases."
And likewise Nārada says:
"When the father has passed away, the sons shall pay the debt according to their respective shares,
whether they are divided or undivided, or whoever may have undertaken that burden."
But while the paternal wealth exists, the son shall not take the property;
that wealth must be given to the creditor, and if he takes it after [the father] has died, he shall be made to pay it back.

When the father has died, one who takes the property is made to pay—meaning that the son, precisely when taking the property after the father’s death, is made to pay. However, when there is a conflict between a debt contracted by the father and one contracted by himself, the father’s debt must be paid like his own. First the debt contracted by the father must be paid; first the debt contracted by the father is to be paid, and afterwards his own.
A debt contracted by the father must be paid by the sons like their own, provided it is proven.
Thus, according to the Smṛti of Bṛhaspati. He (Bṛhaspati) himself states what is not to be given:
"A loan for a wager, a useless gift, that which was promised out of lust or anger, a suretyship, and the remainder of a fine or a tax—these the sons shall not be made to pay."

*Sauram*—that which is caused by the production of liquor. *Ākṣikam*—that which is caused by defeat at gambling. *Vṛthādānam*—that given to dancers and the like. The rest is easy to understand. Regarding the subject of useless gifts (*vṛthādāna*), there is another Smṛti text: "A gift given to a messenger, a panegyrist, a wrestler, a quack physician, a gambler, a corpse, a flatterer, or a wandering bard—in these cases, the gift becomes fruitless."

*Cāraṇas* are singers; *cāṭas* have been mentioned previously. Kātyāyana has stated regarding what was promised: "Whatever has been promised, whether recorded in writing or spoken as a loose promise—that one should know to be a debt arising from passion (*kāmaśruta*) owed to a woman who previously belonged to another."
*Muktaka* means that which is devoid of writing. Likewise, *krodhapratiśruta* has been described by that same [author]:
"That which is spoken out of anger after having caused injury or destroyed property, yet is intended to bring satisfaction, should be known as *krodhapratiśruta*."

This is the meaning: when, having committed an act of violence or the destruction of property out of anger, one promises, "I shall give wealth to satisfy him," that debt is said to be born of anger. In this context, "suretyship" (*prātibhāvya*) is intended to mean that which is to be paid by a surety for appearance (*darśana-pratibhū*). And so says Manu: "A son is not liable to pay for suretyship, a frivolous loan, what is due from gambling, what is due from liquor, nor the remainder of a fine or a tax."
"But regarding surety for appearance, there shall be the rule previously enjoined.

This means that the rule previously stated—that the son ought to give the surety—is the rule here. The meaning of the two terms "fine" (*daṇḍa*) and "remainder of the fine" (*daṇḍaśeṣa*), as well as "toll" (*śulka*) and "remainder of that," has been clarified by Uśanas:
"A fine, or the remainder of a fine, a toll, or the remainder of that very toll."
But a son must not pay that which is not legally enforceable. [258] "Not legally enforceable" means pertaining to a gambling debt (*saurika*).
Now, it is stated that the grandson must pay; regarding this, Manu says:

A debt that is defective or repudiated by the father must never be paid. "Defective" means tainted with fault due to being caused by the vices of gambling and the like. "Repudiated by the father" means rejected or denied by him. If it has been established by evidence—whether the father himself witnessed it or denied it—it must be paid; for "a debt must be paid by sons and grandsons when it is proved by witnesses in case of denial."

Thus says Yājñavalkya. Here, the phrase "not to be given" (*adeyam*) is an elliptical expression for all that is not to be given; therefore, whatever else has been stated regarding sons should also be understood to apply to grandsons. Regarding what must be paid by the citizens (or the community), Kātyāyana states: "A debt seen [contracted] by the father, or one inherited in due order from the grandfather, which is free from defects and has not been cleared by the sons, must be paid by the grandsons—so says Bhṛgu."

The meaning of this is as follows: "Inherited from the father" means that which has come down from the father without dispute, by virtue of having been given by one's own father. "Passed down in succession from the grandfather" means free from defects—that is, devoid of any defect that would render it non-transferable. "Not withdrawn by the sons" means not set aside by the sons due to such factors as incurable diseases. And so says that same [author]: "That which must always be given by the fathers, in their absence, should be given from that wealth;
or else, in the absence of those [fathers], that wealth should be given to their owner by the sons or grandsons."

The meaning is that when paternal wealth exists, the debt must be paid from that very wealth; even in the absence of wealth, it must be paid by virtue of being a son or a grandson. However, it was stated previously that grandsons shall not pay for suretyship in any form whatsoever. Regarding this matter, Viṣṇu has stated a specific rule: "If the debtor has died, renounced the world (*pravrajita*), or been away for twenty years, the debt must be paid by his sons or grandsons; beyond this period, it need not be paid by those who do not desire it. "Renounced" means one who has become a *saṃnyāsin*. "Twenty" refers to twenty years. The meaning is that if the debtor has been away for a period of twenty years while holding the wealth. The phrase "beyond this period, by those who do not desire it" means that after the sons and grandsons, those born later—such as great-grandsons and so forth—who do not wish to pay, need not pay it. Furthermore, this recovery of the debt after twenty years applies to cases where no property was previously requested; if it was requested, it must certainly be paid. As Hārīta says:
As long as the duration of its validity remains, it shall be written down without any cancellation (*nirapākṛti*).

Here, "cancellation" (*apākaraṇa*) refers to recording the entry of the wealth received, the execution of a counter-document (*pratipatra*), the formal entry of the legal transaction in a place where witnesses and other requirements are present, and so forth. For this very reason, Yājñavalkya states:
"Or, once the debtor has paid the money, one should write [the discharge] on the back of the document."
Or the creditor shall give back what has been received, marked with his own hand.

When the debtor is unable to pay the entire debt, he should, having paid according to his capacity, write upon the back of the previously executed document: "This much has been paid by me. Or, the creditor, having received the money that was due, should give it [in writing] upon the back of that very document, marked with characters written in his own hand, stating: "This much has been received by me. Alternatively—the creditor should give the debtor a *upagata* (receipt) marked with characters written in his own hand. Although this has already been enjoined previously, it is stated here again for the sake of clarity and in connection with the context; thus, there is no redundancy. Regarding what should be done with the document when the debt is paid in full, the same author says:
One should tear up the document upon paying the debt, or else have another one made for the sake of clearance.

Having paid the entire debt either gradually or all at once, one should tear up—that is, destroy—the previously executed document. However, when the document is located in a difficult place or has been lost, then for the sake of clearance—meaning for the purpose of terminating the status of debtor—one should have another document executed. The creditor, too, should give a certificate of clearance to the debtor; this is the meaning. He [Yājñavalkya] himself states that the entire debt must be paid when there are witnesses present.
[260] "And that [debt] which has witnesses should be paid with witnesses.

That debt which was contracted in the presence of witnesses must be repaid in the very same presence. Regarding the non-payment of debt (*ṛṇādāna*), the son, grandson, great-grandson, and the heir (*dāyabhāk*), as well as the wife and others, are entitled to discharge the debt. Their order is as follows: first the son; in his absence, the grandson; in his absence, the great-grandson—this is the established sequence. Yājñavalkya states the order when there is a concurrence of different claimants: "The one who takes the inheritance (*rikthagrāhī*) shall be made to pay the debt, and likewise the one who takes the wife (*yoṣidgrāha*)."
"The son is the heir to one who has no other property to rely upon and is himself without a son. Thus it is said.

The meaning of this is as follows: when a man who has no son—that is, one devoid of a suitable son or other heirs—dies while possessing wealth, the heir to his property (*rikthagrāhī*) must be made to pay whatever debt he left; "the king" is the understood subject. In the event of the loss [of the estate], the inheritor of that inheritance, such as a brother, must be made to pay; this is the sense. In the absence of such a person, the one who takes the wife (*yoṣidgrāha*) [is liable]. He who takes the wife of a *svairiṇī* from among the three types of *svairiṇīs*, or the first among the three types of *punarbhūs*, having transgressed the prohibition [against such unions], is the "one who takes the wife. And so says Nārada: [Text of Nārada: ...he who takes the wife of a *svairiṇī* from among the three types of *svairiṇīs*, or the first among the three types of *punarbhūs*, having transgressed the prohibition [against such unions], is the "one who takes the wife. And so says Nārada.
Other women who have had previous husbands are said to be sevenfold in sequence;
among them, the *punarbhū* is of two kinds, while the *svairiṇī* is of four kinds.

A maiden who is either one whose virginity remains intact or one defiled by the taking of the hand in marriage is called a *punarbhū* (a remarried woman) when she undergoes the rite of re-consecration (*punaḥ-saṃskāra*).
A woman who disregards the laws of the land and, having been given by her elders to one man, commits an act of violence against another is proclaimed as the second [type of adultery].
Whether she has borne children or not, if a woman, while her husband is still living,
out of desire resorts to another man, she is the first type of unchaste woman (svairiṇī).
She who, having abandoned her husband from childhood, has resorted to another man,
and then goes back to her husband's house, is proclaimed as the second type.
But when her husband has died, she who rejects the brothers-in-law and others who have approached her and,
out of desire, approaches another man is proclaimed as the third [type of harlot].
She who has come from another land, purchased with wealth, and who, afflicted by hunger and thirst,
approaches you saying "I am yours"— she is proclaimed as the fourth type.
The last among women who have lived according to their own will and the first among those who have been remarried—
whosoever marries these two shall pay the debt contracted by their husbands.
But she who, within seven days, takes refuge with another man while still pregnant,
shall either pay her husband's debt or he may abandon her in that same manner.
"For one who dies without wealth and without a son, the debt of the one who took the wife departs;
he alone incurs the burden of the debt, and it is not recorded that the wealth belongs to anyone else. Thus [it is said].

In this context, "one possessing wealth" (*dhanin*) means one who possesses the inherited property; such a person is the "receiver of the wife" (*yoṣidgrāha*). He shall be made to pay the debt. In his absence, the one who has property dependent on another (*anyāśritadravya*) [shall pay]. One whose property is dependent on another—that is, not yet obtained—is "one with property dependent on another"; the meaning is "one whose wealth goes to himself. Then, by a negative compound (*nañsamāsa*), the opposite of that is meant: one for whom the inheritance has been obtained by another. He who is designated as unfit to receive the inheritance due to defects such as impotence and the like—he too must be made to pay. As for the interpretation that: "In the absence of an inheritor of the estate (*rikthagraha*), the receiver of the wife; in the absence of the receiver of the wife, one with property dependent on another; in his absence, the son; in his absence, if there are grandsons or great-grandsons of one who lacks sons and grandsons, they alone are to be made to pay"; and that if there is no inheritance-taking by the great-grandsons and others, the debt need not be paid by them—[this is incorrect], because in the phrase "the inheritors of one who lacks a son" (*putrahīnasya rikthinaḥ*), the word "inheritance" (*riktha*) refers specifically to the receiver of the wife.
He alone incurs the debt; it is not recorded that the wealth belongs to anyone else.

Thus, according to the statement of Nārada. Consequently, the mutual contradiction between the rules that "in the absence of a wife-seizer (*yoṣidgrāha*), the son shall be made to pay the debt," and "in the absence of a son, the wife-seizer" is as follows: When it is stated that "in the absence of a wife-seizer, the son [is liable]," this establishes the primacy of the wife-seizer and the status of the son as a secondary alternative (*anukalpa*), just as in the rule, "In the absence of *soma*, one presses *pūtīka* plants.
