This being the case, if it were then stated that "in the absence of a son, the wife-seizer [is liable]," it would result in a contradiction with the aforementioned primary and secondary alternatives. Thus, there is a mutual inconsistency. Moreover, if this were so, when both are present, neither would be liable to pay, because the liability of one is predicated precisely upon the absence of the other; and when both are present, the absence of either is impossible. Therefore, intending that the discharge of the debt itself would thus remain unfulfilled, [the author says]:
Among those who take the wealth, the wife, or the son, he who takes the wealth shall bear the debt;
a son who is not [legitimate] shall bear the debt for his mother and her husband; and one who takes a wife shall bear the debt for her husband and their children.

Thus, relying on the words of Nārada, the resolution of the contradiction has been made. Consequently, regarding the two interpretations, Aparārka explains the word ending in the plural number, *rikthinaḥ* (inheritors), in the phrase "of the heir of one who is sonless" (*putrahīnasya rikthinaḥ*). In response to the expectation, "To whom should those who take the wealth, the wife, or the son be made to pay?"—[the answer is] they are to be made to pay to the creditor (*uttamarṇa*), that is, to his son and so forth. When there is no son or other [heir], in response to the expectation, "To whom should they be made to pay?"—the phrase "of the heir of one who is sonless" means: of the creditor who lacks a lineage of sons and so forth, whoever is the heir (*rikthī*) capable of taking the inheritance, such as a *sapiṇḍa* or others—to that heir they are to be made to pay. Here, "*rikthinaḥ*" is the genitive singular. Vijñānayogin, following the desire of earlier teachers, has adopted this method of explanation by resorting to excessive effort through objections and their resolutions. As for the point that previously it was shown that the debt must be paid by sons and grandsons, and thus sons and grandsons—who are free from defects such as impotence—are qualified as heirs solely for the purpose of discharging the father's debt; and because, by its own natural sense, the words "son" and so forth are appropriately used in the sense of "noble son" and so on. Here, this is suspected: when sons and others do not exist, who would discharge that debt? In response to this expectation, this statement is begun to define other successive agents. Since an explanation according to the straightforward path in my stated manner is established, following a circuitous route is to be rejected. Kātyāyana, however, states a specific distinction:
And one who has fathered children while minors, or who has relied upon another for protection, shall repay that debt; this is well known as the debt concerning children while minors and so forth.

"He should give"—the meaning is "he should cause [them] to be given. This too has been stated for the sake of clarity. Since the wife has the authority to discharge the husband's debts, whereas children have no such authority, Bṛhaspati says on this point: "What has been borrowed by a paternal uncle, a brother’s son, a wife, a slave, a pupil, or a dependent for the sake of the family, the borrower ought to pay."
And so Kātyāyana says: "When a man has gone abroad or even died, a debt contracted for the sake of the family must be paid by the wife, the mother, the pupil, or the son; thus says Bhṛgu."
Nārada also says:

"But a woman who, having sons, abandons her son and resorts to another man—her entire property (wealth) shall be taken [by the first husband]; for a woman who is destitute of wealth, the son alone [shall take it]."
One should know that the omen of an eclipse is caused by calamity;
likewise, so too is that which is performed for a maiden's marriage or for funeral rites for the deceased.
All of this must be returned to the master by the family,
whether it was done for the sake of the family or, in case of incapacity, taken by one who was ill.

The meaning is that when the mistress of the household is incapable of maintaining the family, the debt must be paid by the master. And this refers to cases where the debt has been promised or subsequently approved, because of the traditional teaching of Kātyāyana: "That which was promised to be given, and that which was approved [to be given]. Regarding this, Kātyāyana states a specific rule concerning women:

If a woman has been told by her husband who wishes to marry her again, "You must pay this debt," she shall be compelled to pay it even if she is displeased, provided that the money was borrowed for the sake of the woman herself. [264]

If she has not agreed [to pay], then even in the absence of her husband’s wealth, she must discharge the debt by earning money through service as a laborer. However, Aparārka states that when there is a connection to the husband’s estate, the widow has the right to discharge the ordinary debt from whatever property exists, according to the principle of discharging debts from the inheritance. The author of the *Candrikā*, however, maintains that in this case, it is understood from the context that even if she has not relied upon her husband’s wealth, if she has not agreed [to pay], she is not to be made to pay. Regarding the succession of creditors, Nārada says:
"But what is to be given to a Brāhmaṇa who has no descendants, and who is no longer with us..."
One should offer it to the *sakulyas*; in their absence, to his *bandhus*.
But when there are no agnates, nor relatives by marriage or kinsmen, then one should give it to Brahmins; if they too are absent, one should cast it into the water.
In this context, the mention of the "Brāhmaṇa" is also indicative of the fire. "Deposit" (nikṣepa) refers to the oblation (homa). As the author of the *Saṃgraha* has said:

"If the property belonging to a debtor should somehow come into the possession of a Brāhmaṇa, [it shall be treated as a deposit] in the absence of heirs, beginning with the son and ending with the Brāhmaṇa, who are entitled to inherit."
"One should offer an oblation with the middle leaf of the *palāśa* tree;
then one should cast that wealth into the water with the mantra beginning 'yat kusīdam'.
Thus is stated the mantra beginning with "yat kusīdaṃ mayy anena" (whatever debt is mine by this).
Thus [ends the work of] the illustrious Vīragajapati, Lord of Gauḍa; Lord of the ninety-six million Karṇāṭakas; Sovereign of Jamunāpura; Protector of Huśanasāhi Suratrāṇa;
Son of the illustrious Durgāvarpu; One of supremely pure conduct; Supreme King of Kings and Great Lord.

The Chapter on the Recovery of Debts (*ṛṇādāna*) within the Section on Legal Procedure (*vyavahārakāṇḍa*) of the *Sarasvatīvilāsa*, a compendium of law (*smṛtisaṃgraha*) composed by the illustrious Great King Pratāparudra Mahādeva.
Now, the rule for the legal category known as *upanidhi* (deposit) is stated.

Previously, a debt was defined as that which is given into another's hand with reference to a prior accumulation; whereas a deposit (*upanidhi*) is property given into another's hand solely for the purpose of safekeeping, without such reference. Therefore, the occasion for *upanidhi* follows immediately after the section on the recovery of debts (*ṛṇādāna*). A deposit is that which, being sealed and without any mention of its specific nature, quantity, or particularities, is entrusted into another's hand out of trust for the sake of protection. As Yājñavalkya says: "That which is placed in the hand of another without describing its contents, while remaining in its container..."
"That substance, being a sealed deposit (*aupanidhika*), must be returned exactly as it was.
However, Nārada states the distinction between a sealed deposit (*upanidhi*) and a formal pledge (*nikṣepa*):
"That which is deposited in a sealed container, uncounted and unrecognized..."
"One should know that this applies to a sealed deposit (*upanidhi*); the learned call [this] a deposit (*nikṣepa*).
Regarding this, Manu states a specific rule:
"In one who is of noble birth, endowed with good conduct, knowledgeable in dharma, and truthful..."

"A wise man should deposit a trust with one who has a large following and is upright. Regarding "one with a large following"—meaning one who possesses many kinsmen—Bṛhaspati describes the nature of a deposit (*nyāsa*):
"Out of fear of kings, thieves, and the like, or from the desire to deceive heirs..."
"Property deposited in another's house is proclaimed to be a *nyāsa* (deposit).

Although the nature of *upanidhi* and *nikṣepa* was already explained during the discussion on the nature of the eighteen titles of law (*aṣṭādaśapada*), it should be understood here for the sake of proximity, as it was previously interrupted. And this [deposit] must be returned exactly as it was given, according to Yājñavalkya’s Smṛti: "It must be returned in that very same manner. On this point, Bṛhaspati says:
"That which is given in the presence of witnesses and that which is given in secret are declared to be of two kinds."
That [body] must be protected like a son; yet it perishes without regard [for one's efforts].
Whatever merit may arise from giving gold, silver, garments, and so forth,
that same merit belongs to one who protects a deposit exactly as he would one who has come for refuge.
Just as there is guilt for a woman in betraying her husband, or for a man in killing his son or friend,
so too is there guilt for men in consuming or neglecting a deposit entrusted to them.
"One should not take back the object deposited; for its destruction brings dishonor.
Here, by the word *nyāsa*, various types such as *upaniṣdhi* (sealed deposit) and others are intended. In the *Rāmāyaṇa*, however, it is said:
"Having given his sandals as a deposit (*nyāsa*) for the kingdom again and again..."
Thus ends the description of the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) upon the sandals; likewise, regarding "it should be returned":
one should not take the substance offered for the *nyāsa*, for its loss brings dishonor.
It should be understood that [the following] is for the purpose of returning such items according to these and other rules. On this point, he (the author) states an exception (*pratiprasava*).
If it should meet with destruction due to an act of God or the king,
there is no fault in that case, provided the deposit is returned together with the goods belonging to the receiver.

The word "of the receiver" (*grahituḥ*) is to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence. Since it has been stated that the phrase "together with the property of the receiver" (*grahītṛdravyasahitam*) serves to determine the absence of negligence (*upekṣā*) and other such faults, it should be understood that even if the property of the receiver exists, if there is a presence of dependence on other causes for its destruction, then fault indeed remains. The mention of "the king or fate" (*daivarājagrahaṇa*) is intended as an illustration of any cause for which the receiver must provide compensation. Yājñavalkya states a specific rule: "But he shall not be made to pay what has been stolen by the king, by fate, or by thieves.
The words "done through deceit" (*jihmakāritam*) are to be supplied. However, in the case of non-deceitful action, he is certainly to be made to pay, as Nārada says:
"That which is lost together with the object by the receiver is [the loss] of the giver;
likewise if it is caused by fate or the king, provided it was not brought about by his own dishonesty.
For he himself says:
If [the deposit] is lost when it has been sought for and offered, the borrower must restore it and be fined an equal amount.

If the owner seeks it—meaning requests it—and the borrower does not give it back, then even if subsequently the loss or destruction (*bhreṣa*) of the object occurs due to the king or other causes, nevertheless the borrower must restore the property to the owner by calculating its value, and he shall be fined an equal amount by the king. Regarding this, Bṛhaspati states a specific rule: "If the borrower should cause the deposit to be lost through negligence or indifference..."
"If, when requested, he does not give [the object], he shall be made to pay it with interest.

Regarding this, the author of the *Candrikā* states (Vya., p. 179): "In the case of loss, he should be made to pay by way of its value; however, in the case of no loss, he should be made to pay the object itself. The general measure of interest stated in the section on non-payment of interest (*akṛtavṛddhi*) is to be applied in the case of loss. But in the case of non-delivery—'If, when requested, he does not give, it increases by five percent.'"

Thus it is stated specifically in that very [text]. The measure of interest (*vṛddhi*) is to be inferred. By stating "by neglect through separation," he shows that if there is destruction due to neglect while the deposit is together with the depositor's own property, the rule for interest does not apply. Therefore, in that case, only the value prescribed by another Smṛti—"one who has neglected [the deposit] shall be made to pay an equal amount"—is to be given. And thus, even if there is destruction of what was not returned when demanded due to acts of God (*daiva*) or the King (*rāja*), only the principal (*mūla*) is to be given to the depositor; for since the fault is merely the delay in returning it, it is improper to give the deposit along with interest. And to the King, a fine equal to that [value] is to be paid.
Some explain this statement differently:
"If the borrower should lose the deposit through negligence or indifference,
or if, when being asked for it, he does not return it, he shall be made to pay it back with interest."

*Chalana* means deception. Or, if the receiver of a deposit (*nyāsa*) should lose that deposit through negligence or through its depletion; the mention of *nyāsagrahaṇa* (the taking of a deposit) is intended to include both a formal deposit (*nikṣepa*) and a sealed deposit (*upanidhi*). He must be made to pay an amount equal to the value [of the deposit], and he must be fined an equal amount. In the phrase "or if, when asked, he does not give," the word "or" (*vā*) has the sense of "but" (*tu*). If, at the time of being asked, it is said, "If it is not given now, then interest must be paid," and this is accepted by the receiver, then he should rightfully pay it with interest. If, however, due to some other cause, distraction, inability to return it, or greed, the receiver does not give it after being asked, this case falls under the section on the non-payment of debt (*ṛṇādāna*).

"If that which is requested is not given, it increases by five percent"—thus says Kātyāyana; so they say. But that is incorrect, because the distinction between the two topics of "recovery of debt" (*ṛṇādāna*) and "deposit" (*upanidhi*) has been demonstrated by the context. It is precisely here that the rules pertaining to the section on interest (*vṛddhi*) extend. For this very reason, Vyāsa said:
If [the goods] are consumed, he shall be made to pay with interest; if they are neglected, he shall be made to pay the full amount;
if the property is destroyed through negligence, he shall be made to pay a small fraction less.

Regarding this, Varadarāja says: "If it is eaten, he shall be made to pay with interest; if it is lost through negligence, he shall be made to pay the equivalent amount; if it is lost despite care, he shall be made to pay less by one-fourth. Thus says the eminent knower of the *Brahma-vidyā*. In that very same work, Varadarāja states: "The price for purchase and the deposit intended for purchase likewise increase through compound interest (*cakravṛddhi*) until it becomes fivefold. [269]

The price of purchase and the purpose of purchase are rooted in the doubt between buyer and seller. Interest on a deposit or a pledge shall be one and a half times [the principal] after three months, and triple after [six months];
beyond that, it shall increase according to the rule of compound interest (*cakravṛddhi*).
"But whatever man should suddenly seize the property of another by means of stratagems, he must be executed publicly in various ways...

Thus [it is said]. Varadarāja states that this refers to the case of low-born persons (*nīca*). Bhāruci, however, maintains that even in the case of low-born persons, this applies except for deposits (*upanidhi*). Regarding this, Bṛhaspati states a specific rule:
Where a debtor denies what was received, the judge, having established the fact through witnesses or by means of an oath,
shall cause him to pay the deposit and an equal amount as a fine.
And this refers to cases where there are witnesses; in the absence of witnesses, what was deposited in secret must be recovered in secret. Thus says Manu:
"In whatever manner a person deposits an object in the hand of another, in that very same manner it should be received back; as the delivery was, so shall be the recovery."

*Āya* means establishing; *graha* means taking possession. Regarding a secret gift, Bṛhaspati states the legal decision: "In a case where a dispute arises concerning a secret transaction, it is recorded in the Smṛtis that divine proof (*divya*) is the means of investigation for both parties."
A "deposit" (nidhi) is a "sealed deposit" (upanidhi). The meaning is: of one [of two] between both. On this point, Nārada says:
"This same rule is seen to apply to borrowed goods, articles held for delivery, and so forth;
likewise to artisans, sealed deposits, open deposits, and counter-deposits."

Regarding these items such as those borrowed for a specific purpose (*yācita*), this is the rule: it should be understood that the same procedure that applies to a deposit (*upanidhi*)—concerning its return and so forth—applies here as well. What is called "borrowed" (*yācita*) is clothing, ornaments, and the like, which have been requested and brought for festivals such as weddings; subsequently, that very object is placed in the hand of another with the instruction, "Give this back to the owner. However, some have stated the definition of "entrusted" (*anvāhita*) and "placed" (*nyāsa*): "Placed" (*nyāsa*) means the act of depositing an item in the hands of a family member while the owner of the house is absent, after first showing it to him. It must be handed over after informing the owner of the house. In this way, he explains that gold and other materials entrusted to a goldsmith or similar artisan for the purpose of making a bracelet or other ornament are denoted by the term *nyāsa*. "Counter-deposit" (*pratinyāsa*), on the other hand, is based on a mutual agreement regarding reciprocal interests, such as: "You must protect this of mine, and I shall protect this of yours. Bṛhaspati, however, states a specific distinction.
"This same rule has been declared regarding property that is deposited, borrowed, given as a craft-fee, pledged, or brought for safekeeping, as well as in the case of one who has come for refuge.

Regarding the matter of craftsmen, there is no fault if damage occurs to worn-out clothing and the like; however, if damage occurs to new clothing and the like, the artisan—whether a weaver, a washerman, or another—must be made to pay an amount equal to the value. In legal proceedings concerning "damage caused by the king or by fate," the decision must be reached through the very principles previously stated. Specific details regarding washermen and others will be explained further below.

Thus ends the section on the legal title known as "Deposits" (*upanidhi*) within the *Vyavahārakāṇḍa* of the *Sarasvatīvilāsa*, a compendium of law composed by the illustrious Great King Pratāparudradeva.
Now, the rules concerning the legal title known as "Partnership" (*saṃbhūyasamutthāna*) are set forth.
On this point, Nārada says:
"Where merchants and others perform an undertaking collectively, that collective enterprise is recorded in the legal treatises as a head of dispute (vyavahārapada)."

In the matter of non-payment of debt (*ṛṇādāna*), the increase produced from the capital lent belongs to one person alone; here, however, it belongs to many. Therefore, it is logical that this section should follow immediately after the section on non-payment of debt. Nevertheless, because there is no occasion for the section on deposits (*upanidhi*) immediately following that, and according to the aforementioned principle, the deposit follows immediately after non-payment of debt; thus, the proper occasion for this section is later. And so says Nārada:
"When those acting together through a means for the sake of profit perform an undertaking, the deposit which serves as their support should be recovered by them according to their respective shares."
The foundation is the means. The deposit is the depositing of goods.

Regarding that which is equal, excessive, or deficient—whatever portion belongs to whom, and of whatever kind—in that case, the treasury shall be established according to the income, the expenditure, and the growth.
The meaning is that for a small portion there is a small [share], and for a large portion there is a large one.
Collaborative work should be performed by those who are pure, brave, and knowledgeable regarding income and expenditure;
by those of noble birth, skillful, untiring, wise, and experts in the nature of goods.

The reading *nāṇakavedibhiḥ* occurs in some versions. *Nāṇaka* refers to dīnāras and other coins marked with various local mints. Vyāsa, however, speaks of the business of those who act in partnership: "Whether in the presence or absence [of witnesses], those who deceive one another should carry out buying and selling according to the nature of their various wares."
[272] "Those who conceal their goods shall pay the toll on the road;
otherwise, those standing outside the toll station shall be made to pay double.
Alternatively, by the permission of all, a single person may perform the duty for everyone.
If a single man, approved by many, should give wealth or cause a legal document (*karaṇa*) to be executed on their behalf, it shall be considered as having been executed by all of them.
Regarding disputes among those who act in partnership, Vyāsa himself has stated:
"Those very persons are declared to be the examiners and witnesses for one another in matters of doubt or in cases of fraud, provided they are not influenced by mutual enmity."
But when they are joined by malice, then he (Yājñavalkya) says the same:
"Whosoever among them is known to be a deceiver in buying or selling, he shall be cleared by oaths; this rule applies in every legal dispute."

"He is to be cleared by the members of the court"—this is the ellipsis. And this refers to the case of sea-faring merchants (*sāṃyātrika*); Lakṣmīdhara states that in other cases, there are other witnesses available. When fraud is established by proof, the rule of Yājñavalkya—"They should exclude the dishonest one from his share" (*jihmaṃ tyajeyur nirlābham*)—remains in force. "Dishonest" (*jihma*) means a deceiver; the meaning is that the partners in the joint enterprise should expel him after depriving him of his profit. Nārada states an exception to this:
"When a failure in the performance occurs therein due to fate or the king, it is declared to belong to all of them; it should be apportioned according to their respective shares."
But if one who was not designated, being restrained, should destroy [the property] through negligence,
they shall take from him that portion which he lost due to his lack of instruction, and whatever remains beyond that.
"Unappointed" means either not commissioned or being forbidden; this is the meaning. Regarding this, that same author states the specific rule:
"But he who, out of fear of fate or the king, protects [the property] by his own power, they should give him a tenth part, and take the remainder from him."
Kātyāyana also says: "But he who recovers property from a thief, from water, or from fire, a tenth part of that shall be given to him; this rule applies to all kinds of goods."
Regarding this, Bṛhaspati states a specific rule:
"That which is given by those assembled together must be requested back in the same manner;
he who does not ask for it loses his share of the profit."
Hārīta states a specific rule regarding those who live by collective labor, such as agriculture:
"If loss of the field occurs due to the sowing of foreign seeds by anyone, that [loss] must be made good by that very person for all those who live by agriculture."
The mention of "external seeds" is intended as an illustration for all the implements of agriculture. Regarding artisans, Bṛhaspati states a specific rule:
"Where goldsmiths and others perform their craft collectively, they shall receive wages corresponding to their work in proportion to their respective shares."
"Nirveśa" means wages. Kātyāyana states the various types of shares:
"Instructors, those skilled in seeds, and teachers—these artisans shall receive one, two, three, or four shares respectively, in ascending order."

Bṛhaspati states the distinction for those who construct palaces and the like: "For those who work together to build a palace, a temple, a pond, leather goods, utensils, and so forth, the leader indeed deserves a larger share."
Manu, however, states the specific rule regarding the officiating priests:

"The officiating priests, having assembled as invited at a sacrificial session (sattra), shall perform their duties according to their respective ranks and likewise receive their sacrificial fees. [274]

*Sattra* means a sacrifice. Since in that [sacrifice] the sacrificers themselves are the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), there is an absence of separate priests; therefore, those very sacrificers—namely the *adhvaryu*, the *brāhmaṇācchaṃsin*, and so forth—should receive the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) prescribed for those specific priests by mentioning their particular titles. The meaning is that they should divide and take the total sacrificial fee among themselves.
"In whatever ritual whatever specific fees for individual parts have been prescribed, he alone should take them; all [the sacrificers] together should not share them."

In some places, the reading is "or indeed all [the priests]. That refers to the subject of sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) given by multiple performers, and that applies specifically to each individual case. For example, only those who perform the *stotra* chants—the *chandogas*—should receive their share; however, the principal fees (*pradhānadakṣiṇā*) are to be distributed by calculating proportional shares. Regarding this, the same author states the specific rule: "Among all [the priests], the primary ones are the *ardhins* (receivers of half); others are *ardhins* by virtue of receiving half of that [half]. Those who receive a third part are the *tṛtīyins*; those who receive a fourth part are the *pādins*."

The *mukhyas* (principal priests) are the *adhvaryu*, *brahmā*, and so forth; the *aparas* (secondary) are the second group, the *prastotṛ* and so forth; the third are the *parihartṛ* and so forth; and the fourth are the *grāvastut* and so forth. The designations *ardhin*, *pādin*, and *tṛtīyin* are etymological (*yaugika*). In such scriptural passages as, "Having initiated the *gṛhapati*, the *adhvaryu* initiates the *brāhmaṇācchaṃsin*," it is heard that they initiate the *ardhins*; thus, the designations *ardhin* and so forth are applied to the *maitrāvaruṇa* and others. Since these are etymological, it is understood by their force that there is a restrictive rule for the allotment of shares as stated. On this point, Manu says:
If an officiating priest dies during a sacrifice and thus causes his own duty to be abandoned,
a share proportionate to his work must be given to him by the co-performers.

"With co-performers" means with those who act in concert. Others say that it should be given by the sacrificer together with the performers. Still others say that in the case of the ritual action, it should be given together with the performers who have relinquished their respective shares. In all three views, the meaning is this: at the time of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), the group of co-performers or the sacrificer should bestow the fee upon the performer of a portion of his own work and upon the one who performs the intermediate task, according to each respective rite. He himself states an exception to this in certain cases: "And if, after the fees have been given, he should fail to perform his own work..."
He shall receive the entire share, but he must have it performed by another.

"By another"—that is, by someone standing nearby among those belonging to his own group. For if it were performed by just anyone else, there would be the consequence of subverting the specific designations such as *ādhvaryava* (the duties of the Adhvaryu) and so forth. This should be understood to apply similarly when another officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) has died. On this point, Nārada says: "In the event of the misfortune of the priests, another shall likewise complete that work; he shall receive a share of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) accordingly determined for him."
As for that which was stated by Bṛhaspati:
"If anyone among those engaged in a ritual act should die,
the rite must be performed by his kinsman or by all the collaborators together."

Thus, as for that which was stated by Śaṅkha: “If a priest should die while the *savana* has commenced, his kinsman (*sagotra*) or disciple shall complete that duty; but if there is no relative, he should choose another priest,” all of this should be understood as referring to a sacrifice performed by priests who do not belong to a subordinate group (*avāntaragaṇa*). This is the view of the author of the *Candrikā* (Vya. p. 187). Regarding a specific point here, Viṣṇu says: “If a priest dies after [the ceremony has begun], one should choose another; the fee belongs to the one previously chosen. He adds that the one summoned later receives something. Kauṭilya explains the meaning of the word “something” (*yat kiṃcit*): “In the *agniṣṭoma* and other rites, if the officiating priest fails after the *dīkṣaṇīyā* offering, another summoned [priest] shall receive a fifth share. After the sale of the *soma*, a fourth. After the removal of the *pravargya* vessels, a third. After the *agniṣṭomīya* rite, a half. After the morning libation (*prātaḥsavana*), three-quarters. After the midday libation (*mādhyaṃdinasavana*), when the fees have been distributed, it becomes the whole. Thus says Varadarāja. Bṛhaspati states a specific rule regarding the one among dancers and others who knows the rhythm (*tāla*).
This indeed is the duty of dancers proclaimed by the virtuous:
one who knows the rhythm receives one and a half shares when the singers receive equal portions.

Among singers, dancers, and those who share equally, one who knows the musical rhythm (*tāla*) receives an exceedingly large portion here—meaning he receives a share that is half more [than the others]. Regarding thieves acting in concert, the same author states the distinction:

"But whatever has been brought from a foreign land by thieves by the king's command, they shall give a sixth part to the king and divide [the remainder] among themselves according to their respective shares."

"The principal [shareholder] shall receive four parts; the hero shall obtain three parts; the capable one shall take two parts; but the others shall have equal shares. This refers to goods brought from a foreign land, meaning from an enemy's territory. This rule applies to items recovered from a difficult-to-reach place. Regarding recovery from a place where goods are easily obtained, Kātyāyana says:
Whatever wealth may have been seized from a foreign kingdom by thieves under the king's command,
they shall divide it according to the rule, having set aside one-tenth for the king.

The meaning is: "without transgressing the previously mentioned rule beginning with 'four parts'. Regarding this, it is said: "If anyone should obtain the possession of those [goods] that have been dispersed, an equal distribution must be made for the sake of their release."

This statement refers to matters other than those defined by technical terminology (*pāribhāṣika*). Even regarding technical terminology, it is intended to show that [the rule] does not apply according to its own specific scope.

Thus ends the section titled "Joint Undertaking" (*saṃbhūyasamutthāna*) within the *Vyavahārakāṇḍa* of the *Sarasvatīvilāsa*, a compendium of law (*smṛtisaṃgraha*) composed by the illustrious Pratāparudra Mahādeva Mahārāja.
[277] Now, the legal head of dispute known as *dattāpradānika* (non-delivery of what has been given) is examined; regarding this, Nārada says:

"Having given property improperly, he who desires to take it back—that is known as the title of dispute called *dattāpradānika* (non-delivery of what was given). Since this establishes that items such as a pledge (*ādhi*), a deposit (*upanidhi*), and stolen goods are not subject to being given away, its connection is as a supplement to the three titles of *ṛṇādāna* (recovery of debts), *upanidhi* (deposits), and *saṃbhūyotthāna* (partnership). Although it is also a supplement to the rules on the partition of inheritance (*dāyavibhāga*) because it establishes that women's property is not to be given away, nevertheless, according to the principle of the majority, it should be understood as a supplement to those three. On this point, Manu says:
That which is not to be given, that which is to be given, that which has been given, and that which has not been given:
in legal proceedings, the path of giving is to be understood as fourfold.

*Adheya*—unfit for giving; *deya*—fit for giving; *datta*—firmly established; *adatta*—to be revoked. It has been recalled that the nature of what is unfit for giving and so forth was explained in the introductory section (*upoddhāta-prakaraṇa*). Thus, there are four types of paths of giving.

Here, [the author] states the eight things that are not to be given. Regarding that, Bṛhaspati first states the definitions and classifications of what is unfit for giving: "Common property, children, wife, and so forth, one's entire estate, a deposit, and what has been borrowed..."
"Likewise, what has been promised to another should not be given; thus it is remembered as being of eight kinds.

That which is called "not to be given" (*adeya*) is that which is unworthy of being given. For this very reason, even when such a thing is given, there is no cessation of one's own ownership (*svatva*) culminating in the transfer of ownership to another. Thus says Gautama: "Because the giving of what is not to be given is prohibited, the transfer of ownership to another does not take place. And likewise Viṣṇu: "'What is not to be given should not be given'—the meaning is that 'what is to be given' is that which is worthy of being given. And likewise Hārīta: "The giving of what is not to be given, deceit, and the consumption of *kalañja*..."
The taste of the mouth of a drunkard—these four are likewise equal. Thus it is said.

On this point they say: the consumption of *kalañja* is simply its tasting, as in the case of the tasting of the mouth of a drunkard; for [the prohibition of giving] is taught in conjunction with that. Some, however, say that *kalañjana* is *gṛñjana* (a type of garlic). Others, though, say: even if the giving of what should not be given is taught in conjunction with the eating of *kalañja*, which causes loss of caste, there is no greater sin in this [act of giving] by that much alone. The Teachers say that the full knowledge of the sin is obtained only through a careful consideration of the rules for penance (*prāyaścitta*). And so Manu, having introduced the eight things that must not be given, says:
"He who gives [it] is a deluded soul; that man must perform penance.
Regarding the nature of penance (*prāyaścitta*), Viṣṇu says:
"In the case of deceit (*jaihmya*), having fasted for three nights, one becomes pure by means of the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*)."

Likewise, for one who drinks liquor, having tasted it from the mouth, there is a fast of one night; if done intentionally, the consumption of the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) is prescribed. For giving what should not be given (*adeyadāna*), Gautama says there is a threefold *kṛcchra* penance, while Gautama himself states that for giving what should not be given, there is the *sāntapana* penance. Regarding the eating of *kalañja*, falling from one’s caste (*pātitya*) is established by all the *smṛtis*. Among things that should not be given, because sons, wives, and so forth are not to be given away, the expiation for giving them has been stated. Therefore, the giving of substances that ought not to be given is prohibited. On this point, some say: the prohibition against giving what should not be given is indeed based on a reason, and is not without reason. To explain: a common object should not be given without the permission of others; if there is such permission, it certainly may be given. However, even when the giving of property such as a son or wife is performed, ownership (*svatva*) does not depart. Ownership is a mental act; being of the nature of a conceptual resolve (*saṃkalpa*), it does not vanish. Rather, the ownership pertaining to it departs only through a mortal sin (*mahāpātaka*) or similar offense; this is established by the principles governing the acquisition of wealth. For this very reason Viṣṇu says: "One who gives away a son, a wife, and so forth, becomes fallen. Here, the word "giver" (*dātṛ*) also implies the "seller" (*vikretṛ*). And thus Gautama says: "In the absence of distress, for giving away a son, a wife, and so forth, one should perform a six-year penance. That, however, refers to the time of famine. He states the period for other times: "One should perform a twelve-year penance. As for what was said by Vasiṣṭha—having stated, "In times of distress, parents may give or take away a son," he then says: "One intending to adopt a son, having summoned relatives and informed the king, should offer oblations with the *vyāhṛtis* in the middle of his own dwelling and then adopt one who is neither too distant nor too close a relative" (VaDh 15.6). He himself explains the meaning of the word "distress": "The absence of a son is indeed 'distress'. By the word "or" (*vā*), which has a conjunctive sense, the inability to maintain one's family during a time of famine is added. Thus, the qualification "in distress" applies equally to both the adopter and the giver. Therefore, because this giving is Vedic in nature, it is not contradictory to what was stated previously. As for a deposit (*nyāsa*), if permitted by the original owner, it may indeed be given. What has been promised to another may also be given with that person’s permission. The same applies to what has been requested. This is agreed upon by everyone.

But for what reason is one's entire property (*sarvasva*) not to be given away? It is not because it lacks the status of being a fixed means [of subsistence] like a son, wife, and so forth—which would otherwise constitute a great sin (*mahāpātaka*). For ownership (*svatva*) indeed arises through a mental act (*mānasikī kriyā*), just as ownership arises in the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) when there is a sacrificial fee consisting of one's entire property (*sarvasvadakṣiṇā*), or just as royal ownership arises when one's entire property is seized as a fine for a grave crime (*mahāsāhasa*). Furthermore, the renunciation of one's entire property by one who is dispassionate (*virakta*) is not prohibited; therefore, the reason for prohibiting such renunciation must be stated.

On this point, some say: "Since livelihood cannot be established by the renunciation of everything, and because the body—which is the instrument for practicing Dharma—cannot be sustained, it is not proper to renounce everything for the sake of maintaining that body. Rather, even for those who are dispassionate, one should take what is necessary for one's own livelihood and give away only the remainder. This is incorrect, because for those who are dispassionate, the maintenance of the body can be accomplished through a livelihood consisting of wandering for alms and so forth.
[Objection: But surely, the giving away of all one's possessions has been prescribed as a duty?

Otherwise, the statement of Hārīta—"Even in times of distress or when one has become dispassionate, not everything is to be given"—would be rendered without scope. Regarding this, Lakṣmīdhara and others cite an indicative authority (*jñāpaka*): "In the Viśvajit sacrifice, one should give away all one's possessions," and "One should not give a lion. This prohibition of giving a lion indicates that the giving of "all one's possessions" is itself prohibited.

Regarding this, some say: "In the case of the injunction ‘in the Viśvajit one gives away all one’s property’ (*sarvasvam*), the word ‘all’ (*sarva*) refers to everything except for the horse (the *kesarī*). For here, since the word ‘property’ (*sva*) denotes what belongs to oneself, and because things such as sons—which belong to oneself—cannot be given away, there is no cessation of ownership over them."

That is not so; the teachers say that the injunction "one should give away all one's possessions" (*sarvasvaṃ dadyāt*) indeed possesses a prohibitive aspect in order to enjoin the giving of everything. However, the injunctions regarding the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) consisting of all one's possessions refer to objects other than those that ought not to be given. This is because, in the case of children, wife, and so forth, ownership (*svatva*) exists in the form of a relationship characterized by the status of progenitor and progeny; thus, children, wife, and the like are indeed one's own property. And it was stated previously that this [ownership] is revoked by great sins (*mahāpātaka*) and the like. Consequently, the word "all" (*sarva*) does not have a restricted application (*saṃkucadvṛtti*). For this very reason, it was established by the Guru that in the rule "the Audumbarī post is to be entirely covered," the word "all" does not have a restricted application. Furthermore, the seizure of all possessions by a king is prescribed in cases of violent crimes (*sāhasa*); even when an object is taken by force, ownership arises [in the king]. Moreover, that is not a "giving" (*pradāna*), but rather the confiscation of all possessions because [the offender] is subject to punishment. In the present context, however, the discussion concerns the act of giving (*dāna*) as its subject matter; therefore, we have no concern with that [case of punishment]. Furthermore—
That which has been deposited with another, that which has been borrowed, a pledge,
that which is held in common, a trust, as well as one's sons and wife, and even one's entire property, when there is a male heir.
The teachers say that even when a living being is beset by the most dire calamities, there are things that must not be given away— specifically, that which has already been promised to another.

Thus, in order to bring about consistency between the statement of Nārada and the statement of Bṛhaspati—namely, the statement by Bṛhaspati beginning with "common property such as sons, wives, and so forth," and the statement "even in times of distress, those who are detached"—the qualification "provided there is a lineage" (*anvaye sati*) must be accepted. This means that when the substance constituting the seed of the ancestral lineage (*vaṃśaparamparā*) exists, one must not give away one's entire property. Even for those who are detached, if a progeny exists, the giving away of all one's possessions is neither desired nor appropriate.

If it is argued that prohibitory injunctions are intended solely to forbid the gift of one's entire property to one who still has descendants, this is true; such is the view of the authors of the *Candrikā*, Kulārka, Vijñānayogin, and others.

Lakṣmīdhara and others, however, maintain that the prohibition regarding the relinquishment of items that ought not to be given is scriptural (*vācanika*), not logical (*naiyāyika*). Otherwise, the prescriptions for expiation (*prāyaścitta*) and punishment (*daṇḍa*) would be contradicted. Thus says Pitāmaha:
"The man who gives [such things] is a fool and becomes liable to expiation."

Śaṅkha also prescribed this penance: "Having given what should not be given, one should fast for three nights after returning that gift. Furthermore: "He who, out of delusion, accepts what has not been given, and he who bestows what should not be given—both of these are to be punished by a king who knows the Dharma."

The term *adattagrahaṇa* (taking what is not given) is intended as an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) of taking even that which should not be given (*adeya*). Therefore, it should be understood that the punishment for one who accepts what is not given and for one who accepts what should not be given is stated in various [legal] texts. From the mention of "taking what is not given or what should not be given," it is understood that the king must also effect the restoration of what has been taken. The author of the *Candrikā* states that because a gift cannot be accomplished by means of what is not given or what should not be given, the transfer of ownership to another does not arise. Consequently, the view of Lakṣmīdhara and others—that this prohibition against the renunciation of all property is based on scriptural injunction (*vaidha*)—is indeed correct.
But was it not stated previously that it is proper to give [a gift] only when the owner of the substance—such as a universal (sāmānya) and so forth—has granted permission?

That is not so; it should be understood that according to the opinion of Lakṣmīdhara and others, the primary owner alone has authority in that matter, and another does not have it merely by his permission. In common worldly practice, there exists a conventional transaction known as *kutta*, whereby one takes a house, field, or the like from the primary owner, and the increase or decrease of its value must be borne solely by the *kauttika* (the acquirer). And if it is argued that this [debt], called *kutta*, which is designated by the term "accumulation" (*upacaya*), should indeed be included within the section on "Deposits" (*gopya*) under the title of the legal dispute concerning "Recovery of Debt" (*ṛṇādāna*), because its technical designation as "accumulation" is established through the transfer of ownership based on a specific condition; [The response follows: ...then [we reply]. It is not so; the title of law known as *ṛṇādāna* (non-payment of debt) proceeds by depending upon two categories: that which is to be cleared (*śodhya*) and that which is to be released (*mocya*). Debt without collateral is "to be cleared" (*śodhya*); debt with collateral, consisting of the nature of a pledge to be guarded, is "to be released" (*mocya*). Thus, the title of law called *ṛṇādāna* is of two kinds. This is because in the world, there is no possibility of the two forms of "to be cleared" and "to be released" within what is commonly termed "interest" (*upacaya*), which is synonymous with "usury" (*kutta*). Furthermore, in the case of non-payment of debt, the interest accrues to the creditor (*uttamarṇa*), whereas in the case of usury, it accrues to the debtor (*adhamarṇa*); therefore, the category of usury is not included therein.

Others say: the inclusion of the pledge (ādhi) within the subject matter must be stated. When the discharge of the debt incurred by Devadatta has occurred, there is indeed the status of being an object to be released in the present dispute; however, because the performance of ancestral rites (*pitṛkriyā*), which are to be performed as long as one lives, was accepted under the form of a pledge, he cannot be released through that [discharge of the debt]. Just as the initiation rite (*upanayana-saṃskāra*) ceases when its constituent part—the act of teaching—ceases, so too, since the duties of the initiated, such as "the teacher is to be supported while young" and "he is to be served in return when aged," persist for the duration of one's life, initiation itself likewise persists for the duration of one's life through those duties.

Not so; for the legal proceeding (*vyavahāra*) under discussion does not concern property that has been deposited. On the contrary, because it involves the possibility of a partial loss (*apacaya*), whereas such loss is absent in the case of a pledge (*ādhi*). Furthermore, since the type of interest known as *kuttā*—which is accumulative (*aupacayika*)—cannot be subsumed under the title of "Recovery of Debts" (*ṛṇādāna*), its inclusion under "Non-payment of what was Given" (*dattāpradānika*) is logical. The title of "Non-payment of what was Given" is established based on fourfold giving. As stated previously, the path of giving is fourfold: what is given, what is not given, what ought to be given, and what ought not to be given. Giving is of two kinds: conditional (*sopādhika*) and unconditional (*nirupādhika*). Since giving in the form of *kuttā* is conditional, the secret point is this: because it takes the form of a conditional gift, the accumulative interest is included therein. An accumulative matter proceeds by taking as its object the repayment of Devadatta’s debt and the performance of rites for the gods and ancestors (*devapitṛkriyā*) occasioned by that purpose; thus, it is included within "Non-payment of what was Given."
Household property and land inherited in succession from one's father or grandfather must not be given away without the consent of a son or grandson who has attained prosperity.
On this point, Manu says:
"If a person gives wealth to someone who asks for it for the sake of dharma or artha,
and that wealth subsequently does not serve that purpose, it shall become something that must not be returned by him."
Nārada has stated that there is only one kind of person worthy of receiving gifts: "Whatever wealth remains after supporting one's family is what should be given;
he who gives while withholding [the surplus] from others incurs sin."
Regarding this, Kātyāyana states the distinction:
"One's entire property, with the exception of the house, as well as whatever wealth is required for the maintenance of the family and so forth—that may be given; otherwise, it shall not be given."
"One's own" means what has been acquired by oneself.
Men are not indifferent toward their wives, sons, or kinsmen;
they possess sovereign power over their own property in all matters.
The meaning is that they have authority over wealth acquired by themselves. Vyāsa says: "A gift to the blind and others yields a hundredfold merit; a gift to a daughter yields infinite merit;
a gift at a rite for the ancestors yields a hundredfold merit; and a gift to one's mother is said to yield a thousandfold."
A gift given to a sister of the same womb yields inexhaustible merit equal to a hundred thousand.
Dakṣa says: A gift given to one's mother, father, teacher, a friend, a humble person, a benefactor,
or to those who are miserable, helpless, or distinguished, becomes fruitful.
Bṛhaspati says: "A gift given to a Śūdra is said to have one quality; to a Vaiśya, it has two qualities;
to a Kṣatriya, they say it has three qualities; and to a Brāhmaṇa, it is traditionally held to have six qualities."
A thousand [cows] for a *śrotriya*, twice that for a sub-teacher (*upādhyāya*),
three times that for a teacher (*ācārya*), and twice that for those who have maintained the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*).
A hundred thousandfold for one who performs the domestic rites, but infinite for one who maintains the sacred fire;
a hundred thousandfold for a Soma-sacrificer, but infinite for an expounder of the Veda.

Or, in the reading *iti vā*: "spiritual" (*ātmike*) means established in the knowledge of the Self. Bhāradvāja says: "A gift (*paṇya*) is the price; it may be given out of satisfaction, affection, or for the sake of a return favor. They say that a gift consisting of a single [object] should be preceded by water."
Without the offering of water, the gift of Dharma does not exist.

On this point, Āpastamba says: “All gifts are preceded by water. On this point, Gautama says: “The giving of alms is preceded by the word ‘Svasti’ and by water; likewise among guests (and those who give) in matters of Dharma. On this point, Bṛhaspati says:
“One should bestow the woman’s property upon her own kinsmen, but one should avoid [giving it to] him [the husband].”

The meaning is that the woman alone has the right to the woman's property (strīdhana), and no one else. However, in the absence of female relatives (kulyā), it goes to the male kinsmen; and in their absence, to the twice-born (dvijāti).
Nārada, however, states seven such categories.

It is recorded that what is given is of seven kinds: as the price for merchandise, as wages, out of satisfaction, out of affection, as a return for a favor, as a bride-price (*śulka*), and for the sake of a benefit. [285] That which is given as the price for merchandise purchased, as wages for work performed, out of satisfaction to actors and the like, out of affection to friends, in the form of a return favor to one who has helped, as a bride-price to the kinsmen of a maiden for the purpose of marriage, and that which is given for the sake of spiritual merit (*adṛṣṭārtha*)—all these seven types of gifts are indeed given and are not to be reclaimed. On this point, Bṛhaspati says:
Wages, the price for merchandise, the bride-price, a gift to a benefactor,
and that given through faith, favor, or affection— this is remembered as the eightfold [gift].
Manu also says: "A gift given to one's mother, father, a teacher, a friend, a humble person, or a benefactor, as well as to the poor, the helpless, and those who are distinguished, becomes fruitful."
What is received as a dowry, what is obtained through valor,
and what is given with the permission of the wife, kinsmen, and the owner— such a gift shall attain validity.
Yājñavalkya states the specific rule regarding immovable property:
"The acceptance of immovable property, especially, should be public;
and what has been promised as a gift must be given, and once given, it must not be taken back."
Kātyāyana says:
He who, having voluntarily promised a gift to a Brāhmaṇa,
does not give it, shall be made to pay it like a debt and shall incur the first amercement.
By failing to give what was promised and by misappropriating what has been given,
a mortal is born for a hundred billion eons in the animal realm.
Even after having given a promise, one should not give to one who is not engaged in [proper] action. And so says Hārīta:
"That which has been promised by word alone, but not fulfilled through action, is a debt connected with dharma both in this world and in the next."

The meaning is that it is like a debt promised. Now, Nārada states that there are sixteen kinds of what is not given (*adatta*): "But what is given under the impulse of fear, anger, or grief; likewise, through bribery, jesting, exchange, or fraud."

That which is done by children, the deluded, those who are not independent, the afflicted, the intoxicated, or the insane; and that which is done with the desire for gain, thinking, "This person is my agent" and "This is my deed."
If one speaks of an unworthy recipient as being worthy, or performs an act joined with unrighteousness,
whatever is given through ignorance is considered "not given" in its sixteenfold form.
In this context, the word "impulse" (*vega*) is connected individually with each of the terms "fear," "anger," and "sorrow. Regarding this, Kātyāyana states:
"What is given by one who is under the sway of lust or anger, one who is distressed, impotent, insane, or deluded, and what is given through error or in jest—that one may take back again."
Bhāradvāja says:
That which is given to the perpetrators out of fear, as a remedy for the insults of those who are destitute of wealth, is called *bhādāna*.
Nārada has stated the definition of *utkoca* (bribery):
"That which is given for the sake of accomplishing a task is proclaimed as *utkoca*. The word *utkoca* is also feminine in gender; another definition of it has also been stated by that same author.
From the reporting of thieves, violent offenders, evildoers, and adulterers;
from the discovery of what was stolen or lost; and likewise from the instigation of such persons.
But whatever has been obtained by these [means] is called a bribe (utkoca).
Therefore, Kātyāyana states the specific rule:
"But if one who has been appointed to official duties should receive a bribe,
he shall be made to pay that entire sum as a fine, plus an additional eleventh part."
But if one who has not been appointed should accept a bribe for the sake of performing a task,
there is no fault in him provided it is for the purpose of rendering a reciprocal service.
The rest is easy to understand. Dependence has been stated by Nārada:
"All subjects are dependent; the lord of the earth is independent.
Disciples are traditionally held to be dependent; independence resides in their conduct."
Wives, sons, slaves, and whatever property one possesses are not independent;
however, the master of that which has come down through inheritance is independent.
A child is to be known as being like one still in the womb until the eighth year;
from that point until the sixteenth year, he is called a *bāla* (child) or a *paugaṇḍa*.
One who knows legal procedure is independent with respect to others, except for his parents;
for even if he is advanced in age, he remains dependent while they are alive.
Of these two as well, the father is superior, because the importance of the seed is observed;
in the absence of the progenitor, the mother [is superior], and in her absence, the elder brother.
Those [gifts] arising from wind, bile, and phlegm are declared to be "low" and "insane.

The rest is easy to understand. Wealth obtained for the sake of a sacrifice that is spent on gambling and the like—even though given, it is considered "not given" because it must be recovered; thus, there are sixteen types of such gifts. According to the statement of Kātyāyana, the status of being "not given" applies to what is given by one who is distressed, provided it concerns a religious duty: "Whether given by one who is healthy or by one who is distressed, if it was promised for the sake of a religious act..."
"But if he dies without having given it, the son shall be made to pay; there is no doubt in this matter.
Viṣṇu also states: "What was obtained from a thief must be recovered by means of officiating at sacrifices or teaching. Another Smṛti also says:
"A Brahmin should seek to recover his wealth from a thief who has taken it without permission."
"By officiating at sacrifices for them or by teaching them, he is just like a thief. Thus [it is said].
A thief is one who takes what is not given. Nārada says: "That which was sold through trickery, that which was given through trickery, and that which was promised [but not fulfilled]..."
Where one would not perceive even a substrate, all that should be completely turned back.

Yoga—this refers to the specific condition (*upādhi*) by means of which purchases, sales, gifts, and receptions are performed; upon the removal of that condition, the purchase and other transactions cease. Bharadvāja states that the revocability of the giving of wealth and so forth is as follows: "When a gift is given to worthy recipients without regard for any specific purpose, they call that the 'giving of wealth' (*arthadāna*), and its fruit is indeed only of this world."

The meaning is that there is no invisible (adṛṣṭa) purpose [in such giving]. That which is given to women out of attachment, or out of passion to those who are unworthy, is called "desire-giving" (kāmadāna).
That which is given to others out of shame in an assembly,
the seers of reality call that gift "the gift of shame."
That which one gives out of joy upon seeing or hearing something dear is called "joy-giving" (harṣadāna); its fruit is seen right here in this very life.
That gift which is bestowed upon loved ones during times of prosperity or adversity is called worldly; thus, it is given for the sake of visible results.
The wise say that these things which are not given are as if they were given;
regarding this, Nārada says:
"He who takes what is not given out of greed, and he who gives what should not be given," [both incur sin].
Both of these ought to be punished by a king who knows the Dharma.
Bṛhaspati also states:
"One who consumes what has not been given, as well as one who gives what ought not to be given, shall be punished.
By specifying "through greed" as the cause, it is indicated that there is no fault in giving or not giving when done out of ignorance.

Thus ends the twenty-ninth chapter, titled "The Section on Deposits," within the *Vyavahārakāṇḍa* of the *Sarasvatīvilāsa*, a compendium of legal codes composed by the illustrious Great King Pratāparudradeva.
Now, having accepted [the obligation], the rule regarding the category known as "failure to serve" is stated;
on this point, Bṛhaspati says:
