The wise have observed in the treatises that there are five kinds of attendants;
four kinds are laborers, while the remaining five are slaves.
The triple Vidyā is declared to be characterized by the Ṛg, Yajus, and Sāman;
for its sake, one should perform service to the teacher as enjoined by the scriptures.
It is fourfold by way of knowledge, discernment, desire, and purpose;
yet this one [nature] is further divided among these according to the difference in activity.

Skill is said to be knowledge; it consists of the refinement of gold, base metals, and so forth, as well as dancing and other arts. Having acquired that, one should perform service in the teacher's house.

The knowledge concerning the manufacture of bracelets, armlets, and the like, as well as the performance of dance, song, and so forth—and by the use of the word "and," also including the construction of pillars, pots, and the like—is called *śilpavijñāna* (the science of arts and crafts). Nārada states the meaning of the term *antevāsin* (apprentice):
"Desiring to acquire his own craft with the permission of his relatives, he should dwell in the presence of a teacher for a period of time that has been well-determined."
The meaning is that one should make firm the limit of time prescribed by the teacher, thinking, "He must remain in my presence for this long. The same author also states what the teacher's duty is:
"The teacher, having provided food in his own home, should instruct him;
he should not make him perform other work, and should treat him like a son."
Nārada says:
Until he has completed his acquisition of knowledge, the disciple should serve his guru with self-restraint;
and the same applies toward the guru’s wife and virtuous son.
This instruction applies to all three who have studied the three Vedas:
"Having returned home and having presented the teacher’s fee to the guru, he may go to his own house; this is declared to be the conduct of a student."
"To his own home" means he should go to his own house. Kātyāyana, however, states a specific rule:
"But he who does not cause [the pupil] to learn the craft, yet causes him to perform other works, shall incur the first *sāhasa* fine; from that, the pupil withdraws."
Even if he is trained, a pupil may practice according to his own desire;
whatever work he performs therein, the fruit thereof belongs to the teacher alone.
In this regard, Hārīta says:
"Having mastered the craft, the apprentice, having circumambulated the teacher at the proper time and having honored him according to his ability, departs."

These are the four kinds of servants and so forth: the student (śiṣya), the resident pupil (antevāsī), the hired laborer (bhṛtaka), and the overseer of work (adhikarmakṛt). Thus it is said: "The student, the resident pupil, the hired laborer, and fourthly the overseer of work—these are to be known as wage-earners; whereas slaves are those born in the house and so forth."

The wise have declared that their lack of independence is their common characteristic; however, the distinction based on genus and action, as well as their specific function, has already been described.
Action, too, should be known as twofold: indeed, both impure and pure.
Impure action is said to be the work of a servant; pure action is remembered as that which is performed [by oneself].
The cleaning of house doors, impure places, streets, and refuse heaps; the touching of private parts, the state of being defiled by food remnants, and the taking up and discarding of feces and urine.
Then, finally, there is the attendance upon the lords with one's own limbs according to their desire.

"By desire" means by the wish of the master. "With his own limbs" means with his own hands and so forth. "Finally" refers to the attendance upon—that is, the cleaning of—the last [act], which is the voiding of feces and urine. Inauspicious work is to be understood as such; other than this, it is auspicious. Here, the *śiṣya* is one who seeks the knowledge of the Vedas; the *antevāsī* is one who seeks the knowledge of crafts. He who performs work for a wage is a *bhṛtaka*. One who supervises those performing work is to be known as an *adhikarmakṛt*. The rest is easy to understand. Furthermore, the *bhṛtaka* is also of three kinds.
Among these, the soldier is the highest, the farmer is middling, and the porter is the lowest; thus is the hired laborer of three kinds.

As for those born in the house and so forth: "One born in the house, as well as one purchased, one obtained, one received from an heir, one supported during a time of distress, and likewise one who was entrusted by his master."
I was liberated from great bondage; won at a stake in battle, I approached you saying, "I am yours"; and one whose life was spent in renunciation has been made [your slave].
One who becomes a slave through food, as well as one brought [as a slave] by a mare,
and one who sells himself— these are declared in the scripture to be the fifteen kinds of slaves.

One born in the house of a female slave is "born in the house" (*gṛhaja*). One who is "bought" (*krīta*) is one acquired from another owner for a price. One who is "received" (*labdha*) is one obtained from that same person through a gift or other means. One who has "come by inheritance" (*dāyādupagata*) is a slave belonging to a father or other relative. One who is "maintained during a famine" (*anākālabhṛta*) is one who was saved from death during a time of scarcity in exchange for slavery. One who is "entrusted" (*āhita*) is one made a pledge by the master through the accumulation of wealth. A "slave for debt" (*ṛṇadāsa*) is one who entered into servitude through the clearing of a debt. One "captured in war" (*yuddhaprāpta*) is one seized after being defeated in battle. One "won at a wager" (*paṇejita*) is one who, having agreed to the condition, "If I am defeated in this dispute, I shall become your slave," is subsequently won. One who says "I am yours" (*tavāham*) is one who has personally accepted the status of a slave. One who has "fallen from the religious life" (*pravrajyāvasita*) is one who has lapsed from the state of renunciation. One who is "made" (*kṛta*) is one who has reached an agreement, "I will be your slave for such a length of time. A "slave for food" (*bhaktadāsa*) is one who has entered into servitude at all times solely for the sake of food. One "brought by a female slave" (*vaḍavāhṛta*)—a *vaḍavā* being a domestic female slave—is one brought by her; out of desire for her, he marries her and enters into servitude. He who sells himself is here termed a "seller"; thus there are fifteen types. Among these fifteen, Nārada states the manner of expressing the servitude of some: [The following verses of Nārada would follow here.]
In that regard, the first four classes are not released from servitude except through the favor of their master; for them, servitude is hereditary.

The first category consists of the four types: those born in the house, those purchased, those obtained by inheritance, and those who have come as gifts. He himself also states the manner of liberation from servitude for others:
"That lowest of men who, being independent, sells himself—he is the most wretched of them all, and even he is not released from servitude."

The phrase "by the favor of the master" is to be supplied here as well. Thus, the meaning is this: those born in the house and the others, ending with the self-seller as the fifth, are released from slavery by the favor of the master, and not otherwise. However, those such as the one supported during a famine are released from slavery by saving the life of the master. As Nārada says: "Whosoever among these should protect (or gladden) the master from a life-threatening danger, he shall be released from slavery and receive a share like that of a son."

The meaning is: "among these fifteen kinds of slaves. This is what is being stated: for those beginning with the *gṛhajāta* (born in the house) up to the fifth, the *ātmavikretṛ* (self-sold), there are two causes for the removal of slavery: the favor of the master and protection from a life-threatening danger. However, for those who were enslaved during a time of distress (*anākālabhṛta*), the only cause is the protection of the master’s life. Regarding the one who has fallen from the religious order (*pravrajyāvasita*), Kātyāyana states a specific rule: "A slave who has fallen from the religious order must be released by no one. Yājñavalkya also says:
One who has fallen from the religious life becomes the king’s slave for as long as death lasts.
"One who has fallen from the religious life" means one who has strayed from renunciation; he is the king’s slave. The meaning is that he belongs to the sovereign alone and not to anyone else.
Indeed, a man who has fallen from the religious life shall be the slave of the king alone.
For him there is no liberation, nor is there purification in any way whatsoever.

Thus, according to the traditional teaching of Nārada, the general term "man" (nara) refers specifically to the Kṣatriya and the Vaiśya, because servitude is prohibited for a Brāhmaṇa. As Kātyāyana has said:
"Where the three twice-born castes have fallen from their renunciant vows, one should cause the Brāhmaṇa to be banished; as for the Kṣatriya and the Vaiśya, Bhṛgu says they shall be made slaves."
And so says Hārīta:
"There are only two outcastes by action in this world, who are to be shunned from afar:
he who has fallen away from the life of renunciation, and he who has entered the life of renunciation in vain."
For this very reason, Kātyāyana says: "One who has been maintained [as a slave] during a time of distress is released from slavery by giving a pair of cattle."

And so Viṣṇu says: “By the gift of increasingly greater wealth, one is released. Thus, it is a matter established by logic that for those who are slaves due to debt (*ṛṇadāsa*) and others, there is liberation from slavery upon the cessation of the underlying condition, such as the debt. For instance, a slave who was made to work during a famine is released by the surrender of two cows; a pledged slave (*āhitadāsa*), however, is released from the creditor’s slavery once the debt held by the pledgor has been repaid; a slave for debt (*ṛṇādāsa*) is released by the clearing of the debt he himself incurred. As for the three specific types of slaves—those won at a stake (*paṇajita*), those captured in war (*raṇaprāpta*), and those who have come of their own accord (*upagata*)—they are released by the gift of another slave capable of performing all the tasks that they themselves were required to perform. A slave by contract (*kṛta*) is released from the bondage of servitude; a slave brought by a mare (*baḍavāhṛta*) is released by the abandonment of sexual intercourse with her. Nārada speaks of those who are pseudo-slaves (*dāsābhāsa*).
Those who have been stolen by thieves, those sold, and those who have been seized by force as slaves—these must be released by the king; slavery is not permitted with respect to them.
As for that which was stated by Kātyāyana:
"He who, being dependent, offers himself [saying] 'I am yours,' shall not obtain his desire; the former owner shall regain him."

That [penalty] refers to the case where one is not independent due to being another's slave. However, in the case of mere lack of independence, either a substitute for the slave should be made to pay, or he himself should perform the servitude. Nārada states the method for release from servitude:
"He who, with a well-disposed mind, wishes to make his own slave a non-slave, should take from the slave's shoulder a water-pot filled with water and break it."
One should remove [the water] from his head with water containing rice grains and flowers;
then, having said three times, "He is not a slave," one should release him as he runs forward facing the east.

And this same rule applies equally to a female slave (*dāsī*), because in the term "slave" (*dāsa*), the gender and number are not intended to be significant as they refer to the subject of the injunction. Viṣṇu, however, states a specific exception: "She who is married by a slave becomes a female slave. Kātyāyana also says:
"A female slave who is married by a slave shall likewise attain the status of a slave;
for her husband is her master, and since their master is dependent upon his own owner, [the woman] belongs to him."

Regarding those two—the male and female slaves—the term "master" (*svāmī*) or "lord" (*prabhu*) implies, by the force of the context, that he is the master of the slave, the female slave, and their wealth. For this very reason, Nārada states:
"Whatever wealth a slave may possess, the master is considered its lord.
By this, it should be understood that the master alone is the lord even of the slave's property. Bṛhaspati describes the fruit of liberation from slavery:
From that time forward, he should be addressed as one protected by the favor of his master;
his food may be eaten and gifts may be accepted from him, for he becomes esteemed by the virtuous.
"And those sons born of her who are the offspring of her husband or of another,
if the progenitor is the master, the lord shall not compel the female slave to work. Thus says Vyāsa.
If a maidservant belonging to one man becomes a servant to another, he may approach her after paying a bride-price; otherwise, she deserves slavery.

However, Bhāruciprabhṛti and others maintain that if one has procreated offspring upon a female slave after paying the bride-price (*śulka*), that offspring belongs to him alone due to the predominance of the seed (*bījaprādhānya*); whereas if he approaches her without having paid the bride-price and offspring is produced, that offspring belongs only to the owner of the slave. Badarāyaṇa, however, says it belongs to both, stating:
"Therefore, according to the law (*dharma*), offspring is recognized as belonging to both the father and the mother.
Regarding this specific case of female slaves, Nārada states:
Servitude may exist among the castes in the direct order of succession, but not in the inverse order;
for Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras lose their independence by [entering such service].
But one should never cause a Brahmin to perform servitude, even if he is of the same caste.
And so says Kātyāyana:
"Service by a Brāhmaṇa toward the three [lower] castes is to be known as never occurring;
service among the castes occurs only in the direct order, not in the inverse order."

Just as taking a wife is done in accordance with the natural order (*ānulomya*) and not against it (*prātilomya*), for Viṣṇu records that "the status of a slave is like that of a wife. Regarding this, Uśanas states a specific rule:
"Neither a teacher, nor a *sapiṇḍa*, nor a Brahmin, nor those of the lowest castes deserve the state of slavery; nor does a twice-born man who is superior in learning."

This is the meaning: for a Brāhmaṇa, one born of the lowest caste (*antyayoni*) is not a slave, even if he is superior in learning; likewise, for a Kṣatriya and others, a Brāhmaṇa is not a slave. However, it should be understood that among those of equal caste, one who is superior in learning is not a slave, and even one born of the lowest caste is not a slave. Regarding this, Kātyāyana states a specific rule:
"But a Śūdra, whether purchased or unpurchased, one should cause to perform the work of a slave;
for he was created by the Self-existent One himself solely for servitude."

Thus ends the twenty-ninth chapter, titled "Service after Agreement," within the Section on Legal Procedure (*vyavahārakāṇḍa*) of the *Sarasvatīvilāsa*, a compendium of law (*smṛtisaṃgraha*) composed by the illustrious Great King Pratāparudradeva.
Now, the rule for the section titled "Non-payment of Wages" is stated; regarding this, Manu says:
"Henceforth, I shall declare the non-payment of wages."

Beyond this—meaning immediately after the section titled "Service by Agreement" (*abhyupetyāśuśrūṣā*). In the preceding section, it was stated that for those who have entered into a contract or been won at stake, a substitute may be employed in order to fulfill what was promised. Here, however, wages must be paid in order to fulfill what was promised; otherwise, that promised wage must be recovered. This is the connection. Nor does this fall under the category of "Non-delivery of What Was Given" (*dattāpradānika*), because in that case it is said that what has been given is treated as if not given, but there is no mention of the recovery of what was given. Therefore, there is a distinction between these two. Having kept this in mind:
"Hereafter I shall explain the non-payment of wages.
In this context, it should be understood that the phrase "hereafter" (*ataḥ param*) has been employed. Regarding this, Nārada states:
"The master of the work shall pay wages to the servant in the proper order."
That which is determined regarding an action—at its beginning, middle, and end—[is the essential nature of that action].

The meaning is that one should divide the wage—which has been determined in terms of its total amount by saying "I shall give this to you"—into three parts and pay them at the beginning, middle, and end of the work. Now, if it is argued that since the nature of laborers was defined in the previous section, the method of paying their wages and their livelihood should have been explained right there: [The response follows: It is true that the nature of laborers was indeed defined in the previous section; however, because they are numerous and diverse, and because their livelihoods vary according to their specific duties, the details regarding their wages and livelihoods were not mentioned there. Therefore, they are explained here. Furthermore, since the payment of wages is a matter of great importance, it is treated separately. Moreover, the method of payment for laborers is distinct from that for those who serve through affection (*preman*), and thus it is necessary to explain it here. Finally, the wages of those who serve out of affection will be described later in the section on *dharma*. Thus, there is no fault in explaining this here. As for the term *bhṛti* (wage), it is derived from the root *bhṛ* (to support) with the suffix *ktin*, meaning that which supports or maintains a person. Alternatively, it is derived from the root *bhṛ* (to carry) with the suffix *ktin*, meaning that which is carried or received. It is synonymous with *vetana* (remuneration). The word *karma-kara* (laborer) is formed from the root *kṛ* (to do) with the suffix *aṇ*; it refers to one who performs work for the sake of receiving wages. The word *vṛtti* (livelihood) is derived from the root *vṛt* (to exist) with the suffix *ktin*, meaning that by which one exists or subsists. It is synonymous with *jīvana* (means of living). The phrase "at the beginning, middle, and end" means at the commencement, the midpoint, and the conclusion of the work. The word *tridhā* (threefold) indicates the division into three parts. The word *dadyāt* (should give) implies that he should pay the wages in accordance with the agreement. The particle *iti* marks the end of the explanation. The word *ca* (and) serves to connect this with the preceding context. The word *iti* at the very end concludes the entire section. It is synonymous with *nīti* (conduct), *maryādā* (boundary/standard), and *ācāra* (customary practice). Not so. Since they share the same legal status as students, slaves, and the like, the mere nature of laborers was described there by way of introduction, because the occasion for discussing the payment of their wages was not required at that point. For those learned in the Nyāya system maintain that what is to be explained must be prompted by a desire to know (*jijñāsā*). It is precisely by relying on what was stated in the section on "Non-payment of Wages" (*dattāpradānika*) that the section titled "Failure to Perform Agreed Service" (*abhyupetyāśuśrūṣā*) arises; thus the connection is established. And therefore, since the desire to know arises only in accordance with that [preceding discussion], the explanation of slaves acquired through gambling, won in battle, or who have come of their own accord follows from that, as does the explanation of those born in the house and others, and subsequently the explanation of laborers and the like due to that context. Thus, only their essential nature was explained in the preceding section. However, the method of paying their wages was not discussed there; that alone is elaborated upon here. Regarding this, Kātyāyana states a specific rule:
But when the wages have not been fixed, the merchants, cowherds, and farmers shall receive a tenth part of the profit,
the cattle, and the crops, respectively.

"Daśabhāgam" means a tenth part (*daśamabhāgam*). "Govīryam" means milk; the phrase "respectively" (*yathākramena*) is to be understood as the ellipsis. If the master of the work does not give [the fee], then Yājñavalkya says: "But he who causes work to be done without having fixed the wages must be made to pay a tenth part of the profit from trade, cattle, or crops by the king."
Bṛhaspati, however, has stated a specific rule:
"The plowman shall take one-third or one-fifth.
On this point, he himself states an alternative:
"Those supported by clothing and shelter should take a one-fifth share from the produce;

however, those supported [by food] should take a third part from the harvested crop. This is the meaning: a cultivator should take a fifth part from the harvested crop if his food and clothing are thereby provided; otherwise, he should take a third part. Thus, even regarding contractual labor (*pāribhāṣika-bhṛti*), if the laborer is skillful, then something more should be given; when he is unskilled, nothing more—so says Yājñavalkya.

If one should exceed the prescribed place and time, or should obtain profit in an improper manner, it shall be at the pleasure of the owner; however, if there has been extra effort, a share of the profit should be given.
Yājñavalkya describes the manner of paying the stipulated wages for work performed by multiple laborers:
"Whatever amount of work one performs, that much shall be his wage;
however, if the task is impossible for both together, they should perform it according to the agreement if it is achievable."
"As it has been heard"—that is, as it has been defined. But Bṛhaspati states a specific rule:
"A hired servant must not practice even the slightest deception toward his master;
he incurs a loss of wages, and from that, ruin ensues."

From that—namely, from the legal proceeding—the loss of the hired servant from his master; the meaning is "defeat. That is to say, the defeated hired servant shall suffer the loss. And so says Nārada:
"Whatever implements for work have been entrusted to them for the sake of the task, those must be protected with trustworthiness and never with deceit."

Regarding these masters of labor: whatever implements of work, such as plows and the like, have been placed in the hands of the servants for the purpose of activities such as agriculture, that must be protected by them without deceit; otherwise, there will be a loss of wages—this is the implication. Regarding the performance of work, Viṣṇu says: "If a servant, having received wages, does not perform the work, he shall forfeit double the wages. This refers to cases where the person is capable. As Nārada says: "When a hired servant, having received wages, does not perform the work..."
If he is capable, he shall be compelled to pay double that amount as well as his wages.
On this point, Kātyāyana says: "But he who, having undertaken a work, does not have it completed, must be compelled by force to do so; failing to do so, he deserves punishment."
On this point, Bṛhaspati states: "A hired servant who, though not ill, fails to perform his work as prescribed (as ordained) out of arrogance,
shall be fined eight kṛṣṇalas, and his wages shall not be paid."
Nārada says:
If he abandons his work before the time is complete, he shall suffer the loss of his wages;
but if he departs due to a fault of the master, he shall receive payment for as much work as has been performed.

On this point, Viṣṇu states: "A hired laborer who abandons his work before the term is completed shall forfeit the entire wage (or pay it). He shall pay one hundred *paṇas* to the king. Furthermore, whatever is lost through his own fault must be made good to the employer, except in cases of damage caused by fate or the king. If the employer dismisses the laborer before the term is completed, he shall pay him the full wage and one hundred *paṇas* to the king, except for faults on the part of the laborer. Yājñavalkya says: "The carrier, however, shall be made to pay for goods that have been lost, provided the loss was not due to the king or an act of God."
And one who creates an obstacle to the departure is declared by tradition to be liable for double the amount.

If he abandons the work after it has begun, he shall forfeit the seventh part of the wage; if on the way, the fourth part; if at the halfway point, half; and if he abandons it entirely, he shall be made to pay the full amount, as shall the one who causes him to abandon it.

When he abandons him before setting out on the journey that has already commenced, he must pay a fourth part together with the wages; at the halfway point, he must pay half. Furthermore, when the master abandons the laborer at certain places, then the master must also give what was previously mentioned to the laborer. Regarding this, Kātyāyana states a specific rule:
"But he shall not be made to pay for what has been stolen by thieves, or burnt, or carried away by water. "Carried away" (ūḍha) means taken away. Regarding courtesans, Nārada says:
Having received the nuptial fee (*śulka*), a courtesan who does not wish to comply shall pay double;
likewise, one who pays the fee but does not wish to comply shall suffer the loss of that fee.
Bṛhaspati has stated an exception to that:
"A mare that is wide-mouthed, agitated, or unsteady, one devoted to the duties of a king,
or one who does not come when summoned, is declared to be an unspeakable (vile) *baḍavā*."

*Baḍavā* means a prostitute. Regarding this, Nārada states a specific rule: "A man who, having enjoyed a woman, does not pay the bride-price (*śulka*), may have intercourse with her in a non-natural manner by striking her with teeth, nails, and so forth."
He who approaches a woman in an improper place, or causes her to dwell with many men,
shall be made to pay eightfold the nuptial fee (śulka) and an equal amount as a fine.
In the *Matsyapurāṇa*, another specific rule is shown:
"If a courtesan, having accepted her fee, goes elsewhere out of greed,
the king shall cause her to pay a fine and shall also cause her to return the man's belongings."
Those lovers who reside in her house and for whom the courtesan is the primary concern—
they are known to provide a definitive resolution regarding matters arising from her.
On this point, Bṛhaspati says:
"If a servant, having been commissioned by his master,
performs an inauspicious act for that purpose, the master shall incur the guilt therein."
The meaning is that the fault lies with the owner alone in that case. On this point, Nārada says:
"One should bring back the goods that carry the freight when their time is full;
one should restore what is broken or lost to the receiver, except in the event of a common disaster."

*Saṃplavaḥ*—the clashing together of one thing with another or with a different substance. Regarding this, Hārīta says: "He who, having built a house on another's land, should dwell there after paying the *stoma* (rent), must take that [structure] and depart, leaving behind the grass, wood, bricks, and so forth."
But having stayed on another's land without a formal agreement,
one who departs against his will should by no means take grass, wood, or anything else.
Whatever grass, wood, or bricks have been laid down,
he must report all of that to the owner of the land as it is being removed.
By the word *stoma*, a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) is given to them for the purpose of experiencing the houses of others.
And he who, having obtained a dwelling through affection, makes it his own for a long time—
for him, as he departs, there is no other [fees] than the *stoma* consisting of wood.

The meaning is that otherwise the king would seize [the animal]. Within this context, the rule concerning the legal proceeding known as "Disputes between Owner and Herdsman" is stated. On this point, Nārada says:
"From a hundred cows, a heifer shall be the fee; from two hundred, a milch cow."
Every year, O cowherd, the milking takes place on the eighth day.

Every year, a heifer—a cow that has passed the stage of being a calf—must be given as wages to the herdsman, based on the hundred cows he is protecting. However, when there are more than one hundred cows, the meaning is that on the eighth day, instead of a heifer, a cow with its calf and the entire milk yield (*saṃdoha*) must be given. *Saṃdoha* means the milking of all [the cows]. As Bṛhaspati says:
"Likewise, the herdsman shall receive the entire milk of the cow for whom he works on the eighth day."

However, with the consent of the owner, the milk-based wages are indeed refundable. Regarding this, Manu says that from among ten milch cows, one should take the most excellent heifer for the sake of the wages, as she is the milk-wages:
"But the cowherd who is paid in milk shall milk the best [cow] out of ten.

Here, *parām* means "the most excellent"; *daśataḥ* is formed with the suffix *tasi* used in all case-endings in the sense of selection, meaning "from among the ten milch cows. Nārada states what must be done by both the owner and the keeper:
Or the cowherd should bring them back every day at the end of the night;
and once they have been delivered, the cowherd should bring them back again in the evening.
"Upānayet" means he should take possession of them. For this very reason, Yājñavalkya says:

"Just as a cowherd should return the cattle entrusted to him in the evening, so [should he do]. Here, "cowherd" (*gopa*) means a cattle-keeper. The meaning is that however many were entrusted in the morning, that same number must be returned. And likewise Bṛhaspati says: "He should return everything in the evening. However, regarding the non-return of all the animals, Yājñavalkya states:
"One who has received wages must make good those [animals] lost or carried off through negligence."

*Kṛtavetanaḥ* means one who has received wages; that is to say, the keeper (*pālaka*). The mention of "negligence" (*pramāda*) is intended to indicate the faults of the keeper. Therefore, in cases involving theft or death [of the animal], if the keeper is faultless, he shall not be made to pay. For this very reason, Manu says: "A keeper is not liable to pay for an animal that has been carried off by thieves, provided he has raised an alarm and reported it to his own master at the proper place and time."

The proclamation by means of trumpets, flutes, and other instruments is for the purpose of making it known to many people. The "place" intended is where the owner is located; the "time" is one that is not excessively delayed. When, having failed to deliver [the animal] to such a place or at such a time due to his own fault, he reports it in another place or at another time, then he is held liable to pay a fine according to the nature of his offense. Regarding certain specific circumstances, Vyāsa states that the keeper is blameless:
"In the event of the capture of the keeper, the destruction of the village, or the upheaval of the kingdom, whatever may be lost or stolen, the keeper is not culpable therein."

Regarding this, Manu states a specific rule: "But the keeper alone shall restore what is lost, destroyed by worms, killed by dogs, or died in a dangerous place, provided it was not due to human negligence."

"Lost" means its location is unknown—where it is staying. "Destroyed by worms" means ruined or consumed by insects. "Killed by a dog" means struck down by a dog. "Died in a dangerous place" means died in mud or similar terrain. "Deprived of human effort" means deprived of the means of subsistence (*bhukti*). [304] And for this reason, it must be reported to the owner; otherwise, it is understood that the keeper would incur guilt. To clarify this very point, the same author says:
"If a calamity should befall the cow, the cowherd shall strive to remedy it to the best of his ability.
If he is unable, he should quickly return and report it to the owner."

Regarding a different procedure, Viṣṇu states: "If the property is lost, he shall give the value of the lost animal to the owner; if the animals are attacked by wolves or other predators during the day while the herdsman is not guarding them, the fault lies with the herdsman. From the mention of "day," it is understood that there is no fault at night. As Manu says: "But when goats and sheep are hemmed in by wolves and the herdsman does not come to their aid, whatever wolf may forcibly kill shall be the herdsman's fault."

The meaning is "toward which individual. *Anāyatī* means "not making an effort," that is, "remaining indifferent"; or alternatively, *anāyatī* means "not running away. As for what was stated by Nārada: "If, among those cows being grazed together in the forest, a wolf should kill one while they are penned, the herdsman is not culpable in that case."

This concerns cases where [the animal] is incapable [of being returned]. Viṣṇu states regarding the subject of the purity or impurity of a herdsman: “When animals have perished, [the herdsman] is purified by showing their tails, horns, and so forth. The meaning is that the herdsman should show the tail and other parts—which have become the remains of the dead animal—in the forest in order to dispel the suspicion of theft. And that observation of signs is an illustration for all types of hired laborers (*bhṛtaka*). Thus says Viṣṇu: “Upon the destruction of a hired laborer, one should report the laborer or his remains to the king. Because of the mention of the “king,” this refers specifically to the case of a royal laborer.

Thus ends the [305th] chapter, titled "Non-payment of Wages," within the Section on Legal Procedure (*vyavahārakāṇḍa*) of the *Sarasvatīvilāsa*, a compendium of law (*smṛtisaṃgraha*) composed by the illustrious Great King Pratāparudra Mahādeva.
Now, the legal procedure concerning the title known as "Sale by One Who Is Not the Owner" is stated;
herein, Nārada says:
"But that which is performed as a purchase or indeed a sale by one who is not the owner..."
That, however, should always be understood as invalid in legal proceedings.

In the preceding section, it was stated that wages (*vetana*) are subject to rescission; here, however, the connection is that what has been purchased (*krīta*) is subject to rescission. Furthermore, regarding the non-delivery of what has been given (*dattāpradāna*), it was explained that what has been given is essentially as if not given; whereas here, there is the rescission of what has been purchased, but what has been purchased is not essentially as if not purchased—therefore, there is a distinction between the two. On this point, Nārada says: "Having recovered property sold by one who is not the owner, the true owner shall obtain it."

The meaning is that the owner may take back his own property sold by one who is not the owner from the person in whose possession it is found. As for what the author of the *Candrikā* stated—"And this refers to an object sold without the owner's consent"—that is incorrect; for if the owner’s consent exists, the transaction does not fall under the category of "sale by one who is not the owner. Furthermore, as Manu has said:
"One who is not the owner sells the property of another without the owner's consent..."

"Unauthorized" (asaṃmataḥ) means one who lacks correct knowledge; that is to say, one who deceives the owner. When it is asked, "What is this 'property of another'?", Bṛhaspati states: "A deposit, a loan for use, a formal entrustment, what has been taken, what has been borrowed, and a pledge—when these are sold in secret by someone, he is declared to be a non-owner (asvāmī)."
The definitions of deposits and the like have already been stated previously. "In secret" means privately. Kātyāyana states:
One should rescind a sale by one who is not the owner, as well as a gift and a pledge. [306]

By this statement, it is understood through the *daṇḍāpūpa* logic that the owner should recover his own lost, stolen, or misappropriated property from the hands of a non-owner, even before the sale has been completed. Regarding this matter, Viṣṇu states a specific rule: "If one sells another's property openly and unknowingly, he is not at fault in that case; the owner shall recover that property. "Unknowingly" means without knowing the seller’s lack of ownership. In that context, regarding the purchase of another's property, "he is not at fault" means the buyer incurs no guilt as a thief. It follows, however, that the seller does incur such guilt; he is to be punished like a thief. But the buyer is not, provided the sale was "openly"—for if he purchases another's property secretly out of greed, knowing it to be so, then the buyer also incurs the guilt of a thief. Thus says the Smṛti: "If one sells [property] either secretly or openly for a low price, then both the buyer and the seller are to be punished like thieves. On this point, Bṛhaspati says:
That which is purchased inside a house, outside a village, at night, from an unreliable person,
or for an inadequate price— this should be known as fraudulent purchase (*upadhikraya*).

"From an *asat* person"—the meaning is from a person such as a *caṇḍāla* or similar outcaste. Some say that the inclusion of the term *asat* is intended as an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) for slavery and other conditions that signify a lack of ownership, and thus refers primarily to gamblers and the like. However, the same author states that purchase by fraud (*upadhikraya*) is what constitutes a fault:
"But there is no fault in that which was purchased for a price and previously reported to the king; one becomes a thief only through fraudulent purchase."

*Stenaḥ* means a thief; the meaning is that he is to be punished like a thief. On this point, Kātyāyana says: "But the owner of the lost property (*nāṣṭika*) shall have that wealth [recovered] through his own kinsmen. *Nāṣṭika* refers to one whose wealth has been lost. The meaning is that he should have his lost property recovered through his kinsmen acting as witnesses. Bṛhaspati speaks to the purchaser: *krītvā vikrīya vā kiṃcid yasyehānuśayo bhavet | so 'ntardaśāhāt tad dravyaṃ dadyāc caivādadīta vā || pareṇa tu daśāhasya na dadyān nāpi dāpayet | ādadāno dadac cāiva rājñā daṇḍyau śatāni ṣaṭ ||* "Whether having purchased or sold something, if a regret should arise for anyone here, he may give back or take back that object within ten days. But after the ten-day period, one should neither give it back nor cause it to be given back; both the one taking it and the one giving it shall be fined six hundred [paṇas] by the king."* *Bṛhaspati* says to the purchaser: *krītvā mūlyena yaḥ paṇyaṃ duṣkrītam iti manyate | vikretuḥ pratideyaṃ tat tasminn evāhny avikṣatam || dvitīye 'hani dātavyaṃ dviguṇaṃ saha vāhanam | trtīye 'hani naṣṭaṃ cet tṛtīyāṃśena saṃyutam || pareṇa tu na dātavyaṃ grāhyaṃ vā krayinā kvacit | ato 'nyathā hi dūrasthe doṣavati krayiṇi ||* "Whoever, having purchased a commodity with its price, considers it a bad purchase, must return it to the seller on that very same day if it is undamaged. On the second day, it should be returned along with the conveyance, but double the price. If it is lost on the third day, it should be returned together with a third part [of the price]. Beyond that, it need not be returned, nor should it be accepted anywhere by the purchaser, unless the purchaser is at a distance or is at fault."* *Bṛhaspati* says: *anvāhite 'puṣkalake kraye vikraye 'pi vā | svāmī dadyād dhanam mūlyaṃ na ced anvāhinī bhavet || naṣṭaṃ vinaṣṭaṃ kṛmibhir agninā vā jalena vā | bhukte 'nyena na dātavyam anāhite na cārpitam ||* "In the case of a deposit, a partial sale, or even a full sale, the owner shall pay the value of the money if the depositary is not available. If it is lost, destroyed by worms, fire, or water, or consumed by another, it need not be paid back, provided it was not deposited or delivered."* *Bṛhaspati* says: *naṣṭo deyo vinaṣṭo vā dāhyo vā dāhakāribhiḥ | prāptam anyair athāpy anyair na deyaṃ dāyakair vinā ||* "If it is lost or destroyed, it must be made good by those who caused the fire or destruction.
