Thus ends the thirty-fourth chapter, titled "The Section on the Union of Man and Woman," within the section on legal procedure (*vyavahārakāṇḍa*) of the *Sarasvatīvilāsa*, a compendium of law (*smṛtisaṃgraha*) composed by the illustrious Great King Pratāparudra Mahārāja.
Now, the rule for the section entitled "Inheritance" (Dāyabhāga) is being stated by the king Pratāparudradeva, the son of Puruṣottamabhūmīndra; thus, the law of inheritance is being expounded.

In the preceding section, the law concerning the union of husband and wife (*strīpuṃsayoga*) was expounded. Here, however, partition (*vibhāga*) proceeds with reference to the very same husband and wife; thus, there is a logical connection between them by way of the relationship of the dependent and the basis upon which it depends. Nor should it be argued that, based on the Smṛti text stating "no partition exists between husband and wife," there can be no partition at all between a man and a woman. For a partition between husband and wife will indeed be described. Furthermore, in some cases there is a partition among men, in some cases among women, and in some cases between both husband and wife; thus, there is no contradiction whatsoever. What is called inheritance (*dāya*) is the collective property belonging to the group consisting of the father and sons.
"The property of the father is to be divided; the wise call it inheritance," so says the Smṛti. "To be divided" means worthy of partition. Bṛhaspati also says:
"Whatever wealth of his own the father gives to his sons, or which is given [to them] by him..."

"that inheritance... [iti]. Since the word *pitṛ* (father) ends in an agentive suffix in the phrase "the father gives the wealth to the sons," it must be supplied [from the context]. Thus, the word *dāya* (inheritance) is derived as having the object-case (*karman*) as its primary sense. By this, the general definition is established: "inheritance" (*dāya*) is a substance pertaining to the collective relationship between father and son. The author of the *Saṃgraha* also states: "That substance which has come through the father, and that which has come through the mother..."

"It has been stated [that inheritance] by the word *dāya*; now its division is being described. This is the definition according to Bhāruci, Aparārka, and others: "The paternal property that is fit for division is *dāya*. That alone is correct, because it applies consistently to both the division of religious duties (*dharma*) and the division of material wealth (*dravya*).

Nor should it be argued that because rituals such as the *agnihotra* and *vaiśvadeva* lack the status of paternal property (*pitṛdravyatva*), the definition [of inheritance]—"paternal property is to be divided"—does not apply there; for Viṣṇu’s statement, "Paternal wealth is of two kinds: that which is to be enjoyed and that which is to be performed," indicates that while fields, cattle, and so forth are to be enjoyed, the *agnihotra* and other rites are to be performed, thereby establishing that even the *agnihotra* and similar acts possess the character of being paternal. For this very reason, Yājñavalkya says:
"A householder should perform the *smārta* rites daily in the marriage fire."
Or even when brought by a donor, it [is offered] into the Śrauta fires used for Vedic sacrifices.

Karka states that even after the connection of marriage, this fire remains indeed the *vaivāhika* (marriage) fire. By the phrase "or [the fire] brought at the time of inheritance," the division of the *agnihotra* and other rites is mentioned; and that *agnihotra* and so forth must be understood as belonging to the father alone. Otherwise, the rule "the ritual act is performed in the *smārta* marriage fire" would be contradicted. Regarding this, Karka says: "The fire of one who has no brothers is the *vaivāhika*; for those who have brothers, it is only that which was brought at the time of inheritance—this is the settled rule. And thus, "at the time of inheritance"—that is, at the time of the partition of the estate—"brought as inheritance" means accepted as such. Thus says Bhāruci.

"In the case of partition during the father's lifetime, the brothers shall divide the fire brought from the house of a *śrotriya* by the eldest; here, the status of being 'paternal' (*paitṛkatva*) is applied figuratively to the fire. In the case of partition after the father's death, they shall divide the fire brought by the father; since it was brought by the father, its 'paternal' status is primary. In this view, such a fire is indeed brought by the father for his own brothers."

On this point, some say: "The phrase 'brought at the time of giving' specifies another time for the acceptance of the *agnihotra*. Bhāruciprabhṛti and others do not accept this, because if that were the case, it would follow that the fire could be accepted without having been consecrated (*asaṃskṛtya*).

Some, however, maintain: “An alternative time for the fetching of the fire (*agnyāharaṇa*) has been stated in the Smṛti: ‘This is the time for their inheritance. Herein lies the truth: there are two views—that the nuptial fire is either worldly (*laukika*) or non-worldly (*alaukika*). In the view that it is worldly, since the recitation of the mantras in this context is for the purpose of accomplishing the ritual gift (*vaidhadāna*), its function is solely as a purifier of the agent (*kartṛsaṃskāraka*); it cannot be said to be a purifier of the fire itself. To claim that merely fetching the fire or merely churning it constitutes a purificatory rite is improper. This is because Karka’s commentary establishes that being fetched or being churned possesses the same status as being produced from crystal or being a forest fire, stating: “The marriage ceremony should be performed with a fire produced from crystal, or fetched from the house of a Vedic scholar (*śrotriya*), or from a forest fire. Nor is it reasonable to say that the very production of crystal is the purificatory rite for what is produced from crystal, or that the state of being a forest fire is the purificatory rite for a forest fire. Therefore, the nuptial fire is indeed worldly. For this very reason, Āpastamba has stated: “If the fire is destroyed, one should fetch fire from the house of a *śrotriya* or by means of churning; having fasted and performed the penance (*prāyaścitta*) beginning with ‘[if] the wife...’, one should offer oblations as before. The commentator (*vṛttikāra*) states: “Even when the fire is destroyed, this same rule applies. Consequently, the statement that prohibits the performance of the *agnihotra* separately for those who have merged their fires becomes logically consistent.

The meaning is as follows: at the time of partition, there is a mutual division of the fires brought forward for the sons. Regarding the fire used for marriage (*vaivāhika-agni*), if one holds the view that it is non-worldly (*alaukika*), its non-worldly nature follows from the scriptural injunction: “One should establish the fire with ‘Bhūr Bhuvaḥ Suvar Om’,” which is extended by *śrauta-atideśa* (scriptural analogy). For this very reason, even during the state of non-partition, the injunctions for performing the *Agnihotra* separately and the *Vaiśvadeva* and other rites separately become logically consistent. They say that the word *vā* (or) indicates these two alternative views. For this same reason, Āśvalāyana stated: “In the event of the loss of the fire, having performed the entire sequence of purificatory rites ending with the *yugaloja*, one should sacrifice again. The separate mention [of the rule] “Or [the rule applies] to the *Śrauta* fires used for the *Vaitānika* sacrifices” is for the purpose of making it known that, in every respect, there is no partition of the *Vaitānika* fires.

On this point, they say: according to the view that the nuptial fire (*vaivāhika-agni*) is non-worldly (*alaukika*), "division" (*vibhāga*) consists simply in each person performing the rites separately. According to the view that it is worldly (*laukika*), "division" consists in the mutual acceptance of the fire; so say Lakṣmīdhara and others. This will be explained in detail in the *Vibhāga-saṃdeha-nirṇaya*. However, Bhāruci, Aparārka, and others do not accept the definition of Asahāya, Vijñānayogin, and others, who state: "That which becomes the property of another solely on the basis of its connection with the owner is denoted by the word 'inheritance' (*dāya*). They argue that this is incorrect because the causes of ownership, such as purchase (*kraya*) and so forth, cannot serve as the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) here. Nor should it be said that the word "only" (*eva*) excludes purchase and the like, for there is no common usage such as "the buyer is an heir (*dāyāda*)" or "he takes the inheritance. In that case, since women are unworthy of inheritance due to the Vedic text, "Therefore women are powerless and without inheritance," it follows that the property of a woman (*strīdhana*) is not denotable by the word "inheritance" (*dāya*); this will be clarified later. Bhāruci says: "Division (*vibhāga*) is the separation of either a substance (*dravya*) or a duty (*dharma*). Vijñānayogin, however, says: "Division is the allocation of various owners of a collective mass of property to specific portions thereof. Bhāruci does not accept this, stating: "Because it is absent in the case of the division of duties (*dharma-vibhāga*). By "division of duties" is meant the division of duties alone. This refers to the separate performance of the Vaiśvadeva and the five great sacrifices (*pañca-mahāyajña*), as well as the performance of ancestral rites (*paitṛka*) and so forth. And this division of duties must be performed even by some who are utterly destitute and lack property, because of Gautama’s Smṛti: "In division, there is an increase of merit (*dharma-vṛddhi*). For those desiring an increase of merit, a division of duties alone may be made. For this very reason, Viṣṇu says: "Or he may divide the duties alone"; the phrase "for those who are utterly destitute" is to be supplied. From this it is known that division is established even by mere intention (*saṃkalpa*) without a formal technical designation (*paribhāṣā*), just as the act of appointing an appointed daughter (*putrikā-karaṇa*) is established by mere intention without a formal designation.

For those possessing wealth, however, the division of religious duties (*dharmavibhāga*) occurs immediately after the division of property: "Brothers who have divided [their inheritance] shall perform [rites]; by no means those who have not divided. This is because it is stated with reference to religious duties such as the *vaiśvadeva* sacrifice, which are to be performed by those who have divided their property. Consequently, for those without wealth, the performance of religious duties—even without the consent of others—is itself the "division of religious duties" (*dharmavibhāga*). For those possessing wealth, there is the "division of property" (*dhanavibhāga*). Thus, there are two kinds of division. For this very reason, Viṣṇu stated: "Division is of two kinds: rooted in ritual action (*karmamūla*) and rooted in inheritance (*dāyamūla*). In this context, although the word *dāya* (inheritance) has a general meaning, it refers specifically to "wealth" (*dravya*), as it results in that specific sense. Here, by the word *dharma*, the *agnihotra* and other such rites that serve as the means to achieve that [duty] are meant. The "division of religious duties" is indeed accepted by the authors of the *smṛtis* such as Manu and Yājñavalkya, by the commentators on those *smṛtis*—namely Asahāya, Medhātithi, Vijñāneśvara, and Aparārka—and by the authors of legal digests (*nibandha*) such as the author of the *Candrikā*. To illustrate: [The text continues with citations and further arguments.]
If they live for ten years with separate religious duties and separate activities,
those brothers should also be known as divided from the paternal estate.

Thus, the classification of property (*dharmavibhāga*) has been stated. In that regard, *vibhāga* (separation) is the practice of separate religious duties for up to ten years by one’s own accord, without the consent of others. As it is said:
"Whatever else has been acquired by oneself without detriment to the paternal estate, as well as what is obtained through friendship or marriage, shall not belong to the co-heirs."

Thus, for one who possesses nothing other than benevolence (*maitrī*) and the like, the very apprehension of benevolence and so forth constitutes its "division" (*vibhāga*). This should be understood to apply here as well. For this very reason, Manu stated:
"Thus has been declared the law concerning women and men, which is designated as sexual pleasure (*rati*);
[now] the acquisition of offspring in times of distress and the law of inheritance—learn these."

On this point, Bhāruci says: "By the term *dāyadharma*, both the division of inheritance (*dāyavibhāga*) and the division of religious duties (*dharmavibhāga*) are indicated. The meaning of the statement is: "Understand the division of inheritance and the division of religious duties as they are being described by me. Although the word *dāya* (inheritance), which denotes property subject to partition, already includes religious duties, it is nevertheless stated explicitly as *dāyadharma* for the sake of clarity. Regarding the phrase "from the paternal wealth" (*paitṛkād dhanāt*), the ablative case is used with the elision of the suffix *-lyap* (as in *upajīvya*). Some hold that this is intended to demonstrate the *kaimutikanyāya* (the principle of "how much more so"), showing that even the practice of separate religious duties for ten years while subsisting on paternal wealth is indeed a cause for partition. Others, however, maintain that it means "having abandoned the paternal wealth," interpreting it as an elision of the suffix *-lyap*. They argue that otherwise it would contradict the statements of Manu and others, such as "without harming the paternal wealth. This latter view alone is correct, as the author of the *Nibandhana* states: "This very position is the superior one."
"At whatever time, by whatever method, and by whomsoever it is performed;
for whomsoever, in whatever manner, and according to which scripture it is observed. Thus [it is said].

Regarding the nature of the paternal or maternal inheritance, at what time—such as "when the mother's menses have ceased," and so forth—and by what manner or method, such as through equal or unequal shares, and with whom—such as with the father, mother, sisters, and others—the partition is to be declared; thus, that category of legal dispute in which this collection of fourfold procedural rules is defined is the title of law known as "Partition of Inheritance. On this point, the author of the *Saṃgraha* states a specific rule:
"The division of the father’s property may take place even while the mother is living;
however, she possesses no independent ownership, for without her husband, there is no such independence for the mother."

"Even upon the division of the mother's property while the father is still living, as long as there are sons, the husband is not the master of the woman's wealth. Here, one instance of the word *pati* denotes "owner," while the other denotes "husband. By this, it is implied that while the father is living, no division of property should be made, and while the mother is living, no division of her property should be made for the sons and others. And so says Manu:
"After the father and the mother have passed away, the brothers, having assembled together, shall divide the paternal inheritance; for they have no authority over it while the two are alive."

"Anīśāḥ" means "not independent. Thus says Hārīta: "While the father lives, sons have no independence regarding the taking, giving away, or pledging of property (*arthādāna-vi-sarga-ākṣepa*). [350] "Taking of property" (*arthādāna*) means personal enjoyment; "giving away" (*visarga*) means expenditure; "pledging" (*ākṣepa*) means the act of punishing servants and attendants for their offenses. "Lack of independence" (*asvātantrya*) means not engaging in the taking of property and so forth by one's own will without the father's permission. Likewise, there is a lack of independence regarding religious duty (*dharma*), such as not engaging independently in separate sacrifices (*iṣṭa*) or public works (*pūrta*). And thus, according to the author of the *Candrikā*, a son must perform rites such as the *agnihotra* only when permitted by his father, not without permission. According to Aparārka, however, a son has the right to perform rites such as the *agnihotra* even without permission. The settled rule depends on custom (*ācāra*). Since two types of settled custom have already been mentioned previously, they are not stated here. As for what Devala also says:
When the father has passed away, the sons shall divide the father’s wealth;
however, they have no ownership over it while the faultless father remains alive.

Thus, here the meaning of *asvāmyam* (lack of ownership) is *asvātantryam* (lack of independence), because independence is established for sons by the very fact of their birth. This will be elaborated upon later. By the inclusion of the term "faultless" (*nirdoṣa*), it is shown that even when the father is at fault, the sons possess that independence. Therefore, even while the father is present, if he suffers from defects such as incapacity, the eldest son has independence regarding the acquisition and expenditure of wealth; it should be understood that for the younger brothers, there is dependence on the eldest. For this very reason, Śaṅkha and Likhita state: "But when the father is incapable, the eldest, or the next [in order] who knows the business, shall conduct the affairs of the family with his permission. By the word "that" (*tat*), the eldest is meant, because at that time he alone possesses independence. By the phrase "who knows the business," it is indicated that the term "next" refers to the younger brother. The author of the *Candrikā* says: "And the mention of 'incapable' is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) of one who is distressed and so forth. By this mention of "incapable," it is known that when the father has become dependent due to old age or similar causes, the partition of his wealth occurs by the will of the sons alone, even against his wish. And so says Nārada:

"One who is diseased, one who is angry, one whose mind is attached to sensual objects, and one who acts contrary to the scriptures—such a father has no authority over the partition [of the estate]. The implication is that, rather, the sons themselves are the masters. For this very reason, he (the same author) says:
"Or rather, the father himself, established in his [proper] age, should divide the sons.

"Established in his age" means one who possesses unimpeded independence. By the use of the words "the father himself" (*pitaiva*) and the restrictive particle *eva*, the meaning is that only the father has the authority to perform the division provided he is free from defects such as illness; otherwise, the authority belongs to the sons. Thereafter, the sons shall divide the property equally.
When the mother’s menses have ceased, when the sisters have been given in marriage,
and when the father has desisted from sexual pleasure and his desires have subsided;

Regarding *ramaṇe*: the meaning is "in order to enjoy" within the sphere of enjoyment. By the phrase "one whose desire has ceased," the mother's cessation of her menstrual flow (*rajas*) is indicated; and by the phrase "when [the father's] desire for another wife has ceased," it is understood that there is no partition [of the estate] while he still possesses such a desire. Consequently, the expression "after the father's [death]" indicates one time for partition, and that is partition during the father's lifetime (*ajīvadvibhāga*). The expression "when the mother's menstrual flow has ceased" indicates the time for partition during the father's lifetime (*jīvadvibhāga*). Thus, two times for partition have been stated. As for the father's desire, since it does not exceed the scope of partition during his lifetime, it does not constitute a separate temporal distinction.
Śaṅkha and Likhita state the result of partition:
"The joint ownership of brothers while their parents are alive is ordained;
even after that, it continues for the sake of their prosperity, together with those three."
"They may well live together in one place and attain prosperity," so it is said;

the sense is that this is because there is no separate expenditure for each individual. However, upon partition, "dharma attains prosperity. And thus Gautama states: "Upon partition, there is an increase in dharma" (GDh 28.4). When it is asked how this occurs, Nārada says:
"A single dharma prevails among brothers who are undivided."

"When there is partition, their religious duty (*dharma*) also becomes separate for each. Here, *dharma* refers to that which arises from the worship of ancestors and deities and so forth. And thus says Bṛhaspati:
"For those living under a single household fire, the worship of ancestors, gods, and twice-born [brahmins]..."
That which is one for those who are united would become the same in every single household if they were divided.

Therefore, even for those who have not divided the estate, merit (*dharma*) produced by their own *agnihotra* and other rites is indeed accomplished. However, it should be understood that when division does take place, the increase of merit—as described in the two views of Gautama and others—is to be kept in mind. Since the position of equal division is stated here as being universally applicable, Yājñavalkya says that in this matter, if the father should, by his own will, adopt the position of equal division, then the wives who have sons should be made sharers of equal portions:
"If he should make equal shares, the wives should be made equal-sharers."

Or, if even when there is an obstacle [to partition], the father should by his own will adopt the position of equal shares with himself, then the wife should receive a share equal to that of his own portion. Regarding this, Bhāruci says that the statement of Āpastamba—“No division exists between husband and wife”—is to be understood as applying only where there is a scriptural injunction for joint status (*sahatva*). Therefore, Yājñavalkya says:
“It is recorded in tradition that among brothers, between husband and wife, and between father and son, suretyship, debt, and witness testimony belong to those who are undivided.”

Here the Vijñānayogin says: "Is it not the case that prior to the partition of husband and wife, there is no prohibition against acting as a guarantor (*prātibhāvya*) and so forth? For, since there is no partition between them, such a qualification would be purposeless. Furthermore, the absence of partition has been shown by Āpastamba: 'No partition exists between husband and wife' (ĀpDh 2.14.16)."

True. There is no partition regarding those rites to be accomplished by the *śrauta* and *smārta* fires and their fruits, but this does not apply to all rites or to material possessions. For instance, having stated, "No partition exists between husband and wife," when the question arises as to why it does not exist, the author provides the reason: "For from the taking of the hand (*pāṇigrahaṇa*), there is joint status in rites as well as in the fruits of merit" (ĀpDh 2.14.17–18). The meaning of this is as follows: since from the time of the taking of the hand onwards, joint status in rites is heard in the injunction, "The husband and wife should establish the sacred fires" (*jāyāpatī agnīn ādadhīyātām*), therefore, because of their joint entitlement (*sahādhikāra*) at the establishment of the fires (*ādhāna*), they have joint entitlement in those rites accomplished by the fires established through that *ādhāna*. Likewise, due to the traditional law (*smṛti*) stating, "The *smārta* rite is performed in the marriage fire" (YDh 1.97), there is likewise joint entitlement even in those rites accomplished by the fire established through marriage. Consequently, in rites such as the *pūrta* (works of public utility) which do not depend on either type of fire, the entitlement of husband and wife is established as being separate. Similarly, joint status of husband and wife is heard in regard to the fruits of merit and so forth, such as heaven, in passages like, "May they two initiate the undecaying light in heaven. It should be understood that joint status applies to the fruits of those meritorious and non-meritorious acts in which there is joint entitlement; however, this does not apply to the fruits of *pūrta* works performed with the permission of the husband.

But surely, even regarding ownership of property, jointness has been stated: "And in the case of the acquisition of property, they do not teach that there is theft when the husband is away on a journey or when a gift is made for a specific occasion" (ĀpDh 2.14.19–20).

True. By this [verse], the wife’s ownership over the property is demonstrated, but not the absence of partition. For, after stating "and in the possession of property," the reason for that is given: since Manu and others do not teach that there is theft when a husband is away on a journey, or when performing occasional obligatory duties such as feeding guests or giving alms, therefore the wife also possesses ownership over the property; otherwise, it would indeed constitute theft. Consequently, even for the wife, a division of property occurs by the husband's will, but not by her own will.

The opinion of Aparārka, however, is as follows: "There is no partition of inheritance for women at all, because of the Vedic text: 'Therefore, women are powerless and do not inherit. Consequently, the wealth of the wives should be given according to the husband's wish. As for the word 'equal' (*sama*), it means that the husband's share should not be made less; rather, a share equal to his, or even a larger share, may be given. This is to be understood because the use of the word 'if' (*yadi*) in the phrase 'if he should give' (*yadi kuryāt*) indicates that it depends on his will, and thus the giving of the share is voluntary."

In this regard, the following is the established truth: according to the opinion of Bhāruci, when there is a plurality of wives, the division belongs to them alone. According to the opinion of Vijñānayogin and others, there is no fixed division for the wife; rather, the wives receive an equal share along with the sons. However, according to the opinion of Aparārka and others, there is neither a separate division for the wife nor an equal division with the sons; rather, she is to be given something according to the husband’s wish. Regarding these three positions, the commentators state the arrangement according to caste: “For Brāhmaṇa wives, there is an equal division with their own sons. For Kṣatriya wives, however, there is no separate division for the wife, nor an equal division with the sons; rather, whatever may be given is to be given according to the husband’s wish. For Vaiśya and Śūdra wives, there is a separate division for the wife. They say that in this arrangement, custom (*ācāra*) alone is the root authority.

Regarding this, Śaṅkha and Likhita state: “When the father is alive, the division of inheritance is permitted—either openly or privately—in accordance with dharma. The meaning is that the method of division permitted while the father is alive must be carried out either “openly,” such that it takes place in the presence of kinsmen and others, or “privately,” in secret, “in accordance with dharma”—that is, by a righteous method. Kātyāyana describes that very method: “When the parents and the brothers take the entire collection of property in equal shares, that is called a division in accordance with dharma.”

*Dharmya* means not departing from *dharma*, because of the scriptural injunction for equal division without distinction, such as: "Manu divided his inheritance among his sons. Although unequal division is seen in the scriptures, it is not to be practiced because it contradicts worldly custom and contradicts other Vedic texts; thus, it is restricted that they take the middle portion with equal shares. For this reason, since it is not to be practiced in this Kali age, the options regarding the *uddhāra* (preferential share) for the eldest and others have not been set forth. Indeed, there is a prohibition: "One should not practice even a *dharma* that does not lead to heaven and is hated by the world," as for example: [355] etc.

Even though there is an injunction stating, "One should provide a large bull or a large goat to a *śrotriya*," it should not be practiced because it is loathed by the world; just as, despite the injunction regarding cows, "One should sacrifice a barren cow dedicated to Mitra and Varuṇa as the *anūbandhyā*," it is not practiced because it is loathed by the world. And it has been said:
"Just as the duty of *niyoga* (levirate) or even the slaughter of the *anūbandhyā* [cow]..."
"Likewise, even the division of the *uddhāra* does not exist at present. Here, "at present" means in the Kali age.

Just as Āpastamba also, having stated "one who is living should divide the inheritance equally among his sons," and having introduced the view of some that "the eldest takes [all]"—meaning the eldest's taking of the entire estate—as the opinion of certain authorities, and having shown the method of preferential distribution (*uddhāra-vibhāga*) according to those same authorities by stating, "In a specific region, gold, black cows, black land, a chariot for the eldest, the father’s personal ornaments, the household decorations, and the ancestral wealth of the wife [belong to the eldest]," he subsequently rejected it, saying, "That is contradicted by the scriptures."

And for this reason, the deficiencies in the explanations of commentators such as Aparārka regarding the rule "the eldest [shall take] the eldest's share" have not been exposed here. In this case of partition during the father's lifetime, the division is optional. On this point, Nārada says:
"When dividing his own estate, the father shall receive two shares."

And this refers specifically to the case of having an only son. Thus Śaṅkha and Likhita have stated: "If he should be an only son, he may take two shares for himself. Here, the word "he" (saḥ) refers to the father under discussion. "Should be an only son" means that he has reached an advanced age and the time for obtaining another son has passed. Furthermore, this concerns the division of wealth alone and not the division of religious duties (*dharma*), because there is no purpose for a double share in the division of religious duties. Yājñavalkya states that where a son, due to his capacity to earn wealth, does not wish to take his own share from the paternal estate, the father should perform the act of separation by giving him as much as he accepts.
"For one who is capable but does not exert effort, there is a separate rite consisting of giving something [else]. [356]

Furthermore, when a partition is made by sons while the father is still living, it must also be carried out according to the method of equal division prescribed in the statement of Kātyāyana beginning with "the entire collection of property. This is because there is no other scripture that establishes a different method for a partition made by sons during the father's lifetime; and because of the traditional teaching (smaraṇa) of Paiṭhīnasi: "Likewise, when the paternal inheritance is being divided after the father has died, the division among the brothers is equal," and because of the statement of Hārīta: "The division is equal when the father is dead. The meaning is that the division of the estate (*riktha*) performed by brothers after the father’s death must indeed be by equal shares. "Inheritance" (*dāyādya*) means hereditary wealth. The phrase "of the brothers" refers specifically to those who have equal ownership and equal caste, since it will be stated later that the share of those of equal caste who are impotent (*klība*) and so forth is excluded, while for those of unequal castes, shares are obtained in proportion to their relative status. Yājñavalkya states that just as sons are equal sharers in the estate, they are also equal sharers in the debt.
"Sons shall divide the inheritance and the debt equally after the death of their parents.
Here, "debt" refers specifically to that which is paternal, because there is a rule that non-paternal debt must be discharged together [with the inheritance]. For this very reason, Kātyāyana says:
"Debt contracted for the sake of the family by a brother, a paternal uncle, or a mother..."
"At the time of partition, all of that must indeed be given by the heirs.
Regarding this, Kātyāyana states a specific rule: "A debt contracted for the sake of dharma, or given out of affection, or one for which he himself was responsible..."
"One should divide that which is visible, but not the gift from paternal wealth.

This means that one must indeed divide the three types of debt that are "visible"—that is, known—namely: that which was intended for religious purposes (*dharmārtha*), that which was given by a father out of affection, and that which was assigned by the father himself as something to be discharged by the sons.
But how is this so? [357]

Regarding the statement, "If one should divide [the estate], the wives should be made equal sharers," the word "share" (*aṃśa*) is explained otherwise here because women are not entitled to a gift. How then is it that Yājñavalkya stated:
"When they are dividing [the inheritance] after the father's death, the mother shall also take an equal share"?
Thus it is said; and how by Vyāsa:
"The wives of the father who have no sons are declared to receive equal shares;
and all those paternal grandmothers are declared to be equal to mothers."

Thus [it is asked]: how is it that Viṣṇu states, "Mothers take shares according to their sons' portions, as do unmarried daughters"? For if women were unworthy of inheritance, then the statement regarding mothers and the others, ending with the daughters, being heirs to shares would be illogical.

"Not so; here the word *aṃśa* does not denote a share of inheritance (*dāyabhāga*), but rather denotes merely a portion of a collection of property. Therefore, some say that the aforementioned fault does not apply. Others, however, maintain that because words such as "mother" (*mātṛ*) refer specifically to a woman who is a parent, even a mother shall take a share—that is, a share of the inheritance—in a partition made while [the father] is still alive. As for the opinion of Medhātithi, it has already been stated according to the system of the social classes (*varṇa*). Vasiṣṭha states: "Now, regarding the division of inheritance among brothers, and those women who are childless: for them, until the acquisition of a son" (VaDh 17.40–41). The meaning of this is: those women who are the father's wives and are childless—meaning they have offspring within the womb—for them, until the acquisition of a son, i.e., until birth, they remain living together; then, after the signs of the offspring born have appeared, there is a division of inheritance among the brothers.
Surely, why is the straightforward meaning—that here there is a partition of inheritance among brothers and childless women—being abandoned?

It is said in reply: it is abandoned because it would result in a contradictory meaning, namely that childless women [retain their share] "until the birth of a son," and because a partition of inheritance is impossible for women who are ineligible for inheritance. For this very reason, another Smṛti states: "A mother who possesses no property of her own shall receive an equal share upon partition from her sons."

*Asvadhanā* (destitute of her own property): the meaning is that a mother who lacks her own specific woman’s property (*strīdhana*) shall receive a share equal to that of the sons when a partition is made during their lifetime. Here, the mention of the "mother" is intended to include co-wives and others by way of illustration. The rule that "mothers take shares corresponding to the shares of the sons" implies that because of the specific qualification *asvadhanā*, if she possesses her own property and it is possible for her livelihood and the performance of duties requiring wealth to be accomplished through that alone, she does not receive a share. Furthermore, if it is impossible to accomplish both livelihood and wealth-based duties with her own property alone, she does not even receive an equal share of her own assets; rather, it is understood that she receives only a smaller share according to her needs. Similarly, if the mass of property to be divided is very large, even for the destitute mother and others, they do not receive an equal share, but rather a share less than equal according to their respective needs—this is understood from the utility of the qualification *asvadhanā*. This is intended to indicate that the wife's taking of a share is not based on her status as a co-heir like the brothers, but rather on the basis of her need. It is not, however, due to the utility of the qualification *samam* (equal), for even if an unequal share were taken, the word would not be rendered meaningless; this is because, in the case of a partition during the father's lifetime, it was stated previously that the husband may, by his own will, give the wives even a larger share. In this case of partition during the father's lifetime, the mother's share should be given according to the brothers' wishes, whether equal or greater. It should be understood that the word *samam* is used to preclude a larger share that might otherwise be obtained when there is no such wish and the divisible estate is small. Therefore, having considered all of this, Yājñavalkya [stated]: [Note: The provided text ends mid-sentence regarding Yājñavalkya's verse.]

Having stated, "If he should divide [the estate] into equal shares, the wives should be made equal sharers," [it is further specified that this applies only to those] "to whom no woman's property (strīdhana) has been given by either the husband or the father-in-law."

Thus it has been stated. The meaning of the statement is that if *strīdhana* (women’s property) has been given, those wives have no right to a share. For this very reason, the author of the *Candrikā* said: "Therefore, in this case, there is no division of inheritance (*dāyavibhāga*) which establishes the mother's ownership; rather, it should be understood as the taking of wealth only to the extent necessary for her needs" [359]. In his commentary on the verse "Of the brothers, or of husband and wife," Vijñānayogin states: "Therefore, the wife also possesses ownership over the property; otherwise, it would constitute theft. However, that [statement] does not establish a right to inherit, but should be understood as referring merely to ownership regarding the feeding of guests, the giving of alms, and so forth. Aparārka, however, maintains that in the phrase "if he should make equal shares," the word "share" (*aṃśa*) refers to a portion of the divisible property. Consequently, since wives do not have a right to a share, the rule that "whatever may be given according to the husband's wish" is intended to mean exactly that. Thus, according to all three views, women do not possess a right to the inheritance (*dāyabhāktva*), but rather a right to a share (*aṃśaharatva*). And that [right to a share], which depends on the relative abundance or scarcity of *strīdhana*, should be understood as previously explained. According to the opinion of the *Bhāṣyakāra*, however, it should be understood that the division of property for the wives of *Śūdras* is established by worldly custom (*lokācāra*).

As for that which was stated by Viṣṇu: “And unmarried daughters shall receive a share corresponding to the share of a son,” since he employs the qualification “unmarried,” it is understood that they may take a share corresponding to a son’s portion according to their capacity for the purpose of their own marriage, but not that they have a right to inherit a portion for the sake of their maintenance as mothers do. For this very reason, Devala stated: “To the maidens, the father’s wealth—the matrimonial property—should be given. “Matrimonial property” (*vaivāhikaṃ vasu*) means wealth intended for the purpose of marriage. Therefore, Yājñavalkya said:
"And the sisters, having given a fourth part from their own shares. Thus [it is said].

The meaning of this is as follows: sisters who have not been consecrated (*asaṃskṛtāḥ*) must be consecrated by their brothers. Having done what? Having given them a fourth part from their own respective shares. By this, it is understood that daughters are entitled to a share after the death of the father. Here, the phrase "from their own share" does not mean that a fourth part should be extracted and given from each individually allotted share. Rather, whatever the caste of the girl, she is to be made a recipient of a fourth part from the share of a son of that same caste. This is what is meant: if that girl is of the Brāhmaṇa caste, then she receives a fourth part of whatever share belongs to a Brāhmaṇa son. For example: if someone has a Brāhmaṇa wife, and there is one son and one daughter, then all that paternal property should be divided into two parts; one of those parts should be divided into four, and having given a fourth part to the daughter, the son should take the remainder. Or, if there are two sons and one daughter, even then the paternal wealth should be divided into three parts; one of those parts should be divided into four, and having given a fourth part to the daughter, the two sons should divide and take the remainder. Or, if there is one son and two daughters, then the paternal wealth should be divided into three parts; one of those parts should be divided into four, and having given two parts to the two daughters, the son takes the entire remaining share. In this manner, the application should be made for brothers and sisters of the same caste, whether they are equal or unequal in number. But when there is one Brāhmaṇa son and one Kṣatriya daughter, then the paternal property should be divided into seven parts; the three shares belonging to the Kṣatriya son should be divided into four, and having given a fourth part to the Kṣatriya daughter, the Brāhmaṇa son takes all the remainder. Or, if there are two Brāhmaṇa sons and one Kṣatriya daughter, then the paternal wealth should be divided into eleven parts; among those, the three shares belonging to the Kṣatriya son should be divided into four, and having given a fourth part to the Kṣatriya daughter, the two Brāhmaṇa sons take all the remainder. In this way, wherever there is a disparity of caste among the brothers and sisters—whether their numbers are equal or unequal—it should be inferred everywhere accordingly.

Now, one might argue that the interpretation—“having given a portion, namely the fourth”—is appropriate, meaning that one gives the substance required merely for the sacramental rites with the intention of giving a fourth part; however, this is incorrect because it contradicts the scriptural injunction:

“The brothers shall each separately give their own property to their sisters from their respective shares; they shall give a fourth part from each of their own portions, for those who refuse to give shall become outcasts. [361]

The meaning of this is as follows: brothers such as Brāhmaṇas and others should give to their sisters, beginning with the Brāhmaṇī, from their respective shares prescribed for their own caste—as will be stated later in the verse, "A Brāhmaṇa shall take four shares"—the fourth part, that is, a quarter-share from each of their own individual portions. It is not said that a fourth part is to be given by extracting [a portion] from one's own share; rather, a fourth part is to be given separately to each individual maiden from the single share prescribed for her specific caste. The method of distribution when there is a disparity of caste or a disparity in number has already been explained. Since it is heard in the text, "They would be outcasts if they refuse to give," that there is sin in non-giving, it is understood that giving is mandatory. If it is argued that here too the mention of "fourth part" is not intended, and what is intended is merely the giving of enough wealth for the performance of sacramental rites (*saṃskāra*), [then we reply:]...
No, for there is no evidence that the giving of a fourth part is not intended even in the two aforementioned Smṛtis, and because it is heard in scripture that there is sin in not giving it.

As for what has been said by some—that if the intention were to give a share, the case of one with many brothers would result in great wealth while the case of one with many sisters would result in poverty—[that is incorrect].

This has already been refuted by the aforementioned method. For it is not stated here that a fourth part is to be given after setting aside a portion belonging to oneself, such that [the objection] would apply. Therefore, after the father's death, the daughter is also an heir to a share; however, previously, she receives only whatever the father gives her, because there is no specific statement to the contrary.
And all of this is the opinion of Asahāya, Medhātithi, Vijñānayogin, the author of the Pradīpa, and others.

Bhāruci, Aparārka, and others do not accept this view: that after the father’s death, or while the father is alive, a daughter is not entitled to a share; rather, while the father is alive, he may give whatever he wishes to his daughters. Upon the father’s death, even the brothers must provide for the unmarried daughters what is necessary for their sacraments (*saṃskāra*), and for those who are unsettled (*apratiṣṭhitāḥ*), they must provide what is necessary for their establishment (*pratiṣṭhā*). However, they do not claim that such daughters are entitled to a fourth share. The scriptural passages prescribing a fourth share are intended to provide the means for sacraments or the means for establishing them. In the statement of Viṣṇu, “A share must be given to the unmarried and the unsettled,” it is understood that the giving of a share applies specifically to sisters characterized by the qualifications of being unmarried and unsettled. And that [share] is understood to be for the purpose of establishment or marriage. As for the traditional rule stating, “They would be outcasts if they refuse to give,” which prescribes sin for non-payment, it should be understood to mean that there is sin if one fails to provide for their establishment through the requisite wealth, or if one fails to perform their sacraments through the requisite wealth. Whether the father is alive or dead, the daughters are entitled to whatever is given. Since these Smṛti texts are rooted in reason (*nyāyamūla*), it is improper to assume an unseen spiritual result (*adṛṣṭa*) when a visible purpose is established. This is the opinion of Bhāruci, Aparārka, Yajñapati, and others. For this very reason, Bṛhad-Viṣṇu stated: “One should perform the sacraments of unmarried daughters according to one's own means. Regarding this, Śaṅkha states a specific rule: “When the inheritance is being divided, the daughter shall receive her personal ornaments, wedding gifts, and woman’s property (*strīdhana*). Here, “ornaments of the daughter” refers to the jewelry worn by the girl herself, and “woman’s property” refers to the mother’s wealth. On this point, Bodhāyana says: “The daughters shall receive the mother’s ornaments and her inherited property, or else other [gifts]. “Inherited” means passed down through the maternal lineage. “Other” refers to anything else given at the brother’s discretion, which the maidens may receive. Yājñavalkya provides an exception to the rule that “the daughters shall receive the inherited property.”
"The daughters [inherit] the remainder from the debt; in their absence, the lineage.

This means that the daughters shall divide the mother’s wealth according to the prescribed order, [specifically] the remainder from the debt—the residue remaining after the discharge of debts incurred by her. What is meant is this: the debt contracted by the mother must be discharged by the sons alone, not by the daughters; however, the daughters shall take the mother’s wealth that remains after the debt has been cleared. And this is logical, for it is said: "A male is born when the male seed is in excess; a female is born when the female seed is in excess."

Because female constituents (*stryavayava*) are more abundant in daughters than in sons, the woman’s property (*strīdhana*) goes to the daughters; because male constituents (*pitrvayava*) are more abundant in sons than in daughters, the father’s property (*pitṛdhana*) goes to the sons. Regarding this, Gautama has shown a distinction: “The woman’s property belongs to the daughters who are unmarried (*aprattā*) and those who are unsettled (*apratiṣṭhitā*). The meaning of this is: when there is a combination of married and unmarried daughters, the woman’s property belongs only to the unmarried; and among the married, when there is a combination of settled and unsettled, it belongs only to the unsettled. “Unmarried” means not yet wedded; “unsettled” means destitute. To address the question of who should take the remainder of the mother’s property after debts have been cleared in the absence of daughters, he says: “In their absence, the lineage (*anvaya*). “In their absence” means in the absence of daughters; “the lineage” refers to the sons and others who should take it. Vijñānayogī maintains that this is already established by the rule “they shall divide [the estate] after the parents,” and is stated here for the sake of clarity. However, Bhāruciprabhṛti and others explain the statement “the daughters [take] the remainder of the mother’s [property]” differently: in the absence of sons, the daughters shall divide the mother’s property. In their absence, the male lineage—such as paternal uncles and others—should take it, according to the Smṛti text: “The heirs (*dāyāda*) shall obtain [the property] after [the owner]. “After” means in the absence of the owner’s daughter and so forth. “Heirs” refers to the owner’s daughter, paternal uncles, and others. For this very reason, it was said by the author of the *Saṃgraha*: [text follows].

"Whatever property has come down through the father and whatever has come down through the mother is designated by the term *dāya* (inheritance); its partition is now being described. Thus [it is said].

Since property obtained through the mother is denoted by the term *dāya* (inheritance), the right to inheritance belongs only to the sons and not to the women, because of the Vedic scripture stating, "Therefore, women are powerless and non-inheritors (*adāyādāḥ*)," and because of the Gautama-smṛti which says, "There is no division of inheritance for women, because they are powerless. Thus, [the authors] establish that in the absence of brothers, daughters may receive their mother’s ornaments and so forth, and whatever is given at the will of the brothers; only that should be taken, and nothing else. Regarding this, Hārīta states a specific rule:
Manu has declared that brothers must provide for the marriage of maiden sisters who are deaf-mute, born blind, or physically deformed, out of the paternal inheritance.

*Aneḍamūkāḥ*—those incapable of speaking or hearing. *Vikalāṅgāḥ*—those with deficient limbs or those with redundant limbs. Because of the general reference to "paternal inheritance" (*paitṛkād rikthāt*), the meaning of the statement is that all the inheritance should be given to the bridegroom by the brothers, and they [the brothers] should perform the sacramental rites for them. Some say that there is no sacramental rite of marriage for those afflicted by defects such as being mute or deaf; however, it should be understood that this view is refuted. Manu also states who are unworthy of a share: "The impotent and the outcast, those born blind or deaf, as well as the insane, the idiotic, the mute, and those who are devoid of sense-organs, do not receive a share. (MDh 9.201)

The meaning of this is as follows: by the mention of the dual number in the phrase "the impotent and the outcast are without shares" (*anaṃśau klībapatitāv*), they are to be maintained by brothers who are entitled to inheritance, or by those who take the estate, or by those who take the wife. By the mention of the dual number in "the blind from birth and the deaf" (*jātyandhabadhirau*), they indeed have a share; however, even though they possess a share, they are to be maintained because of the existence of the sacrament of marriage (*vivāhasaṃskāra*). By the use of the word "likewise" (*tathā*), the secret point is that if the lame and others are eligible for the sacrament of marriage, they are both sharers of the inheritance and must be maintained. By the use of the cumulative conjunction in "the insane, the idiotic, and the mute" (*unmattajaḍamūkāś ca*), they too must certainly be supported, but they are not sharers of the inheritance—the remainder being that this applies provided they are not eligible for marriage. The phrase "and whoever are devoid of sense-organs" (*ye ca kecin nirindriyāḥ*) is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) that includes women as well; thus, the protection of women who are devoid of sense-organs—such as co-wives, daughters, sisters, and so forth—and of men such as brothers, their sons, paternal uncles, and maternal uncles, must be performed. Some, however, say that "devoid of sense-organs" refers to those whose sense-organs, such as the nose, have been destroyed by disease. As for what was stated by Nārada:

An enemy of his father, an outcast, a eunuch, and one who has been expelled from caste—even these sons of the body (aurasa) shall receive no share; how much less, then, those born of the wife (kṣetraja)?

"Cast down"—meaning one who has committed a great offense and been expelled by his kinsmen. "The outcast (patita) and the eunuch (ṣaṇḍa)" are clear. "Hatred toward the father" refers to a form such as "this is not my father"; for otherwise, if hatred were to arise in sons due to the father's partiality, a share would have been ordained for them in that case. Vasiṣṭha also says [365]: "But those who have entered other stages of life (āśrama) are non-sharers"—the remainder being "having neglected the householder stage. For this very reason, Devala says: "When the father has died, the impotent, the leper, the insane, the idiot, and so forth (including the blind), the outcast, the offspring of an outcast, and one wearing the marks of an ascetic (liṅgin) do not share in the inheritance."

The meaning is that when the father has died, eunuchs and others do not become heirs. A "liṅgin" refers to one who has taken religious vows, such as a perpetual celibate (*naiṣṭhika*) or a forest-dweller (*vanastha*), as well as a Kṣapaṇaka, a Pāśupata, and so forth. Regarding the phrase "the offspring of an outcast," this refers to a son born during the state of [the father's] outcasting; for there is no contagion of the defect of outcasting upon a son born prior to that event. It will be explained later that the worldly relationship between father and son ceases in cases such as outcasting. And thus Viṣṇu states: "Only their legitimate (*aurasa*) sons are entitled to a share, but not the offspring born after [the father] has been outcasted by performing an act that causes loss of caste. Nor are those born of women in the inverse order of castes (*pratiloma*) entitled to a share, nor their descendants, even in regard to the grandfather’s property. In the phrase "when the father has died," the word "api" (even) is to be supplied, meaning that whether the father is dead or even if he is not dead, eunuchs and others do not take a share—thus it should be explained. And thus Āpastamba says: "While living, he should divide the inheritance among his sons equally, excluding the eunuch, the insane, and the outcast. "Excluding" means setting aside. The word "ca" (and) indicates those unworthy of marriage. The author of the *Candrikā*, however, says: "The statement 'when the father has died' is intended to indicate the time of partition. According to him, it must be understood that at the time of partition, even those characterized by impotence and so forth are non-heirs, and not only those characterized by impotence, deafness, and the like. As for what was stated by Yājñavalkya:

"Those born of the body (aurasa) and those born of the wife (kṣetraja) of these [fathers] are entitled to shares provided they are free from defects"—this should be understood as referring to the Dvāpara and other ages, because in the Kali age, the son born of the wife (kṣetraja) is prohibited. Thus, sons who are entitled to no share may nevertheless obtain the grandfather's wealth in the absence of diseases or other conditions that would bar their inheritance; for it is said:
"Their sons, being free from defects, shall receive the share of their father's inheritance."

Thus, according to the statement of Devala. "Defects" refer to impotence and the like. On this point, Yājñavalkya says: "One who is impotent, one who is outcasted, one born of such [an outcast], one who is lame, one who is insane, one who is dull-witted, one who is blind, or those with incurable diseases and so forth—these should be maintained by the family, yet they shall receive no share of the inheritance."

"Born of that" (*tajja*) means born from one who has fallen [from caste]. The first term [in the compound] is intended to include those who are devoid of sense organs and so forth. "Maintenance" (*bharaṇa*) lasts as long as life, according to the *Manusmṛti*: "They must be maintained for as long as one lives. Regarding the specific rule for the shares of those of different castes, Yājñavalkya says:
"The sons of a Brāhmaṇa [father] shall have four, three, two, and one shares respectively according to their caste;
the sons born of a Kṣatriya [father] shall have three, two, and one shares; but the sons born of a Vaiśya [father] shall have two and one shares."

A Brāhmaṇa has four wives; a Kṣatriya, three; a Vaiśya, two; and a Śūdra has only one wife—thus, three [classes of wives] are shown according to the sequence of the castes (*varṇa*). In this context, those born of a Brāhmaṇa are referred to by the word *varṇa*, meaning the Brāhmaṇa and other castes. The suffix *śas* is used here in the sense of distribution (*vīpsā*). Therefore, in each respective caste, those born of a Brāhmaṇa shall receive four, three, two, and one shares respectively. This is what is meant: those born of a Brāhmaṇa from a Brāhmaṇa woman each receive four shares; those born of him from a Kṣatriya woman each receive three; those born from a Vaiśya woman, two; and those born from a Śūdra woman, one each. Regarding "born of a Kṣatriya" (*kṣatrajāḥ*)—meaning those born of a Kṣatriya—the term "by caste" (*varṇaśaḥ*) carries over. Those born of a Kṣatriya from a Kṣatriya woman each receive three shares; those born from a Vaiśya woman, two; and those born from a Śūdra woman, one each. Regarding "born of a Vaiśya" (*viḍjāḥ*)—meaning those born of a Vaiśya—they receive two and one shares respectively. Those born of a Vaiśya from a Vaiśya woman receive two each; those born of a Śūdra woman from a Śūdra man receive one each, because for a Śūdra there is only one wife and thus no wife of a different caste. For the sons of these [lower-caste wives], there is only the single equal division previously mentioned. This was stated by Yājñavalkya in accordance with another *Smṛti*, since in his view marriage to a Śūdra woman is forbidden for a Brāhmaṇa. As he himself has said: [367] "Because it has been stated by that very [author]:”
"That is not my opinion, because in that case he himself is born [as the son] therein.
By "that," the marriage to a Śūdra woman performed by a Brāhmaṇa is referred to. Regarding the property to be divided, Kātyāyana says:
"That which belongs to the grandfather, that which belongs to the father, and whatever else has been acquired by oneself..."
Even upon the partition among heirs, all of this is divided.

"Acquired by oneself" means acquired by oneself through the use of property not partitioned from the father or others. Otherwise, that which is acquired by oneself would be non-partible property. As Yājñavalkya says:
"Whatever else is acquired by oneself without detriment to the paternal estate, as well as what is obtained from a friend or received at marriage, shall not belong to the heirs."
But he who recovers property that was seized and had come into his possession by succession need not give it to the co-heirs; nor need he give what has been acquired through learning.

That which was acquired by oneself without depleting the property of one’s parents; *maitram*—that obtained from a friend; *audvāhikam*—that obtained through marriage; such [property] shall not belong to the heirs (*dāyāda*), namely the brothers and others. Furthermore, regarding that which has come down by succession—that is, any property inherited through paternal lineage which was seized by others and not recovered by the father and others due to incapacity or other reasons—if any among the sons recovers it, he need not give it to the other heirs; rather, the recoverer alone shall take it. Regarding this, Vijñānayogin stated that among the sons, whoever recovers it with the consent of the others need not give it to the heirs. Aparārka does not accept this, for since they have no entitlement to that share even with the consent of the others, such a statement would be redundant. Śaṅkha says that [the recoverer] receives a fourth part of the estate.

"But if one person alone recovers land that was previously lost, others shall receive their shares in due order after he has given them a fourth part. Regarding the word "in due order" (*kramāt*), the term "who has arrived" (*abhyāgatam*) is to be understood as the ellipsis. The meaning of the phrase "whatever else is acquired by oneself" has been clarified by Manu as follows: Thus: [368] "If a younger brother acquires property through his own effort while the elder brother is present, the latter shall not lose his share; rather, the former shall give him a fourth part of that acquisition. "Acquired through his own effort" means obtained by his own labor or by means of his own science (*vidyā*). "While the elder brother is present" means while the elder brother is alive and capable of exerting himself. "The latter shall not lose his share" means that the elder brother does not forfeit his right to a portion of the estate. "Rather, the former shall give him a fourth part" means that the one who acquired the property must give a fourth part of it to the elder brother. This applies even if the elder brother is indolent or lacks learning, provided he is capable of exertion; for if he were incapable, the rule would be otherwise. Alternatively, this may be interpreted as referring to the case where the elder brother is absent or deceased, and the younger brother recovers ancestral land that had been lost. In that case, the elder brother's share is determined according to the rules of inheritance. Furthermore, the meaning of the phrase "whatever else is acquired by oneself" is explained by Manu: "What is gained by science, what is gained by valor, and gifts from friends—these are defined as self-acquired property; over these, the father has no power. "Gained by science" refers to wealth obtained through learning such as grammar or logic. "Gained by valor" refers to wealth obtained through prowess in battle or other forms of martial skill. "Gifts from friends" refers to wealth received as a favor from relatives or others. "Over these, the father has no power" means that the father cannot claim a share of such property, nor can he bestow it away at will. However, this does not apply to the case of a son born after the partition of the estate, for it is said: "A son born after partition shall take a share from the father's possessions; if there is nothing, he shall take a share from the brothers. Thus, the meaning of the verse is established. Furthermore, regarding the phrase "if one person alone recovers," the following is stated: "If a single brother recovers ancestral property that was lost, he shall not be deprived of his share; rather, he shall give a fourth part to the others. "Ancestral property" refers to the estate of the father or grandfather. "Lost" means abandoned or forgotten. "Recovered" means found again. "He shall not be deprived of his share" means he retains his own portion. "Rather, he shall give a fourth part to the others" means he must give a fourth part of the recovered property to the other brothers. If the recovery was made with the assistance of all the brothers, then the entire property is divided equally among them. If, however, it was recovered by one alone, then he gives a fourth part to the others and keeps three parts for himself. This applies to both movable and immovable property. If the property was recovered through the efforts of all the brothers, then it is divided equally. If it was recovered by one alone, then he gives a fourth part to the others. If the property was recovered by the father alone, then the sons have no claim to it unless they have contributed to the recovery. If they did contribute, they shall receive a share according to their contribution. If the property was recovered by the mother, she shall retain it for herself, or it shall be divided among the sons if they assisted her. If the property was recovered by a wife, she shall retain it for herself, or it shall be divided among the sons if they assisted her. If the property was recovered by a slave, the master shall take it; if the slave recovered it through his own effort, he shall receive a share. If the property was recovered by a friend, the friend shall retain it unless it was recovered with the consent of the family. If the property was recovered by an enemy, it shall be confiscated by the king. If the property was recovered by a stranger, it shall be returned to the rightful owner. If the property was recovered by a child, the guardian shall manage it until the child reaches majority. If the property was recovered by a woman, she shall retain it for herself unless she has a husband or son who can manage it. If the property was recovered by a renunciant, it shall be offered to a worthy recipient. If the property was recovered by a mendicant, it shall be shared among the community. If the property was recovered by a king, it shall be used for the welfare of the subjects. If the property was recovered by a deity, it shall be used for the maintenance of the temple. If the property was recovered by a Brahmin, it shall be used for Vedic study and charity. If the property was recovered by a Kshatriya, it shall be used for protection and justice. If the property was recovered by a Vaishya, it shall be used for agriculture and trade. If the property was recovered by a Shudra, it shall be used for service and manual labor. If the property was recovered by a mixed caste, it shall be used according to their specific duties. If the property was recovered by an outcaste, it shall be confiscated by the state. If the property was recovered by a forest-dweller, it shall be used for the sustenance of the forest community. If the property was recovered by a hermit, it shall be used for ascetic practices. If the property was recovered by a yogi, it shall be used for spiritual advancement. If the property was recovered by a philosopher, it shall be used for the dissemination of knowledge. If the property was recovered by a poet, it shall be used for the patronage of literature. If the property was recovered by a musician, it shall be used for the performance of music. If the property was recovered by an artisan, it shall be used for the production of crafts. If the property was recovered by a merchant, it shall be used for commerce. If the property was recovered by a farmer, it shall be used for cultivation. If the property was recovered by a laborer, it shall be used for wages. If the property was recovered by a servant, it shall be used for maintenance. If the property was recovered by a guest, it shall be used for hospitality. If the property was recovered by a beggar, it shall be used for alms. If the property was recovered by a traveler, it shall be used for provisions. If the property was recovered by a messenger, it shall be used for communication. If the property was recovered by a spy, it shall be used for intelligence. If the property was recovered by a soldier, it shall be used for military equipment. If the property was recovered by a physician, it shall be used for medicine. If the property was recovered by a teacher, it shall be used for instruction. If the property was recovered by a student, it shall be used for tuition. If the property was recovered by a priest, it shall be used for rituals. If the property was recovered by a sacrificer, it shall be used for sacrifices. If the property was recovered by a donor, it shall be used for charity. If the property was recovered by a receiver, it shall be used for acceptance. If the property was recovered by a giver, it shall be used for distribution. If the property was recovered by a taker, it shall be used for appropriation. If the property was recovered by a seller, it shall be used for sale. If the property was recovered by a buyer, it shall be used for purchase. If the property was recovered by a lender, it shall be used for lending. If the property was recovered by a borrower, it shall be used for borrowing. If the property was recovered by a creditor, it shall be used for debt collection. If the property was recovered by a debtor, it shall be used for debt repayment. If the property was recovered by a witness, it shall be used for testimony. If the property was recovered by a judge, it shall be used for adjudication. If the property was recovered by a scribe, it shall be used for record-keeping. If the property was recovered by an accountant, it shall be used for accounting. If the property was recovered by a treasurer, it shall be used for treasury management. If the property was recovered by a steward, it shall be used for household management. If the property was recovered by a gatekeeper, it shall be used for security. If the property was recovered by a guard, it shall be used for patrol. If the property was recovered by a scout, it shall be used for reconnaissance. If the property was recovered by a guide, it shall be used for direction. If the property was recovered by a counselor, it shall be used for advice. If the property was recovered by a minister, it shall be used for administration. If the property was recovered by a general, it shall be used for command. If the property was recovered by a herald, it shall be used for proclamation. If the property was recovered by a bard, it shall be used for praise. If the property was recovered by a minstrel, it shall be used for song. If the property was recovered by a dancer, it shall be used for dance. If the property was recovered by an actor, it shall be used for drama.

Whatever one may acquire through labor without depleting the paternal estate—by "labor" is meant such things as agriculture and so forth produced by toil—the term "paternal property" (*pitṛdravya*) here includes the use of the word "father" (*pitṛ*) as an indicator for [undivided] family property. "Without depleting" means without causing injury. Vyāsa also says:
"Whatever wealth one acquires by one's own power without depending on the paternal estate..."
One should not give that to the heirs.

Thus he spoke. Prajāpati also said: "Wealth obtained by a woman through learning, valor, or labor; that which is received as the honey-mixture (madhuparka); that which is friendly; and that which is received at marriage—these are not to be divided among brothers."

That which is obtained through *vidyā*—whether by the study of the Vedas, by teaching them, or by explaining their meaning—one should not give that to the heirs; the acquirer alone shall take it. Regarding such cases, Bhāruci has already explained at length that even though the property resides in a single person, there is still a state of "divisibility" (*vibhaktatva*). Kātyāyana states the nature of wealth acquired through learning (*vidyādhanasvarūpa*): "But that which is obtained by means of learning after having presented oneself [to a teacher] on the basis of a wager, one should know that as *vidyādhana*; it is not subject to partition."

That which is obtained from a disciple, from officiating as a priest, from answering questions, from resolving doubts through inquiry, from praising excellent knowledge, from debate, and from thorough study;
They say that the wealth acquired through learning is not subject to partition;
this applies to what is obtained by surpassing others through knowledge, even if it was preceded by gambling.
Bṛhaspati states that the wealth acquired through learning is not to be divided:
"That which is obtained by means of a promise for instruction, received from a pupil,
or whatever is gained by a priest— this, according to Bhṛgu, is the wealth of learning."

*Prādhyayanam* refers to the acquisition of learning, such as the composition of treatises on grammar (*ghaṭikāśatakādi*). "Learning without wealth" (or "learning through the gift of food") is also included here. In this context, the phrase "whatever has been acquired by oneself" is to be understood as applying to all subsequent items. Therefore, each of the following is connected with the condition "without detriment to the paternal estate": that which is acquired through friendship (*maitram*) without detriment to the paternal estate; that which is acquired through marriage (*audvāhikam*) without detriment to the paternal estate; that which is inherited in due order (*kramāyātam*) without detriment to the paternal estate; and that which is obtained through learning (*vidyayā labdham*) without detriment to the paternal estate. Accordingly, all of the following must be divided among all the brothers: that which is acquired through friendship by way of a return favor without detriment to the paternal estate; that which is obtained through an *āsura* or other form of marriage without detriment to the paternal estate; that which is inherited in due order or set aside without detriment to the paternal estate; and that which is obtained through learning acquired at the expense of the paternal estate. Furthermore, because the phrase "without detriment to the paternal estate" applies to all cases, even property obtained through a gift (*pratigraha*) without detriment to the paternal estate must be divided. If this phrase did not apply to all cases, there would be no need to mention "friendship," "marriage," and so forth. If it is argued that the mention of "friendship" and the rest is meaningful precisely to indicate that what is obtained through friendship and so on—even if it involves detriment to the paternal estate—is not subject to division, then that view contradicts established custom and conflicts with the statement of Nārada regarding property obtained through learning.

"He who maintains the family of a brother who is acquiring learning shall receive a share from that wealth of learning, even if he himself is unlearned. If this were a separate sentence from the rule "without detriment to the paternal estate," then the non-divisibility of what is obtained through a gift would result in a contradiction with established custom. This very point was clarified by Manu, who previously stated, "without diminishing the paternal estate," and so forth. The definition of the non-divisibility of wealth acquired through learning was stated by Kātyāyana:
Furthermore, whatever wealth is obtained through a spell acquired by means of devotion to another person—
that is called "wealth acquired through a spell."

In this context, the word *para* (other) refers to that other individual which is distinct from one's own undivided share. The word *bhakta* (share) is employed as an indicator for the substance (*dravya*) itself. Consequently, it should be understood that the phrase "without contradicting the paternal estate" appropriately applies as a supplement to the entire rule. Now, an objection may be raised: it need not be stated that "what is obtained by a friend or others, provided it does not conflict with the paternal estate, is indivisible," because there is no possibility of its being subject to division. It is well known that whatever is obtained by someone belongs to him alone and not to another; furthermore, a prohibition presupposes a prior possibility of occurrence.
It is said:

"But that which is obtained by those who are united, all of them shall have equal shares in that"—this is an exception to what was previously established. Regarding this, Hārīta states: "One should not divide the *yogakṣema* according to their respective activities. *Yoga* is the acquisition of what has not yet been acquired. Laugākṣi explains the meaning of the term *yogakṣema*: [text follows].
"Those who perceive the truth say that *kṣema*, *pūrta*, *yoga*, and *iṣṭa* are indivisible; indeed, they declare even the bed and the seat to be so.

This is the meaning: by the word *yoga*, the *iṣṭa* rite—which is the cause for obtaining what has not yet been obtained and is accomplished through the sacred fires (*śrauta*) and the domestic fires (*smārta*)—is indicated. By the word *kṣema*, the *pūrta* rite—which is the cause for preserving what has already been obtained, such as the construction of tanks and gardens—is indicated. Both of these, even if inherited from a father, are indivisible even if acquired in opposition to the paternal estate.

Some, however, say that those who provide security and well-being—such as the king, ministers, and domestic priests—are meant; others say it refers to the royal umbrella, chowries, weapons, vehicles, and so forth. "The path" (pracāra) refers to the route for entering and exiting houses, gardens, and the like; that too is indivisible. Nārada, however, states a specific rule:
"Even in the case of one to whom his mother has given her own wealth out of affection, this same rule is seen to apply, for the mother is as beloved as the father."

The word "one's own property" is to be understood as the remainder. This is the rule—the rule regarding indivisibility—which has been stated with reference to what was given by a father. As for that which was stated by Uśanas regarding the indivisibility of land: "What is indivisible even among those of the same lineage, even up to a thousand generations, is the officiating priest, the field, the document, prepared food, water, and women. [371]
This refers to the case of a son born to a Brāhmaṇa from a Kṣatriya wife;
land received as a gift must not be given to a son of a Kṣatriya or other [lower caste].
Even if their father should give it, once he is dead, the son of the Brāhmaṇa wife shall take it.
