for it is said: "That twice-born man who, having initiated a pupil, teaches him the Veda in its entirety along with the secret portions (rahasya), him they call an Ācārya."

It must first be accepted that this *Smṛti* was composed for the purpose of removing doubts regarding the meaning of the term "teacher" (*ācārya*) by means of diligent application to the *Śruti* and *Smṛti*. Furthermore, when analyzed through logic (*nyāya*), the intended purport (*tātparya*) of the *Smṛti* must be stated in accordance with the specific sense in which it culminates. In this regard, although it may appear that "the meaning of the word is the act of teaching" (*kriyāyogaḥ śabdārthaḥ*), nevertheless, the *Smṛti* does not have mere action as its sole purpose. If that were the case, it would result in the definition being merely a figurative explanation (*lakṣaṇā*). But this is not possible; for if the definition had been intended merely as "he who, having initiated a pupil, teaches him the *Śruta*," then the mention of the injunction (*vidhi*) would be useless. Being thus inappropriate, it would imply that the speaker is unreliable (*anāpta*). However, when the definition is intended to apply precisely to that which is enjoined, the mention of the injunction is direct (*āñjasī*). Therefore, one should accept that the definition—beginning with "he who... (*yas tu...*)—is formulated after first indicating, by means of the injunction, the very essence of teaching (*adhyāpana*) as established by the rule. Nor is it untenable to intend both meanings simultaneously due to the consequence of a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*); for in a sentence dependent on the speaker’s intent, the author of the Sūtras, by employing the word "meaning" (*artha*) in the *Codanāsūtra*, has declared such a split to be no fault. Finally, the word "but" (*tu*) serves to distinguish the definition of an *Ācārya* from the mere act of teaching performed by an *Upādhyāya*.
Now, if it is argued that teaching itself cannot be an object of injunction because it is already established by other means, [we reply: no.

Not so; for one who asserts that [the duty of teaching] is obtained from another source must explain what that source is: is its acquisition from the injunction to study (*adhyayana-vidhi*), or rather from livelihood (*vṛtti*)? It cannot be the first, because it has already been stated at the beginning of the treatise by the Guru that the injunction to study, being devoid of a specific qualification (*niradhikāra*), is incapable even of enjoining its own subject matter; this should be understood from that very source. Nor can it be the second, because the purpose of livelihood for teaching is also mediated solely through the status of a teacher (*ācāryaka*); thus, since they do not carry out the injunction for the sake of producing the status of a teacher, there is no acquisition of teaching from any other source. Therefore, in the absence of an injunction, it is improper to describe teaching—which is otherwise unestablished—as a defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*). Consequently, the fact that teaching is something to be enjoined is established. Alternatively, since a Smṛti text cannot have mere worldly usage as its fruit, it must be accepted that its fruit lies in the performance of the injunction for granting a boon (*vara-dāna-vidhi*), which depends upon the determination of the meaning of the term "teacher" (*ācārya*). In that context, within the Vedic injunction for granting a boon—"A boon should be given to the teacher"—the referent of the word "teacher" is taught as the recipient (*sampradāna*). Now, the referent of the word "teacher" is not the connection with the act of teaching at the stage of being a recipient, because that [act] has already passed away. Nor is the mere essential nature (*svarūpa*) the referent, because if that were obtainable even without an injunction, the injunction would be purposeless. Furthermore, the Smṛti cannot employ a figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) based on a past connection with the action, for it is inappropriate to accept that a Vedic or Smṛti text employed for the purpose of determining the true meaning of the term "teacher" should have as its primary intent a secondary or inferior meaning. Moreover, that which is not currently perceived cannot be indicated by such a sign. In the expression "a lion in a cage," the lion is indicated by the cage, but here there is no specific form characterized by a past connection with the action. Therefore, by the force of the injunction for granting a boon, it is understood that the word "teacher" denotes an unseen entity (*adṛṣṭa*) capable of persisting in the state of being a recipient beyond the connection with the action; and when looking for the action that produces that status, the Smṛti is relied upon as having the purpose of enjoining the action that serves as the defining characteristic. Thus, a root-Vedic text consistent with that is to be inferred: "Having initiated him, he should teach."

Now, if it is argued that in order to establish that study is prompted by the injunction for becoming a teacher (*ācāryakaraṇavidhi*), one must establish the inference of a Vedic text in the form of an *adhikāravidhi* stating "one who desires to be a teacher should teach"; and why, instead, infer a Vedic text regarding mere application (*viniyoga*) in the form "having initiated [the pupil], he should teach," where the status of being a teacher is the meaning of the optative suffix (*liṅ*)?

Not so. Since the *smṛti* passage is solely intent upon restating the definition of the teacher (*ācārya*) as it enters into the injunction for granting the boon (*varadāna*), it must be accepted as merely indicating the application (*viniyoga*) of the action that produces the extraordinary category of the "teacher" required by that injunction. It does not have the status of an injunction regarding its subject matter (*adhikāravidhi*), because that would entail unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*) and because there is no such requirement. The state of being a teacher (*ācāryatva*) is the ground for the application of the word "teacher," since suffixes such as *-tva* and *-tal* have the nature of expressing an abstracted ground for application. And that state of being a teacher is an unseen (*adṛṣṭa*) result accomplished through teaching that has initiation (*upanayana*) as its constituent part; therefore, let the injunction authorize only that much and nothing more. Thus, for the purpose of fulfilling the requirement of the injunction for granting the boon, the *smṛti* requires only the status of an injunction regarding the application of the action, and nothing more than that—neither an extraordinary result (*apūrva*) nor a fruit belonging to the sphere of the subject's qualification (*adhikāra*). Consequently, both the lack of requirement and the complexity are evident. Furthermore, since the status of being a teacher is neither pleasure nor the cessation of pain, it cannot be imagined to be a result produced by an injunction (*naiyogika*) comparable to heaven and the like. However, if it is expressed by the optative suffix (*liṅ*), then even though it is neither pleasure nor the cessation of pain, the teacher possesses a third purpose accessible only through the Veda. Thus, even in the case of a directly perceived Vedic text, the fact that the injunctions concerning the student (*adhyetṛ*) and others are established as being intent upon that alone is proven; hence, there is no inconsistency whatsoever in the case of an inferred text.
If it is argued that, in this way, the Bhavanātha has proposed the following verbal formulation: "One should effect the status of an Ācārya by means of teaching, having brought [the pupil] near."

The intention of Bhavanātha is as follows: although that unseen result (*adṛṣṭa*) which is the fruit of the action is indeed the meaning of the optative suffix (*liṅ*), such that the ultimate verbal formulation (*vacanavyakti*) is precisely "one should cause [the pupil] to study," nevertheless—because that unseen result is established by tradition (*smṛti*) as being designated by the term "teacherhood" (*ācāryaka*), and because in that form it is desired by the teacher as a means of obtaining rewards such as gifts—it serves, by virtue of being an object of desire (*kāmyatā*), to establish the qualification (*adhikāra*) for the act of teaching as its own domain. It does not do so simply by way of an injunction (*niyoga*) like a mandatory (*nitya*) injunction and the like. To demonstrate this, the verbal formulation "one should bring about teacherhood through teaching" (*adhyāpanena ācāryakaṃ bhāvayet*) has been presented in order to explain the connection of the instrumental factor (*karaṇa*) derived from the context (*aupādānika*). For this very reason, after presenting such a verbal formulation, Śālikanātha says: "By implication (*arthāt*), there is the qualification for one who desires to become a teacher. The intention is that the verbal formulation was presented in accordance with that [result] precisely to reveal the attainment of qualification through implication.

But surely, since the sentence is intent upon the application of the ritual action for the purpose of producing the status of an *ācārya* required by the injunction for granting the boon, it follows that the optative suffix (*liṅ*) is a restatement (*anuvāda*) of that injunction; thus, the intended view that the status of an *ācārya* is denoted by the optative suffix would not be established. Even if, due to the absence of a mention in proximity, it is not a restatement of the injunction regarding the state of being a "grasper" (*grāhaka*), nevertheless, just like the optative in the sentence concerning the "taking up" (*ādāna*), it would indeed be a restatement of the injunction regarding the state of being a "prompter" (*prayojaka*).

Not so; for in the case of the *ādhāna* (fire-consecration), since the refinement (*saṃskāra*) resides in the fire, it is impossible for it to be denoted by the optative suffix (*liṅ*), and thus the optative is accepted as a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the efficient force (*apūrva*) that prompts the action. However, in the case of the teacher’s refinement produced by teaching, since it resides in the one who teaches, it is indeed possible for it to be denoted by the optative suffix; therefore, the optative need not be accepted as a mere restatement.

But even so, since the consecration (*saṃskāra*) of the teacher is included within the injunction for one who possesses authority (*sādhikāra*), it may—like the consecration of the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*)—be conducive to gain; yet, because it cannot itself bring about authority, it cannot be the instigator (*prayojaka*) even with respect to teaching. Thus, the intended status of being the instigator of study would be utterly dismissed. Otherwise, the consecration of the officiating priests would likewise be the instigator both of officiating as a priest and of performing a sacrifice.

It is not so; for even though the office of teacher (*ācāryaka*) enters into the scope of an injunction involving a specific qualification (*sādhikāra-vidhi*), it is desired by the instructor as something that brings about rewards such as the granting of boons (*varadāna*). Since, in reality, it serves as the basis for the qualification to teach, its status as a motivator (*prayojakatva*) is possible. However, although the consecration of the officiating priest (*ṛtvij-saṃskāra*) brings about rewards, it is dependent on others because it must be accomplished through acts such as the selection (*varaṇa*) performed by the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) under his authority. Because it cannot be accomplished by one’s own will due to this dependence on another, it does not independently establish a qualification; thus, the possibility of its being a motivator is absent. This is the distinction. Therefore, it should be understood that the ultimate syntactical form intended by the proponent is precisely "having initiated [the pupil], he should teach" (*upanīyādhyāpayet*). Consequently, the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) is established against the reason based on the fact that [the Veda] is a means to worldly purposeful action (*laukikārthakriyā*) and so forth.

Some offer this rebuttal: [the compound] *laukikārthakriyāsādhanam* is a *bahuvrīhi*, meaning "that ownership (*svatva*) for which worldly purposeful action (*arthakriyā*), such as acquisition and so forth, is the means (*sādhana*). The sense is: "because it is to be accomplished by worldly purposeful action. Therefore, one should understand that, even in the opinion of Vijñāneśvara, there is neither a contradiction with the text nor a logical inconsistency.

That is incorrect. To abandon a *tatpuruṣa* compound and resort to the inferior *bahuvrīhi* compound is like a man fleeing from the fear of mud who ends up falling into filth. Thus, once it is established that ownership (*svatva*) is a worldly (empirical) fact, the following rules of Gautama—“The owner [is one who acquires property] through inheritance, purchase, partition, seizure, or finding; for a Brāhmaṇa, what is received is additional; for a Kṣatriya, what is conquered; for a Vaiśya and a Śūdra, what is earned”—are methods of acquiring wealth with visible purposes. However, the five means beginning with inheritance (*riktha*) are common to all. Inheritance (*riktha*) means the acquisition of inheritance—that is, the birth of a son or similar offspring which establishes ownership over the wealth of a father or other relative. Accordingly, Gautama himself stated that it is the cause for obtaining paternal wealth: “By birth alone does he obtain ownership, so say the Teachers. “By birth alone” means by the very birth of the body in the mother’s womb. For this very reason, Viṣṇu says: “Ownership is acquired by birth. Bhāruci states: “[This applies] to a son alone, but not to an appointed daughter (*putrikā*). The author of the *Candrikā* explains *saṃvibhāga* as a division that effects ownership over specific portions of the property belonging to sons and others. Vijñāneśvara, however, maintains: “Inheritance (*riktha*) is an unobstructed gift (*dāya*); partition (*saṃvibhāga*) is an obstructed gift. Although the word *riktha* can refer even to an obstructed gift—as seen in the rule “the heir (*rikthagrāha*) shall be made to pay the debt”—nevertheless, here an unobstructed gift is intended. Otherwise, there would be a redundancy with the word *vibhāga*. He argues that by the word *vibhāga*, an obstructed gift occurring after that time is indicated, because partition itself is not a cause of ownership. Bhāruci and others do not accept this; they argue that in the case of an unobstructed gift, birth is required in addition to the relationship, whereas in the case of an obstructed gift, the absence of an obstacle is not the cause, as it is trivial. *Parigraha* is the appropriation of water, grass, wood, and so forth found in forests and such places that has not been claimed by another. *Adhigama* is the discovery of a treasure-trove and the like. Among these, the son, the buyer, the co-partner, the appropriator, or the finder becomes, respectively, the owner of the father’s wealth, the purchased item, the partitioned share, the seized object, or the discovered find. Similarly, what is “received” (*labdha*)—that is, obtained through acceptance—is the specific mode of acquisition for a Brāhmaṇa. Likewise, for a Kṣatriya, what is “conquered” (*vijita*) is what is obtained through victory. For a Vaiśya, what is “earned” (*nirviṣṭa*) is what is obtained in the form of wages from agriculture and so forth. For a Śūdra as well, what is “earned” is what is obtained in the form of livelihood through service to the twice-born and so forth. This is how the meaning of Gautama’s Smṛti, which concerns the basis of acquisition, is to be understood. Therefore, the meaning is that this Dharma-smṛti is a traditional authority (*smṛti*), just like the grammar and other treatises which concern the basis of correct words.

The truth here is this: Gautama has composed this statement with great effort, reiterating the very means of acquiring ownership well-known in the world—such as acceptance of gifts and so forth—and then regulating them for the sake of *adṛṣṭa* (unseen spiritual merit) by specifying the castes, such as the Brāhmaṇas and others. Thus it is said:
"O Brāhmaṇa, whatever wealth they acquire through a censurable act, they become pure by relinquishing it, and by silent recitation (*japa*) and austerity alone."

When ownership (*svatva*) is understood solely through the scriptures, that which is acquired by reprehensible means—such as accepting gifts from the unworthy (*asatpratigraha*) or trade—is not considered ownership at all; therefore, it is not to be divided among one's sons. However, when ownership is understood as worldly (*laukika*), then even what is acquired by accepting gifts from the unworthy constitutes ownership, and thus it must be divided among one's sons. As for the statement, "They are purified by its renunciation," this refers to the penance (*prāyaścitta*) for the acquirer alone. For the sons and others, however, ownership arises by virtue of inheritance (*dāya*); thus, they have no connection with the fault. There are seven lawful sources of wealth: inheritance, acquisition, purchase, victory, ... [the rest of the verse follows].
Application, the yoga of action, and the acceptance of gifts from the virtuous as well.

This is because of the traditional teaching (*smaraṇa*). If ownership (*svatva*) were merely worldly (*laukika*), then in some cases the transfer of another’s ownership would occur through mere intention (*saṃkalpa*), and the cessation of one’s own ownership would likewise occur through mere intention. In other cases, however, the cessation of ownership occurs only through a great sin (*mahāpātaka*), not through mere intention. Consequently, it has been explained in the *Lipsā-sūtra* that the relationship between father and son, as well as the relationship between husband and wife, ceases upon the occurrence of a great sin and the like.

Now, one might object: let ownership be worldly, but let the state of being an owner (*svāmya*) be non-worldly (*alaukika*). As the author of the *Saṃgraha* said, following the principles of logic (*nyāya*): "He in whose hand something exists is not necessarily its owner."
"Does another's property not come into the hands of others through theft and the like?
Therefore, ownership must arise solely from the scriptures, and not even from experience.
Thus, the meaning is that ownership is to be understood exclusively through the scriptures, and is not accessible through any other means of valid cognition.

Not so; for when one of two things—ownership (*svāmya*) and property (*asvatva*)—which share an identical status regarding their acquisition and preservation, is established as being worldly (*laukika*), it must be understood that both are thereby established. Therefore, we consider it correct that, according to the text, the fact that property is accomplished through worldly transactions (*laukikakriyā*) is the very reason for its worldly nature, because of its invariable concomitance (*avyabhicāra*). Thus, it is proven that since property is worldly, the sequence of the transfer of ownership follows the logic of the Naiyāyikas alone, and is not based on scriptural injunction (*vācanika*). As it was stated by Vijñānayogin: "As for the traditional legal texts (*smaraṇa*) such as 'the wife, the daughters,' etc., even those are intended to remove confusion when many [claimants] are contending on the basis of their connection to the owner, by establishing the sequence of the transfer of ownership based on the principle of degrees of proximity (*pratyāsatti-tāratamya*)."

[Objection: But surely, by resorting to the logic of the wife and the daughter, the wife’s right to inherit her husband’s share would follow. If that were so, then even for wives who have not been partitioned from the estate, their right to inherit the husband’s share would follow, since the logic to be stated later—namely, "the wife is declared to be half the body"—is equally applicable. If this is argued:

Not so; for since there exists a fixed share of property for each individual among those whose wives are divided, the rule regarding the wife and daughters applies precisely there. However, in the case of those whose wives are undivided, because there is no fixed property belonging to the husband individually, it is impossible for them to take the husband’s share from the collective property; therefore, it should be understood that the rule regarding the wife and daughters pertains to the case of divided [property].

Now, if this were the case, then the wives of all brothers who have passed away without being partitioned would not be entitled to receive their shares. For it is so recorded in the Smṛti: "The wives of those [brothers] who were unpartitioned inherit that property," the implication being that this applies when all the brothers are absent.

To this it is replied: since the inheritance of wives who have not divided [the estate] is restricted by its being determined to terminate with each individual, the principle applies just as it does for those who have divided; therefore, even in the state of non-division, the wives alone are the heirs. In that regard, the opinion of Viṣṇu is that no distinction should be made between a wife who has daughters and a wife who has no daughters. In the passage beginning "the wife and the daughters" (*patnī-duhitaraḥ*), the term *patnī-duhitare* is an elliptical citation of a portion of the original. Furthermore, in the phrase "the wife and the daughters" (*patnī-duhitaraś ca*), Manu indicates the principle of relative proximity (*pratyāsatti-tāratamya*).

"The father shall take the inheritance of one who has no son, and the brothers as well. In this case, the sequence is not intended to be significant because of the use of the word "or" (*vā*). Regarding its essential meaning, the author of the *Saṃgraha* says: "The wealth of a deceased wealthy man who is destitute of a son [belongs to the father and brothers] without distinction."
By whom, then, should this now be received? This is what is being stated here.

The meaning of this is as follows: when there arises the inquiry as to who should now take the wealth of a wealthy man who has died without a primary or secondary son—after his death—the answer is that it should be taken by the father and others. Now, since there may be no relatives nearby who have rendered various kinds of assistance compared to the father and others, this rule is stated by Manu. Therefore, having recognized that secondary sons are closer than the father and others, the author of the *Saṃgraha* explained that the intent of the verse "the father shall take the property of one without a son" is "one who is devoid of all sons"; this is indeed faultless. However, because secondary sons are superior to the father and others due to their capacity for both visible and invisible (spiritual) benefit, they are more proximate than them. Likewise, even the wife, through her visible and invisible benefits and upon consideration of the *Śruti*, *Smṛti*, and other sources, is superior to the father and others and is thus more proximate than them. Consequently, the intent is to be understood as follows: it is only in the absence of the wife that Manu states, "the father shall take the property of one without a son. For this very reason, Bṛhaspati, after declaring that the wife is more proximate than others by virtue of her relationship characterized by visible and invisible benefits in the absence of secondary sons, has shown that the wife alone is entitled to share in the husband's wealth even while the father and others are still living.
In the Vedas, in the Smṛtis and Tantras, and in worldly custom,
the wise have declared that a wife is half of one's own body, sharing equally in the fruits of both merit and demerit.
For one whose wife has not passed away, half of his body still lives;
while even half a body remains alive, how could another [wife] be taken?
When paternal kinsmen— such as fathers or brothers— are present,
the wife of a deceased man who leaves no son shall take his share.

Here, by the second half-verse beginning with “half the body is considered [hers],” etc., the wife’s close proximity to the father and others in the accomplishment of both visible and invisible benefits is stated. As for the meaning of the individual words: *āmāne* means in the Veda; in such passages as “the wife is indeed half of this self,” the meaning is “half of the self’s body. *Smṛtitantre* means in the treatises on Dharma (law). [As it is said: “If a wife drinks liquor, he falls along with half his body;
for one whose half-body has fallen, no atonement is prescribed. [407]
In such passages as these, "worldly custom" (lokācāra) means a treatise on matters approved by worldly custom. [The phrase] "What wise man would abandon his wife, who consists of half his body?

and so forth, refers to action whose fruit is merit or demerit, because of the joint entitlement [of husband and wife] therein. "Of one without a son" (asutasya) means of one devoid of both primary and secondary sons. "Wife" (patnī) refers to one consecrated by a praiseworthy marriage—such as the Brāhma form—which confers eligibility for sacrifice, according to the Pāṇinian Smṛti rule: *patyur no yajñasaṃyoge* ("the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied after *pati* when joined with *yajña*"). By this, a wife purchased (*krītā*) is excluded from the term "wife" (*patnī*), since she lacks the status of a *patnī*. Thus, another Smṛti states:
But a woman who has been purchased with money is not called a wife;
she is not for rites to the gods nor for rites to the ancestors—the wise know her to be a slave.

To show that in the absence of the status of *patnī* (wife), a woman provides only visible benefit (*dṛṣṭopakārakatva*) and not invisible benefit (*adṛṣṭopakārakatva*), it is said, "they call her a slave-girl" (*dāsīm viduḥ*). The statement by the author of the *Candrikā*, "In this context, some say that one who has been consecrated by the marriage sacrament (*vivāhasaṃskṛtā*) is called a *jāyā* or *patnī*," is untenable; for the marriage sacrament does not establish the status of *patnī*. Indeed, the status of *patnī* is nothing other than the relationship between husband and wife (*patibhāryāsaṃbandha*). And that relationship consists essentially in the act of acquisition and being acquired (*ārjyārjakarūpa*). Furthermore, that [relationship] is purely worldly (*laukika*). For this very reason, the status of wife ceases upon a great sin (*mahāpātaka*) and the like; there remains only the notion of being a wife based on past status. Nor do the rules regarding mantras at the wedding produce the status of wife, because that status is established through the formal giving (*vaidhadāna*), as stated by the Teacher in the *Lipsāsūtra*. Thus they say.

That is not so; for the Guru has stated that what pertains to the wife is merely *svatva* (ownership/right) in the worldly sense, and not *patnītva* (the status of being a wife), because *svatva* and *patnītva* are distinct. He says: "She is called a *patnī* due to her connection with the sacrifice (*yajña*), and she is 'one's own' (*sva*) due to her connection with the owner. The meaning of this passage from the Guru’s work—that even in cases such as a mortal sin (*mahāpātaka*), there is a severance of *bhāryātva* (the state of being a wife)—is as follows: *bhāryātva* is indeed *svatva*, but not *patnītva*; otherwise, once penance (*prāyaścitta*) has been performed, the status of *patnītva* would not return. This is precisely the intention of the author of the *Candrikā* and others, as well-observed in the statement: "A woman consecrated through a *brāhma* or other [approved] forms of marriage is called a *jāyā* and a *patnī*. And for this reason, Bṛhaspati declares that even in the ancestral rites (*pitrya-karman*) of the husband, the wife alone takes precedence over the brother and others.
"In the absence of a son, however, the wife shall [perform the rites]; in the absence of a wife, the uterine brother.
The words "in the offering of the *piṇḍas*" are to be supplied as the ellipsis. Regarding this, Vṛddha-Manu says:
"A sonless widow, protecting the bed of her husband and remaining steadfast in her vows..."
The wife alone shall offer that funeral cake and take the entire share.

In the latter half [of the verse], the sequence of meaning (*arthakrama*) should be understood according to the sequence of the recitation (*pāṭhakrama*). The wife receives the husband’s share first, and afterwards she should offer the funeral cake (*piṇḍa*); the meaning is that while she is present, the brother or others do not. This same explanation should also be applied to the rule: "Among these, the one who offers the cake is the heir to the share; in the absence of each preceding one, each subsequent one [is so]. For it is stated there that the taking of the share is itself the cause for offering the funeral cake. "Guarding the bed" means being well-restrained. Prajāpati explains the meaning of the word "entire" (*kṛtsna*) in the phrase "she shall receive the entire share."
Having taken moving property, immovable property, gold, silver, grain, liquids, and clothing, one should cause the śrāddha for the monthly, six-monthly, and other rites to be performed.

One should honor paternal uncles, preceptors, daughters' sons, husbands, fathers-in-law, maternal uncles, as well as elders, the protectorless, and guests, by means of offerings to the ancestors (kavya) and works of public utility (pūrta).

*Ārupya* refers to tin, lead, and so forth. *Kavya* refers to food intended for the ancestors (*pitaras*). *Pūrta* refers to excavations and similar works of public utility. What is meant by this is as follows: having taken her entire share together with the immovable property, the wife—according to the wealth she has received—must accomplish the collection of religious duties (*dharmajāta*) that serve as means for the welfare of both herself and her husband, including those rites requiring wealth such as the three types of *śrāddha* and *pūrta*. As for that which was stated by Bṛhaspati:

"Whatever various kinds of property, such as inherited wealth (*ādhi*) and the like, are recorded as having been divided, the wife whose husband has died shall receive them, with the exception of immovable property. [409]

The meaning is that whatever diverse property, such as land and so forth, consisting of both immovable and movable things, is recorded as belonging to the husband, all of that the wife receives in the case of partition. Because of the mention of "partitioned," it is understood that in the case of non-partition, the brothers and others living together shall receive the wealth of the deceased sonless man; this, though already stated previously with its reasoning, is made known here again. As for the statement, "that [property] the wife [receives], excluding immovable property," this refers to a wife who has no daughters. If it were intended to apply to the wife alone [without regard to daughters], [the following would occur].
Having taken moving and stationary property, gold, base metals, grain, liquids, and clothing, one should cause the Śrāddha for the monthly, six-monthly, and other periods to be performed.

"The author of the *Candrikā* [states] that there would thus be a contradiction with the previously cited statement. Herein lies the intention of the *Candrikā*-author: when there is a concurrence between a wife who has no daughter and a wife who does have a daughter, the immovable property belongs only to the wife who has a daughter, not to the one who lacks a daughter. When the wife herself is without a daughter, then the immovable and movable property belongs to her alone and not to another, such as a mother who does have a daughter; for it has been stated that she is *bahiraṅga* (external/secondary) in comparison to the wife. Nor should it be argued that, in order to avoid this contradiction, this statement refers to a case where the wives are divided (*vibhakta-patnī*); for he himself states this very thing in order to reject such an arrangement."

"Even if she is established in virtuous conduct (*vṛtta*), a woman does not deserve immovable property (*sthāvara*) even when a share has been made [for her]. The meaning of this statement is that the entitlement to immovable property, which constitutes the maintenance of the lineage, depends upon possessing a lineage; therefore, a woman who is devoid of that [lineage] does not deserve immovable property, even if she is established in virtuous conduct and even in the case where the property has been partitioned. "When the husband has died, a woman who protects the family receives the husband's share."

For as long as life lasts, ownership over her exists in the case of giving, mortgaging, or selling. (410) "Mortgaging" means pledging as security. As for women, however, even in the state of being divided [from their husbands], they are entitled only to maintenance. A woman brought [into the household] for the purpose of sexual enjoyment is called a "woman brought for enjoyment.
But as for a woman purchased by purchase, she who was bought for the sake of sexual enjoyment by one desiring offspring—
Whether she has been taken as one's own or belongs to another, she is still designated as "woman."

The wife of another—namely, the beloved of another—is defined as the referent of the word "woman" (*yoṣit*) in the rule: "He who seizes a woman shall be made to pay the debt. Regarding such a woman, Kātyāyana states that she has no share in the inheritance: "But when the husband has died, the wife is entitled only to food and clothing;
however, she receives a share of the undivided property until her death."
The second half [of the verse] concerns the wife: even for an undivided wife, there is a share. As that same author says:
"A sonless widow, preserving the bed of her husband and remaining steadfast in her vows, may enjoy [it] until death with patience; after [her death], the heirs shall take possession."
And this should be understood to apply to fathers-in-law and others who are incapable of providing maintenance. As Bṛhaspati says:

"One should give a funeral cake (piṇḍa) every year, or a share of the field, at one's own discretion. The meaning of the word *piṇḍa* here is property sufficient for the mere means of subsistence. Nārada states the small amount of such property required for the mere means of subsistence:
A virtuous woman whose husband has died shall receive thirty-four āḍhakas and forty paṇas every year.

"Year by year" means every year. An *āḍhaka* is a quantity of grain measuring one hundred and eight less than two hundred *prasṛtis*. A *paṇa* is a *kārṣāpaṇa*; others say it is an eightieth part of a *vyāvahārika-niṣka*. Kātyāyana states that what has been given to women must be protected: "The livelihood derived from immovable property that was given to women by the father-in-law cannot be revoked by his successors once the father-in-law has died. [411]

The mention of the "father-in-law" is intended as an illustration for all those who provide maintenance; and the mention of "immovable property" is intended as an illustration for all forms of wealth. Therefore, it should be understood that even other wealth given to women for their livelihood cannot be taken back by others. Kātyāyana states an exception to this rule:
"A woman devoted to service of her elders is entitled to enjoy her allotted share;
if she does not perform such service, he may compel her to work for her food."

The phrase "having taken the allotted share" is to be understood as the ellipsis. Regarding this, Viṣṇu states the means of livelihood for supporting [the wife] for as long as one lives: "Every year, forty paṇas and twenty-four āḍhakas; or else, for as long as one lives, one hundred kārṣāpaṇas or half of that. He says the same regarding even those who commit improper acts: "For those who have transgressed the bounds of propriety, the taking of the allotted share must be performed. "Those who have transgressed the bounds" refers to unchaste women. As for their maintenance, that which was stated by Manu is as follows:
"One should apply this very rule even to women who have become outcasts (patitā)."

"Food and clothing should indeed be given to them, and they should dwell near the house. This refers to cases where the husband is the provider. Likewise, the entire collection of scriptural statements prescribing the maintenance of women should be understood as referring to wives who have not been partitioned from the estate. And as for the verse: "A sonless widow, remaining faithful to her vows, should protect the bed of her husband... [and so forth].
"Let her enjoy [the estate] until death; the heirs shall obtain it after [her passing].
Thus: "Whether immovable or movable, base metals, grain, or clothing—when the husband has died, a woman who protects the family receives the husband's share."
"The ownership over that [property] lasts as long as life for the purposes of giving, mortgaging, or selling.

[414] If it is argued: "In that case, since the father himself is one who provides visible benefit through the performance of *śrāddha* rites, he is more proximate than the daughter; therefore, in the absence of a wife, how can the daughter take the property?"—do not say so.
For it has been stated by this very [text]: "While she remains, how could another take the wealth?

Indeed, although she is separated from the father by the relationship of visible benefit (*dṛṣṭopakāra*), she is nevertheless not separated by the relationship of the body (*śarīrasambandha*); thus, in both respects, the daughter alone is foremost.
If that is so, then the occasion for the rule "the father shall take" would arise only in the absence of a daughter.

Not so; even now, there would be no occasion for him [the daughter's son]. In the absence of a daughter, the daughter's son belongs to that same category [of heirs] because he is more proximate than the father and others;
thus, "In the lineage of one who has neither sons nor grandsons, the daughter's sons, performing the cremation, shall obtain [the inheritance].
And: "But for the ancestors, the grandsons and the daughter's sons are considered fit to offer the *svadhā*."

And because of this recollection of Viṣṇu: "Thus, Dhāreśvara, Devasvāmin, Devarāta, Śrīkara, and others have stated that the collection of texts prescribing that wealth goes to the daughter refers exclusively to the *putrikā* (appointed daughter). The author of the *Candrikā* refutes that opinion. Thus says the text of the *Candrikā*: 'The opinion of Dhāreśvara, Devasvāmin, and Devarāta should be understood as discarded, being imagined through the madness of ignorance regarding their own established tenets (*pratitantrasiddhānta*).'—'Own established tenet' means one's own system. Vijñānayogīśvara also refuted it, as in the *Mitākṣarā*: 'Nor does this refer to the *putrikā*, because in the section on sons, both the *putrikā* and her son are declared to be equal to an *aurasa* (legitimate) son by the rule: "The son of an appointed daughter is equal to him. The intention of Dhāreśvara and the others is this: there are exactly ten types of secondary sons along with the *aurasa*. Since the son of an appointed daughter and the self-made son are products of one's own imagination, they do not possess the status of a son; rather, they merely have a share in the inheritance. Therefore, whether one accepts the two compounds *putrikaiva sutaḥ* ("the appointed daughter herself is the son") or *putrikāyāḥ sutaḥ* ("the son of the appointed daughter"), the son of the appointed daughter is equal to a grandson, whereas the son who is the appointed daughter herself is equal to a son. Because the wife is more closely related than even the son, the appointed daughter receives the wealth first; thereafter, the wife receives it like a son. This is the logical demonstration for the rule: "The wife, the daughters... where the word *ca* (and) is used. The plural form "daughters" is intended to include daughters who are not appointed, daughters who have been made appointed, and daughters who are the mothers of sons born from an appointed daughter. And therefore..."*

In statements such as "the wealth of a deceased wealthy man who leaves no offspring whatsoever," the term "all offspring whatsoever" (*aśeṣātmaja*) does not include the appointed daughter (*putrikā*). Therefore, for that purpose, the specific mention of the "son of an appointed daughter" (*putrikāsuta*) establishes that he is entitled to half the estate over the legitimate son (*aurasa*). Consequently, among the three types of appointed daughters, the daughter who was formally appointed (*putrikākaraṇa-duhitṛ*) is entitled to the entire property, while the other two daughters are entitled to half each. This view, held by Dhāreśvara and others, is noted here as being appropriate.

That does not hold together: in the expression "the daughter's son," it is not tenable for the word "son" (*suta*) to have a figurative sense based merely on the status of being an heir, because tradition records that in the absence of a biological son (*aurasa*), she alone has the right to perform the post-mortem rites (*aurdhvadaihika*) and other duties for the father. Furthermore, what is called "figurative sonship" is simply the state of being a non-biological son (*anaurasa*). Consequently, since her entitlement to inherit was established previously by virtue of sharing the same security and welfare as a son, enough of this excessive detail.

Some, however, argue that by the word "eva" (only) in the phrase "the wife and the daughters alone," it means that the daughters alone [inherit] when the wife is connected with the sacrifice (*yajñasaṃyogavatī*), and not any other woman; and they say that because of the word "ca" (and), the husband also [inherits]. That is not correct, for if that were the case, the wife’s right to the property would follow immediately after the daughters’, and thus there would be a contradiction with the principle stated previously. Furthermore, here, by virtue of the word "ca," in the absence of a daughter, the son of the daughter (*dauhitra*) is the heir to the wealth, as he belongs to that same category. Thus says Viṣṇu:
"In the absence of a lineage of sons and grandsons, the daughters' sons shall obtain the wealth."
"But for the ancestors, at the utterance of *svadhā*, the grandson and the daughter's son are considered [the offerers].
So also Manu:
"Whether she be appointed or not appointed, whichever son she bears who is similar [to the father]..."
"The grandson's mother is his maternal grandfather; therefore, he should offer the funeral cake (piṇḍa) and take the inheritance. Thus it is said.

In their absence, the parents—the mother and father—are the heirs to the wealth. This is because in a *dvandva* compound, the word "mother" (*mātṛ*) is placed first; and since a *dvandva* functions as a singular, it undergoes *ekaśeṣa*. Because the word "mother" situated in the analytical sentence (*vigrahavākya*) is recalled first, the sequence of meaning is understood precisely from the sequence of recitation. Even regarding the connection with the wealth, when a sequence is required, it follows the very order of perception: first the mother is the heir to the wealth, and in her absence, the father—this is understood. Furthermore, the father is common to other sons as well, whereas the mother is not common; thus, there is a greater degree of proximity (*pratyāsatti*).
Immediately thereafter, the sapinda and others shall take the wealth of each respective person.

According to this statement, the mother alone takes the property first. Because of the mother’s superior proximity to both parents, it is logical that she should take the property first; in her absence, the father becomes the heir—this is the opinion of Vijñāneśvara. However, the author of the *Candrikā* establishes that the father alone has the primary right to take the property, based on the *Viṣṇu-smṛti*: "In his [the son's] absence, it goes to the father; in his absence, it goes to the mother. Between the opinion of the *Candrikā*-author and that of Vijñānayogin, the latter alone is correct, as it is established upon the foundation of reason (*nyāyamūlatayā*). By this, the claim by Śrīkara—that the parents take the property by dividing it between them—should be understood as refuted.
In the absence of a father, the brothers are the sharers of the wealth. As Manu has said:
"The father shall take the inheritance of one who has no son, or else the brothers.
Furthermore, as stated by Dhāreśvara:
The mother shall obtain the inheritance of a son who dies without offspring;
and when the mother also has passed away, the father’s mother shall take the wealth.

According to this statement of Manu, even while the father and mother are living, if the mother has passed away, the paternal grandmother alone shall take the wealth, not the father; for wealth taken by the father passes to sons even of different castes (*vijātīya*), whereas wealth taken by the paternal grandmother passes only to those of the same caste (*sajātīya*). Vijñānayogin does not accept this view, because the taking of wealth by sons of different castes has also been stated in such passages as, "They shall have shares of four, three, two, and one," and so forth. Among brothers as well, uterine brothers (*sodara*) shall first take the property, because those of different wombs (*bhinnodara*) are more remote from the mother. In the absence of uterine brothers, those of different wombs are the sharers of the wealth. In the absence of brothers, their sons are the sharers of the wealth according to the order of the fathers, based on the rule, "The allotment of shares is according to the father. In the absence of the sons of brothers, the *gotraja*—namely the paternal grandmother, the *sapinda*s, and the *samānodaka*s—are the sharers of the wealth. Among them, the paternal grandmother is the first to receive the wealth.

Regarding the statement, "And when the mother has also passed away, the father’s mother shall take the wealth," although it follows that the paternal grandmother (pitāmahī) should take the wealth immediately after the mother, Vijñānayogin maintains that because the succession of the [paternal] father and the others down to the brother's son is fixed, there can be no insertion of anyone in the middle; furthermore, the statement "the father’s mother shall take the wealth" merely intends to establish her entitlement to inherit. Therefore, she takes the property after the son of the [paternal] father, and thus there is no contradiction. The author of the *Candrikā* does not accept this view.
And if the mother has also passed away, the father’s mother shall take the wealth.

Because of this statement regarding the order of succession, and because of the *Viṣṇu-smṛti* which states: “The wealth of one who dies without a son goes to his wife; in her absence, the mother and father shall take it; in their absence, the mother of the father, then the brothers, and then the *sapiṇḍas*,” it follows that after the mother, the paternal grandmother (*pitāmahī*) is entitled to inherit the property. Regarding this, they say that the opinion of Vijñānayogin alone is correct. In the absence of the paternal grandmother, the *sapiṇḍas* belonging to the same lineage (*gotra*), such as the paternal grandfather and others, are the heirs to the wealth; for those *sapiṇḍas* who belong to a different lineage are included under the term "kinsmen" (*bandhu*). Among them, in the absence of the father’s descendants, the paternal grandfather, the paternal uncles, and their sons are the heirs in successive order. In the absence of the paternal grandfather’s descendants, [the heirs are] his great-grandmother, the paternal grandfather, his sons, and his grandsons. In this manner, the inheritance by *sapiṇḍas* of the same lineage should be understood to extend up to the seventh degree.

"Whoever is the nearest among the *sapiṇḍas* shall take the wealth of that [deceased]," according to the traditional law (*smṛti*). In their absence, those who share the same water (*samānodaka*) are the heirs. They are to be understood as seven generations beyond the *sapiṇḍas*, or until the knowledge of birth and name ceases. As Manu says:
"The status of *sapiṇḍa* ceases with the seventh person."
"But the status of *samānodaka* ceases after the fourteenth generation;
according to some, beyond that it is called *gotra* because of the loss of memory regarding birth and name.
By this, the sequence stated by the author of the *Saṃgraha* [is established].
Even in the absence of daughters, the mother shall obtain the wealth;
likewise even when the father exists, so long as there is a line of descendants consisting of the sons of co-wives.
In the absence of such a mother, the father’s mother shall take the wealth;
even while the father exists, so too in the case of a lineage consisting of sons born of Kṣatriya wives.
Even in the absence of the paternal grandmother, the father shall obtain the wealth.

Thus, it should be understood that [this position] is refuted. Since this sequence is rooted in the logic devised by Dhāreśvara, and since it has already been refuted by Viśvarūpa and others by resorting to methods such as *adhyāhāra* (supplying ellipses), we do not refute it here; furthermore, it contradicts the logic stated previously. As for what was said by that very same author:
"If there are both uterine brothers and non-uterine brothers—these two types of brothers—then even when a non-uterine brother exists, only the uterine brothers are entitled to the inheritance."

Thus, because it is rooted in sound reasoning, that [view] is to be respected. However, other relatives are shown in another Smṛti according to the order of proximity: "The sons of one's father’s sister, the sons of one's mother’s sister, and the sons of one's maternal uncle are to be known as one's own (ātma-) relatives."
The sons of one's father’s paternal aunt, the sons of one's father’s maternal aunt,
and the sons of one's father’s maternal uncle are to be known as paternal kinsmen (pitṛbāndhava).

"The sons of one's mother's paternal aunt, the sons of one's mother's maternal aunt, and the sons of one's mother's maternal uncle are to be known as maternal relatives (mātṛbāndhava). [419] Thus it is said. In the absence of these *gotraja* (agnate) heirs, there is a connection through cremation (*daha*). In that regard, because they are more proximate (*antaraṅga*), first the self's own relatives (*ātmabāndhava*) are the heirs; in their absence, the father's relatives (*pitṛbāndhava*); and in their absence, the mother's relatives (*mātṛbāndhava*)—this sequence is to be understood. Nor should it be argued here that, because the mother is more venerable than the father, her relatives should inherit the property even before the father's relatives.

Because of the traditional teaching (smṛti) that "the mother is more venerable than the father and others," it follows that the mother alone is more worthy of honor, not the maternal relatives; thus, we consider it logical that the right to inherit the property belongs to the maternal relatives only after those of the paternal side. In their absence, the teacher (ācārya) inherits:
"That twice-born man who, having initiated a pupil, teaches him the Veda..."
They declare such a person to be a teacher who possesses the entirety [of the tradition] along with its secret mysteries.

By this, it is indicated that just like a relationship by birth (*yonisaṃbandha*), a relationship through learning (*vidyāsaṃbandha*) is also a cause for inheriting wealth. In the absence of the former, the pupil (*śiṣya*) inherits, because a relationship of learning exists even in the case of a pupil. For this very reason, Āpastamba states: “In the absence of sons, the *sapiṇḍa* who is the nearest; in his absence, the teacher (*ācārya*); in his absence, the resident pupil (*antevāsī*). By this statement, it is shown that in the phrase “in the absence of sons, the nearest,” the relationship by birth is the cause for inheriting wealth, whereas in the phrase “in his absence, the teacher,” etc., the relationship of learning is the basis for inheriting wealth. In the absence of a pupil, the fellow-student (*sabrahmacārī*) is equal to a brother. In his absence, any learned *śrotriya* Brāhmaṇa may take the property, according to the traditional teaching (*smaraṇa*) of Gautama: “Learned *śrotriyas* shall divide the estate of a childless Brāhmaṇa. This is the view of Vijñāneśvara. Bhāruci and others, however, maintain that since fellow-students are equal to brothers, the property goes to the *śrotriya* Brāhmaṇa only after the non-existence of their sons, their wives, and so forth. Asahāya and others, however, state that following the relationship by birth, due to the relationship of learning, this wealth first goes to the teacher; in his absence, to the teacher’s son; in his absence, to the teacher’s wife; in his absence, to the fellow-student; in his absence, to a virtuous *śrotriya* Brāhmaṇa; in his absence, to any *śrotriya* whatsoever; and in his absence, to any Brāhmaṇa whatsoever. As Manu says: [420] (Manu 9.186–187) *anapatyasya putrasya mātā dāyam avāpnuyāt |* *mātary api ca vṛttāyāṃ pitur mātā hared dhanam ||* *ṛṇe dhane ca sarvasmin pravibhakte yathāvidhi |* *paścād dṛśyeta yat kiṃcit tat sarvaṃ samatāṃ nayet ||* “In the case of a son who dies without offspring, the mother shall receive the inheritance. And when the mother has also passed away, the father’s mother shall take the wealth. When all debts and assets have been divided according to rule, whatever may subsequently be discovered, all that should be brought to equality. Thus he says.
"But in the absence of all [these heirs], Brāhmaṇas who are learned in the three Vedas, pure, and self-controlled shall be the heirs to the estate; thus the Dharma is not violated.
Therefore, the king must never take the property of a Brāhmaṇa.
"Because of the traditional law (smṛti) stating that 'the property of a Brāhmaṇa must never be seized by the king,' and because of the statement of Manu; it has also been said by Nārada:
'In the event of the loss of property belonging to a Brāhmaṇa, if there is no heir whatsoever...'"
"It must be given to a Brāhmaṇa alone; otherwise, the king would become a sinner.
As for that which was stated by Manu:
"But in the absence of all others, the king may take [the property] from the other castes."

Thus, the meaning is that among the castes other than Śūdras—namely the Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas—the king shall take that wealth only in the absence of heirs down to the fellow-student (*sabrahmacārin*), but not a Brāhmaṇa. However, for a Śūdra, the wealth goes to the king upon the absence of heirs down to a brother; as it is said:
"In the absence of a uterine brother of a Śūdra, the king shall obtain that wealth.

Having thus stated that the inheritance belongs primarily to the lineal descendants through the blood-relationship (*yonisambandha*), Yājñavalkya now describes the order of succession for the lineal descendants through the relationship of learning (*vidyāsambandha*).
The heirs of forest-dwellers, renunciants, and students are, in order: the preceptor, the virtuous disciple, the spiritual brother, and the fellow ascetic.

The forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*), the ascetic (*yati*), and the student (*brahmacārin*)—in their respective order and in reverse order—are the heirs to the property (*riktha*) of the teacher, the good disciple, the spiritual brother (*dharmabhrātṛ*), and the fellow-ascetic (*ekatīrthin*). There are two types of students: the temporary (*upakurvāṇa*) and the lifelong (*naiṣṭhika*). The wealth of the temporary student is taken by the mother and others; the wealth of the lifelong student is taken by the teacher, because in that case the connection through learning is weightier than the connection through blood. As for the wealth of the ascetic, the good disciples take it. The ascetic is of four kinds, distinguished as *kuṭīcaka*, *bahūdaka*, *haṃsa*, and *paramahaṃsa*. In the absence of a teacher, the wealth of the *kuṭīcaka*, *bahūdaka*, and *haṃsa* is taken by the disciple. However, for the *paramahaṃsa*, since there is no teacher, the disciple alone takes it. The wealth of the forest-dweller is taken by the spiritual brother who is a fellow-ascetic. A "fellow-ascetic" (*ekatīrthin*) is one belonging to the same stage of life (*āśrama*). A "spiritual brother" (*dharmabhrātṛ*) means one who has been accepted as a brother through being a disciple of the same preceptor. Vijñāneśvara understands this as a descriptive compound (*viśeṣaṇasamāsa*) meaning "one who is both a spiritual brother and a fellow-ascetic. As for the traditional teaching of Vasiṣṭha stating, "Those who have entered other stages of life are not entitled to shares," that is intended to mean simply that there is no connection to inheritance by one's own will.
One should accumulate wealth for the sake of a day, a month, six months, or likewise for a year; once it has been accumulated, one should spend it in the month of Āśvayuja.
Since this was stated with reference to the forest-dweller (vānaprastha),
he should at that time wear garments for the purpose of covering his private parts,
and likewise take up the various requisites for yoga as well as sandals.

This is because it was stated with reference to the *yati* (ascetic). It should be understood that this exposition of the division of property is indeed appropriate, as even for the *naiṣṭhika* (lifelong celibate), there is still a connection with clothing and other necessities for the sake of maintaining the body. On this point, the venerable Lakṣmīdhara says: "The wealth of one who has died without offspring and without a wife goes first to the wife; in her absence, to the daughter; by the use of the word 'and' (*ca*), in her absence, to the daughter's son (*dauhitra*); in his absence, the mother and father shall take it; in their absence, it goes to the brothers; in their absence, the kinsmen (*bāndhava*) shall take it in due order. First, the inheritance passes to the wife and others within the group of the self (*ātmavarga*); after that, it passes to the group of the father (*pitṛvarga*), such as the father, paternal uncle, and their sons; after that, it passes to the group of the grandfather (*pitāmahavarga*) up to the seventh degree; after that, to the *samānodaka* relatives; in their absence, to the kinsmen of the self; in their absence, to the kinsmen of the father; in their absence, to the kinsmen of the mother, ending with those learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*). This being the case, the wealth goes to the daughter immediately after the wife, and it passes to her daughters regardless of whether they have children or not. Thus, the statement "the daughters" becomes meaningful. For this very reason, the plural number in "brothers" (*bhrātaraḥ*) is also employed without regard to the distinction between brothers who have children and those who do not. For this same reason, the singular number is used in "the wife" (*patnī*). When two wives—one with children and one without—occur together, the right belongs to the one with children, not to the one without. For this reason, in the phrase "her son" (*tatsutaḥ*), when the sons of brothers both with and without children are present, the inheritance belongs only to the one with children. The same applies to subsequent cases. As for the plural in "of fellow students" (*sabrahmacāriṇām*), it is for the sake of showing respect for those living in different places, just as for those living together. And that [inheritance], which is otherwise obstructed and belongs to the daughter alone apart from the ownership of the [deceased] daughter herself, attains the status of unobstructed inheritance in the presence of a daughter's son during the stage when it would otherwise go to the daughter. By the particle "and" (*ca*), which serves to include what was not explicitly mentioned, it indicates that the daughter's son also acquires ownership at the same time. Similarly, in the phrase "so too the brothers" (*bhrātaras tathā*), the word "so" (*tathā*) is connected to the word "their sons" (*tatsuta-*) and thus follows the connection with the word "just as" (*yathā*), because of the necessary connection between the relative pronoun *yat* and the demonstrative *tat*.

And thus the logical sequence (*anvaya*) is as follows: immediately after the inheritance has gone to the father, the sons of that [father], who are denoted by the word "brothers" (*bhrātṛ*), have an unobstructed right to the inheritance. Likewise, even when his own sons exist, the inheritance remains unobstructed for them. As for what Vijñānayogin stated—"In the case of the term 'parents' (*pitarau*), by the power of the *ekaśeṣa* compound, first the wealth goes to the mother, and in her absence, it goes to the father"—that is not correct; for, like the plural number, the dual number also indicates equal primacy, and thus both possess exactly equal ownership over that property. However, Somaśekhara argues: "But because of the statement, 'A male [child] is born when the semen is in excess,' and in accordance with the Vaiṣṇava text stating that 'one should take a share corresponding to the contribution of the seed,' it is logical that such a share should be taken. This is not so. If that were the case, then since the maternal constituent persists in the paternal line up to the brothers' sons, the taking of the inheritance would occur only there, and not in the line of the great-grandfather. As Bhāruci said on the occasion of commenting on the Vaiṣṇava text [423]: "'The word *bīja* (seed) denotes the funeral cake (*piṇḍa*). Here, the intended meaning is precisely the continuity of the funeral cakes to be offered. Because of the *sāpiṇḍya* relationship of the mother with the father, and because both are mentioned, the father alone has primacy, and in his absence, the mother alone [has it]. This very intention should also be understood regarding the Vaiṣṇava text cited by the author of the *Candrikā*.

The truth of the matter here is as follows: just as sons have an unimpeded right to inherit the paternal estate by virtue of being sons, so too in the case of daughters and others, if there exists a line of male descendants (putra-santati), their ownership [of the estate] is likewise by virtue of being the son of that [daughter]. Therefore, it is said, "her son" (*tatsuta*). If it is objected: "In this context, by the word *tat* (that), only a brother who is himself sonless is referred to, and not a brother in general; thus, it appears that the son of such a brother does not possess the right to inherit without impediment," [the response is as follows:]

Not so. Since the word *bhrātṛ* (brother) is a relative term, it is understood from the word *bhrātṛ* itself that [the brother] belongs to one who has no son; however, by that word alone, there is no reference (*parāmarśa*) to a brother qualified by the specific relation of belonging to one who has no son, because the purport of the word does not extend that far. Nor should it be argued that, even as heirs to the estate, the debts incurred by him must be discharged by his brothers' sons, for if that were the case, it would contradict the general legal tradition (*smaraṇa*) stating, "The heir to the property (*rikthagrāhī*) shall pay the debt. Nor can it be said that such a position is accepted because the discharge of that debt is established by universal worldly practice; rather, their obligation to discharge that debt arises from their being heirs to his property by virtue of a prior relationship (*bhūtapūrvagatyā*). In this regard, the following statement of Viṣṇu applies: "In the absence of [heirs] ending with the daughter's son, the mother and father shall take [the property]. Thus, in the absence of those [heirs] ending with the daughter's son—implied by the particle *ca* in Yājñavalkya’s statement, "The wife and the daughters..."—the mother and father shall take the wealth in accordance with the offering of the funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*). After the succession has passed to the daughter's son, the wealth goes only to his son, not to the mother and father.

The truth of the matter here is as follows: even in a case where there is an obstacle (*sapratibandha*), the fact that the inheritance (*dāya*) remains unobstructed (*apratibandha*) despite the existence of a lineage of sons is to be understood as the intended meaning of Yājñavalkya’s statement through the use of the words "ca" (and) and "eva" (only). Based on the force of the rule, "The inheritor of the estate (*rikthagrāhī*) shall be made to pay the debt," it is logical to clear that debt by relying on actual status as an inheritor of the estate. However, ownership (*svāmya*) itself remains entirely unobstructed. Consequently, the daughter's son (*dauhitra*) possesses an unobstructed right to inherit, whereas the daughter does not. If the daughter were also to have such a right, then upon her death, the inherited property would pass to her mother and father; however, this is contrary to the consensus of all learned authorities. In the case of a daughter who lacks offspring—either because she has no children or because she was appointed as a *putrikā* (appointed daughter) but lacks a male descendant—the inheritance would, upon her death, pass either to her own daughter or to her paternal kinsmen. Yet, this too is not logical. Thus, it is recorded in the Smṛti: [The text continues with the relevant verse.]
"And they take the paternal inheritance of a daughter who has no son;
the father, brothers, sons, and others born of the same lineage (gotraja) are indeed not [the primary] kinsmen (bandhava). Thus it is said.

"Relatives" (*bāndhava*) refers to maternal uncles and so forth, as well as paternal cousins on the mother's side (*paitṛṣvaseya*) and others. Thus Viṣṇu states: "The inheritance of one who dies without offspring does not go to the relatives. The meaning of this is as follows: the property (*riktha*)—that is, the obstructed inheritance (*sapratibandho dāyaḥ*)—of women who have no offspring, or of a man who has no offspring, passes only to those of the same lineage (*sagotra*) who are born of the same caste (*jāti*). It does not, however, pass to the kinsmen (*jñātīn*) of daughters who have no offspring or whose lineages consist of appointed daughters (*putrikā*), because they do not belong to the same *gotra*. For this very reason, Hārīta says regarding the wife: "A sonless woman, preserving the bed of her husband and remaining steadfast in her vows..."
"The patient one should eat until death; the heirs shall obtain [the property] after [his passing].

In this regard, because of the Smṛti rule "of one who is sonless" (*aputrāyāḥ*), and because of the Smṛti rule "the inheritance of one without offspring does not go to relatives" (*anaptyarikthaṃ na bāndhavagāmi*), and because it is accepted that the words "sonless" (*aputra*) and "without offspring" (*anapatya*) have the same meaning, the wealth—even for a daughter accompanied by the lineage of an appointed daughter (*putrikā*)—does not go to her daughter after her, nor to that appointed daughter. For this very reason, he (Yājñavalkya) himself says: "It does not go to the appointed daughter, nor to the relatives; rather, the kinsmen of the heir of the sonless one shall take the wealth."

On this point, some say: "In the phrase 'the wife and the daughters indeed' (*patnī duhitaraś caiva*), the daughter's son (*dauhitra*) is drawn in by the word 'and' (*ca*). He is specifically determined by the restrictive particle 'indeed' (*eva*). Therefore, it is established by the practice of those learned in the three Vedas that even wealth destined for the daughter's son goes instead to the mother and father in the absence of a daughter's son; it does not go to her son. Thus, the wealth intended for the daughter, having passed to the daughter's son, looks toward him alone when his own son exists. However, there is this distinction: in the absence of all heirs down to the daughter's son, the inheritance does not pass to the daughter's son’s son; rather, because they are more closely related than he, it reverts to the mother and father."

If it is argued that, in the absence of a daughter, since there is no transmission through her, and because the transmission through the son’s daughter (*dauhitra*) is closer than the transmission through the mother and father, one should therefore resort to the mother and father immediately after the daughter—this is not so.
For the son’s daughter has a proximity even greater than that of the mother and father;
in a lineage lacking sons and grandsons, the son’s daughters shall obtain the inheritance.
But at the offering of *svadhā* for the ancestors, the grandsons and daughters' sons are considered [the ones who perform it].
Thus says the word of Viṣṇu:
"Whether she has been formally appointed or not, if she bears a son who is her equal,
by that grandson the maternal grandfather shall receive the funeral cake (piṇḍa) and he shall inherit the wealth."

Thus says the *Manu-smṛti*. Here, the phrase "or as one not formally appointed" (*akṛtā vā*) is for the sake of illustration; for it is stated that the son of a formally appointed daughter (*kṛtā putrikā*) is entitled to half a share by virtue of being a son, and thus possesses the right to inherit without obstruction. Just as the maternal grandfather becomes the grandfather of a grandson through the son of an unappointed daughter, so too does he become so through the son of an appointed daughter. By this [it is meant]: "The son of an appointed daughter must perform the *śrāddha* for his maternal grandfather according to the rule."

This view is also refuted; for since the son of an appointed daughter (*putrikā-suta*) is enumerated among sons, it follows that the term "son of an appointed daughter" refers specifically to the daughter’s own son (*pautra*). Regarding the interpretation of the intent behind these two statements from Manu and Viṣṇu, the elders disagree. They maintain that the *śrāddha* for the maternal grandfather by the daughter’s son is necessarily conditional, and unlike the *śrāddha* for one's own father, it does not occur without a specific cause. For instance, according to the traditional teaching of Viṣṇu: "He from whom one receives [wealth] should perform the *śrāddha* for him";
thus, the *śrāddha* for the maternal grandfathers must certainly be performed by the inheritor of the wealth.
A daughter's son must always perform this according to the rules for the sake of expiating the debt.

Thus, according to the Smṛti of Vyāsa, the performance of the Śrāddha for the maternal grandfather by the daughter’s son is based on his receiving the inheritance. As for that which was stated by Pulastya:
"The maternal grandfathers are traditionally held to be three, beginning with the mother’s father;
the sons of the daughters should perform their Śrāddha just as they do for their paternal ancestors."

Thus, it should be understood that this refers to the *mātāmaha-śrāddha* (ancestral rite for maternal grandfathers) as enjoined following the *pitṛ-śrāddha* (ancestral rite for paternal ancestors). As stated by Pitāmaha:
"Wherever the paternal ancestors are honored, there the maternal ancestors must also be honored. It should be performed without distinction; otherwise, one would go to hell."
Vyāsa also says:
"A twice-born man should satisfy his father and his maternal grandfather with the śrāddha;
thus he becomes free from debt to his ancestors and attains the world of the sacrificers."
Also in the Skanda Purāṇa:
"Having performed the ancestral Śrāddha for the three beginning with the father,
one should likewise perform it for the maternal grandfathers for the sake of discharging that debt."
As for what was said:
"The son of an appointed daughter (putrikā-putra) should perform [the rites] for his maternal grandfathers by rule;
furthermore, because of his connection to both [families], he should perform the funeral rites for both."

On this point, some maintain: "The son of an appointed daughter (*putrikāputra*) is indeed of two kinds: one is related through the maternal grandfather (*mātāmaha*), and the other is related through both the father and the maternal grandfather. Through the relationship with the maternal grandfather, the *śrāddha* for the maternal grandfather must be performed; through the relationship with both, the rites for both must be performed. This is the intended meaning: because the term "son of an appointed daughter" is understood as a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*), he is denoted by the word "maternal grandfather" (*mātāmaha*). However, if it is understood as a descriptive compound (*karmadhāraya*)—namely, "the son who is an appointed daughter"—then [it refers to the rule]: "The son who is born from her shall be my son."

Thus, by virtue of this technical rule (paribhāṣā), the son of an appointed daughter (putrikāputra) has a connection with his maternal grandfather, whereas the other [son] possesses a connection to both.

To this it is replied: Viṣṇu states that the daughter’s son has the same entitlement as a son regarding the *śrāddha* for his maternal grandfather: “The maternal grandfather’s *śrāddha* for the daughter’s son is without cause. “Cause” here means the taking of inheritance. The meaning is that the daughter’s son has an obligatory entitlement to perform the maternal grandfather’s *śrāddha*. On this point, Bhāruci says: “By stating ‘without cause,’ Viṣṇu implies by way of a different formulation that the daughter’s son’s agency arises when other immediate performers—such as sons and so forth—are present. Here, by the word “and so forth” (*ādi*), the wife is intended; thus, even in those rites accomplished through fire and Vedic knowledge, women have an entitlement.

"Only the wife should offer that *piṇḍa* and receive the entire share"—by the force of such scriptural statements, they have the right in that regard. And likewise Gautama says: "The daughters' sons have a permanent (*nityavat*) entitlement to the *śrāddha* for their maternal grandfather. The suffix *-vat* is used here in its own sense (i.e., as an adverbial modifier). Therefore:
"Whether she has not given birth or has given birth, whichever son she bears who is similar [to him]..."

"The grandson's son [pautrī] shall offer the funeral cake (piṇḍa) to his maternal grandfather and inherit his wealth"— this [rule] should be understood as referring to the son of a daughter who has been designated as such (putrikā), specifically concerning the wife denoted by the term *patnī* and the son of a daughter appointed as an heir (*putrikākaraṇa*).

Now, if it is argued that statements such as "whether she has been formally adopted or not" refer specifically to the *putrikā* (appointed daughter) through the word "adopted," whereas the word "not adopted" refers to daughters born of *gāndharva* and other forms of marriage—on the strength of the statement "by him, the maternal grandfather becomes the grandson of his son"—wherein both [the father and the maternal grandfather] attain the status of a grandson because the *putrikā* herself is a son and her son is a *dauhitra* (daughter's son); and since in a *gāndharva* marriage the *sapiṇḍya* and *sagotra* relationship with the maternal grandfather are not terminated, the status of "grandson" belongs to those two alone, and thus they have a mandatory entitlement to the *mātāmaha-śrāddha*, while the mere *dauhitra* does not— [Response: This is not so. For even in the case of a *gāndharva* marriage, the *sapiṇḍya* and *sagotra* relationship are indeed terminated by the birth of a son; therefore, the entitlement to the *mātāmaha-śrāddha* belongs to the *dauhitra* alone, just as it does for the son of a *putrikā*. Furthermore, the mention of "whether she has been adopted or not" is intended to include all types of daughters, not solely the *putrikā*. Moreover, the rule regarding the *mātāmaha-śrāddha* applies to the *dauhitra* regardless of whether he was born of a *putrikā* or otherwise. Thus, the entitlement is established for the *dauhitra* in every case.

Not so. Since the taking of wealth is based on the wife—as seen in the rule, "one should offer the funeral cake and take the wealth"—and since the term *patnī* (wife) indicates a connection with Vedic sacrifice (*yajña-saṃyoga*), thereby excluding women married through the Gāndharva and other such forms of marriage, the sons of her grandsons can only very distantly claim the wealth derived from the wife. Furthermore, by the force of the term *pautrī* (daughter's son), even in the case of the son of a daughter born of a Gāndharva or similar marriage, there is no status as a *dauhitra* (daughter's son); rather, that designation is merely figurative (*upacāra*). Therefore, what was stated previously is indeed correct.

Now, if it is argued that there is a contradiction between these two Vaiṣṇava statements—namely, "He from whom one receives [wealth] should perform a śrāddha for him," and "The maternal grandfather’s śrāddha by a daughter’s son is without cause"—then:

Not so. Here the opinion of the venerable Bhāruci remains established: “Whosoever is entitled to perform the rite, from whomsoever he may take the wealth—with that combined property, acting as his representative for that purpose, he should perform the rite for him. This is the underlying principle: in cases where there are many sons or many daughters’ sons, regarding the performance of the *navaśrāddha* and *ṣoḍaśaśrāddha* rites among the funeral ceremonies (*aurdhvadaihika*) for a father or maternal grandfather, the authority does not belong to many, but to one alone; this is what was stated by Bhāruci based on the force of the context (*prakaraṇasāmarthya*), which should be understood. Someśvara, however, says: “By the denotative power of the statement itself, setting aside the context, the rule ‘whoever takes [the wealth] from whom, he shall perform the *śrāddha* for him’ refers to an heir (*rikthagrāhin*) other than a son or a daughter’s son. And this was stated immediately thereafter by Viṣṇu: “The sixteen *śrāddhas* should be performed by one capable person alone out of the extracted wealth. The mention of the sixteen *śrāddhas* is indicative of the *navaśrāddhas* as well. Thus says Gautama: “One should not perform the *navaśrāddha* or the *ṣoḍaśaśrāddha* with the combined wealth”; here, the word *ca* (and) includes the *parivyayaṇa* rite. By the word *samudita* (combined), it is known that the entitlement belongs to one alone and not to others. In Viṣṇu’s statement, the word *śakta* (capable) implies both capacity and entitlement. Thus the meaning is this: the word *eka* (one) denotes the principal; the principal is the eldest, and if he is the one entitled, he alone is the rightful performer. Otherwise, the meaning is established by the immediately following rule. The word *śakta* means one who is physically robust. Among the daughters’ sons, he alone is the one entitled.
