Hence, this is not a case of "loss of essential nature" (*svarūpahāni*), which refers to the destruction of the object itself. Therefore, the objection is refuted. Furthermore, the term "loss" (*hāni*) is used

Not so; for in the expression "the loss of land" (*bhūmer hāniḥ*), since the genitive case is prescribed in the sense of the object (*karman*), the meaning of the sentence is established as "twenty-year possession destroys the land. In the case of "ten-year possession destroys wealth," the destruction of its very nature (*svarūpahāni*) alone is stated.
Now, one might object:
"The king should conduct legal proceedings by means of the truth, having set aside deception" [Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.1].

If it is argued that logic (*nyāya*) must be applied solely by following the truth (*tattva*), this is not so. In this context, *chala* (quibble) is intended to be non-essential (*atattvātmaka*), and not essential (*tattvātmaka*). For we observe the settlement of legal disputes (*vyavahāra-nirṇaya*) by resorting to quibbles that are essentially true. Thus it has been said: "The two-fold movement [of speech] is illustrated in accordance with both factual and quibbled [arguments]."
Thus, resorting to equivocation (*chala*) has been stated as one possible course for legal procedure (*vyavahāra*). Otherwise:
"Dharma, legal procedure, custom, and royal edict—this four-legged legal procedure consists of these, each subsequent one subverting the preceding."

By this *smṛti* [text], one should prevent the subversion of *dharma* by subsequent practices (*vyavahāra*), customs (*caritra*), and royal decrees (*rājaśāsana*) which are based on the pursuit of quibbling (*chala*). If this pursuit of quibbling were considered real, it would result in the lack of authority for the authors of the *smṛtis*. Therefore, in the phrase "having set aside quibbling, [one should decide] by means of the truth" (*bhūtena*), it should be understood that the mention of "quibbling" refers specifically to quibbling that is unreal in nature. For this very reason, the author of the *Candrikā* and Vijñānayogin state: "If he denies [the claim], he shall pay when proven; if he is proven only in part, [he shall pay for that part]."

Thus, on the occasion of explaining that statement, it was said that one must resort to *chala* (quibble) here. Vijñānayogin also, by stating that "in disputes concerning immovable property, one should avoid ordeals," thereby asserting that there is no ordeal in matters of possession (*avaṣṭambha*), and by stating that "even in the case of 'the land [is lost] to him who sees it and does not speak,'" there is a loss of the fruit [of ownership], has accepted a decision based on *chala*; this has been cited merely as an illustration.

Regarding this, some say: "If it is asked, 'How can the performance of separate actions and the practice of separate religious duties for ten years—given the absence of any one of the causes of ownership such as inheritance, purchase, partition, or acquisition, and the consequent absence of a cause for ownership—constitute the production of ownership for a person who acts separately and follows separate duties?'"

It is said: ownership is understood from the statement, "divided from the paternal wealth. For instance—it was stated previously that what is called "partition" (vibhāga) is the establishment of each individual among multiple owners over property that was previously a collective whole; and this is understood from the scriptural injunction. As it is said: "If the pledge is not released when the debt has doubled, the pledge shall perish [and become the property of the creditor]."

Thus, regarding this point, Vijñānayogin stated that there is a scriptural cessation of one's own ownership and the acquisition of another's ownership; likewise, the author of the *Candrikā*, asserting that there is no partition according to the *Chāndogya* [text], stated that there is a scriptural acquisition of ownership.

Now, one might argue: "In the *Candrikā*, regarding the rule that 'the pledge is lost when it has doubled,' the author accepts that the pledge may end in exchange (vinimaya), citing the example of sesame seeds and so forth; he states that the fact that such an exchange causes the transfer of ownership (*svatva*) is established by worldly usage (*lokasiddha*). Therefore, here too, based on worldly usage, let the acceptance of a thing—even if it is based on indifference or for one's own benefit—be considered a cause of ownership. This must be rejected, as the answer has already been given by the very verse: "Of land, to one who looks on and does not speak" (*paśyato ’bruvato bhūmeḥ*). Furthermore, even in that case, the *Candrikā*-author himself stated previously that the conclusion must be either that the transfer ends in a formal gift (*vācanika-dāna*) or that the exchange ends in a purchase, since the substance exchanged serves as the price of a sale. It was also stated during the commentary on the rule "the pledge is lost," etc., that what is called the "formal nature" (*vācanikatva*) of ownership is its technical or conventional nature (*pāribhāṣikatva*). However, that technical nature cannot be asserted here, because the person remained silent for the duration of years and seasons. Moreover, the meaning of the *Candrikā* passage—that "in reality (*paramārthataḥ*)" there is no taking of an inheritance—is this: "In reality" means according to the actual state of things (*vastuvṛttyā*). "Taking of an inheritance" means partition (*vibhāga*). Even in the absence of that, the brothers are indeed already divided from the paternal wealth. This is the underlying intention: ownership is simply the fitness for disposal at will (*yatheṣṭa-viniyoga-arhatva*), and that is established by birth alone. Partition arises only when there exist the various causal factors (*kāraka-hetu*)—such as mutual agency, witnesshood, suretyship, giving and receiving, buying and selling, partnership, and the discovery of treasure—and so forth. This is because these factors are accepted as indicators (*jñāpaka*) precisely by virtue of being causal agents (*kāraka*). [446]
Divided brothers may perform [the rites] together, but not those who are undivided from one another.

Thus, those [signs] which are prohibited for those who have not divided their property indicate that a division has been accomplished. Just as the "concomitants to be established by the second" (*dvaitīyīkasādhyānubandha*) produce a distinction in the scriptures and thereby serve as indicators of difference—being regarded by the Mīmāṃsakas as "causal factors" (*kārakahetu*)—so too should it be understood here. In this case, ownership (*svatva*) arises by birth alone among brothers; nevertheless, because there is an absence of a causal factor for division until the end of ten years, once the status of those grounds of support as causes of division is established, the division of ownership itself becomes manifest as established. This is the opinion of the author of the *Candrikā*, which has been restated here as a worthy view. And thus, regarding the use of the word "api" (even/also) by the author, his intention is that when those indicative signs (*liṅga*) are present, a partition must necessarily exist.

As for what was stated by the author of the *Candrikā*—namely, that through the series of texts beginning with "within ten years," etc., he described the capacity and incapacity of physical signs (*liṅga*) on the grounds that, in case of doubt regarding partition, no divine ordeal (*divya*) may be employed and thus a partition must be made again—that is incorrect. For even within ten years, the capacity of physical signs is equal to that of written evidence and witnesses; however, the intent is simply this: because physical signs are more powerful after ten years, there is no need for them even when written evidence and witnesses exist. As for the non-employment of divine ordeals, it is based on the scriptural injunction, since Viṣṇu records: "In the absence of all [other means], a partition must be made again. This refers to the absence of all indicators such as written documents and causal factors. Someśvara and others maintain that the word "partition" (in this context) is intended to mean that when brothers are incapable or impoverished, something should be given according to their own will, just like the partition of a wife's property.

That is not so; for if everything were non-existent, there would be no entry into the divine [law], and since one’s own preferred position would likewise not enter [the discussion], Bhāruci says that the partition must be made as purely [as possible]. This very position is correct. However, some state the intention of Someśvara and others as follows: "When the doubt regarding the partition has been removed, the partition being established, they say that brothers who have gone abroad are entitled to whatever may be given"—thus all is faultless. These two views, which are worthy of the author of the *Candrikā*’s approval, have been restated here. [447]
If they live for ten years with separate religious duties and separate activities,
those brothers should also be known as divided from the paternal wealth.

By this [statement], it is established that in the absence of physical property (*dravya*), a division of religious duties (*dharma*) must be made for those who are utterly destitute, based on such Smṛti texts as: "In a division, there shall be an increase in merit" (*vibhāge dharmavṛddhiḥ syāt*). Therefore, those who have performed separate religious acts and separate rites for up to ten years without conflict with the paternal estate are indeed considered divided; for it has been stated by Bhāruci that a division of religious duties can be undertaken by one person alone even without the consent of others. It has also been stated at the very beginning of this section that such a case is indeed denotable by the term "division. Furthermore, it has been stated that heirs have no claim over property acquired without conflict with the paternal estate. Consequently, it should be understood that even when there exists property acquired without conflict with the paternal estate, because that property is indivisible, the "division" here remains restricted to the division of religious duties. The ablative case in the phrase *paitṛkād dhanāt* ("from the paternal wealth") is used in the sense of an elided gerund (*lyablope*).

In this regard, the essential meaning of Bhāruci’s opinion is as follows: regarding the phrase "they should live for ten years," because the ablative case is employed here through the elision of a verbal suffix (*lyap*), those who have remained separated from their paternal property for up to ten years—whatever they subsequently acquire through friendship and so forth is non-partible; however, what is acquired through friendship and so forth within the ten-year period is indeed partible. It is established by the logic of *kaimutika-nyāya* (the principle of "how much more so") that what one has personally earned during the state of non-separation through friendship and so forth is partible. As Viṣṇu says: "That which is not paternal, that which is received from the womb, that which is obtained through religious duty, that which is obtained through friendship, that which is obtained through learning, and that which is accidental—all this is partible until ten years [have passed]; after that, everything is partible. Regarding this, Bhāruci says: "Not paternal" (*apitrya*) means there is no paternal wealth present. This is an adjective qualifying the following three. "From the womb" (*gārbha*) refers to a woman's property. "Religious duty" (*dharma*) refers to sacrifices, charitable works, and the like. "Friendship" (*maitra*) refers to what is obtained from a friend. "Learning" (*vaidya*) refers to what is obtained from knowledge. "Accidental" (*ākasmika*) refers to what is obtained unexpectedly, such as through gifts and so forth. Among these five types of property, the latter three are non-partible because they were not divided when there was no division of religious duties. They remain non-partible even when there exists a division of religious duties in the form of remaining together for a period of ten years. The intention here is that the phrase "until ten years" is an indicative mark (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the absence of a division of religious duties. Nor is this a scriptural statement [of Viṣṇu].
Conciliation, subterfuge, and division—when equal in strength, these may be employed for up to ten days; when unequal, they should be used for no more than nine years.

It should not be said that, according to the statement of Bharadvāja—which teaches the cessation of unequal division (viṣamavibhāga) up until nine years—the unequal division does not cease after nine years; for this statement does not have that as its purpose. To explain: this statement was made in the context of discussing doubts regarding partition. Furthermore, the force of the words themselves appears to indicate exactly that: "Brothers who have been divided [should] live for ten years with separate duties and separate activities... (Baudhāyanadharmasūtra 2.2.1.10).

Thus, it has been established that residing for a period of ten years, characterized by the attributes of having distinct properties and distinct activities, is the cause of partition. This would be contradicted if the intent were merely to establish an unequal partition; for, by the force of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) in the phrase "the brothers are divided," the indicated (*liṅgin*), namely partition itself, would be contradicted, since the marks of partition cannot result in the transfer of ownership to another. Furthermore, because a legal proceeding may be valid even when following a figurative interpretation (*chala*), one must therefore resort to the ablative case alone in that context, understood as being used where a verbal suffix (*lyap*) has been elided.

That is not so, because it has been stated that the grounds for partition possess the nature of causal factors (*kāraka*) and thus have the capacity to produce partition; furthermore, ownership by sons is established by their very birth, and the pursuit of a quibble regarding its essential nature (*tattva*) is cited as being logically improper.

Thus, this is the summary here: when there is doubt regarding partition, the determination is made in some cases by a written document, in some by witnesses, in some by cognate kinsmen (*jñāti*), in some by agnates (*bandhu*), and in some by a combination of these. In the absence of these, the determination is made by evidentiary causes (*kāraka-hetu*). When both types are present, the evidentiary cause is indeed the primary rule. However, by means of indicative causes (*jñāpaka-hetu*), the determination is made only by those that have been in effect for up to ten years, and not by others. This implies that for indicative causes that have remained in effect for up to ten years, the determination is made by evidentiary causes themselves, as they have attained the nature of evidentiary causes. But this much is the distinction: since partition is established immediately by evidentiary causes through their very nature, the determination by them occurs at once; whereas for those evidentiary causes that function as indicative causes, the period is up to ten years. In the total absence of all these, since no divine ordeal (*divya*) is to be employed, the partition must be carried out in its pure form. Even when the partition is established by the aforementioned causes, something should be given to the litigating brothers; thus, everything is faultless.

Thus ends the section on the division of inheritance within the Legal Proceedings (Vyavahāra) book of the *Sarasvatīvilāsa*, a compendium of Smṛti compiled by the illustrious Pratāparudra Mahādeva Mahārāja.
Now, the rule for the word-element called *sāhasa* is stated.

Previously, the consideration of what is to be given and what is not to be given was established within the thirteen titles of law (*vivādapada*). As Viṣṇu stated: "Legal procedure (*vyavahāra*) has two origins. It originates in two ways: by being rooted in what is to be given (*deya*) and by being rooted in punishment (*daṇḍa*). Thus, the phrase "having two origins" describes the two causes of legal procedure. Likewise, the *Gautama-sūtra* states: "It has two origins and two outcomes. The word "legal procedure" is understood to follow here. Regarding this, the Commentator (*Nibandhanakāra*) explains that the meaning of "having two origins" is that the section from the non-payment of debt (*ṛṇādāna*) up to the partition of inheritance (*dāyavibhāga*) is rooted in what is to be given, while the fivefold group beginning with violence (*sāhasa*) is rooted in punishment. Even though [this was] stated by Manu and others...
Of these, the first is the non-payment of debt; then the deposit, sale without ownership, partnership, and the non-delivery of what has been given.
Non-payment of wages, breach of contract,
rescission of purchase and sale, and disputes between an owner and a herdsman;
The law concerning boundary disputes, verbal assault, and physical assault;
theft, violence, and the abduction of women.
The wise know these eighteen points in legal procedure.

Thus, the titles of legal procedure (*vyavahārapada*) have been stated in their sequential order in the manner described. Here, after verbal abuse, physical assault, and adultery, the partition of inheritance (*dāyavibhāga*) follows in sequence. However, the author of the *Nibandhana* has stated that the thirteenth title of dispute is "inheritance" (*dāya*). There is a great contradiction between these two views. It is resolved as follows: thus it was stated by Nārada: "Recovery of debts, deposits, partnerships, resumption of what has been given, and breach of service after entering into a contract;"
Non-payment of wages, as well as sale without ownership, non-delivery after purchase, and likewise rescission of a gift made out of affection;
Non-performance of agreements, disputes, and the son born of the field; the relationship between husband and wife, partition of inheritance, and then violence.
"Likewise, verbal abuse, as well as physical assault, gambling, and miscellaneous matters have been declared... [thus it is said].

The statement of the commentator follows the words of Nārada; therefore, the Gautama-sūtra, which is to be explained by him, likewise conforms to the words of Nārada. It is in accordance with this very [view] that we have also stated the arrangement (*saṃgati*) of the titles of law (*vivādapada*). And thus, the word "atha" (now) in the phrase "atha sāhasam" (now, violence) is employed to indicate that the section from the non-payment of debt (*ṛṇādāna*) up to the partition of inheritance (*dāyavibhāga*) is based on what is to be given (*deya*), whereas the pentad beginning with violence (*sāhasa*) is based on punishment (*daṇḍa*). Consequently, the arrangement is established as the occasion for explaining punishment immediately after the explanation of what is to be given. Furthermore, although there is no mutual distinction between verbal abuse (*vākpāruṣya*) and physical assault (*daṇḍapāruṣya*), they are treated separately here for the purpose of distinguishing between the smallness and greatness of their respective punishments. Thus, the arrangement of all three sections has indeed been stated. As for what was said by Vijñānayogin—that there is no mutual arrangement among the titles of law—that should be understood as being directed against him.
Kātyāyana states:
"An act that is performed impulsively is declared to be *sāhasa* (an act of violence).
Nārada expresses this very same point.
"Whatever action is performed impulsively by those arrogant of their strength, that is called *sāhasa* (violence); here, *saha* is said to mean strength.
Thus, the meaning is that the seizure of common property or the property of another, when carried out by relying on force, is *sāhasa*. For this very reason, Yājñavalkya says:
“Sāhasa is defined as the forcible seizure of common property.
Viṣṇu states that this is of four kinds: “Violating another’s wife, theft, both [forms of] harshness, and injury to others. Bṛhaspati, however, says:
“The abduction of a human being, theft, violating another’s wife,” and so forth.
Harshness and both [of these] constitute the fourfold category of violence (sāhasa).

It should be understood that the sequence of these two statements is not intended [to be definitive], as there is no purpose for it. As for what was stated by Śaṅkha and Likhita: "Theft, assault, injury, and violence are denoted by the term *sāhasa*," one should understand therein that since sexual intercourse with women (*strīsaṃgrahaṇa*) does not exceed the nature of theft, both sexual misconduct and theft are subsumed under the term "theft" (*caurya*). Furthermore, its definition is separately stated in the legal treatises as being threefold: first, middling, and likewise highest.

The first form of *sāhasa* (violence) is recorded as the destruction or seizure of fruits, roots, water, and so forth, as well as the implements of agriculture, by those who are incapable [of paying compensation] and the like.
Regarding clothing, livestock, food, drink, and household utensils—
by this very same method, the middle amercement is prescribed.
Malice through the use of poison, weapons, and the like; violating another's wife;
and whatever else obstructs life—this is recorded as the highest degree of violence (uttama-sāhasa).
For that [first type of person], the application of punishment is seen by those learned in the treatises as ten *aparādhas*; for the middle [type], it is five hundred *aparādhas*.
[453] For the highest degree of violence, a fine of more than one thousand [paṇas] is prescribed;
or else, death, confiscation of all property, or banishment from the city.
In the case of the highest violence, the punishment declared is the cutting off of that limb.

The meaning is as follows: where a fine of one thousand and eighty *daṇḍas* is prescribed, that is designated as the highest amercement (*uttamasāhasa*). A fine amounting to five hundred and forty [paṇas] is designated as the middle amercement (*madhyamasāhasa*). A fine amounting to two hundred and seventy [paṇas] is designated as the lowest amercement (*adhamasāhasa*). And so says Yājñavalkya: "A fine of one thousand and eighty paṇas is the highest amercement;
half of that is declared the middle, and half of that is recorded as the lowest."
Some explain this statement as follows:
"The highest fine (uttamasāhasa) consists of a penalty of eighty-one thousand paṇas."

Thus, this statement prescribes a punishment (*daṇḍa*) and does not prescribe a technical name (*saṃjñā*). According to this view, the words "in the case of the highest *sāhasa*" (*uttamasāhase*) are in the locative case. That which has a thousand *paṇas* as its measure is called *sāhasra*. That which exists together with eighty is *sāśīti*. The meaning is that in the case of the highest *sāhasa*, the punishment is one thousand and eighty *paṇas*. *Uttamasāhasa* is the *sāhasa* pertaining to the highest category; *madhyamasāhasa* is the *sāhasa* pertaining to the middle category; and *adhamasāhasa* is the *sāhasa* pertaining to the lowest category. Its other name is *prathamasāhasa*. And so, the meaning is as follows:

The seizure of fields and other property belonging to a superior person, as well as the seizure of property belonging to a middling person, and likewise the seizure of property belonging to an inferior person; similarly, the seizure of a superior object such as a horse, gold, or jewels, a middling object such as a buffalo, rice, or wheat, and the seizure of an inferior object such as an earthen pot—these constitute, respectively, what is designated as "highest," "middling," and "lowest" [theft]. This will be explained further on: "The punishment is the highest *sāhasa*," and so forth. They say that there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between the terms, where the word [denoting the fine] is used figuratively with respect to hundreds. [454] Regarding the first case, "ten times more" (*daśāpara*) refers to minor objects; for those minor objects whose value is ten *āparas*, the punishment ranges from double their value up to eightfold, sixteenfold, thirty-twofold, and sixty-fourfold. In the case of minor objects, the rule of determination regarding the *māṣa* value applies to Śūdras, Vaiśyas, Kṣatriyas, Brāhmaṇas, and ascetics. The same should be inferred for the case of "a hundred times more" (*śatāpara*). In the case of an object worth a thousand, the cutting off of limbs and so forth should be applied.

In this context, since no specific [substance] is mentioned for the number one hundred and so forth—as in the case of "eighty thousand *paṇas* and so on"—and because it would be inappropriate to assume a price for earthenware vessels and the like based on the action [of breaking them] by assigning such a number, an eighth part of a *paṇa*, namely a *māṣa* or a *kākaṇikā*, is to be assumed. It is stated in the *Divyamātṛkā* that in this section on legal procedure (*vyavahārakāṇḍa*), a *paṇa* measured as eight *māṣas* must be accepted; therefore, this should be understood.
Regarding this, Yājñavalkya states the specific rule:
"The punishment of reproach (*dhig-daṇḍa*), or the punishment of speech (*vāk-daṇḍa*), the punishment of wealth (*dhanadaṇḍa*), and likewise the punishment of death (*vadha*)."
"Indeed, they should be applied here either individually or collectively, according to the nature of the offense.

The meaning of this is as follows: the *dhig-daṇḍa* (punishment of reproach) consists of censuring [the offender] in one's mind by saying "shame! (*dhik*). The *vāk-daṇḍa* (punishment of speech), however, consists of harsh words. The *dhana-daṇḍa* (punishment of wealth) is well known. And the *vadha-daṇḍa* (punishment of corporal punishment) extends up to the separation of the body from life. These four types of punishments—either individually (*vyasta*), one by one, or collectively (*samasta*), two, three, or all four—should be applied according to the gravity of the offense. Manu states the sequence for their application: "One should first apply the punishment of reproach, and immediately after that, the punishment of speech."
"The third is the fine of property, and after that, the punishment of death.
Since it is impossible to prescribe such a specific rule for punishment for every individual case, Yājñavalkya states the general method for doing so:
"Having ascertained the offense, the place, the time, and also the strength [of the offender]..."
[455] He should inflict punishment upon those deserving of punishment according to their age, their actions, and their wealth.

Having ascertained the offense, punishment should be applied to those deserving of it according to that offense. As Viṣṇu has stated: "In the case of seizing goods of superior, middling, or inferior quality, the punishment shall be in accordance with their value. The meaning of this has been clarified by Manu, as follows: "Gold, gems, silk, women, men, elephants, horses, and the property of gods, Brahmins, and kings—this is to be known as 'superior' (dravya)."
But items of middling value are as follows: clothing, excluding silk; likewise animals, excluding cows;
iron, excluding gold; and likewise rice.
"The word *vrīhi* (rice) is indicative of barley, wheat, and so forth. Earthenware vessels, seats, beds, bones, wood, skins, grass, and the like,
as well as camp-food and prepared food, are declared to be minor items (*kṣudradravya*)."
Thus, the general rule is that one should be punished for the three types of objects according to the first, middle, and lowest fines, as in the case of the *sāhasa* offenses. Manu himself says:
"Whatever punishment has been declared by the wise for the three types of *sāhasa* offenses, that same punishment applies to theft as well, according to the sequence of the three types of objects."

Because the punishment for *sāhasa* (violence) and *steya* (theft) is identical, they constitute a single category; nevertheless, the secret point is that even according to that view, the extension of the punishment is not contradictory because they are mentioned separately. Viṣṇu, however, states a specific distinction even by way of the inclusion of caste: "The punishment has been declared; for learned Vaiśyas, Kṣatriyas, and Brāhmaṇas, the offenses in cases of theft are double the subsequent ones. This is the meaning: whatever punishment has been declared for a particular theft, if the theft is committed by a Śūdra, it should be made eightfold; if the theft is committed by a Vaiśya, sixteenfold; if the theft is committed by a Kṣatriya, thirty-twofold; and if the theft is committed by a Brāhmaṇa, sixty-fourfold punishment should be imposed. In this manner, the punishment should be inferred for thefts committed by Vaiśyas, Śūdras, and others.
For a Brahmin, it may be a hundredfold, or even a full hundred times more.

This is because of the recollection of Viṣṇu. One should prescribe double for those of lower status, since he himself has stated: "One should prescribe double for one who is base. The author of the *Nibandhana* explains that "base" refers to [inferiority] by birth, conduct, or wealth. It should not be argued that, just as in the *Divyamātṛkā*, the rule regarding the performance of ordeals (*samayakriyā*) is prescribed for a Vaiśya at two-fold value, for a Kṣatriya at three-fold, and for a Brāhmaṇa at four-fold—thus indicating a gradation in the performance of ordeals according to the numbers one, two, three, and four for Śūdras, Vaiśyas, Kṣatriyas, and Brāhmaṇas respectively—so too here the determination of punishment should be made by calculating an eighth, sixteenth, twenty-fourth, or thirty-second part. This is because these two scriptural injunctions—one prescribing punishments and the other prescribing ordeals—are rooted in the Veda and lack a basis in mere logic; therefore, this gradation is expressly textual (*vācanika*). Regarding this, Viṣṇu states a specific rule: "For stealing ten *kumbhīs* of grain, one should be made to pay eleven times the amount. The author of the *Candrikā* notes that a *kumbhī* is synonymous with a *droṇa* and a *khārī*. After making him pay that wealth eleven times over for the theft of twice that amount, punishments such as mutilation of limbs or death should be applied as appropriate. Regarding this, Manu states a specific rule: [Manu 8.320–321] "For stealing more than ten *kumbhīs* of grain, the thief shall be punished with corporal punishment. For stealing more than a hundred, he shall be put to death. For stealing gold, silver, or precious gems exceeding twenty *kṛṣṇalas*, the thief shall be punished with the highest amercement. [Manu 8.326] "For stealing men, women, or fields, the thief shall be punished with the highest amercement; likewise for stealing large animals such as elephants, horses, and camels. [Manu 8.327] "For stealing small animals, cotton, salt, or cooked food, the thief shall be fined eleven times the value. [Manu 8.328] "For stealing thread, wool, cow-milk, curd, ghee, oil, sugarcane, molasses, or honey, the fine shall be five times the value. [Manu 8.329] "For stealing vegetables, roots, fruits, flowers, firewood, water, or grass, the fine shall be one *māṣa*. [Manu 8.330] "In the case of stealing articles used for household purposes, or for religious rites, or for medicinal purposes, the king shall determine the fine after considering the time and the purpose. [Manu 8.331] "For stealing goods belonging to a temple, or for stealing a deposit, or for stealing a Brāhmaṇa's property, the thief shall be punished with the highest amercement. [Manu 8.332] "For stealing a Brāhmaṇa's clothes, a vehicle, a bed, a seat, flowers, roots, or fruits, the fine shall be two *māṣas*. [Manu 8.333] "For stealing meat, fish, birds, clarified butter, milk, curd, or oil, the fine shall be five *māṣas*. [Manu 8.334] "For stealing perfumes, medicinal herbs, dyestuffs, or fibers, the fine shall be one hundred *paṇas*. [Manu 8.335] "For stealing gems, pearls, coral, or conch-shells, the fine shall be five hundred *paṇas*. [Manu 8.336] "For stealing goods of little value, or for stealing large quantities of base metals, the thief shall be made to pay eleven times their value. [Manu 8.337] "For stealing goods of great value, the thief shall be punished with the highest amercement; for stealing human beings, he shall be put to death. [Manu 8.338] "For stealing a Brāhmaṇa's property, even if it be of small value, the thief shall be punished with the highest amercement; for stealing a Śūdra's property, he shall be fined one hundred *paṇas*. [Manu 8.339] "For stealing a Brāhmaṇa's clothes, a vehicle, a bed, a seat, flowers, roots, or fruits, the fine shall be two *māṣas*. [Manu 8.340] "For stealing meat, fish, birds, clarified butter, milk, curd, or oil, the fine shall be five *māṣas*. [Manu 8.341] "For stealing perfumes, medicinal herbs, dyestuffs, or fibers, the fine shall be one hundred *paṇas*. [Manu 8.342] "For stealing gems, pearls, coral, or conch-shells, the fine shall be five hundred *paṇas*. [Manu 8.343] "For stealing goods of little value, or for stealing large quantities of base metals, the thief shall be made to pay eleven times their value. [Manu 8.344] "For stealing goods of great value, the thief shall be punished with the highest amercement; for stealing human beings, he shall be put to death. [Manu 8.345] "For stealing a Brāhmaṇa's property, even if it be of small value, the thief shall be punished with the highest amercement; for stealing a Śūdra's property, he shall be fined one hundred *paṇas*. [Manu 8.346] "For stealing a Brāhmaṇa's clothes, a vehicle, a bed, a seat, flowers, roots, or fruits, the fine shall be two *māṣas*. [Manu 8.347] "For stealing meat, fish, birds, clarified butter, milk, curd, or oil, the fine shall be five *māṣas*. [Manu 8.348] "For stealing perfumes, medicinal herbs, dyestuffs, or fibers, the fine shall be one hundred *paṇas*. [Manu 8.349] "For stealing gems, pearls, coral, or conch-shells, the fine shall be five hundred *paṇas*. [Manu 8.350] "For stealing goods of little value, or for stealing large quantities of base metals, the thief shall be made to pay eleven times their value. [Manu 8.351] "For stealing goods of great value, the thief shall be punished with the highest amercement; for stealing human beings, he shall be put to death. [Manu 8.352] "For stealing a Brāhmaṇa's property, even if it be of small value, the thief shall be punished with the highest amercement; for stealing a Śūdra's property, he shall be fined one hundred *paṇas*. [Manu 8.353] "For stealing a Brāhmaṇa's clothes, a vehicle, a bed, a seat, flowers, roots, or fruits, the fine shall be two *māṣas*. [Manu 8.354] "For stealing meat, fish, birds, clarified butter, milk, curd, or oil, the fine shall be five *māṣas*. [Manu 8.355] "For stealing perfumes, medicinal herbs, dyestuffs, or fibers, the fine shall be one hundred *paṇas*. [Manu 8.356] "For stealing gems, pearls, coral, or conch-shells, the fine shall be five hundred *paṇas*. [Manu 8.357] "For stealing goods of little value, or for stealing large quantities of base metals, the thief shall be made to pay eleven times their value. [Manu 8.358] "For stealing goods of great value, the thief shall be punished with the highest amercement; for stealing human beings, he shall be put to death. [Manu 8.359] "For stealing a Brāhmaṇa's property, even if it be of small value,
One deserves death for the theft of men of noble birth, and especially women, as well as for the theft of all kinds of jewels.
Regarding those of noble birth, that same author states a different range of punishment:
"For one who abducts a man, the punishment declared is the highest amercement;
for the abduction of a woman, however, it is the forfeiture of all property; but for one who abducts a maiden, there is the death penalty."
For minor articles, however, those whose value is less than one *māṣa*, the fine shall be five times their value. As Nārada has said:
"In the case of wooden vessels, grass, and the like, as well as earthenware, bamboo, articles made of bamboo, sinews, bones, and skins..."
For the theft of branches with moist roots, as well as fruits and roots, products of cow's milk, sugarcane derivatives, salt, and oil;
"For cooked grains, prepared foods, fish, and meat—
indeed for all items of small value— the fine shall be five times their price.

As for the statement of Viṣṇu, "In the case of theft of minor goods, the fine is double the value," this should be understood as referring to objects of little utility, such as earthenware bowls and the like.

Viṣṇu, however, states a specific rule: "For the theft of gems weighing one *prāṇa*, one *kalañja*, or more, there shall be the amputation of a hand, or death, or being made to climb a pit of hot ashes (*kukūla*). A *prāṇa* is a specific measure consisting of four *māṣas*. A *kalañja* is a *dharaṇa*. As Viṣṇugupta has said:
"Five *guñjās* make a *māṣa*; four times that [weight] is a *prāṇa*. Those expert in the measurement of gems call four *prāṇas* a *kalañja*, which is a *dharaṇa*."

On this point, some say that by the force of the word "fourfold" (*caturguṇaiḥ*), the *māṣa* does not consist of twenty *guṇas*, because that which is being enjoined is primary; since it is proper to refer to the primary element, they claim that the *prāṇa* consists of six *māṣas*. This alone is correct, as such is the established usage. A *kalañja*, however, is two *prāṇas*, according to the definition: "A *kalañja* is a pair of *prāṇas*. This arrangement follows worldly custom. All of this should be understood to apply when punishment is meted out based on physical force, as Manu and others have stated this in the context of *sāhasa* (violence). As for that which was stated by Manu:
An act committed by force against one who is present is *sāhasa* (violence);
it becomes *steya* (theft) when it is done by stealth, having deceived the victim.
There is an alternative reading: *yadi kṛtvāpahnūyeta* ("if, having committed it, one should deny it"). And so Kātyāyana says:

"That which is a denial accompanied by kinship, as well as that which is a forcible seizure, shall indeed be *sāhasa* (violence); theft (*steya*) is declared to occur upon denial. [458] Thus it is said.

This has been explained by commentators such as Medhātithi, Asahāya, Yajñapati, and others, as well as by Vijñāneśvara and others. "Anvayavat" means accompanied by a connection [of witnesses], that is, in the presence of guards of property, royal officials, and so forth. That which is done by force (*prasabham*), through the exertion of power—such as the seizing of another's wealth—is *sāhasa* (violence). On the other hand, that which is done otherwise, being designated under the category of theft (*caurya*), is *steya* (theft); this alone is the definition. It was stated previously and will be stated again that even when done by the exertion of power but not in the presence of the king or others, it is indeed *sāhasa*. Therefore, one should consider the interpretation of Medhātithi and others to be merely conceived by their own intellects. For this very reason, Bṛhaspati says:

"Now, hear about theft by force (*sāhasasteya*), which arises from anger and greed. Regarding this, the author of the *Candrikā* states: "Theft by force (*sāhasa*) means theft characterized by violence. On this point, Vyāsa says:
"Having thoroughly identified the perpetrator, along with his accomplices and kinsmen..."
"A king should put them to death by various means of execution that cause terror.
Thus it is said; and also in another Smṛti:
"Likewise, those who seize captives and those who carry off the elephants of kings..."
"And those who kill by force, one should impale such men on stakes. Thus [says the law]. Bṛhaspati also says: "In cases of open murder, as well as for secret assassins..."
"Having identified [the culprit] correctly and seized his wealth, he should be executed by various means of death.

In this context, the phrase "by various means of death that cause terror" indicates that the infliction of terror is an alternative among the various methods. He [Yājñavalkya] himself states the manner of executing a secret killing: "Where the execution is visible, but the executioner is not seen..."
That [person] must first be understood by the king through inference.
"He is to be recognized by his association with the virtuous, or again by signs such as his lips;
he may also belong to the class of assassins or thieves.
Regarding this, Yājñavalkya states a specific distinction:
A thief is apprehended by his captors through stolen goods, or by a footprint,
or likewise through a prior criminal act, or by residing in an impure place.

This is the meaning: he who is proclaimed by the people as "this is a thief" is to be seized by the pursuers—the king’s men, the police, the constables, and so forth. *Loptra* refers to a portion of the stolen goods, or a sign such as a digging tool and the like. *Pada* refers to the footprint left on the ground by the thief. One who has previously been notorious for theft is one guilty of past offenses. An *aśuddhavāsaka* is one who dwells in an improper place. Furthermore, another person may also be seized on suspicion due to the concealment of caste, name, and so forth;
likewise those addicted to gambling, women, and drinking, and those whose faces and voices appear parched and altered.

Those who inquire about the property and houses of others while moving about in secret, those who have no income yet possess great expenditures, and those who sell goods that have been lost— [these are spies].

These and other methods for apprehending thieves are set forth in the *Mānava Dharmaśāstra*; they are not elaborated upon here because they are well known in the world. However, one cannot determine that "this person alone is the thief" and cast him down based solely on these signs. Thus says Nārada:
"One should carefully examine whether the stolen property was dropped from another's hand unintentionally, or whether it was discarded by thieves."
Likewise:
"Unreal things appear like real ones, and real things appear like unreal ones;
various phenomena are seen in this way, therefore investigation is appropriate. Thus it is said.

Since the status of a thief must be determined by removing doubt through human means of proof such as witnesses and so forth, as well as divine means of proof such as the balance ordeal (*dhaṭa*) and others, for what purpose has he ceased [his inquiry] with his own experience in order to set forth the methods for apprehending thieves established in the world? On this point, Manu speaks regarding the subject of theft alone:
"The king, whose eyes are his spies, should know that there are two kinds of thieves who seize the property of others: those who are open and those who are hidden. [460]
Bṛhaspati also says:
"Thieves are recorded as being of two kinds: those who act openly and those who act in secret;
they are divided into a thousand varieties by means of their intelligence, skill, and deceit."
Nārada states the definition of both types of thieves: "In this regard,
open cheats include those who use false weights and measures,
as well as bribe-takers, those who employ fraud, gamblers, and prostitutes."
"And those who produce counterfeits, as well as those who live by giving auspicious directions.
Those who live by giving auspicious directions are "those whose livelihood is the giving of auspicious directions. As Vyāsa said:
"In this world, those who live by giving auspicious directions deceive both women and men."
"For ignoble people, though wearing the outward marks of the noble, seize wealth through deception. Thus it is said.

The rest is easy to understand. Regarding this, Viṣṇu states: “These [offenders] are to be punished strictly according to the nature of their offense. The meaning is that these—namely, open thieves—are not to be fined in proportion to their wealth, but rather according to the gravity of the fault. Included by the word “and” (ca) are counterfeiters, those using false scales, those who live on bribes, those who employ deceitful means, gamblers, prostitutes, forgers of false coins and the like, and those who subsist on giving auspicious predictions. Even merchants and others, though possessing great wealth, are not to be fined in accordance with their assets; rather, they are to be punished according to the offense. The meaning is that the specific fine is prescribed by determining its value based on the principle: “for this particular fault, such is the punishment.”

Viṣṇu describes the nature of concealed thieves: "Those who are tainted by offenses, who are hidden, and who are secret thieves—the pickpocket, the housebreaker, and those who cut the knots of cattle or women—should be punished together. *Doṣā* means night. This very same meaning has been clarified by Nārada: "Those who wander at night equipped with tools and the like, remaining unobserved and whose place of residence is unknown, are to be known as concealed thieves."

The phrase "at night" is intended to indicate the most common occurrence, for such thieves can also exist during the day in places such as forests where there is no light. He himself states their classification:
"The one who carries off [goods], the breaker of walls, the plunderer of travelers, the cutter of knots, and the thief of cattle from women and men—the thief is recorded as being of nine kinds."

One called an *utkṣepaka* is one who, having ascertained the inattention of wealthy people, takes the wealth kept nearby; or, as Bhāruci says, one who, for the purpose of showing coins and the like, immediately misappropriates them by sleight of hand. A housebreaker (*saṃdhibhettā*) is one who, having observed a breach at a place where someone enters a house, stays there and breaks through the wall—meaning, one who constructs a tunnel and so forth. A highwayman (*pānthamuṭ*) is one who plunders the wealth of travelers in deserts and similar places—a "stealer in plain sight," so to speak. A knot-cutter (*granthibhedaka*) is one who cuts the knots of garments and so forth in order to seize the wealth. The rest is easy to understand. Regarding these, Yājñavalkya states the punishment for the *utkṣepaka* and the *granthibhedaka*: *utkṣepakagranthibhedau karasandaṃśahīnakau / kāryoṃ dvitīyāparādhe kṣipraṃ tv ekakarau nṛpe // aṅgulīr granthibhedasya chedayet prathame grahe / dvitīye hastacaraṇau tṛtīye vadham arhati //* "A *utkṣepaka* and a *granthibhedaka* should have their hands and thumbs cut off; in the case of a second offense, they should be deprived of a single hand each. For a *granthibhedaka*, the king should cause the fingers to be amputated upon the first seizure [of property]; on the second, both hands and feet; on the third, he deserves death."* The remainder is clear. Among those [categories of thieves], Yājñavalkya declares the penalty for the *utkṣepaka* and the *granthibhedaka*.
Those who commit robbery by breaking into houses or by cutting through knots [of goods] shall have their hands cut off at the wrist.

"Hand-cutting" (karasaṃdaṃśa) refers here to the thumb and forefinger, intended as the instrument for seizing another's property. Manu states the punishment for one who breaks into a house: "Those thieves who, having broken into a house, commit robbery at night..."
Having cut off their hands, the king should impale them on sharp stakes.
The word "that" (*tat*) is to be understood as the remainder [of the sentence]. Vyāsa, however, states a specific rule:
"Having broken various kinds of locks, one obtains wealth from the house;
having restored everything to the owner, he should be placed upon a sharp stake."
Bṛhaspati states the punishment for one who steals while looking on:
likewise, one who robs travelers should be hanged from a tree by the neck.
Manu, however, states a specific distinction.
"In the case of breaking a joint, one should break [the fingers] at the first seizure;
at the second, the hands and feet; at the third, he deserves death.
Here, "fingers" refers to the index finger and the thumb.

"For the first offense involving the theft of the Vedas, there shall be the cutting off of the fingers and the thumb," according to the traditional teaching of Bṛhaspati. Vyāsa states the punishment for a thief who steals women or men:
"The stealer of a woman is burned upon an iron bed, or by a fire of straw."
The thief of a man, having had his hands and feet cut off, shall be stationed at a crossroads.

Bṛhaspati states the punishment for the theft of a cow: "Having cut off the thief's nose and bound him, one should cast him into the water. Vyāsa states the punishment for the theft of horses and cattle:
In the case of stealing a horse, one should cause the thief to be executed after cutting off his feet and hips;
but for the stealer of a beast, one should cut off the foreleg with a sharp weapon.
Regarding this, Nārada states a specific rule:
"For one who steals a large animal, the punishment is the highest amercement;
for a medium-sized animal, the middle amercement; and for a small animal belonging to a Śūdra, the first amercement."

The middle [fine] is the middle amercement; the first is the first amercement. Regarding theft of gold and other such items, Manu states the punishment: "For the theft of gold, silver, and other such superior goods, and for all kinds of gems, if the value exceeds one hundred [paṇas], the penalty is death."
For an amount exceeding fifty [paṇas], the cutting off of the hand is prescribed;
for amounts exceeding one hundred, one should determine a fine eleven times the value.

The infliction of punishments ending in the breaking of limbs or death applies only to Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, and the like, but not to a Brāhmaṇa. Thus says Yama: "A corporal punishment for a Brāhmaṇa shall never be imposed;
rather, one should cause a Brāhmaṇa who has committed an offense to perform even menial tasks."
"Brāhmaṇas and cows are not to be killed; such is the Vedic revelation in this world.

Regarding this, the author of the *Candrikā* states that "tending cattle and the like is a censurable occupation," while Bhāruci and others maintain it refers to "residence in a prison. For this very reason, Hārīta says:
"Since the twice-born are not to be killed, shaving the head is considered their form of execution."

It was established at the beginning of this section that even for a *brāhmaṇa* who is an assassin (*ātatāyin*), killing is not permitted. As for what was stated by Viṣṇu—that where execution is prescribed, there restraint of the senses (*indriyanirodha*) must be performed—the senses are ten: five organs of cognition and five organs of action, consisting of speech, hands, feet, anus, genitals, ears, skin, eyes, tongue, and nose. Some maintain that their "restraint" consists of cutting them off.

That is not so, because it contradicts the previous statement. Rather, "confiscation" (nirodhana) refers to the binding of the hands and feet with chains and the like; "restraint of speech" (vāṅnirodha) is the binding of the mouth. As for what was stated by Sumantu: "For a Brāhmaṇa, the substitute for execution is the restraint of the eyes" (*cakṣurnirodha*), here "restraint" means plucking out [the eyes]. Nor should it be argued that because this statement employs the specific term "eyes," it is intended to be restrictive and thus subsumes the previous statement under itself. For this very reason, Bhāruciprabhṛti and others have said: "In the case of a grave offense, the substitutes for the execution of a Brāhmaṇa—namely, shaving the head, exile from the country, imprisonment, and plucking out the eyes—should be applied respectively according to the gradations of the offense. However, the author of the *Candrikā* states:

"‘A corporal punishment for a Brāhmaṇa never occurs’—by the force of the word ‘never’ (karhicit), it is said that ‘eye-restriction’ means binding the eyes or applying a skin-patch over them, but not plucking them out. The elders maintain that this alone is correct. Yājñavalkya states that even for a woman who has committed a great offense, there is a punishment ranging from the amputation of limbs to death: "And a woman who is extremely corrupt, one who kills a man, provided she is not pregnant... [464]
And having bound a stone in water that breaks a dam, one should cause it to enter [the water].

Especially one who is corrupted, excessively corrupted, or extremely wicked—that is, a killer of an embryo (bhrūṇahanī), meaning one who causes an abortion; and she who is a slayer of a man. Furthermore, one who administers poison or sets fire, or who kills her husband, her elders, or her offspring—having deprived her of her ears, hands, nose, and lips, one should cause her to be killed by oxen.

Here too, the phrase "not pregnant" (agarbhiṇīm) is understood to apply, according to Vijñāneśvara. The meaning is that one should cause her to be killed—that is, put to death—by oxen, meaning by very fierce bulls. Regarding this, Yājñavalkya states the punishment for those who assist thieves:
If those who know [the truth] provide a thief or a murderer with food, shelter, fire, water, spells, or the means for his escape, they shall receive the highest fine.

The meaning of this is as follows: *bhakta* is food; *avakāśa* is a dwelling place; *agni* is fire for the purpose of dispelling cold from the hands and so forth; *udaka* is water for one who is thirsty; *mantra* is consultation with a thief—by this, instructions on the methods of theft are indicated; *upakaraṇa* is the equipment for theft, such as the provision of shovels and the like for the purpose of constructing tunnels and so forth; *vyaya* is travel provisions (*pātheya*). Regarding the phrase "even though knowing," Bhāruci states that for those who do not know, there is the middle amercement (*madhyama-sāhasa*);
furthermore, those who are capable yet remain indifferent are also partakers in that fault.

Thus, from the Smṛti of Nārada, it is understood that for neglecting a thief and similar offenses, the punishment is indeed the highest amercement (*uttamasāhasa*). In that case as well, it applies only when there is intentional knowledge; however, Bhāruci maintains that if it is done unintentionally, the middle amercement (*madhyamasāhasa*) applies. With this very intention, Kātyāyana says: "The instigator, the accomplice, likewise the one who points out the way, the shelterer, the giver of weapons, and the giver of food for criminal acts [are all liable]."
Or he who provides instruction and demonstrates its destruction,
who is engaged in the task of indifference, who points out faults, and who expresses approval.
"But one should determine their punishment according to their capacity.
Regarding this, Yājñavalkya states a specific rule:
"He who causes another to commit an act of violence (sāhasa) shall be made to pay double the fine."

"And whoever, having spoken thus, causes me to be the giver, he shall pay fourfold"—the meaning is that he shall be made to pay. Regarding a killing where the perpetrator is unknown, Yājñavalkya states the means for identifying the killer:
"In the case of one killed by an unknown assailant, the son and kinsmen [should immediately investigate] the quarrel..."
And women who are devoted to other men should be questioned separately regarding him.

The daughter of a relative killed by an unknown person, as well as his nearby kinsmen, should be questioned immediately regarding the quarrel, asking, "With whom did he have a dispute? The rest is easy to understand. Regarding this, Manu states an exception: "A twice-born man traveling on a journey whose means of subsistence are exhausted, taking two stalks of sugarcane or two roots from another's field, does not deserve to be punished."
"Those staying on a road may take a single handful of chickpeas, rice, wheat, barley, mung beans, or black gram, provided they are not prohibited [by the owner].
Regarding the specific rules for the seduction of women, Saṃvarta says:
Listen now to the signs of women who do not desire it, yet are subjected to force, as they occur repeatedly during their encounters.
A woman who bears nail and tooth marks, who is emaciated, who has been tormented by the seizing of her hair,
and who has been instantly ravaged, is one defiled by forceful violation.
Crying out loudly and weeping in the presence of the people, she spoke his name, saying: "In this manner I have been defiled by him."
One should grieve for her by such signs as these:
her breasts made into wounds, her ornaments and hair cut off, and her eyes closed like buds.
[466] Having been brought into the assembly by the king and his courtiers, and having investigated the matter himself at that very moment,
whatever innate statement he may utter should be carried out with diligent effort.
In this dispute, one should not accept the testimony of witnesses;
because the accused has already been proven by his conduct, it is not necessary to administer an ordeal.

The intention of the author of the *Candrikā*, who states that "in this case, the decision must be made by the king based on signs alone, neither through ordeal nor through witnesses," is as follows: it is not that witnesses and ordeals never apply in this matter; rather, when a decision has been reached by the king and his assessors, there is no need for witnesses or ordeals, and thus they do not come into play. However, when a woman in love, longing for her husband, deceives him by feigning nail-marks on her breasts, tooth-marks on her lips, and so forth, then there is scope for witnesses and ordeals.

Yājñavalkya states a specific rule regarding the approach of a widow: "One who approaches a widow of her own accord, one who does not run to the rescue when a cry for help is raised, one who raises a false cry for help, and one who touches a woman of the highest caste— all these are outcastes (caṇḍālas)."
One who feeds Śūdras or renunciants at rites for the gods or the ancestors;
one who makes an improper oath; and one who performs the duties of an unfit person—[these are excluded].
One who obstructs the virility of bulls, Śūdras, or cattle;
one who denies a common property; and one who causes the destruction of a maidservant’s fetus.

A father and son, a sister and brother, a husband and wife, or a teacher and pupil— anyone who abandons another among these, provided they have not fallen from their caste, shall be subject to a fine of one hundred [paṇas].

One who approaches a widow of his own will without her husband’s authorization is a *svacchandavidhavāgāmī*. One who, though capable of doing so, does not run to the rescue when his own family is crying out in distress due to fear of thieves and the like is a *kruṣṭe nābhidhāvakaḥ*. One who makes an improper oath is an *ayuktaśapathakṛt*. One who destroys the virility, that is, the capacity for procreation, is a destroyer of manhood. Regarding the reading "of trees and small animals," Vijñāneśvara explains that one who causes the falling of fruits and flowers from trees and the like by the application of medicinal substances such as asafoetida (*hiṅgu*) is meant. Each of these is liable to a fine of one hundred *paṇas*. As for that which was stated by Bṛhaspati:
But he who should lustfully desire her by force, one shall seize all his wealth;
having cut off his penis and testicles, one shall cause him to be paraded around on a donkey.

This, however, applies to one who is other than a Brāhmaṇa and desires a Brāhmaṇa woman; the phrase "he should desire another's wife" is understood as the remainder [of the rule]. Manu, however, states a specific exception: "Having branded the Brāhmaṇa, he should banish him from his own kingdom;

but a Brāhmaṇa, even for a great offense, he shall not cause to be killed. Rather, having marked him on the forehead, he should expel him from his own kingdom. And the branding should be performed in the shape of a vulva. Thus says Vṛddha-Vasiṣṭha.

"For drinking liquor, branding with the sign of a tavern flag; for theft, branding with one's own footprint; for killing a Brahmin, branding on the hip with the image of a donkey; and for violating the Guru’s bed, branding with the image of a female organ.
Thus [it is said]. Manu, however, states a specific distinction:
For violating the teacher’s bed, the mark of a female organ should be made; for drinking liquor, the sign of a tavern banner;
for theft, the footprint of a dog; and for killing a Brahmin, the figure of a headless man.
A headless man is a *kabandha*. The rest is easy to understand. Yājñavalkya states the specific rule regarding sexual intercourse with the wife of a king:
"Those who set fire to fields, houses, forests, villages, pastures, or threshing floors, as well as one who approaches the wife of a king, shall be burned by a fire of straw."

The meaning is that [the offender] should be wrapped in mats made of *vīraṇa* grass or straw and then burned. This specific rule is undertaken because there would otherwise be the contingency of imposing the death penalty on those who merely burn fields and the like. Nārada, however, having stated that adultery with another's wife is of three kinds, declares the specific punishments for each:
"That is declared to be threefold: first, middle, and highest.
[The first is] conversing with another's wife at an improper place or time, or in a secluded spot."

[468] Gazing with a sidelong glance, laughter, and the first act of boldness; the sending of perfumes, garlands, incense, ornaments, and garments—these are remembered as the preliminary signs of passion.
Enticing with food and drink is recorded as the middling form of violence;
likewise, sitting together in a secluded place and mutual physical contact [are also included].
And the seizing by the hair is correctly recorded as *saṃgrahaṇa*.

The meaning is this: he who engages in conversation in an improper place, such as a grove, or at an improper time, such as in darkness or in a secluded and desolate spot, and who remains for a long time together on the same bed or similar seat, is also engaged in *saṃgrahaṇa* (sexual misconduct). This refers to a case where the man is suspected [of intent]; for another [who is not suspected], there is no fault. Thus Manu says:
"But he who, having not been previously invited, speaks even for a valid reason, shall incur no fault whatsoever, for there is no transgression on his part."

And this [definition] refers specifically to cases other than side-glances, leering looks, and so forth, but rather to the mere circumstance of staying on the same couch together. Thus Viṣṇu says: "Enticement, side-long glances, laughing, and staying together in one place are the means of seduction. Likewise Gautama states: "If one who has touched another's wife is stubborn, he should be seized. "Stubborn" means he consents to the touch. And Manu says:
"He who touches a woman in an improper place, or she who, being touched, tolerates it—when there is mutual consent, all that is recorded as *saṃgrahaṇa* (seduction)."

Viṣṇu, however, states a specific rule: "He who says, 'This was enjoyed by me through delusion,' is to be accepted [as guilty]. Here, "delusion" (moha) is indicative of pride and other such motives. As Manu says: "Whether out of pride, or delusion, or out of self-conceit, he who himself declares, 'This was previously enjoyed by me'—that is recorded as *saṃgrahaṇa* (sexual intercourse)."

And so Gautama says: “In the case of a prohibition, the man shall be fined, and the woman half of that. The meaning of this has been explained by the author of the *Nibandhana*: “A woman who engages in conversation with someone with whom she is forbidden to speak by her husband, father, or others, shall be fined one hundred *paṇas*. A man likewise, having been thus forbidden, shall be fined two hundred *paṇas* if he persists.”

Viṣṇu, however, states a specific rule: "For a man and a woman who engage in sexual intercourse when it is forbidden, the punishment for adultery shall be according to their caste. Bhāruci maintains that this refers specifically to women kept in confinement. Viṣṇu further prescribes the punishment according to the status of the caste: "In the case of approaching another's wife while she is protected, the fine is one thousand and eighty paṇas. This should be understood to apply to cases other than those involving the wives of teachers, female friends, and so forth—as in the following list:
mother, mother’s sister, mother-in-law, maternal uncle’s wife, father’s sister, the wife of a paternal uncle, a friend, a disciple, a sister, her female friend, and a daughter-in-law.
A daughter, a teacher’s wife, one of the same lineage, one who has sought refuge, a queen, one who has gone forth into homelessness, a nurse, a virtuous woman, and one of the highest caste.
One who approaches any one of these women is said to be a violator of the Guru’s bed;
in that case, no punishment other than the excision of the penis is ordained.

Thus says the Nārada-smṛti. Regarding this, Yājñavalkya states a specific rule: "In the case of a woman of the same caste, the highest fine [is prescribed]; in the case of a woman of a lower caste (ānulomya), the middle fine; but in the case of a woman of a higher caste (prātilomya), there shall be death for the man and the cutting off of the ears and so forth for the woman."

The meaning is this: if any of the four castes forcibly violates a protected woman of his own caste or one of another caste, he shall be fined one hundred and eighty *paṇas*. However, when a man of lower caste approaches a protected woman of a higher caste in the natural order (*ānulomyena*), he shall be fined the middle amercement (*madhyama-sāhasa*). Furthermore, when he approaches a woman of his own caste who is unprotected, or one of a higher caste who is protected, in the natural order—as Manu has said:
"A Brāhmaṇa approaching a protected Brāhmaṇa woman by force shall be fined one thousand;
if he has sexual intercourse with her when she consents, he shall be fined five hundred."
"A Brāhmaṇa should be made to pay a fine of one thousand [paṇas] for approaching those two when they are protected;

however, for a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya approaching a Śūdra woman, the fine shall be one thousand. These two refer to the wives of a Kṣatriya and a Vaiśya. In the case of *prātilomya*—that is, sexual intercourse with a woman of a higher caste who is protected—a man of the Kṣatriya or other lower caste must suffer death. And this applies specifically to cases involving protected women and so forth. As Viṣṇu says: "A Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya who has intercourse with a protected Brāhmaṇa woman should be burned by a fire of straw. Manu states the specific rule regarding intercourse with an unprotected woman:

"If a Vaiśya or a Kṣatriya should have intercourse with an unprotected Brāhmaṇī woman, he should fine the Vaiśya five hundred [paṇas] and the Kṣatriya one thousand. Regarding the Śūdra, Gautama says: "If a Śūdra should approach even an unprotected woman of a higher caste, he deserves the cutting off of his organ. Here, the word *api* ("even") is to be construed out of its immediate position [with the preceding clause]. By the statement "he deserves the cutting off of his organ," the confiscation of all his property is established as being conjoined [with this penalty].
"Death or the confiscation of all property for him who approaches her while she is protected.
"Of him" means of this Śūdra. [The rule is:
"A Śūdra who should approach a member of the twice-born castes, whether she be protected or unprotected..."
If hidden, it consists of the linga, the body, and all one's possessions; if not hidden, it consists of mere material wealth.

Thus says the Hārītasmṛti: "For a woman who goes to a man of a lower caste, the cutting off of her ears and other [limbs] must be performed. As Viṣṇu has stated: "For a woman who goes to a man of a different caste, whether in the direct order [of castes] or otherwise, the cutting off of her nose and so forth, or the punishment of death, shall be prescribed. Regarding this, Bhāruci says: "The cutting off of the nose and so forth applies to a woman in the direct order;
for following a man of a different caste, the punishment of death is proclaimed."

Thus he cites the Smṛti. And this instruction regarding punishment is for the king alone, because he alone has the authority over its administration. It does not apply to every twice-born person, because of the prohibition against taking up weapons: "A Brāhmaṇa shall not take up a weapon even for the sake of self-defense. Furthermore: "The punishment of censure and the punishment of verbal restraint—both of these depend upon the Brāhmaṇas. [471]

And because of this prohibition, Śaṅkha and Likhita state a specific rule regarding this matter: "In the case of mutual sexual intercourse between a Kṣatriya and a Vaiśya, both shall be punished. Regarding this, Vijñāneśvara states: "The fines, consisting of one thousand and one hundred paṇas respectively, are to be understood [as applying here]. As Manu has said:
'If a Vaiśya approaches a protected Kṣatriya woman, or a Kṣatriya approaches a protected Vaiśya woman—both of them deserve the same punishment as one who approaches an unprotected Brāhmaṇa woman.'"

Thus he spoke. Bhāruci, however, explains it otherwise: "If a Vaiśya approaches the wife of a Kṣatriya, and then a Kṣatriya approaches the wife of that very same [Vaiśya], a fine consisting of one hundred *paṇas* is to be understood [for the latter]. Likewise, if a Kṣatriya goes to the wife of any other Vaiśya whatsoever, he should be fined one thousand *paṇas*; if a Vaiśya goes to a Kṣatriya woman, he should be fined one thousand *paṇas*. Regarding a maiden, however, Yājñavalkya states a specific rule:
"For abducting an adorned maiden, the highest [amercement]; otherwise, the lowest."
"One should impose a fine for offenses against women of the same caste; however, in the case of the reverse order [of castes], death is prescribed by tradition."

One who abducts a maiden of the same caste (*savarṇā*) who is adorned and intent on marriage shall be punished with the highest fine (*uttamasāhasa*). One who abducts a maiden of a different caste (*asavarṇā*) who is intent on marriage shall be punished with the first fine (*prathamasāhasa*). A Kṣatriya or others who abduct a maiden born of a superior caste shall be put to death. Vijñāneśvara states that, because of the prescription of punishment, the maiden should be taken away from the abductor and given to another. Bhāruci and others, however, maintain that she must simply be punished by the king; yet they say that if the abductor possesses the excellence of a bridegroom (*varasaṃpatti*), she should be given to him, since the Paiśāca form of marriage is permissible in such a case. Dhāreśvara and others, however, state that the mention of the bridegroom’s excellence follows immediately after the discussion of monetary fines; thus, if she is of the same caste, she should be given to him.

Regarding this, Viṣṇu states a specific rule: "There is no fault in the case of women of higher caste when it is done out of desire. This is the meaning: there is no fault for one who abducts a maiden of lower caste who is herself filled with passion. From the very absence of fault, the absence of punishment is understood through the logic of the "cake and the stick" (*daṇḍāpūpika*). Asahāya and others state that this alone constitutes the *āsura* form of marriage. As Yājñavalkya says: "There is no fault in the case of women of higher caste who are willing; otherwise, there is a fine."

Śaṅkha and Likhita state the penalty for defiling a maiden: "In the case of defiling those of lower castes [than oneself], there shall be the amputation of that limb; in the case of superior women, death. The word "in the case of maidens" is to be understood as the ellipsis. Regarding "the amputation of that limb": if one defiles her by inserting a finger and thereby causing a wound in the vulva, that specific limb must be amputated. If one defiles a maiden by force with the hand or other means, the cutting off of the hand must be performed. On this point, Manu states a distinction: "But he who defiles a willing woman does not deserve the amputation of a finger;
however, he should be made to pay a fine of two hundred [paṇas] to prevent a recurrence."

The word "finger" (*aṅguli*) is also indicative of the hand. The phrase "to prevent an over-extension" means for the purpose of warding off an excessive application [of the rule]. Bhāruci says it is "for the purpose of precluding sexual enjoyment. Regarding this, Gautama states a specific rule: "If a maiden defiles another maiden, there shall be the amputation of her limb or the shaving of her head. Regarding this, Manu states a specific rule: "A maiden herself may cause the defilement of a maiden; for her, however, the fine shall be two hundred [paṇas]."

"But a woman who violates a maiden deserves immediate shaving [of the head]. The phrase "should violate a maiden" means she should cause her to have an injury to the vulva. Regarding this prescription of punishment, Bhāruci maintains that it applies universally to maidens of all classes—whether of equal or unequal caste, or whether they are of middling, low, or high status. However, for a man of lower status, such as a Kṣatriya, who approaches a willing maiden against her will out of passion, there is corporal punishment;
whereas one of inferior status who serves a superior maiden deserves death.

This is because of the traditional teaching of Manu: "When one approaches a woman of the same caste who is willing, he shall give a pair of cattle as a bride-price (*śulka*) to her father, if the father so desires; if he does not desire it, he shall pay that very amount to the king as a fine. Regarding women who are imprisoned, female slaves, or likewise female servants, if a man is capable and yet does not prevent intercourse with them, they are all liable for the performance of the task; even in the case of women who are approachable, the man shall be made to pay a fine of five hundred and more.

The word "going" (*gacchan*) is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence]. "Appropriated" (*aparuddhāḥ*) means those who have been barred from enjoyment by another man. A "servant woman" (*bhujiṣyā*) is one whose possession is restricted to a specific man. The phrase "even among those who may be approached" (*gamyāsv api*) is an epithet for these two. This is a restatement (*anuvāda*) to the effect that they are common to all men because they may be approached. As Yājñavalkya has said: "A fine of ten *paṇas* is prescribed for the forcible approach of a servant woman;
if she is unwilling and there are many [approachers], the fine is twenty-four *paṇas* for each."
Regarding this, Yājñavalkya states the specific rule:
"Upon approaching a woman of the lowest caste, however, one should brand him with a mark and banish him;
at that time, a Śūdra becomes a man of the lowest caste himself, and for approaching a woman of the lowest caste, there is death."

The meaning of this is as follows: Regarding the final [caste], the Caṇḍālī—if members of the three higher castes (traivarṇika) are intent on approaching her, one should fine them one thousand paṇas based on the statement, “But for [approaching] a woman of the lowest caste, a thousand,” and having branded them with a contemptible mark in the shape of the female organ (bhaga) by means of a "bad punishment" (kudaṇḍa), one should banish them from one's own kingdom. However, for one who is intent on performing penance (prāyaścitta), there is only punishment. Furthermore, a Śūdra who approaches a Caṇḍālī becomes a Caṇḍāla himself. And for a member of the lowest caste, such as a Caṇḍāla, approaching a woman of a superior caste, the same rule applies; such is the meaning of the statement. On this point, Manu states a specific distinction: [474] Manu says: “[A man of the three higher castes] who has approached a Caṇḍālī shall be punished with a fine of five hundred [paṇas] and branded with the sign of a female organ. “A Śūdra who has approached a Caṇḍālī shall be punished with a fine of five hundred [paṇas] and shall be made a Caṇḍāla. “The same applies to one who has approached a woman of a superior caste.
