If a Śūdra approaches a woman of a superior caste, he shall be fined five hundred paṇas and made a Caṇḍāla. If a member of the lowest caste approaches a woman of a superior caste, the same punishment applies. This is the meaning of the text. [474] Regarding this, Manu says: [474] Manu says: “[A man of the three higher castes] who has approached a Caṇḍālī shall be punished with a fine of five hundred [paṇas] and branded with the sign of a female organ. “A Śūdra who has approached a Caṇḍālī shall be punished with a fine of five hundred [paṇas] and shall be made a Caṇḍāla. “The same applies to one who has approached a woman of a superior caste. (Manu Smṛti 8.372–374) Regarding this, the *Mitākṣarā* explains: “‘Branded with the sign of a female organ’ means marked with a brand in the shape of a vulva. ‘Made a Caṇḍāla’ means that he is to be treated like a Caṇḍāla. ‘The same applies to one who has approached a woman of a superior caste’ means that for a Śūdra who has approached a woman of a superior caste, the punishment is the same as that for
The killer of a Brahmin, the drinker of intoxicants, the thief, and the violator of the Guru’s bed—
all these men are great sinners (mahāpātakin) who deserve to be executed individually.

A drinker of *surā* is one who drinks that which is forbidden as *surā*. A "thief" (*taskara*) is one who steals the gold of a Brāhmaṇa; for, according to the traditional teaching of Āpastamba, "the theft of a Brāhmaṇa’s gold is a mortal sin" (*mahāpātaka*). And this refers to cases other than those involving a Brāhmaṇa: "Even one joined with a mortal sin, a Brāhmaṇa does not deserve death. The king shall instead impose banishment, branding, and shaving of the head."
Even when punishment has been inflicted upon them, their offense remains;
for it is said, "One who has been punished for an *uttamasāhasa* crime should be known as unfit for conversation.

Thus, because they are exceedingly wicked, being equivalent to those guilty of an *uttamasāhasa*, one should understand that they are unfit for conversation even in this case. This very point has been elaborated by Manu:
Indeed, being unfit to eat with, unfit to sacrifice for, unfit to teach, and unfit to marry,
they shall wander the entire earth, excluded from all ritual acts.

"But these, having been branded with the mark, must be abandoned by their kinsmen and relatives; they are to be excluded from speech and salutation—this is the instruction of Manu. As for that which was stated by Bodhāyana—"In the case of killing a Brāhmaṇa, there shall be death and the confiscation of all property for Kṣatriyas and others"—that should be understood as referring to cases involving acts of violence (*sāhasa*). Regarding this, Manu states a specific distinction:
One who destroys a tank should be killed, or punished by the death-purification in water;
if he should repair it, he must pay the highest fine.
Kātyāyana, however, states a specific rule:
"He who should seize, break, or burn an image of a deity,
or even the temple itself, shall incur the first amercement."
[475] But he who should accomplish a transaction by means of a false measure, a counterfeit seal, or a favorable document, shall indeed be made to pay the highest fine.
But Bṛhaspati stated an exception:
"Those who, by the power of mantras or medicinal herbs, cause even a slight degree of exhaustion or perform acts of sorcery (mūlakarman), they should be banished by the king."
The act of subjugation is performed by means of roots and other such substances; for this very reason, Manu says:
"One should put to death those who forge royal edicts, those who corrupt the subjects, those who kill women, children, or Brahmins, as well as those who practice *saṃvanana* (subjugation spells)."

"One should banish those who live by means of enchantment and those who corrupt the constituent elements of the state. The constituent elements (*prakṛti*) have indeed already been explained at the beginning of this section as the sovereign, the minister, the fort, the treasury, the army, the realm, and the ally. Those who live by means of enchantment are those who subsist on the practice of subjugation (*vaśīkaraṇa*).
Thus ends the chapter on the legal category known as "Violence" (sāhasa) within the Sarasvatīvilāsa, a compendium of law (smṛtisaṃgraha) composed by the illustrious Great King Pratāparudra Mahādeva.
Alternatively, regarding the category known as verbal abuse (*vāk-pāruṣya*), Nārada states its definition:
"An insult directed at [another's] country, caste, family, and so forth, accompanied by a disparaging implication."
Speech whose meaning is contrary [to what is beneficial] is called verbal abuse.

Harshness (*pāruṣya*) means making rough. Harshness of speech is the making of speech and mind rough. "Accompanied by the suggested" (*vyaṅgyasayuta*) means joined with a suggested meaning, having a contrary meaning, or having a distressing meaning. This is the sense: "The Easterners are violent" is an insult to a region; "Brahmins are ill-behaved" is an insult to a caste (*jāti*); "The Vaiśvāmitras are devoid of friendship" is an insult to a family (*kula*). By the inclusion of the term "and so forth" (*ādi*), an insult to one's own essential nature (*svarūpa*) is also included. For example, "He is devoid of learning" according to the circumstances is accompanied by a suggestion; as is the attribution of incest, such as "He has gone to his sister," and the accusation of a mortal sin, such as "He is a drinker of wine. But when verbal abuse occurs between those of equal caste and qualities,
the prescribed punishment in the treatise is a fine of twelve and a half paṇas.
Manu states a distinction regarding equality based solely on caste:
"But among all those of the same caste, when there is an offense, the fine is twelve [paṇas] only.

An "offense" (*vyatikrama*) refers to an offense of speech; that is to say, verbal abuse. The meaning is that when there is no distinction such as priority or posteriority in an offense other than speech, and both parties are equally at fault, the punishment shall be exactly twelve paṇas. For this very reason, Sumantu says:
When both have simultaneously engaged in the fault of harsh speech,
if no distinction is observed and the discipline is equal for both, [the offense is shared].

*Vinaya* means training and self-restraint (*dama*). The intention is that, however, in the case of a specific offense, the restraint (*dama*) should indeed be proportionate to that [offense]. For this very reason, Bṛhaspati states:
"When two parties are equal, the punishment is equal; it is recorded as being double for one who is inferior;
and in cases of mutual verbal abuse, a greater [punishment] is prescribed for the superior party."
Regarding this, Nārada states a specific rule:
"He who first brings a false accusation shall certainly bear the guilt;
he who later offers a justification is the one who must pay the fine, whereas for the former, the punishment is more severe."

The meaning is that an offense caused by prior slander is more serious than an offense caused by subsequent slander. Regarding this, Viṣṇu states the distinction: “If two persons of equal status slander one another at the same time, the punishment shall be equal. On this point, Yājñavalkya says:
“If one insults those who are deficient in limbs, organs, or afflicted by disease by means of true, false, or distorted praise, he should be fined twelve and a half paṇas.”
Those with deficient limbs include the hunchbacked and others; those with deficient sense organs include the one-eyed and others; and the diseased include those with leprosy and others.
Punishment should be administered according to the relative superiority or inferiority of their social class (*varṇa*) and caste (*jāti*).

Bhāruci says that *daṇḍapraṇayana* means the "prescription of punishment. Vijñāneśvara says that *daṇḍapraṇayana* means the "thorough application" (*prakarṣeṇa nayana*) or the "determination" (*ūhana*) of punishment. The term *varṇajātyuttarādharāḥ* refers to those who are higher or lower in terms of caste (*varṇa*) and birth (*jāti*). The meaning is that the application of punishment must be carried out according to whether one is higher or lower in caste relative to their birth. For example, if a *mūrdhāvasikta* (who is inferior to a Brāhmaṇa and superior to a Kṣatriya) reviles [another], he deserves a fine of seventy-five *paṇas*—slightly more than the fifty *paṇas* prescribed for the insult of a Brāhmaṇa or a Kṣatriya. A Kṣatriya, having reviled him, deserves a fine of exactly seventy-five *paṇas*, which is less than the fine for insulting a Brāhmaṇa. A *mūrdhāvasikta*, having reviled both of them, deserves that same fine. Furthermore, when *mūrdhāvasiktas*, *ambaṣṭhas*, and others insult one another, their respective fines should be understood as being based on the insults exchanged between Brāhmaṇas and Kṣatriyas, applied in due order. This principle should be inferred in other cases as well. Regarding this, Viṣṇu states: "In the case of verbal abuse committed in the reverse order of castes, the fine is double. The meaning of this is as follows: for a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya who insults a Brāhmaṇa, the fines are double or triple; that is, compared to the fifty *paṇas*, the fine for a Kṣatriya is double at one hundred *paṇas*, and for a Vaiśya it is triple at one hundred and fifty *paṇas*. Thus the punishment is to be understood.
"In cases of offenses committed in the reverse order [of castes], the fines for the castes are double and triple;
therefore, in the direct order, they are recipients of half and half again.
Regarding the case of a Śūdra, Manu states a specific rule:
A Kṣatriya who reviles a Brāhmaṇa deserves a fine of one hundred;
a Vaiśya deserves two hundred or fifty; but a Śūdra deserves corporal punishment.

Vijñāneśvara maintains that "killing" in this context means cutting off the tongue. Likewise, by the same principle of parity, for a Vaiśya and a Śūdra who are immediately following a Kṣatriya in the social order, one hundred and fifty respectively should be understood as the fines for insulting a Kṣatriya. For a Śūdra insulting a Vaiśya, the fine is one hundred. The rest should be inferred accordingly, as stated by Manu: "A Brāhmaṇa should be fined fifty for insulting a Kṣatriya;
for insulting a Vaiśya, twenty-five; but for insulting a Śūdra, the fine is twelve."

Regarding this, Yājñavalkya states the specific rule: "For verbal threats involving the destruction of the arms, neck, eyes, or thighs, the fine is one hundred [paṇas]; for those involving the feet, nose, ears, hands, and so forth, it is half of that."

*Śatyaḥ* means a fine of one hundred [paṇas]. This refers to the meaning that for verbal injury such as "I shall break your foot or other limb," the fine is half of that, namely fifty paṇas. He states the specific rule regarding harsh abuse:
"In the case of an accusation involving a *pātaka* (sin causing loss of caste), the fine is the middle amercement;
and in the case of one involving a minor sin (*upapātaka*), he should be made to pay the first amercement."
[479] And for one guilty of a minor offense (upapātaka), such as saying "you are a cow-killer" and the like,
or for insulting those who possess the three Vedas, a king, or a deity, the punishment is the highest amercement (uttamasāhasa).

The middle [fine] applies to guilds (*jātipūga*), and the first to villages and districts. Guilds (*jātipūga*) are associations of those belonging to the same caste. Regarding this, Bṛhaspati states an exception:
"In the case of verbal abuse, a Brāhmaṇa does not commit an offense against one who is devoid of good qualities."
Having called one who has fallen a "fallen one," or again, having called a thief a "thief."
"From [that] statement, there would be an equal fault... and so forth.

"By statement" means by an equivalent statement; the sense is that where one might prove [the offense] through physical contact (*pāṇi*) and so forth during an accusation and the like, there would be no fault by virtue of the statement alone. Similarly, although many *smṛti* texts prescribing various punishments based on [insults regarding] learning, lineage, country, occupation, body, father, mother, kinsmen, and elders have been compiled by the authors of compendiums upon seeing such insults, we have desisted from doing so here for fear of excessive length, as their actual application is currently absent.

Thus ends the forty-eighth chapter, titled "The Section on Verbal Abuse," within the *Vyavahārakāṇḍa* of the *Sarasvatīvilāsa*, a compendium of legal tradition (*Smṛtisaṃgraha*) composed by the illustrious Great King Pratāparudradeva.
Now, the rule for the legal category known as *daṇḍapāruṣya* (assault) is stated,
as Nārada says: "Assault against the limbs of another person with hands, feet, weapons, and so forth..."
"And injury by means of ashes and so forth is called verbal assault (*daṇḍapāruṣya*).
On this point, Manu says:
"This rule of punishment has been declared for verbal assault according to its true nature."
Henceforth, I shall proclaim the determination of the law concerning physical assault.

As the author of the *Pariśiṣṭa* has said: "Whatever causes suffering, a wound, the shedding of blood, or likewise cutting and piercing for living beings— that indeed is called violence (*daṇḍapāruṣya*)."
Manu states that this [punishment] also has three types, according to the sequence of low, middling, and high: "Its threefold nature is seen through threatening,
seizing without restraint, and the sight of blood from a wound."
"Because of the transgression involving inferior, middling, and superior objects, they say there are exactly three types of *sāhasa* (violence); that is the purification of [the realm] from thorns.
Regarding the casting down of one who is unattached and the striking of one who is fearless, Manu states the punishment for it:
One who cuts the skin shall be fined one hundred [paṇas]; for drawing blood, half of that;
one who cuts the flesh shall be fined six niṣkas, but one who breaks a bone shall be banished.
"Candrikākāra states that one who cuts flesh is a wound-maker. Yama also says:
'For the cutting off of the ear, lip, nose, foot, eye, tongue, mouth, or hand, the highest fine is prescribed; for piercing them, the middle fine is the teacher's [penalty]. [481]"
Bṛhaspati also states:
"Throwing ashes and the like [upon another], or striking with the hand and so forth—this constitutes the first degree of physical assault; in this case, a fine of one *māṣaka* should be imposed."
For striking with bricks, wooden planks, and the like, a fine of two māṣakas shall be imposed;
however, wise men should determine the punishment for a wound according to its severity and the specific circumstances of the blow.
"This punishment has been declared for [adultery with] women of equal status and those of higher status;
it should be understood by the wise as being double or triple, depending on the relative preeminence [of the woman].
And likewise, Yājñavalkya says:
Touching [an outcaste] smeared with ashes or mud is recorded as being ten times the [penance for] a staff;
touching [him] with impure matter, the heel, or spittle is recorded as being double that.
The same applies to the wives of others who are of equal status, but it is double for those of superior rank.
The double fine consists of twenty paṇas. However, Kātyāyana states a specific distinction:
"If [the injury] is caused by vomit, urine, feces, and so forth, the fine shall be fourfold;
it shall be sixfold on the middle part of the body, but is recorded as eightfold on the head."
The meaning is clear. In this regard, Kātyāyana extends the rules for the punishment of verbal abuse to this case of physical assault:

"Just as the punishments for verbal abuse have been declared according to the inverse and natural order of castes, so too shall the punishments be inflicted in cases of physical assault in their respective order."
On this point, Yājñavalkya states:
"The limb of a non-Brāhmaṇa that causes pain to a Brāhmaṇa should be cut off.
If he merely raises his hand [to strike], the first amercement is the punishment; if there is actual contact, it is half of that."
As Bhṛgu said: "If an outcaste should injure a superior person with any limb whatsoever, that very limb of his must be cut off; such is the ordinance of Manu. [482]

Vijñāneśvara maintains that because the cutting off of limbs is prescribed for a Śūdra who has committed an offense against any member of the twice-born (dvijāti), this same punishment applies to a Vaiśya and even to a Kṣatriya who harms another [of a higher caste], as the underlying principle is the same. Regarding "brandishing" (*udgūrṇe*), which means raising a weapon or the like for the purpose of killing: for a Śūdra, however, even for mere brandishing, there is indeed the cutting off of the hand and so forth, according to the Smṛti of Manu: "Having raised his hand or a staff, he deserves the cutting off of his hand. But regarding the touching of a weapon or the like for the purpose of brandishing, Yājñavalkya prescribes half of the first *sāhasa* fine in cases involving those of the same caste.
If the hand or foot is raised [to strike], the fines for both shall be twenty [paṇas] each; but if all of them use weapons against one another, the middle amercement shall apply.
Furthermore:
for pulling at the feet, hair, or goads, or for seizing with the hands, the fine is ten *paṇas*;
for causing pain, dragging, wrapping with a garment, or placing the feet and so forth [upon another], the punishment is one hundred *paṇas*.

For the commission of all these acts together, one shall be fined one hundred [paṇas]. This is what is stated: he who, having seized any one of the feet, hair, garment, or hand, pulls [the woman] away suddenly, shall be fined ten paṇas. He who, having enveloped her with a cloth, squeezed her tightly, and pulled her, strikes her with his foot, shall be fined ten paṇas; this refers to the case of a Brāhmaṇa. And so says Yama:
"One who strikes out of anger deserves the amputation of a foot.
The king shall cut off both lips of one who spits out of arrogance."
One who urinates upon him on the penis, or defecates upon him on the anus,
or seizes him by the hair with his hands, shall have those parts cut off without hesitation.

Even for one who seizes [another] by the hair with only one hand, the rule of cutting off both hands is understood from the use of the dual number. "A man who causes pain with wood or other implements without shedding blood shall be fined twenty-two paṇas; an outcaste (antyaja) who bites [the victim] shall be fined double that. Thus it is said.
To clarify the meaning:
for breaking teeth like a hand, for cutting off the ears or the nose,
for causing a wound, and likewise for striking one who is nearly dead, the middle amercement shall be imposed.
Furthermore:
In cases of obstructing bodily movements, speech, or the eyes and so forth,
as well as in the breaking of the neck, arms, or thighs, the middle amercement is prescribed.
For many who strike one person, the aforementioned fine shall be doubled.

The meaning is this: when many people have gathered together and commit an offense such as causing a fracture against one person, then for whichever offense whatever punishment has been prescribed, it should be understood that a double fine applies to each individual. Regarding this, Uśanas says:

"In cases where no punishment has been declared by all the great-souled ones because of their infinite variety, the infliction of punishment must be carried out after determining the specific nature of the act."
The ellipsis is "because of the infinity of individuals deserving punishment. When one strikes humans or animals for the sake of inflicting pain,
one should impose a punishment in proportion to the greater severity of that suffering.
In cases of striking, cutting, piercing, or causing a wall to fall,
one shall be made to pay fifteen, twenty, or thirty paṇas, as well as the cost of repair.

In the case of striking a wall with a mallet or similar object, or breaking it so that it falls apart, the fines shall be understood to be fifteen *paṇas* and twenty *paṇas* respectively. Furthermore: "One who throws into a house an object that causes pain, as well as one that is life-threatening, shall be made to pay sixteen *paṇas* and the second [type of offender] the middle fine."

The meaning is as follows: one who throws an object such as a thorn, which causes pain, into another's house, shall be fined sixteen *paṇas*; one who throws a life-threatening substance such as snake venom shall be fined the middle amercement (*madhyama-sāhasa*). Furthermore: "In cases of causing pain, drawing blood, or cutting off a limb or member, the fine for small animals increases progressively by double starting from that point. [484]

For the beating, causing pain, drawing blood, or cutting off a branch or limb of small animals—such as goats and the like—the punishment shall be double, fourfold, and sixfold respectively, due to the gravity of the offense; here, by the word "branch," horns and so forth are indicated, while "limbs" refers to the well-known [parts of the body]. For the tearing of branches, the trunk, or the entire tree of those that bear shoots, and for trees that provide livelihood, the fine shall be twenty [paṇas] doubled.

Regarding trees that produce shoots, such as the banyan (*vaṭa*) and others, there are three fines—twenty *paṇas*, forty *paṇas*, and eighty *paṇas*—to be applied respectively for the cutting of branches, the trunk, and the entire tree. For trees that do not produce shoots but provide livelihood, such as the citron (*mātuluṅga*) and others, the same aforementioned fines apply in the aforementioned circumstances. For trees that produce shoots but do not provide livelihood, the fine must be determined accordingly. Furthermore: "For trees grown on sacred sites (*caitya*), in cremation grounds (*śmaśāna*), on boundaries (*sīmā*), in other places, or in temples (*surālaya*), the fine is double that prescribed for ordinary trees."

The meaning is clear. Regarding this, Manu states a specific rule: "In the case of injury to any of the forest trees during their utilization, a fine shall be imposed according to the specific circumstances, without hesitation. Thus it is said.
Regarding this, Kātyāyana states the specific rule: "In the event of injury to the body or the senses, however the penalty may be determined,
the wise should likewise provide compensation for satisfaction and the means for recovery."
He shall be made to pay the expenses incurred for the quarrel and whatever was done for its sake.
Thus, according to the traditional teaching of Bṛhaspati. Regarding this, Manu states an exception:
"When the nose-string is severed, when the yoke is broken, when [the animal] turns sideways or comes facing forward, and likewise when there is a breakage of the axle or of the vehicle's wheel."
Manu has declared that there is no punishment for the breaking of a vehicle's yoke, its thongs, or its reins, nor when one cries out, "Drive on! or "Stop! [485]

The cry "avehi" (go away! uttered by one standing on a cart is protracted (*pluta*), because it expresses a call from a distance; or rather, the reading is "apehi," which means "move aside. By the statement "avehi is the cry," it is understood that there is a fault in not crying out [to warn]. Thus, that same author says: "Even where the vehicle is moving due to the driver's (*prājaka*) negligence, the owner shall be liable for the fine of two hundred [paṇas] in case of injury."
A *vrajaka* is one who goes.

Thus ends the chapter on the title of law known as *daṇḍapāruṣya* (assault) within the section on legal procedure (*vyavahārakāṇḍa*) of the *Sarasvatīvilāsa*, a compendium of traditional law (*smṛtisaṃgraha*) composed by the illustrious Great King Pratāparudra.
Now, the rule for the section titled "Gambling and Betting" is stated.

In the preceding section, theft was examined; because gambling and betting share the same legal status as theft, they follow immediately after it. On this point, Manu says: "Gambling and betting are open forms of theft."
"The king should be diligent in the constant prevention of these two.

Here, *tāskarya* means the state of being a thief (*taskara*). The suffix *ṣyañ* is applied because the word begins with *brāhmaṇa* and so forth. Having become diligent, he should restrain them. Their nature has been described by Nārada:
"Gambling with dice, leather straps, sticks, and the like, performed with deceit."
Playing with dice, sporting with birds, and gambling with stakes—these constitute the category of *samāhvaya*.

The *akṣas* are dice. The *vardhra* is a leather strap; some say it is a bowl made of glass (*kāca*). The *śalākā* is a long, square piece made of ivory or similar materials; some say it is circular, because gambling is played with such pieces in a glass bowl. The rest is easy to understand. The distinction between gambling (*dyūta*) and betting (*samāhvaya*) has been stated at the beginning of this section. Alternatively, their connection is that while the king’s permission is not granted for theft as mentioned in the previous section, here his permission is granted; thus they are linked. For instance, Manu has prohibited gambling, as it destroys truth, purity, and wealth: *Manu said: Gambling is forbidden, for it takes away truth, purity, and wealth.*
But it was permitted by others, provided it was accompanied by the king's share.
"The business presided over by the master of the gambling house is for the purpose of identifying thieves.
Or else: "A gambler, having given the king the share as prescribed, may conduct the gambling openly; in this way, no fault shall be found."
Having introduced the subject of collective action, Bṛhaspati says:
"If anyone should suffer defeat in a duel, the stake that was agreed upon therein must be paid to the owner. [487]

Viṣṇu states that a fourth part of the wager (*paṇa*) must be given to the king by both parties: "In a duel or a formal challenge (*samāhvaya*), a fourth part of the wager must be given to the king. Bhāruci explains that by the phrase "a fourth part of the wager," it is understood that this tax is to be paid by both. Regarding a specific rule here, Viṣṇu says: "Except for wrestlers and buffaloes, one should give to the victor that which was challenged [as a stake], and one should also pay the forfeited wager. The meaning of this is as follows: "challenged" refers to the term *samāhvaya*; setting aside the preferred wrestlers and buffaloes, one should give to the victor any animal other than rams and cocks, whether it be dead or defeated. If he does not give it, it must be provided by the king. Regarding the livelihood of the superintendent of gambling, it is said: "The keeper of the gaming house (*sabhika*) shall take the increase of the stakes (*glaha*). Here, "sabhika" means the official of the assembly (*sabhyah*), and the word "gambling" (*dyūta*) is understood from the context. Yājñavalkya states the measure of the interest (*vṛddhi*).
In a game where the interest on the stake is one hundredfold, the keeper of the gambling house shall take five percent from a fraudulent gambler,
but ten percent from an honest one.

A stake (*glaha*) is defined as a wager devised by gamblers through mutual agreement. Regarding that stake, Vijñāneśvara states that the *śatikā*—which is based on that stake—is either limited to one hundred or exceeds that measure. One who possesses such interest is called a *śatikavṛddhi*. Therefore, from a rogue gambler, the keeper of the gambling hall (*sabhika*) should take five percent (*pañcakaṃ śatam*) for his own profit; from any other [honest gambler], he should take a tenth part of the winnings. Viṣṇu declares his duty: "The keeper of the gambling hall shall conduct the game and shall pay what is due from him. Nārada says the same.
"The master of the gambling house shall conduct the game and shall pay what is won therein.
Regarding this, Yājñavalkya states the specific rule:
"When it has been properly supervised, he shall give to the king the share as prescribed."
“One should cause the winner to recover his winnings and give them to the victor; one who is patient should utter truthful words.

This means that one should cause the winner to recover what he has won by taking it from the vanquished and give it to the victor. To establish trust among those playing the game, one should repeatedly utter truthful statements. [488] Regarding this, Viṣṇu states a specific rule: “If the defeated player does not pay the stake to the keeper of the gaming house, he shall be compelled by the king to pay it; however, the king shall not compel payment for a stake won in a secret gambling match where the king’s share was not paid. The meaning is clear. Regarding disputes over victory and defeat, Yājñavalkya states the grounds for a decision:

For they alone are the observers and witnesses of the legal proceedings. In gambling, those very persons are to be the observers of the proceedings; therefore, those same gamblers should be appointed by the king as members of the court (*sabhyas*), and not those mentioned in the section on witnesses. In that case, there is no prohibition regarding women, children, the elderly, gamblers, and so forth. Furthermore, gambling should be conducted with a single table for the purpose of detecting thieves.

This is the meaning: one should establish a single entrance, a single primary site, supervised by the king, a superintendent, or others. For the most part, those who have acquired wealth through theft become gamblers. Yājñavalkya extends the rules of gambling to betting on animals: "This very same rule is to be known for betting on living creatures and for challenging matches; [it applies] when the stake is one hundredfold or more."

And so forth. Regarding fraudulent gambling, Yājñavalkya says: "Those who play with false dice or by means of trickery (*upadhi*) shall be banished from the kingdom by the king, marked with a brand. "With false dice" refers to dice and the like that are rigged. As for "trickery," this refers to those who play by means of gems, spells, medicinal herbs, and so on, as causes for deceiving the mind; these persons, having been branded immediately, shall be expelled from the realm. Because they are a specific class of thieves, they are to be branded with the foot of a dog. Nārada, however, states a distinction:
"The king should banish from the realm those who play with fraudulent dice;
having placed a rosary around their necks, for that is declared to be their punishment. Thus it is said.

Regarding this, Viṣṇu states a specific rule: “Gauñjikas, cārmikas, and others who are deceivers are to be banished. Gauñjikas and cārmikas are those who deal in leather. On this point, Bhāruci says: because both [the gauñjika and the cārmika] possess skill and operate within the same sphere of activity, their act is indeed theft; thus, these are distinct from ordinary gamblers. However, the other [ordinary gambler] belongs to the category of those to be deceived. Therefore, the gauñjikas and others are not to be punished with fines, but rather they are to be expelled from the country. Consequently, it should be understood that the collection of statements such as “gambling is forbidden by Manu” refers specifically to fraudulent gambling.

Thus ends the chapter on the section titled "Gambling and Betting" within the *Vyavahārakāṇḍa* of the *Sarasvatīvilāsa*, a compendium of legal codes (*Smṛtisaṃgraha*) composed by the illustrious Great King Pratāparudradeva.
Now, as a supplement to the seventeen titles of dispute, the procedure for punishment is stated by Yājñavalkya:
"He who, being independent, should prove a disputed matter, and he who should flee..."
And one who, having been summoned, says nothing at all, is declared by tradition to be defeated and liable to punishment.
If a dispute should arise where no wager has been made, the judge shall cause the defeated party to pay a fine,
as well as his own stake, and the wealth to the creditor.
One who misappropriates deposits and other such items shall be made to pay the wealth to the owner,
as well as a fine equal to that amount to the king, or an amount according to his capacity.
Property that has been lost and subsequently found shall be returned by the king to the owner;
if he cannot prove his ownership by means of identifying marks, he deserves a fine equal to the value of that property.
If property has been recovered by a customs officer or a local guardian after it had been lost, the owner may reclaim it within one year; after that period, the king shall take it.
One who is satisfied does not fail to achieve his purpose, nor shall he be obstructed by the king;
when giving testimony, he should approach the king, and even if he is liable to punishment, that wealth belongs to the other party.
The king, however, should cause the Brahmin master to pay by means of conciliation;
but others who are insolent, he should cause to pay by afflicting them according to the customs of the country.
Yājñavalkya says: If one who has been dismissed searches for [the debt] and pays it, he should be made to pay a fine equal to that amount;
if he lives off it by his own will, he is to be punished and made to pay that same amount with interest.
Manu says: One who fails to produce witnesses shall clearly be compelled to pay a fine for the corruption of witnesses;
once the case has been proven, those witnesses are to be excluded as they have been disqualified by their violation of the duties of witnesses.
If, within seven days of the witness having given his testimony,
illness, fire, or the death of a relative occurs, he shall be compelled to pay the debt and a fine.
False witnesses and those who act deceitfully should each be punished separately;
the fine is twice the amount of the dispute, and it is ordained that a Brāhmaṇa should be banished.
But the lord of the earth should punish that sinner with the punishment due to a thief who enjoys property that has not come to him, even for many hundreds of years.
Yājñavalkya:
But if those appointed to the task of land-measurement should speak falsely, they shall each be punished by the king with the middle amercement for lying.
However, each of those who are to be disciplined—the "lowest" among them—shall receive the first amercement;
others, such as the "elders by silence" and so forth, shall be punished individually according to their respective status.
Those who are to be disciplined, having persisted in falsehood with their very first act of audacity,
cannot all be brought to a final decision if many have been apprehended.
If they should do so out of fear or greed, the punishment shall be the highest fine;
this refers to cases involving knowledge.
If a breach occurs after [the matter] has been proclaimed, they shall be punished with the highest fine.
Thus, after punishing witnesses and others for false testimony due to ignorance and the like, the investigation of the boundary should be undertaken once again.
As it is said: "Having punished those who spoke out of ignorance, he should investigate the boundary again.
Likewise in cases of the breaking of a boundary-mark or the transgression of a boundary.
For the seizure of a field, the punishments are the lowest, the highest, and the middlemost.
Nārada says:
One should fine a cow one *māṣa* as a penalty, and likewise two *māṣas* for a buffalo;
similarly, the fine for goats, sheep, and calves shall be half a *māṣa*.

This is the meaning: if cattle, having eaten the crops in another's field, remain there, stay, or lie down, they should be understood as liable to double the aforementioned fine. For these same animals, the rule regarding pasture land (*vivīta*) is the same as that for donkeys, camels, and buffaloes. A *vivīta* is a fenced enclosure abounding in grass.
As long as the crop is destroyed, so long shall the fruit belong to the owner of the field;
however, he who is the owner of the cattle by virtue of possessing them deserves the previously mentioned punishment.

The owner of the cattle is the master of the herd. There is no fault if [the cattle] enter a path, a village, the edge of a pasture, or a field unintentionally; however, if it was done intentionally, he deserves punishment like that of a thief.

In this regard, large bulls, elephants, horses, the blind, the deaf, the humpbacked, and newcomers are not to be fined at a crossroads. Viṣṇu states: "For one who is capable [of fulfilling an agreement] but fails to do so, the fine shall be the confiscation of all property, followed by banishment from the city. "Capable" means one who is able to observe the agreement—that is, one who is not ignorant. Yājñavalkya states: "Having defiled a twice-born man with forbidden food, the fine is the highest amercement;
for a Kṣatriya, the middle amercement; for a Vaiśya, the first amercement; and for a Śūdra, half of that."
One who deals in counterfeit gold and one who sells forbidden meat should have three limbs amputated and be made to pay the highest fine.

The meaning is this: one who habitually trades with counterfeit gold whose excellence has been produced through the application of chemical transmutation (*rasavedha*); one who habitually sells "bad meat" (*kumāṃsa*), that is, despicable meat such as that belonging to dogs and the like; and by the force of the word "and" (*ca*), one who trades with counterfeit silver and so forth—all these should be deprived of three limbs each: the nose, the ears, and the hands. Vijñāneśvara maintains that by the force of the word "and," they should also be made to pay the highest fine (*uttamasāhasa*) in addition to the amputation of the three limbs. As for that which was stated by Manu: "But the king should [punish] the goldsmith, who is the most wicked of all thorns... [493]
One who acts unjustly should be cut into pieces with razors.
Thus, Vijñāneśvara states that this refers to the case of gods, Brahmins, kings, or gold.
"One who calls an adulterer a thief shall be made to pay a fine of five hundred;
one who abandons wealth that is his means of subsistence shall pay that same amount multiplied eightfold. Thus it is said.
Yājñavalkya states: "In the case of killing a human being, one becomes guilty instantly like a thief;
likewise for those who steal living beings for great personal gain, such as cows, elephants, camels, horses, and so forth."
For the killing of small animals, the fine shall be two hundred;
however, for auspicious beasts and birds, the punishment shall be fifty.
"For donkeys, goats, and sheep, the fine shall be five *māṣakas*; however, for those killed by dogs, the fine shall be one *māṣaka*. [And:
"Those who steal from the king's treasury and those who remain in rebellion..."
"One should cause those who assist one's enemies to be executed by various forms of punishment.
Regarding this, Nārada states a specific rule:
"The weapons of those who live by arms, and the draft animals and so forth of those who live by means of transport..."
The ornaments of courtesans, and the external property of those who live by playing musical instruments.
Whatever tool by which craftsmen live,
the king ought not to seize even when all their property is being confiscated.

The punishment for one who sells the limbs of a corpse, for one who strikes his teacher, and likewise for one who mounts the vehicle or seat of a king, is the highest fine (uttamasāhasa). There is also another Smṛti text:
Manu has declared that one should have Śūdras who bear the marks of the twice-born executed,
even if they deny it in court when proven by evidence.
One should cause the debtor to pay the creditor's due and a small portion of a fine according to his capacity.
Regarding this, Medhātithi stated that this refers to a case involving a debtor who is unable to pay a fine equal to one-tenth [of the debt].
Punishment is traditionally recorded as being of two kinds: corporal punishment and monetary punishment.
Physical punishment, such as beating and so forth, is declared to extend up to the point of death.
The monetary fine, beginning with a kārṣāpaṇa and ending with one's entire property, has been thus illustrated.
Thus,
corporeal punishment is said to be of ten kinds, whereas monetary punishment is of many kinds.
Regarding this, Manu says:
"Manu, the son of the Self-Existent, has declared ten places for punishment:
the genitals, the stomach, the tongue, the two hands, and the feet as the fifth."
"The eyes, the nose, the two ears, as well as wealth and the body. Thus it is said.

This is the meaning: the organ of procreation (*upastha*) is the characteristic mark of women and men; its suppression consists in the restraint of approaching those who should not be approached (*agamyāgamana*), and in the cutting open of the belly—some say this refers to the cessation of food—in cases of theft. In cases of verbal abuse, there is the cutting off of the tongue. In cases of physical assault, [the cutting off] of the hands. In that same case, for seizing by the feet and so forth, [the cutting off] of the feet. In cases of looking at what should be hidden, [the cutting off] of the eyes. In cases of smelling the scent applied to the breasts of another's wife, [the cutting off] of the nose. In cases of overhearing the king’s counsel and so forth, [the cutting off] of the ears. In cases of the theft of wealth, [the cutting off] of the hands; and in cases of great crimes (*mahāpātaka*) involving the theft of wealth, [the cutting off] of the feet. This rule is to be understood as applying to Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras in cases where no specific punishment has been stated. As for the Brāhmaṇa, however, it was stated previously that he is to be executed without being wounded. The mention of "two kinds of punishment" is for the sake of illustration, since other methods are also recorded in the Smṛtis.
"The punishment for him is the shaving of the head, his banishment from the city,
the branding of a donkey's mark upon his forehead, and travel by means of a donkey.
This refers to that Brāhmaṇa.
Shaving the head is prescribed as the punishment for a Brāhmaṇa whose life is at stake;
however, for the other castes, the punishment may result in the loss of life.
Thus, according to the Smṛti of Manu:
"He who recovers from the hand of another property that has been stolen or lost,
without having reported it to the king, shall be fined ninety-six paṇas."
Having ascertained the place, the time, and the portion, as well as the relative strength and weakness of the goods lost, experts should declare that which must undoubtedly be paid.

When materials such as hemp or flax have deteriorated—that is, when the value of goods has declined—those skilled in the increase, decrease, and rise of commodities, being experts in the valuation of goods, shall examine the place, the time, the usage, and the quality or worthlessness of the damaged material; whatever they determine should undoubtedly be paid by the artisans. From the addition of half [the original value], the king should take a tax of two hundred parts.
That which was specially commissioned for the king, or that which was sold as fit for the king, shall go to the king.

In this context, it is prohibited that what is not established [as marketable] should not be sold; likewise, gems and the like fit for a king, even if sold by the king himself, are prohibited. And so says Nārada:
"One who falsely states the quantity, one who departs from the toll-station, and one who engages in fraudulent buying or selling, shall be made to pay eight times the amount."
One who collects a ferry-toll for crossing shall be made to pay ten paṇas as a fine;
this same penalty applies to Brāhmaṇas and neighbors for failing to invite [one another] to a meal.
"In the absence of an invitation" means "at a śrāddha ceremony or the like"—this is the ellipsis.

Thus ends the section on the rules regarding punishments as a supplement to all [preceding topics], in the *Vyavahārakāṇḍa* of the *Sarasvatīvilāsa*, a compendium of legal tradition (*smṛtisaṃgraha*) composed by the illustrious Great King Pratāparudradeva.
Now, the rule concerning the category known as *prakīrṇaka* (miscellaneous matters) is stated.

In the preceding seventeen sections, it was established that judicial procedure (*vyavahāra*) pervades four constituents. "Pervading four" means that it encompasses the four components consisting of the plaintiff, the defendant, the members of the court (*sabhyas*), and the king. Here, in this section called *prakīrṇaka*, the matter is determined solely by the king; such is the connection. This judicial procedure performed by the litigants has thus been explained in brief.
"I shall now declare the legal proceedings concerning the king (nṛpāśraya) and miscellaneous matters (prakīrṇaka).

By the word "this" (eṣa), he refers to the set consisting of the seventeen titles of law (vyavahārapada). Nārada states that these have the king as their basis: "Furthermore, it should be known that the legal proceedings in miscellaneous matters (prakīrṇaka) are dependent upon the king."
The defiance of the kings' commands and the failure to perform their duties.
Likewise, there are the violations of the measurements and boundaries of cities,
as well as the subversions of the duties of heretics, guilds, corporations, and assemblies.
Disputes between father and son, transgressions regarding penance,
the failure to accept gifts, and even the neglect of those in the stages of life (āśramas).
"Furthermore, there would be the fault of confusion regarding the Dharma, as well as the restriction of its practice;
and whatever was not seen among the predecessors—all that would be considered miscellaneous (prakīrṇaka)."

This statement is from Nārada. Among the eighteen titles of law (*vivādapada*) spoken by Nārada, that which is not mentioned in the seventeen titles is designated as *prakīrṇaka* (miscellaneous). Since my own legal compendium (*smṛtinibandha*) is a collection of all *smṛtis*, I have, in accordance with them, determined in their respective places within the titles of law those judicial proceedings (*vyavahāra*) that are fixed solely for the king, according to the requirements of each case. Here, in this title of law called *prakīrṇaka*, I shall state only that which was not previously mentioned, both according to my own work and according to Nārada. To illustrate: the meaning of "obstruction of the king's command" (*ājñāpratīghāta*) is as follows—when a command has been issued by the king such as, "So much wealth is to be given to this Brāhmaṇa or Kṣatriya," he who does not comply must be made to pay that wealth to him and be fined double that amount. Regarding this, Viṣṇu says: "In the case of obstruction of a command, the fine is double. On this point, Bhāruci states: "By the mention of 'double' (*dvaiguṇya*), it is understood that the wealth commanded must be made over to him twice over. The meaning of "performing his duties" (*tatkarmakaraṇa*) is as follows—the "duty" (*karman*) of that king is the administration of the kingdom (*rājya*); "performing" (*karaṇa*) it means doing so without having received the seal-ring (*mudrikā*), for Viṣṇu’s legal tradition states: "If one assumes the office of a superintendent (*adhyakṣatā*) without being appointed, he is to be punished accordingly. "Breaking the measure of the city" (*purapramāṇasaṃbheda*) means: the city is well-known; "measures" (*pramāṇa*) refers to the instruments of force, such as elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry; their "breaking" (*saṃbheda*) is the discovery of the enemy's secrets, that is to say, exposing their vital points (*marmodghāṭana*). "Causing dissension among the subjects" (*prakṛtīnām bheda*) refers to creating division among ministers by reporting mutual slanders. And thus says Saṃvarta: [text follows].
"For slandering ministers and for disclosing the secrets regarding the size and defenses of the city, the middle and the highest fines respectively are declared as the sequence of punishment.

Thus, according to the order: for slandering the constituent elements of the state (*prakṛti*), one shall be fined the middle amercement; for speaking of the city's dimensions and vital secrets (*marmakathana*), one shall be fined the highest amercement. By the use of the word "and" (*ca*), corporal punishment is also to be applied as appropriate. Here, the word *paiśunya* is derived from the root *piśun* with the suffix *ṣyañ* in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāve*): the state of being a slanderer is *paiśunyam*.

"Contravention of the laws of heretics, merchants, guilds, and corporations. This is the meaning: the laws regarding heretics are that in this city, at this specific place, heretics must be stationed; likewise, the laws concerning merchants, guilds, and corporations refer to their fixed locations and positions. Their contravention is what is meant here, not things such as saffron, spring festivals, or swings, because those have been established within the category of "non-sinful acts" (*anapāpakarma*) in the *Samayācāra*. Furthermore, because disputes over these matters involve both plaintiff and defendant, they possess the fourfold character of a legal proceeding (*caturvyāpitva*), and because they are not restricted solely to the king's jurisdiction. "And a dispute between father and son"—this is the meaning: when someone who was separated from his kin, having gone to another country or stayed abroad for a long time, returns and says, "This is my father," or "This is my son"; (the mention of "father and son" is illustrative of wife and so forth), such as "This is my husband," or "This is my wife. In such cases, there are no witnesses, the parties themselves do not know [the truth], and ordeals (*divya*) and the like are not applicable, as it is improper to purify [the matter] through oaths and such. Therefore, because the matter is restricted solely to the king's jurisdiction, the decision must be made by the king alone. Regarding the method of deciding in cases of doubt concerning father and son, Viṣṇu states: "In case of doubt regarding the son, the mother should take him onto her lap; if there is a change [of emotion], the decision is to be made. "Natural state" (*prakṛti*) refers to the absence of sexual desire. This applies to a case where the mother is twenty years old and the son is fifteen. Since such a reaction would be impossible in the case of an elderly mother, Śaṅkha and Likhita provide another means of decision: "The sleeping son should be called and [his reaction] observed. If a decision cannot be reached even by one of these methods, Viṣṇu declares that the heart of the consecrated king himself is the authority: "In this matter, the heart of the king alone is the authority. For this very reason, Kālidāsa said: [The verse follows: *“...”* (Note: The source text provides the Sanskrit for the preceding commentary only). (Note: The provided text ends with the mention of Kālidāsa, implying a citation of his verse on the subject.)
"For the internal functions of the mind are the authority of the virtuous regarding matters that are subjects of doubt.

Thus, the meaning of the phrase "transgression of penance" (*prāyaścittavyatikrama*) is the failure to perform the prescribed penance. Since the performance of such penance is exclusively regulated by the king, when there is a transgression, the penance must be caused to be performed; therefore, the penance must be carried out by the king himself. And so says Devala:
"The king is the one who causes penances to be performed; he is the instructor and the protector of the Dharma. Thus it is said.

The king is the one who assigns the *kṛcchra* penances as expiations for great sins. According to the author of the *Arṇava*, in matters such as the expiation for killing a Brahmin (*brahmahatyā*), the twice-born and others must not undertake the penance without the king’s command. When there is an assault committed by another, the king must protect those learned in the three Vedas (*traividyavṛddha*) regarding their Vedic studies; this is because that protection is exclusively the duty of the king. Regarding the phrase "the neglect (*lopa*) of those in the stages of life" (*āśramiṇām*): its meaning is as follows—the neglect (*lopa*) refers to the abandonment of the duties of those in the stages of life (*āśramiṇaḥ*), namely the student (*brahmacārin*), the householder (*gṛhin*), the forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*), and the ascetic (*yatī*); specifically, the neglect of the duties of the various types of ascetics, such as the *kuṭīcaka*, *bahūdaka*, *haṃsa*, and *paramahaṃsa*, as well as those belonging to a single religious order (*ekatīrthya*). Furthermore, since it has already been established that any among the ascetics who has fallen from his path becomes the king's slave, it should be understood that this rule does not apply to such cases. The fault of total social confusion (*sarvasaṃkara-doṣa*) is indeed evident, and the regulation of their conduct is likewise clear. As for the phrase "and that which was not seen among the predecessors": the meaning is this—when someone in a village is accused but there is no opposing party, yet the villagers claim there is an accusation, the king must make a decision there; other such cases are to be inferred. These duties of the king should have been stated at the very beginning of the section; nevertheless, because they consist of legal procedure (*vyavahāra*), they are stated immediately after the topics of legal procedure (*vyavahārapada*). Alternatively, following the connection between the seventeen titles of dispute (*vivādapada*) and the miscellaneous titles (*prakīrṇakapada*): previously, the prescription of punishment was stated only for the defeated; here, the prescription of punishment is also for the victor—this is the connection between these two. As Yājñavalkya says: [End of excerpt]
But when legal proceedings have been wrongly decided by the king,
the judges, together with the winner, shall be fined a penalty double that of the dispute.

Since the statement regarding punishment does not refer to the victor but rather to the nature of punishment for the members of the court, and because the imposition of punishment upon the members when their faults exist has already been stated at the beginning of the section, the imposition of punishment here is explained as pertaining to the victor. Here, although one might suspect that the status of being a victor belongs to the winner by way of past events and not because he has actually been defeated according to justice, it was previously stated in the seventeen sections that what has been decided there is not to be overturned;
however, "that which was lost due to the fault of the court members must then be paid by the member."
But one should not deliberate upon a matter that has already been decided by those who performed the action.

Thus it is from the traditional law (smṛti). Regarding this matter, however, the commentators have stated that the statement "the legal proceeding (nyāya) must be conducted again when a fault of the court members exists" is intended to convey precisely that. Consequently, the connection has already been explained: that in this context, the legal proceeding must be conducted again. For this very reason, Yājñavalkya says:
[500] "If one who has been defeated by legal reasoning should think, 'I am not defeated,' and returns, he should be defeated again and made to pay double the fine."
On this point, Nārada says: "A legal transaction entered into with women, at night, outside the village, within the house, or with enemies— even if completed, it must be performed again."

The word "of the king" (*rājñaḥ*) is to be supplied [as the subject], because legal procedure (*vyavahāra*) is restricted solely to the king. Thus says Yājñavalkya: "He shall set aside legal proceedings brought about by force or fraud. Therefore, the author of the *Candrikā* maintains that the intended meaning is that one should initiate [the investigation] afterwards, i.e., immediately following the legal proceeding. Regarding this as well, Manu states a specific rule:
A legal proceeding conducted by one who is intoxicated, insane, or excessively terrified, or by a child or an elderly person,
as well as one entered into by unrelated parties, is not valid.
An unrelated case is one devoid of both plaintiff and defendant. And so Manu says:
"Whatever has been decided or adjudicated, wherever it may have occurred, one should know that to be established according to dharma; one shall not reverse it again."
That position which the members of the court determine to be "untrue" or "true" is set aside; however, once instructed, it is brought forth on the basis of the testimony of witnesses.

It should be understood that this refers to cases where the grounds for punishment—such as being committed by a woman—are absent. Furthermore, Yājñavalkya states the application of that wealth which has been collected as a fine by the court officials through unjust means, after a formal judicial decision: "The king, having reported to Varuṇa the fine he has taken according to justice, should himself give it to the Brahmins multiplied thirtyfold."

Whatever punishment was unjustly levied by a previous king out of greed or other motives, one should personally give that to the Brahmins after dedicating it as threefold for Varuṇa. This is because whatever was taken from an unjustly acquired source in the form of a fine must be returned to him. Alternatively, there is another interpretation: "The two-fold course has been proclaimed in accordance with the deception of the elements."

Thus, by following the pursuit of truth rather than the pursuit of cavil (*chala*) within legal procedure (*vyavahāra*), the seventeen titles of dispute (*vivādapada*) have been enumerated. By following the pursuit of cavil, the title of dispute known as *prakīrṇaka* (miscellaneous matters) has been enumerated. And so Bṛhaspati says: "In the case of the corruption of witnesses, assessors, or litigants, there is a retrial;
however, for those defeated by their own words, no rule for a second trial has been stated."

In this context, the injunction that "the king shall look into legal cases" relies solely on the pretext (*chala*) of following his own word, because the case has already been concluded by his own transgression; it does not involve the search for other means of proof (*pramāṇa*), due to the urgency of the injunction which cannot tolerate delay. Regarding this, Manu states a specific rule:
"If the ministers or the judge should decide a case otherwise [than it truly stands], the king himself shall decide it and fine them one thousand [panas]."

Therefore, it is understood from the two words "himself" (*svayam*) and "king" (*nṛpati*) that the administration of justice is strictly restricted to the king alone. Regarding this, Kātyāyana states an exception: "The gift, mortgage, or sale of fields, houses, and slaves made by those who are not independent do not attain validity, unless they have been ratified [by the master]."

The meaning is that what is done by one who is not independent must indeed be reversed; there is no further legal principle [to support it] here. Those described as "independent" are those designated as such by their own authority. Regarding those who are "not independent," Nārada says: "Women, sons, slaves, and other dependents are not independent.
"Dependents" (parigraha) refers to those who live off another's means. On this point, Kātyāyana states a specific distinction:
The master shall annul any transaction performed by one who is not independent;
no other person shall dispute such a transaction, except for that which is done by one who is terrified or insane.

Since the authority to settle disputes involving those who have been driven away out of fear or madness belongs solely to the king, the intention here is that a dispute between the owner of such a person and the one who has brought them back is not entirely improper. Bṛhaspati describes the nature of such a person as follows: "He who, when commissioned by his master for the management of income and expenditure, or for moneylending, agriculture, or trade, is considered to be one whose affairs have been entrusted to him."
"Whatever has been done by him is authoritative—whether gain or loss, expenditure or income—in his own country or abroad; the owner shall not contradict that. On this point, Nārada says:
"They say that even other transactions are invalid when not in times of distress.

Here, the mention of "women" is intended as an illustration for those who lack independence. Thus, it should be understood as an implied meaning that in times of distress, however, even transactions performed by those lacking independence are valid. Regarding this, he (the same author) states an exception:
"Especially regarding house and field, [transactions such as] giving, mortgaging, and selling [are invalid]."
The meaning is that gifts, mortgages, and sales of houses or fields, even when made by one who lacks independence during times of distress, do not become valid. On this point, Kātyāyana says:

"Success, however, has been declared by those who know the essence of the scriptures to be of two kinds: medical treatment, and expiation and punishment; it is remembered as being twofold through these two."
Regarding this, Nārada says:
"A king who, being composed, always views legal cases in this manner,
spreads his radiant fame here in this world and attains the same world as Indra."
Bṛhaspati also says:
Thus, during the day, the king, together with his courtiers, should carry out the administration of justice;
by spreading his fame throughout this world, he shall become a minister of Mahendra.
[503] A king should reach a decision on legal matters by means of witnesses, written documents, and inference;
having spread his fame here on earth, he attains the realm of the Sun.
Manu also says:
"Thus, a king who always conducts all these legal proceedings,
having cast off all impurity, is glorified in the world of Brahmā."
But he who, having restrained desire and anger, perceives his purpose through righteousness—
the subjects follow him just as rivers flow toward the ocean.
For one whose nature is to delight the subjects and who constantly relies upon the elders,
longevity, progeny, wealth, and fame will undoubtedly be attained.

Surely these lords of sages— Manu, Vasiṣṭha, and the masters of yoga— have passed away, free from all envy; yet may the Lord of Bhavānī be pleased with this supreme verbal expression of mine, bound by memory.

Thus ends the "Vilāsa" (Play) on the section known as the *Prakīrṇaka* (Miscellaneous), [composed by] the illustrious Vīra Gajapati, Lord of Gauḍa, Lord of Navakoṭi, Lord of Karṇāṭaka, Lord of Luburiga,
Sovereign of Jamunāpura, Protector and Guardian of Huśana Sāhi Suratrāṇa.
